Seven years ago we all went through the flames; and the happiness of some of us since then is, we think, well worth the pain we endured. Our boy's birthday is the day on which Quincey Morris died, and his mother holds the secret belief that some of our brave friend's spirit has passed into him. We call him Quincey.

'This boy will some day know what a brave and gallant woman his mother is,' said Van Helsing, with the child upon his knee. 'Later on he will understand how some men so loved her, that they did dare much for her sake.'

JONATHAN HARKER.

THE END.
interact.look: A thick bundle of typed pages, tied with ribbon: every diary, every letter, every telegram. No single authentic document in all of it, only copies. Yet the whole truth.
Jonathan's desk, with a blotter, a Ghoorka knife in a case, and a framed photograph of five men and a woman.
Law books, and on the bottom shelf a boy's picture-books, thumbed to pieces.
A fire burns in the grate. On the mantel stands a small, plain bowie knife, kept clean.
Quincey's bowie, in its case, on the mantel. A card reads: 'To Quincey, who is not forgotten.'
Mina stands by the window, her forehead smooth and clear in the evening light. She watches a little boy chase a ball on the lawn.

do.card:
Seven years ago we all went through the flames...

And the happiness of some of us since then is, we think, well worth the pain we endured.

interact.look: The four-poster in which three Lords of Godalming have died. My father lies small and grey among the pillows.

arthur_burden_desk_key.say: The key turns stiffly. Inside lie a folded letter in my father's hand and a small velvet box.

interact.use_fail: Nothing here fits the drawer. I want its key.
interact.look: A lacquered desk with a brass-bound drawer. The drawer is locked; he has kept the key from me all my life.
Physic-bottles, a water-glass, a Bible. The spectacles have been wanted for two days and found by nobody.

interact.take_text: I take his spectacles. He will want them to read any message.
interact.look: Gold-rimmed spectacles, folded under the Bible where the nurse has laid them.

interact.take_text: I take the green bottle of cordial. 'For the evening dose', says the label.
interact.look: Dr. Lenox's travelling cabinet: lint, lancets and a cordial in a green bottle.
Kept high all summer. My father says the cold is waiting for him in the corridor.
The chair in which I have sat for eleven nights.
Burke's Peerage, Debrett and a long row of Hansard. A family that read about itself.
Three candles, and the fourth socket empty. Nobody has had the heart to replace it.
To the stairs and the hall.
My father, the old Lord, propped against his pillows. Time has cut him down to bone, but the eyes are still the eyes of a man who rules a county.
The family physician, with a face trained to give no news.
Thirty could dine here. Lately it has held telegrams, black-edged cards and bills.

interact.take_text: From Mrs. Westenra: 'Lucy begs you will come to Hillingham when your father is easier. Do not stay away for fear of us.'
interact.look: A salver with two letters on it and a pink telegram.
Sir Hugh Holmwood in plaster, with the nose broken in some forgotten game of ours.
Hunting-books, county histories and a red Bradshaw.
Rugs and old ulsters. It smells of dogs.
Enough hearth to roast an ox, now holding a single log.
Carved with the Holmwood arms: three rings on a field of grey.
Nobody sits in this one. It was my grandfather's.
The way up to my father's room.
The steward's office. Brass plate: 'W. Wilkes'.
The front door, and the lime avenue beyond.

interact.go_fail: Locked. It wants a key, and the recess beside the keyhole wants a seal pressed into it, my father's signet.
interact.look: Iron-bound, with a lock of three wards and a recess the shape of a seal. Only the Lord opens it.
Seventy years in service. He has buried one Lord already and is working hard at not burying a second.
A thin gentleman in black, with a document-case held against his chest like a shield.
Crowle of Crowle & Aske, round, rosy and kind. Everything about him is soft except the way he reads other people's faces.
Grey, gabled, very old. A Holmwood has lived here since the Wars of the Roses, and not one of them has lived here cheaply.
Back into the hall.

interact.go_fail: Not yet. I will not leave until he has blessed this, and until I have what I need to say it: the telegram, my mother's ring and my father's letter.
interact.look: The brougham stands waiting. I may go to Hillingham when I hold the telegram, my father's blessing and a ring.
'Ring Green, half a mile.' Someone has scratched 'and a bad road' underneath.
Yews clipped to black pillars, and the chapel beyond.
The Home Wood gate hangs open. It is never open.
My grandfather planted the avenue. I climbed this one at nine and broke my collar-bone.
Lucy's letter lay open on this bench the day I read it twice.
Unlit by day.
He has had the horses harnessed since breakfast.
Leans on his rake and watches the Home Wood. He has not raked anything in an hour.

interact.take_text: I pick the wild rose from the arbour's foot. The thorn takes a drop of my blood, and I do not mind.
interact.look: Lucy's arbour, thick with roses. The wild one at the foot has opened first, as she says it always does.
Lace cloth, a pot of Darjeeling and a plate of what Lucy calls seed-cake and Mrs. Westenra calls cake.
Mrs. Westenra's. She likes it with its back to the wind.
Lucy's.
A bench for reading and for pretending to read.
Full of geraniums, in military ranks.
A dozen pale roses, nearly as pale as Lucy.
A white house, a long lawn, and every window open.

interact.go_fail: Not yet. I have something to ask first.
interact.look: A gravel walk between lavender, to the little white pavilion.
Lucy, in a white morning frock with her hair half down, laughing at something nobody has said.
Lucy's mother, in grey silk, with a heart she cannot spare and a sharp eye for settlements.
Lanky, brown, easy. He was also going to ask. He has the grace of a man who knows.

interact.set_text: We played until dusk, Lucy and I and Quincey, and she knocked my ball into the pond and called it strategy. I could not stop laughing. I had not laughed in a year.
interact.look: Lucy cheats at croquet and loses with enormous dignity.

interact.set_text: She wound it and we danced three turns on the boards of the summer-house with no one watching. I trod on her hem twice, and she forgave me twice.
interact.look: Her old music-box. It plays one waltz and a half.

interact.set_text: She read me 'Maud' aloud, and then looked up and said I was the only person who did not mind a bad reader. We read until the lamp was lit.
interact.look: Tennyson, much underlined.
Two cups, always, and a saucer of lemon.
Mine, by long custom.
Hers, by every custom.
Paper-shaded, lit at dusk.
Back to the lawn.
Lucy, engaged to be married and shining with it.
The footman, hat in hand, hesitating. He holds a yellow envelope.
Blotter, seals, a bowl of wafers and a ledger held shut by a strap.

interact.take_text: I take the ledger. The arrears column runs to four figures, then to five. Rents unpaid for three years; interest due to Crowle & Aske in a hand I do not know. Someone has been paying the tenants' debts out of borrowed money.
interact.look: The ledger of arrears. I open it where the strap has left a crease. Red ink, page after page.
Rent-rolls back to the Restoration.
Hand-coloured maps. The Home Wood is edged in red pencil with a question-mark.
Cold. In July, that means money.
Worn to the shape of one man's anxieties.
For the Harvest Home subscription. It rattles with very little.
Back to the hall.
Grey, upright, thirty years a Holmwood servant. He has the face of a man holding a door shut with his back.
Three rings on a swinging board, painted by someone who has never counted to three.
The pump handle was a gift of my grandfather. It has not given water since.
The Arms' barrel, rolled out onto the green for the occasion. Nobody is drinking from it.
Water-butt.
A hay-cart with a broken axle. It has been broken since Lady Day.
Where old men watch ducks and mutter about Lords.
'The Ring, half a mile.'
Spokesman of the tenants, because he is the only one who has never owed anyone a penny. Hat on, jaw set.
Arms folded over her apron, not unkindly.
White to the eyebrows. His mill-race was my grandfather's gift and my father's loan.
A brass wire loop pegged across a run. Not a rabbit-run; the loop is too big.
Warm still. They did not go far.
A felled oak, two hundred years old, sawn in the dark.
Stiff in the bracken. She was not killed by any poacher's wire; the throat has been torn out.
Struck by lightning in my grandfather's time. Poachers hang their bags in it.
The gate to the lawns.
The keeper, with a shotgun he is not sure he is allowed to use against another man.
Three shapes by a shuttered light: two men and something low at their feet that growls like a dog and is not.
Plain stone and oak, with a cloth that was white once.
Silver, heavy, tarnished along the arms. Someone had polished it recently, I think.
'SIR HUGH HOLMWOOD, BUILDER OF THE RING, FELL AT EDGEHILL ON THE XXIII OF OCTOBER, 1642. HIS BODY WAS NOT RECOVERED.'
'HERE, IN THE YEAR 1643, HIS SON FOUND HIM IN A FIELD AND BROUGHT HIM HOME. HERE HE RESTS.' The last two words have been rubbed bright by thumbs.
'IN THE YEAR 1688 THE LORDSHIP OF GODALMING WAS CONFERRED UPON THE HOUSE OF HOLMWOOD FOR SERVICES TO THE CROWN.'
Worn smooth by four hundred years of Holmwood boredom.
My mother's. She sat here every Sunday of my childhood.
Nobody lit them. I think.
The rope hangs perfectly still. The bell rang once, a moment ago.
A black door set in the north wall, cut with a name: 'HERE HE RESTS'. A dial of years is set into the lock. What year is a man's resting, if not his death?
The yew walk, and daylight.
A woman in grey, kneeling, so still she might have been carved.

do.say: A single stroke of the bell, from the tower, though the rope hangs still. At the far pew, someone kneels who was not there when I came in.

interact.look: Black oak, brass handles, the arms of Godalming. The old man, at last, is perfectly still.
A Holmwood in stone armour, hands crossed. Someone has placed a pebble on his chest.
A Lady Godalming in stone lace, with a stone spaniel at her feet.
'ELIZABETH, LADY GODALMING. SHE LOVED HER SON.' She is the only ancestor with a verb in her epitaph.
The lamp I carried down. Its flame leans toward the farther wall, where there is no door.
Up, to the chapel and the light.
A green-shaded lamp, a pen-tray, and two things laid squarely in the middle of the blotter by someone who meant them to be found.

interact.take_text: I read it standing. The whole estate is mortgaged. My father borrowed against the Ring four years ago, and again last winter, and paid the tenants' arrears out of it so that no one on the Holmwood land would ever be turned out in his time.
interact.look: A long deed with three red seals: the Ring, the Home Farm and the Home Wood pledged to Crowle & Aske, for a sum I had to read twice.

interact.take_text: 'I have kept this from you, God forgive me, because I was afraid you would think yourself a fortune-hunter when you went to Lucy. I mortgaged the Ring so the tenants should not suffer, and I lied to you for four years. Do not lie as I did. A name can bear a debt; it cannot bear a lie. - Your father.'
interact.look: 'ARTHUR - to be opened by my son when the Lord is dead.' My father's hand, much steadier than in life.
Charters, leases, the 1688 patent of nobility. Dull and very heavy.
Marriage-settlements. My mother's is on top, with a ribbon.
Pigeon-holes of rolled parchment, tied with faded tape.
A face I almost know, in a frame gone dark. The glass catches my own face over it.
His chair. I do not sit in it.
Back to the hall.
Eighty tons of Russian oak, newly tarred. She looks small to be carrying fifty boxes and a secret.
Stencilled 'Hildesheim & Co., Varna'. Salt fish for Constantinople, they say; the smell is honest, at least.
Worn by generations of seamen waiting for a wind.
Constantinople, Odessa, Burgas, Varna. Not a word of Whitby, which is a very long way off.
A weathered wayside cross with a lamp. Sailors touch it going out and sometimes coming home.

props.name: The last box on the quay

interact.look: Long, plain, nailed shut, with black earth in the cracks of the lid. Even the dockers walk round it.
Thin, inky and anxious to be elsewhere, holding the ship's papers like a man holding a hot coal.
A heavy man in a braided cap with one hand on the stamp and the other, discreetly, held out.
A widow in black with a tray of beeswax candles, selling them to sailors' wives and, today, to sailors.
An old Orthodox priest in a rusty cassock, who has blessed ten thousand sailors and buried a good many.
Broad, silent, with a rosary wound round his wrist. His men carried the boxes and wiped their hands afterwards.
My first mate, a Roumanian, sturdy and short of temper. A good seaman and a bad listener.
Spruce, tarred, with the sail laced to it. Someone has nailed a small wooden cross to its foot.

interact.go_fail: Barred and padlocked. The hold key is kept somewhere in the ship, not far from where I sleep.
interact.look: The main hatchway to the hold, battened and barred. A key hangs somewhere on this ship; a lever would do as well.
Spare blocks, a marline-spike, tarred twine. Everything a ship needs and nothing a man needs.
The windlass capstan. Six men to the bars in a calm; I have fewer every week.
A stout lantern on the main-boom crutch. It burns all night now, and the men watch it as men watch a sleeping beast.

interact.set_text: High in the north-west, long white mares'-tails are drawing across the sky, thin as combed hair. The swell has begun to run against the wind. That is weather coming, and not far off.
interact.look: Grey above, grey below.
Back to the quay.
Forward to the bows, where the figure was seen.
Aft to the wheel.
Down to the men's quarters.
Warm air, onions and the smell of a stove.
The way to my cabin.

interact.set_text: I search the deck from end to end with a lantern: coils, lockers, the boat. Nothing but wet planks and my own shadow.
interact.look: Wet cable, thick with weed. Nothing hides in it.
The mate paces the deck with a handspike. He sleeps less than I do, and speaks to no one but the weather.
A young hand with a quick laugh. The laugh has gone from him since Cape Matapan.
The youngest hand, who crosses himself every time he passes the hatch.
Big, slow, steady at the wheel in any weather. He stands as though he were rooted to the planks.
A Swede among Russians, grey before his time. He is the man who keeps his eyes lowered when the fog comes in.

do.say: Two of us, the mate and I. The fog does not lift. The deck is clean; even the blood would be a comfort.
Three hands, the mate and I. They sleep on deck now, back to back, with lanterns.
The Bay of Biscay, and wild weather. A hand short, and it is the lost man's mess-kit they will not touch.
A hand short. The crew stand about in twos and threes, and fall quiet when I pass.
We are under way. A fresh east wind, and eight men and myself aboard.

interact.look: Back to the deck.
A straw tick and a rough Russian blanket. I have slept here with the whole Black Sea going over my head.
A canvas cot under the port, for the hours I may spare. When I lie down, the days go by.
A slanted desk with the ship's log open, an inkwell and a steel pen. Every night I must write what I know.
A slate nailed to the bulkhead with the names of the crew in chalk, and a roll showing who may sleep and who may stand.

interact.take_text: My own crucifix, which my mother gave me when I first went to sea. I put it in my pocket.
interact.look: Oilskins, a pipe, my father's compass. Under the oilskins, wrapped in a handkerchief, a small silver cross.

interact.take_text: The beads that were my mother's. I take them down, and I wind them round my fingers.
interact.look: A small icon of St. Nicholas with a red lamp. Beside it hangs a string of beads, black with handling.
Charts of the Black Sea, the Aegean and the Channel, with the course ruled in pencil. The ruled line ends at Whitby.
Swings on its gimbals and throws the shadows about. I have stopped looking at the corners.
Bradshaw's is the wrong book for this ship; Lloyd's Register and a Russian Bible are the right ones.

interact.take_text: I take the brandy. It will be wanted.
interact.look: A small bottle, kept for sickness and for the last night of a bad voyage.

interact.take_text: I take the bottle and set it by the log.
interact.look: A strong, corked bottle. It would float, if sealed with wax, and carry a message farther than any man.

interact.set_text: I search my own cabin: the locker, the bunk, the chart-case, the dark under the cot. Nothing, only a bad smell of damp earth in the corner, a smell I carried down myself.
interact.look: A clean locker; clean, I think, because no one else would open it.
Up to the deck and the air.
Ten boxes, each lashed with rope, each stencilled in Cyrillic: EARTH, WHITBY. They are heavier than they should be.
Ten more. The lids have been nailed and then painted over, like something that is meant to stay closed.

interact.set_text: I walk the length of the hold, finger on every lid. Fifty boxes, as the paper says, fifty exactly. And the ship rides lower than fifty boxes of clay would make her.
interact.look: The last row. I count them with a lantern, finger by finger.
Casks of sand, the other half of the cargo. Cheap, grey and honest; I check them last.
The mate's tool-chest: hammer, chisel, screw-driver. He will have it open on the third of August.

interact.set_text: Box thirteen. A lid with bright nails, no seal, and the earth round it fresh, as though the box has been stirred. I could swear it was not so at Varna.
interact.look: This one has no customs seal on the lid and its nails shine like new. Black dust lies fresh round the base.

demeter_voyage_crowbar.say: The nails scream out of the wood one by one. The lid comes up on black earth, damp and smelling of the grave. The mate was right about the boxes, and he is not here to know it.

interact.use_fail: Nailed shut. I need a lever: the carpenter's crowbar from the forecastle chest.
interact.look: Nailed shut. A crowbar would take the lid off; I do not like what I think is underneath.
Black earth to the brim and a hollow in it the shape of a man.

interact.set_text: A trail of earth from the foot of box thirteen to the forward hatch, wider than a dog's, narrower than a man's; and across it, wet bare footprints, one long, one long. The prints end at the ladder. They do not come back.
interact.look: A smear of black earth on the boards.

interact.set_text: I search the hold with lantern and lead, as the book of Rules says. Behind every row, under every lashing, between every cask. There is not a corner for a man to hide in, only the boxes. I do not like how well I know that.
interact.look: A narrow gap between the casks and the hull.
Something moves among the lashings. It breathes like a man and it is not a man.
Something moves among the lashings. It breathes like a man and it is not a man.
Back on deck.
The cook's iron stove, hot day and night. It is the one place the men will sit with their backs to the room.
Eight places laid and, tonight, one fewer, because Petrofsky's bowl has not been moved.

interact.take_text: The cook shrugs. 'Take it, Captain. It's what's it's for.' I take one head, and then another.
interact.look: Garlic, hung from the beam like beads. The cook swears by it, against colds, quarrels and ghosts.

interact.take_text: I fill a small flask with lamp-oil from the drum.
interact.look: Lamp-oil, for the binnacle and the galley lamp.
Spoons, ladles and a hook where keys are hung. Most of them are not keys.

interact.take_text: I fill a flask with water.
interact.look: Sweet water, rationed. The cask has been drawn down by the thirst of people who do not want to leave the galley.

interact.take_text: A sharp galley knife, good for fish, rope and worse. I take it.
interact.look: Pans, a ladle, and a sack of salt. The cook salts the doorstep when he thinks I am not looking.

interact.take_text: I take a roll of clean lint.
interact.look: Plasters, a roll of lint, a bottle of laudanum. A ship's surgeon is a captain with a steady hand.

interact.set_text: Stores, flour-barrels, salt-beef casks; I tip the lids with the cook watching. No man. Only a rat which looks at me as if I were the stranger.
interact.look: Flour and salt-beef.
Round, red-faced, a lifelong cook who has never in his life been afraid of a stove and has become afraid of everything else.
Up to the deck.
A blanket tucked tight, a pipe on the pillow, a St. Nicholas pinned above. He did not come to this bed on the night he was lost.
Petrofsky sleeps in the lower berth with his boots on. He says the floor has begun to feel cold.
Tidy as a drawer. A Swedish psalm-book lies open at the 23rd.
A big man's bunk, short of a pillow.

interact.take_text: The carpenter's crowbar, two feet of black iron. It will lift a lid, or a lid's nails, or a man's courage.
interact.look: Chisels, adze, spikes and a heavy iron crowbar, kept sharp by a man who thought he was only a carpenter.

interact.take_text: I take a torch. A lantern shows what is there; a torch shows what flees.
interact.look: A bundle of torches dipped in pitch, for the boat in a calm and the hold in a pinch.
A slate left on the mess table, scrawled with names in three hands, with a fourth line crossed out and written again.
Saints nailed over every bunk, St. Nicholas, the Mother of God, St. Elias, with a small iron cross at the foot of each.

interact.set_text: Every bunk, every bag, every oilskin: I turn them all out under the lantern. Prayers, a wedding-ring, a Turkish coin. No man.
interact.look: Sea-bags and oilskins.
A seamed, dark, silent hand who has sailed with me nine years. Tonight he is mending a net with hands that do not look at it.
My second mate, a quiet, bookish man who steers by compass and prays by habit.
Back along the deck.

interact.take_text: I cut a length of good manila from the bitter end. A fathom, no more, and it is enough to hold a man to a wheel.
interact.look: Coiled cable, stiff with salt. A man could lose a hand in it, or find one lost.
The bowsprit points at nothing. The fog begins at its tip.
The red and green lights burn dull in the fog. A passing ship would see them. None passes.

interact.take_text: Petrofsky's cap. I fold it in my pocket for the day his mother asks me what became of him.
interact.look: Lying wet against the rail, a blue knitted cap with a name sewn in the band: PETROFSKY.

interact.set_text: Earth, damp and black, scuffed across the planks right to the stem-head. It is the same earth as the hold. The man who left it came out of the hatch and walked forward, and has not come back.
interact.look: A smear of black earth on the planks.

interact.set_text: The chain-locker, the sail-bin, the dark under the windlass. Nobody, nothing. I find only the wet and a new smell on the wind that is neither tar nor salt.
interact.look: The chain-locker.
Tall, thin, white as paper, standing quite still at the stem-head and looking out at the fog. Looking at me, now.
Back down the steps.
Worn smooth by twenty years of hands. The spokes are the length of a man's reach.

interact.set_text: I tap the glass. The needle trembles and drops another tenth since the forenoon watch. A steady, long fall: weather from the west is coming, and not tonight.
interact.look: A brass barometer in a mahogany case. The needle has been drifting down all morning.
The compass card, steady as a priest. For now the ship points where I tell her.
A chalk-board for the sail-plan. The mate and I argue over it. Today it is mine to settle.
Flags, a bell and a lamp. They would be a great help if there were anyone to signal.
He has offered to steer and watch, and keep the sail trimmed. Those are not a man's whole duties but he has taken them.

do.say: The wheel stands alone. The helmsman is gone, and the spokes are still warm.

interact.look: Black oak, dragon-headed. It was my father's, and before him another's, and every one of them sat in it as if it were a mistake that could be corrected.
A map of the border is pinned under three daggers. The fortress of Severin, burning in red wax, stands where the Turkish ink comes closest.
The counsellor's chair, with a cushion upon it for a back that has served three princes.
Velvet. Vlaicu will not sit in anything without it.
A log the thickness of a man burns on it. Nobody who sits near it is warm.
The coiled dragon of the Order, and beneath it, in faded thread: 'Founded by Sigismund, King of Hungary, in the year 1408. Whoso wears the Dragon keeps the gate of Christendom.'
The annals of the principality in four hands, none of which agree about anything.

interact.take_text: I fill a flask from the barrel. The tower will want it.
interact.look: Lamp-oil for the beacons, in a barrel with the garrison's mark burned in the lid. Half of it is meant for the tower.
Pens, sand and a pot of black ink gone to jelly. A clerk has been working at it since the siege began.

interact.take_text: I take the draft order. It wants a seal.
interact.look: A clerk's neat draft: 'To the captains of the levy: assemble at the camp below the Reed ford...' It has no seal and so no force.
A candle, a stick of green wax and a brass press shaped to fit a ring. It waits for the ring.
To my father's chamber, and the stair beyond.
A narrow spiral up to the battlements.

interact.go_fail: Not yet. The council must be answered, the order sealed and sent, the beacon lit, Radu faced, and my father's hammer in my hand.
interact.look: The great gate and the road to the army. I do not leave until the order is sealed and sent, the beacon is lit, my brother is dealt with and I carry my father's hammer.
Counsellor to my father and to his father. A grey beard, a voice like a closing door, and the best advice in the principality delivered with the worst timing.
Furs, rings and a smile that arrives a moment after the thought behind it. He commands three hundred spears and mentions it often.
My younger brother, back from the Sultan's court with Turkish manners, Turkish silks and an excellent opinion of himself. We have the same eyes. I have never been sure about the rest.
A thin rider in a muddy cloak who has been waiting by the door for an order that has not come.
Wide as a threshing-floor and cold as one. I have not yet slept in it.
An iron-bound chest with a dial of years on the lid. Whatever it holds, my father locked it himself.
Vlad Dracul in marble, wearing the Order's collar. On the plinth: 'Invested 1431, at Nuremberg.' It is the year he is proudest of. It is not the year of the Order.

interact.take_text: I take my father's hammer. It fits my hand as if it had been waiting.
interact.look: Mail, a helm and the heavy iron-headed hammer my father swung on the Danube. It is lighter than it looks, and I am not sure whether I am meant to be flattered.
Letters, a wax-stub and a map of the border with the Turkish side left blank, as though no one dared to draw it.
Five candles. Four of them are lit.
Built for two. Warms one.
Hours, a Livy in Latin and three treatises on fortification, all well-thumbed. My father read to be believed.
Back to the hall.
Boyar Corvin's daughter. She has a clear grey stare and an unfashionable habit of saying exactly what she means. We were children together in this castle. We are not children now.
Cut stone, blackened by seven centuries of other people's fires.

oil.say: I soak the logs through. The smell of lamp-oil is almost cheerful. It wants only fire.

interact.use_fail: It is not wood it wants. Something to feed the flame, and then something to start it.
interact.look: An iron brazier on a stone foot, stacked with split logs. The wood is bone dry, and so is the pitch. It would not light for weeks of trying without something to feed it.

torch.say: The torch touches the oil. A pillar of fire stands on the tower, and across the valley, on the ridge, a second small flame answers.

interact.use_fail: Not that. It wants a flame.
interact.look: The logs are dark with oil. A spark would finish the work.
It roars. On the far ridge the answering flame has doubled.

interact.take_text: I take the torch from its bracket.
interact.look: A resin torch in an iron bracket by the stair door, the only one on the tower that is not burned out.
Shuttered, so as not to be a target.
Green water. Even the pine-needles have given it up.
Back down to the hall.
Thirty years on this tower. He knows every star by the name it has in the barracks, which is not the one in the almanac.
The castle gate is behind me, up the hill. The old road has taken the shape of a long habit.
One arm points to the camp, the other to a ford with a Turkish name someone has tried to scratch out.
Axle cracked, a mattress on top, three children in a heap and a grandmother in front, who has not looked back once.

interact.set_text: I kneel by the prints. Felt-wrapped hooves; silent riders. They came down from the north-east, along the reed-creek, to the river.
interact.look: Many hooves, small, wrapped round with felt: the marks are deep and smeared, not the clean crescents of shod horses. Whoever it was came by night, and does not want to be heard.
A wooden Christ under a little roof, carved by someone who loved wood more than anatomy. Fresh flowers lie at its foot, from people who have nothing else to give.
A candle in a tin, left for travellers by someone who will not know their names.
Lightning took it a long time ago. Wolves use it to mark their ground.
She sits straight, with a rag-wrapped bundle on her knees. She looks through me rather than at me, which is how a prince is looked at on the road.
Three grey shapes at the edge of the lantern-light. They are not afraid of the cart, nor of me. They are weighing something.
Pine knots and a kettle. Twenty men sit round it who have all been telling stories, and are all sure the others are lying.
A trestle by the commander's tent, with a vellum map held down by four stones.
Sheepskins on bracken. A boy sleeps there with his boots on, because he has been told to.
A pavilion for the lords, of which only the pole stands in a convincing line.
Rations: black bread, onions and salt pork. In a country of mountains, the army marches on onions.
Water for the horses, and for the men who would rather it were wine.
Forage, tents, the camp-priest's portable altar and a crate marked 'FRAGILE' in a hand nobody will claim.

interact.go_fail: Which ford? Three crossings, and one army can only be at one. The map-table will tell me, if I weigh what the scout and the prints have said.
interact.look: The track runs down through the reeds to the river. It is a mile of mud, and I should know exactly which ford before I walk it.
Back up to the road and the castle.
Captain of my father's guard, now of mine. A neck like a bull's and the memory of every battle the principality has lost.
Lean, wind-burned, a goatskin cloak over mail. He has just come in from the river, and it shows on his boots.
A Turkish light-horseman, tied to a wagon-wheel, with a dignified sulk. He glares at a spot just left of my face.
A gaunt man in black who was not here a moment ago. He has the stillness of a thing that has never had to hurry, and shadows lie wrong around his feet.
A grey pony with felt tied round its hooves. It fell in the shallows with an arrow in its flank and the river is not yet done with it.
Somebody already planted stakes across the shallows. They are not ours.
Pitch and tow. They were going to burn the bridge-timbers.

interact.take_text: I take the broken standard. I do not know why. A prince should remember what he has fought.
interact.look: A green horse-tail standard on a spear, snapped. A crescent of tin hangs from it by one wire.
Back to the camp.
Light cavalry, felt on their hooves and knives between their teeth. They have not seen me yet.
He crouches in the reeds with a short bow, watching the camp-fires across the water.
A broad man in a steel cap, with a curved sword he does not draw. He is sure that tonight belongs to him.

interact.go_fail: The ferryman stands between me and the boat. He wants his toll.
interact.look: A black flat boat with a lantern at the bow. It goes out into the mist without a rower and comes back without a mark on it, they say. The ferryman must be paid first.
Seven stones, none of them upright. Something older than the school stood here and was not asked.

interact.take_text: I take the coin. 'He will not need it,' I tell the cairn, and the lake seems to hear.
interact.look: A cairn of lake-stones with an iron cross. In the cairn, pressed in by a careful thumb, a silver coin that no passer-by has dared to take.
'Scholars only. The tenth pays more.' The last four words have been scratched deeper by a different hand.
It burns green and gives no shadows.
Standing in the water as it has stood since its roots drowned.
Hooded, tall, and so still that a gull has settled on his shoulder. He does not breathe visibly. He holds out his palm without turning his head.
A slab of black stone with three hollows in its face: one for a bowl, one for a disc, one for a lamp. What goes in them, and in what order, is for the scholar to know.
A single book chained to a slanted board. Nobody opens it for a reason.
A bench scarred by nine scholars' knives. 'Teodor was here.' Nobody knows which Teodor.
The worn hollow where a scholar sat for an entire winter without speaking.
Rows of slates. One bears, in chalk: 'Aqua suscitat. Argentum ligat. Ignis signat.' The last word has been underlined, and then, lower, 'But always in this order.'
It shows the room correctly, and everyone in it but me. I stand a long time before I realise how little I mind.
It burns without smoke or sound. Held near the palm, it gives no heat.
The door to the lake and the ferry.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Vasile has the key; he has the only one, and he knows it.
interact.look: Iron, black, banded with the same hollow-and-disc mark as the altar. The lock has a face like a wolf's.

interact.go_fail: The stair is closed by a black bar that lifts only for the scholar who has attended the Master, performed the rite and read the roll.
interact.look: A spiral stair that goes further than the mountain. The tithe-chamber is below.
Whatever he was, he has not been that for centuries. He teaches in a flat, kind, amused voice, as a cat teaches a mouse the geography of the room.
Another scholar, my age, dark and quick, in a student's black. He keeps the library key on a cord round his neck and takes pleasure in showing it.
A pale boy of seventeen, copying a diagram with trembling hands. He has not been home in three winters.
The only woman in the school, silent, with ink on her wrists and a face I would not wish to meet at a crossroads at midnight.
Books on chains, as the old libraries did. These chains are to keep the books from the readers.
Treatises on storm, hail and thunder, in a flowing hand. 'To raise a tempest, find the storm already in the sky.'
'De Lupis,' 'On the Speech of Beasts' and a leather-bound 'Wolf-Tongue Primer' in a child's hand. The margins are sharp with bite-marks.
Pages that are cold to touch. I decide not to read them.

interact.set_text: I read it twice. Water, silver, flame. Water opens, silver binds, fire seals.
interact.look: A thin red codex on a reading-stand, open at a diagram of three vessels. The opening line reads: 'Three things wake a rite. Water first, to open the way. Silver next, to bind what has come. Fire last, to seal it.'
A black table, scarred round a single circle where something warm once stood.
A great scroll on rollers, signed by every scholar who has ever sat below. Ten names stand against each year. Ink is wet on the last line.
Candles of black wax, burning with a flame that does not wag.
Back to the lecture hall.
The seats are carved from the mountain itself. Ten in a ring, nine worn smooth.
Taken in a winter of thin rain. Nobody remembers his name.
The tenth seat. It is the only one with a cushion, and the cushion is a hide of something black.
A fire that gives a green light and a very faint sound like speech, three rooms off.
A grating set in the floor. Beneath, a breath of warm air that smells of wet iron and horse.
The way back to the school.
He is taller down here, and his shadow now has a shape of its own, which does not agree with his.

dracula_voivode_warhammer.say: The iron head takes the seal at the first blow. The lid slides, cracks, tips onto the flags. I am standing in a hole in the world, and I am not hungry for air.

interact.use_fail: Not that. The lid is lead-sealed oak. It wants weight and iron.
interact.look: The lid is nailed and sealed in lead. I am inside. I have been inside long enough that the idea no longer frightens me. Something heavy would break the lid.
Torn open, from within. A year ago I would have called that impossible.
'Vlad Dracul, Knight of the Dragon.' Beside it, a smaller slab: 'Mircea, his son,' for my elder brother, whom I never knew.
The dragon is cut on the lid, but her face is not. She always said the dragon would be enough.
They were lit when I was carried in. Each one burned down and was replaced, until someone ceased to replace them.

interact.go_fail: The door is barred. The lock wants the Voivode's seal. And I am still lying in a coffin.
interact.look: Iron-bound and stoutly barred from the other side. A recess in the lock is shaped to fit the family ring.
Where the Voivode was blessed, and where the bread of the Mass is blessed. I put my hand near it and feel nothing but cold, which tells me nothing.
It is only wood and silver. I look at it for a long time. It is only a cross; it does not burn; it does not even disapprove. I should have learned something from that.
Where the boyars sat on feast-days with their sword-belts loosened.
Where I sat as a boy, bored, drawing dragons in the dust of the prayer-book.
A new slab, still pale, and a sprig of withered rosemary. 'Ileana Corvin, who waited.' There is a small silver ring on the stone.
Down to stubs.
Down to the family vault, where I was laid.
The castle's old priest, wounded and propped against a pew. A dark stain has crept across his habit. He is looking at me the way men look at the sea before a storm.
Two Norman towers, a great west front, and four hundred years of rooks. Mr. Hawkins says it is the only client the firm has never sent a bill.
A brass plate worn to a shine by thirty years of the housemaid. The door of the office.
A tidy gate and a tidy bell. Mina Murray teaches the junior class here and has views on the bell.
Bolts of calico in the window and, above, my two rooms with the green blind.
A little roofed gate where coffins once waited for the priest. Not today, thank God.
A fountain with a tin cup on a chain, and a motto: 'Ye shall draw water with joy.'
Warm from the sun. A clerk is asleep upon the Times beside it.
Unlit. Lamplighter's ladder leans on the next one, abandoned for his dinner.
'Station 1 mile. London 194 miles.' Someone has added, in pencil, 'and back'.
Stand No. 4. The cabman has a whip, a pipe, and a very low opinion of the Great Western Railway.
Green water and three drowned leaves.
A girl with a basket of violets and a very good memory for faces.
A big man in a drab coat, who has driven half of Exeter to its weddings and the other half to its funerals.
Mahogany, leather-topped, and as orderly as a conscience. A decanter, a blotter, and a calendar open at May.

interact.take_text: I tie the bundle with its pink tape and put it in my breast pocket. Mr. Hawkins has told me to keep it safe.
interact.look: A bundle of heavy cream letters in a small, upright foreign hand. The envelopes bear a Transylvanian stamp and the seal of a wolf's head.

interact.take_text: Mr. Hawkins nods as I pocket the pen. 'Take it. I have three.'
interact.look: A steel pen, a bottle of Stephens' ink, and a pen-wiper in the shape of a hedgehog.
Our own replies to the Count, copied in damp tissue. A history of the purchase in nine letters.
A tall desk with a sloping top and a stool, from which Mr. Pell has watched the street for thirty-one years.
Every volume of Chancery since the Restoration. Only the dust is complete.
Black tin boxes marked with the names of every family in Devon. 'Harker' is not among them; my father never had the money to need a solicitor.
A fire kept up from October to May and sometimes in June. Mr. Hawkins says his bones are older than he is.
Seven minutes fast. Mr. Hawkins likes his clerks early, and the clock knows it.
Deep, hard, and designed to make a man tell the truth.
Four umbrellas, none of them mine, and a cricket bat.
The street door, with the brass plate behind it.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Mr. Pell keeps the key to the muniment room, and Mr. Pell keeps it like a relic.
interact.look: A low oak door with an iron keyhole the size of a florin. The firm's old papers lie behind it.
My employer and, since my father died, something nearer to a father: white-haired, spectacled, kind, and never wrong about a deed.
A narrow man in black alpaca with a pen behind each ear. He has the muniment key on a chain across his waistcoat and will tell you so.
The way back up to Mr. Hawkins's office.

harker_road_box_key.say: The key turns with a grind of old iron. Inside, three bound surveys of London houses: Hampstead, Whitby and Purfleet.

interact.use_fail: I have nothing that fits the lock. Somewhere in this room, a spare key is kept by habit.
interact.look: A black japanned box stamped 'PURCHASES - TRANSYLVANIA - PRIVATE'. Mr. Hawkins has the surveys inside, and a lock that wants its own key.
Rolls and bundles in red tape. A tabby cat has made its bed in 'Smith v. Smith'.
Three-legged, with a cushion that has been sat flat by clerks since the Reform Bill.
Hung from a hook by the shelves. There are scorch marks where the clerks tapped their pipes.
Lumps of broken wax, in every colour. A box of the firm's own old stamps lies on top.
Wet-ringed and ink-spattered. On it, a magnifying-glass and a note in Mr. Pell's hand: 'Surveys NOT to leave the room except by Mr. Hawkins.'

do.say: The air is cold and dry as paper. Everything in this room has been waiting a long time for somebody to need it.

interact.look: The schoolroom door, with a coat-peg for each child.
A chalk-drawn map of the Exe, and under it a line in neat shorthand. Mina has copied it out in longhand beside: 'Courage, mon ami.'
Slates, a ruler, a jar of pens, and a pile of copybooks, marked in red with kind, firm ticks.
'Phonographic Teacher.' Mina has been teaching herself shorthand, so as to be useful to a husband. She has not said which one.
Europe, with Transylvania a smudge of green by a thumbprint. Mina has underlined it in pencil.
Carved with initials, and one confession: 'H.S. loves a ginger cat.'
Cold. The children have drawn a smiling face in the soot.
A red geranium on the sill, the only thing in the room not marked for punctuality.
Mina in her grey school dress, ink on her finger, a pencil in her hair, and the kind of attention that makes one feel the only man in Devon.
Seven years old and standing on the bench to see the visitor properly.
Eleven steps and the smell of calico.
A brass-bound sea-trunk with a four-wheel combination lock, taken from my father's room when he died. I have never opened it.
A narrow bed made with Mrs. Dunmore's hospital corners.
My shorthand notes, a razor-strop, and a half-written letter to Mina, which I keep failing to finish.

interact.take_text: I put the diary in my coat. Mina is right: a traveller who writes nothing down has seen nothing.
interact.look: A stout little book bound in black. Mina gave it to me for the journey and said I must keep it in shorthand 'so that nobody can read your nonsense but me'.
Half packed. Shirts, collars, and a small box of seidlitz powders in case the Count's cooking disagrees with me.
Blackstone, Bradshaw's Railway Guide, a dog-eared 'Murray's Handbook for the Continent', and nothing a young man should be ashamed of.
It shows the same plain face as every other morning: an honest, tired young man who is going somewhere.
Mrs. Dunmore's best, loaned on condition of no pipe.
My landlady: a stout widow with a perfect understanding of the movements of every lodger in the street.
Back to the Close.
'THOMAS HARKER, SURGEON'S ASSISTANT, AND MARGARET HIS WIFE. HE DIED IN THE FEVER OF 1874, SHE FOLLOWED HIM IN THE SPRING. THEIR SON JONATHAN WAS TEN.' Someone has put snowdrops here.
'ALICE ANN, AGED 3 YEARS. SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.' A dead wreath of pimpernels.
'JOB TREMLETT, 47 YEARS SEXTON OF THIS PARISH, WHO DIGGED GRAVES FOR OTHERS AND NOW LIES IN ONE FOR HIMSELF.'
A cross, leaning gently towards the church as if to hear the sermon.
Older than the church, and holding up its limbs like a man who has seen much and said little.
A bench in the sun.
A stumpy Saxon tower and a Georgian porch.
Old stalks, kept in water by someone who loves them. The verger, perhaps. Or Mina.
A bent old man with a billhook and a sharp tongue, who has dug the graves of three generations of Exeter.
The way out, and back to the station.

Ranks of leather-backed volumes of pasted slips. Under TRANSYLVANIA, one entry is marked with a red ticket: 'Geography and Ethnology of the Carpathians, press-mark K.7'. The other entries are only history.

interact.take_text: I take a blank slip. The Museum prints them in a shade of green that makes every reader feel guilty.
interact.look: A shallow tray of printed call-slips: Title, Press-mark, Name of Reader.
Green baize, brass lamps, and a notice: 'Readers are respectfully requested not to lean on the books.'
A sleeping gentleman is using the Peerage as a pillow.
Pinned flat on the wall: Buda-Pesth, the Danube, the Carpathians. The Borgo Pass is a pencilled tick. A reader has written beside Transylvania: 'whirlpool of races'.
A bust of a long-forgotten trustee with a nose broken in 1851.
An inkwell chained to the table by order of the Trustees. Even ink cannot be trusted in London.

npcs.name: The Superintendent of the Reading Room

interact.look: A grave, spectacled man at the high desk, who has never raised his voice and never needed to.
Bald, white-bearded, buried in a folio of Hungarian wills. He has the look of a man who has read the whole of Europe and found it wanting.
My own window, barred inside by a Count's courtesy. Beneath it, a ledge a foot wide and a drop that does not bear looking at.
A rope of ivy thick as my wrist, rooted in the stone. It runs down and to the left. The leaves are torn, as if something heavy had gone down it recently.
A rusted iron ring in the wall, once for a banner-pole. The rust on it is rubbed bright on the lower curve, where a hand has taken weight.
A stone block that has shifted a finger's breadth. Beside it the lime is pale and scraped, as if a boot-heel had caught it.
A dozen bats under the eave. They are all facing the same window: the one on the east corner.

interact.go_fail: It is twenty feet along the face, and I cannot simply walk across a sheer wall. I must find the Count's own way down and across, step by step.
interact.look: Open to the night. The shutters hang back as though somebody has just gone through, and from within comes the smell of old earth.
Shut tight; dust on the sill, no scrape, no bat-dropping. Nobody has used this one for a century.
The way I came in. The wall below is a thousand feet of moonlit drop.

interact.take_text: I fill one pocket with a handful of old coin. The Count has too much to miss it, and I may need to buy a way out.
interact.look: A great heap of gold of every kind: Roman, British, Austrian, Hungarian, Greek and Turkish, covered with a film of dust as if it had lain long in the ground. None of it less than three hundred years old.
A cup set with jewels, and so old that its enamel has worn to the shape of a thumb.
Laid for a meal that was never eaten. Gold plate, a decanter, and no sign of a servant's hand.
Hung with faded velvet. The sheets have not been slept in. I think no one sleeps here.
A nail in the wall, high and plain, with a paler square of plaster below it. A mirror hung here once. There is none in the castle.
A long wardrobe of black oak, and in the shelves, ledgers in an old Latin hand. The last entry is dated the day I arrived.

interact.take_text: I take the poker. It is heavy, and I feel better for it.
interact.look: A heavy iron poker by a hearth that has not seen a fire in my time.
A ring of keys hanging from a hook, each a different age and size.

interact.go_fail: Locked. The lock is as old as the door and the door is as old as the castle.
interact.look: The door that gives, in the Count's own tower, onto the winding stair and the old chapel below.
Back up to the Count's room.

interact.go_fail: Barred. The beam is wedged into its sockets and will not lift by hand alone.
interact.look: A great iron-bound door barred on the inside by a beam, the way the earth-boxes come and go.

harker_road_poker.say: I wedge the poker under the beam and heave. With a groan it comes out of its staples, and I lean it against the wall.

harker_road_vault_key.say: The key opens the hidden lock in the staple, and the beam slides free.

interact.use_fail: I have nothing to lever or unlock the beam with.
interact.look: The bar of the postern: a trunk of oak, shot into iron staples. It will lift if levered.
The largest box, its lid thrown back. Within lies the Count, with open eyes like stones, red lips, and a cheek that has no breath in it.
Earth, fresh from the hills. The smell is unmistakable.
Earth heaped to the brim. They are all for England.
A single tall candle burning at the Count's head, no taller than a thumb, and with no melted wax.
A stone altar cracked across. The cross above it has been taken down and put face to the wall.
A knight's tomb with the head broken. The inscription is Slavonic; I can read 'unreconciled' only.
Old bones, heaped by the wall. Nobody has said a prayer for them.

interact.take_text: I take up the spade. If the thing in the box wakes, I shall at least have an answer.
interact.look: A spade, still stuck in a heap of clay. I could break the Count's skull with it; I have thought of it twice already.
A plank bridge across a deep gully, with the middle plank rotted away. A river roars below.

interact.take_text: I drag out a long, stout plank and shoulder it.
interact.look: A woodcutter's stack, split and left. There is a stout plank among the logs, long enough to bridge a gap.
A fire of broken pine, and above it a cook-pot. The smell is of onion and goat. A little caravan stands in the dark beyond.
Painted wheels and a tarpaulin tied with rope. It is clean in a way that tells me they have been here a long time.
A crude wooden cross with a rag tied on it. Somebody has left a bunch of dried garlic at its foot.

interact.take_text: I take a head of garlic. The peasants taught me that much, and I was a fool to laugh.
interact.look: A wayside offering. I take none of it.
'Bistritz - 28 hours. Buda-Pesth - 6 days.' Someone has scratched out 'Buda-Pesth' and written, in a bad hand, 'God knows'.
A gaunt woman in a red kerchief, who watches me over the cook-pot with a look neither friendly nor threatening.
An old man in sheepskin, leaning on a crook with a whistle at his lips.
Eyes in the gorse, low and yellow. They have been following me for a hundred yards.
Open to the lime trees and a little warm air.
A white door with a small brass crucifix.
A plain iron-framed bed. The sheets have been changed many times; I do not remember any of them.
A tidy bed. Its occupant has recovered, and left a holy picture on the pillow.
An old Magyar peasant sleeps there, with a rosary wound round his fingers.
Bottles of bromide, a water-jug, and a fever chart pinned to the wall: forty-two days of it.

interact.take_text: The doctor said I might borrow his pen to write to my fiancee. I do so.
interact.look: A pen and inkwell left on the table after the doctor's rounds.

interact.take_text: In the lining of my coat, the diary. The leather is torn and stained, but every page is there.
interact.look: A small trunk with my initials, in which the Sisters keep my torn coat, my shirt and my pocket-book.
A large crucifix in silver. I cannot look at it long without weeping.
A little desk where Sister Agatha writes her letters. Paper, a sander, and a half-finished embroidery.

interact.take_text: Sister Agatha lets me have a sheet of her paper.
interact.look: A few sheets of hospital paper with the crest of the Sisters.
A Sister of St. Joseph, small, quick, with gentle grey eyes and a Hungarian-German English all her own.
The hospital's physician: a lean man in a frock-coat who makes his rounds like a drill sergeant and has the voice of a country priest.
An old drover with a bandaged leg, who has been here nearly as long as I have and keeps count of the days with matchsticks.
Mina. She has come, in her travelling dress, white from the long journey, and she is holding my hand.
Back into the cool of the hospital.
Old, wide, humming with bees. The scent of blossom is almost unbearable after the castle.
A bench with one place worn smoother than the rest.

interact.take_text: Sister Agatha has said I may cut one. I choose the whitest and carry it indoors as if it were glass.
interact.look: A bush of white roses, in flower. Sister Agatha says they will be wanted for a wedding.
A shallow well with a rope and bucket. The water is sweet and ice-cold.
A small grey stone with seven names. Under them: 'They served the sick.'
A statue of the Carpenter, with a lily and a moss-grown plane.
A gnarled old man with a watering-can and the placid look of one who has seen every sort of patient go by.
A girl in a shawl, mending slowly from a fever of her own.
Back to the ward.
A white altar-cloth, brass candlesticks and a vase of white roses.
Above the altar, a crucifix and the legend 'Ecce Agnus Dei'.

interact.set_text: I take up a stub and let wax fall on the back of my hand: warm, soft and ready for a seal. I keep a little against the need.
interact.look: A rack of votive candles in red glass. Dripping wax has run down the rack and frozen in long tears.

harker_road_parents_letter.say: I fold the letter once more and set it at the Virgin's feet, among the others. Father, Mother: you are never any further than this.

interact.use_fail: I have nothing yet to leave here.
interact.look: A painted shrine, with fresh flowers and rows of tiny tablets. The hospital's patients leave letters here for those who cannot be reached.
Plain oak, with a kneeler worn by a century of knees.
A stoup of cold holy water at the door.
A grey, kind clergyman, in Buda-Pesth these thirty years for the sake of British sailors and the odd stranded traveller.
Mina, in her travelling dress, with white roses in her hand and Jonathan's name already half on her lips.
Sister Agatha, dressed in her Sunday veil, standing as witness with a look of fierce delight.
White counterpane, blue hangings, and the dent where I read until the candle guttered. It has never once failed to be comfortable.
Brushes, ribbons and a hand-glass. Far too many ribbons.
A girl in it with a pink face and her hair half up. She looks as though she has been told a secret.

interact.take_text: I read it at the window. It is the shortest letter I have ever had from a gentleman, and I read it four times.
interact.look: A thin cream envelope in Arthur's careful, upright hand, addressed to me and not yet opened.
A candle, a novel, a glass of water and a little pot of forget-me-not seeds from Mina.

interact.take_text: I take the inkwell. If I am to write to Mina this week, I shall want it.
interact.look: A squat bottle of black ink. Mamma says I use more ink than the whole of the Admiralty.
Seven white frocks and one blue. I have been told this is unadventurous.
Tennyson, a lady's cookery-book that is only a disguise, and Mina's pressed fern in a green frame.
Where I sit to be pinned into things.
To the stairs and the parlour.
Hannah, with an armful of linen and a look of fond despair.
Set for six. Mamma's count of the guests increases whenever she looks at it.
A stand with a green jar on it and the sad stalks of last week's arrangement. A vase is not a flower until someone has taken some trouble over it.

lucy_summer_escritoire_key.say: The little key turns. Inside are a bundle of Mina's letters tied in blue ribbon, and a pad of good paper.

interact.use_fail: Locked. Mamma keeps the key somewhere only she knows. She would like it to be a proof of something.
interact.look: Mamma's walnut escritoire, with a little brass lock. Mina's letters are kept in the left-hand drawer.
A small table by the window, where the light is best for letters.
A silver tray for cards. It has been very full this week.

interact.take_text: A card in a large, rapid hand. It will not stay in my pocket for long without being read.
interact.look: A card, slightly bent, left by a tall gentleman who would not wait to be announced.
A square piano with music open on it. I have been playing the same page since February.
Chintz roses on a sofa. Real roses in the garden look rather superior.
Mamma's. She sits with her back to the draught and her face to the door.
The visitors' chair. Occupied this month by a succession of men who all want to be somewhere else.
Unlit by day; it is waiting for a better occasion.
Up to the first floor and my own room.
Open to the lawn.
Mrs. Westenra, in grey silk, with a heart she cannot spare and a talent for seeing exactly what she wants to see.

interact.take_text: I pick the wild rose from the foot of the arbour. The thorn takes a drop of blood and I suck my thumb like a child.
interact.look: The arbour is thick with roses, and the wild one at its foot has opened first, as it does every year.

interact.take_text: I cut three white lilies, as tall as my elbow. They will do for the back of any vase.
interact.look: Tall white lilies, standing in a row like bridesmaids.

interact.take_text: A handful of forget-me-nots, small and blue, no taller than my finger.
interact.look: A stone sundial with forget-me-nots growing round its foot. The motto reads: 'I count only the sunny hours'. It must be very slow work.
A bench in the shade, for reading and for pretending to read.

interact.take_text: Dr. Seward must have left it before he went in to Mamma. I read it, and then I fold it very small.
interact.look: A folded sheet left on the bench. It has my name on it in a hand I have seen on medical charts.
Lace cloth, a pot of Darjeeling and a plate of what Mamma calls seed-cake.
Mamma's.
Mine.
Geraniums in military ranks.
A white house with every window open.
Back to the house.
Dr. Seward, young, grave, and visibly rehearsing something under his breath. He holds his hat as though it were a patient.
Mr. Morris of Texas, lounging against the fence like it was built for him. His boots are covered in Surrey.
Arthur Holmwood, tall and fair and very pale with nerves. He has a rose in his buttonhole, and has forgotten it is there.
The narrower bed, nearer the window. Mina took the other, and the key, and the habit of locking the door.
Mina's bed, made with a neatness that is almost a reproach.
Everything I own that is not on the road to Whitby, folded in tissue.
A window-seat, cushioned in faded cretonne, with a long view of the harbour and the Abbey.

interact.set_text: Wet grass, and sand on the toes. I have not been out. Mina says I have; I say I have not. The slippers do not say.
interact.look: My white slippers, which I left clean by the bed last night. The soles are grey with mud, and the hems of my nightgown are wet.
A jug, a bowl and a cracked soap-dish.
I look rather pale this week. I think it is the Whitby light.
Mina's books on one shelf and my novels on another, shelved with a sort of silent argument.
Mina keeps it filled. She says she will not be caught out in the dark.
Down to the street, and up to the cliff.
Mamma, in a shawl, anxious about draughts and about nothing in particular.
Our seat, facing the sea. A brass plate on the back says it was given in loving memory of someone who sat here for forty years. The wind is cold on the back of my neck.
The ruins stand over the town like an unfinished sentence.
Stone steps cut into the cliff, down to the town and the harbour. Mr. Swales swears there are one hundred and ninety-nine.
'Sacred to the memory of a mariner, lost at sea.' I read that on every one of them. The sea has an enormous appetite for stones.
Lichen has taken the last of the name.
The cross leans seaward, as though it has been listening.
Smoothed by generations of people who know exactly what the weather is going to do.
A coastguard's lamp, not yet lit.
'To the Crescent and the town.'
Mina Murray, in a straw hat, with a writing-pad on her knee and anxious eyes.
Old Swales of the East Cliff, nearly ninety, and as hard as the stones he sits among.
Our seat. The wood is cold and damp, and I am sitting on it. I do not remember sitting down.
Black against a dark blue sky, and one window lit that has no business being lit.
There is no bell here. The sound comes from the headland, from the harbour, from inside my own chest, slow, slow, slow.

interact.go_fail: I cannot make my feet move. He is looking at me, and my feet have decided to stay. I will have to hold on to something first.
interact.look: The steps go down into the dark. Down is the way home, if I can stand up.
It flutters at the edge of my sight and is gone when I turn.
Tall, dark, and pale, with eyes that are very red when they look at me. He has been waiting.

do.say: I wake sitting on the seat in my nightgown, with my feet bare on the wet grass. The bell is tolling, and a tall dark man is standing by the Abbey wall, watching me with red eyes. I did not walk here. I did not choose this. I want to go home.

interact.look: Step after step after step, worn into hollows by the feet of sailors' wives. I must go down. I must not lose count.
'In memory of ... who departed this life.' Everyone departs; it is only a matter of whose bell they hear.
The cross points downhill, to the harbour.
Lichen, cold and wet, the same dead colour as the sea.
A bat, flitting in and out of the moon. I used to think they were charming.
A single lamp at the bottom of the steps, swinging in the wind.
Mina, in her dressing-gown with a shawl over her arm and her hair in a plait. She looks as though she has been running.
Blue hangings, white counterpane, and a heap of white flowers on the pillow, which Dr. Van Helsing says is medicine. They smell exactly like a kitchen.
A great ugly wreath of garlic blossoms. I am told not to take it off.
Pen, paper, ink. A long, steady sheet of paper with nothing yet written on it. The window beyond it is open to a night I am going to remember for a very short time.
My father's letter, written to me when I was ten, with forget-me-nots pressed in every fold. I held it in Whitby on the night I would have died, and it held me back. I know what I shall do with it.
Someone has sat in it every night this month. I have stopped asking who.
Tennyson, and Mina's pressed fern in its green frame. The shelves look as bright as they did in the spring; it is odd that they should.
Dr. Seward in the bedside chair, asleep, his hand on my wrist. The best friend any foolish girl ever refused.
Mamma, asleep in an armchair with her hands folded over her heart, on Dr. Van Helsing's strict orders.
Miss Hallam's desk: a ledger, a bell, and a pen-tray laid out as if for inspection.
Shorthand primers, a ruler, and a tin of hairpins I confiscated from the third form.

interact.take_text: I take a hairpin. It has got more people out of trouble than any other single invention.
interact.look: A stout steel hairpin, the sort Pitman's disciples use to clean their pens.
Initials cut with a compass-point, and a poem to a boy called Ernest.
Tidy to a fault. Edith Marsh sits here and trusts nobody's blotting-paper but her own.
Dora Pike's desk, with a page of sums folded very small under the lid.
Eleven small hats, eleven small shawls, and one rain-cape that belongs to nobody.
Banked for the summer. The kettle on top is the only warm thing in the room.
Blind, noble and chalk-dusted. The girls draw spectacles on him in Lent.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Miss Hallam holds the key, and Miss Hallam will not lend it while a prize is missing from her cupboard.
interact.look: A narrow door with a keyhole. Miss Hallam keeps it locked since the winter of the burst pipe.
The way out, to my rooms and to the station.
The headmistress, upright as a ruler, with spectacles she looks over rather than through.
A girl of thirteen with a notebook of her own, in which she records, I suspect, the faults of her elders.
Pale, quiet, a good hand at sums. Her sleeve-cuffs have been turned and re-turned until they are thin as paper.
A heavy table with four ink-rings and a place worn pale by two generations of elbows.

mina_records_hairpin.say: I slide the hairpin under the tangled type-bars and ease them apart. Two of them click free, like a sigh.

oil.say: A drop on every pivot and a little on the carriage rail. The machine stops groaning.

mina_records_ribbon.say: I wind the new ribbon onto the spools, black and sleek as a cat's back.

interact.use_fail: That will not help the Remington.

interact.take_text: I take the oil-can's last good drops, decanted into a medicine phial.
interact.look: A little can with a long spout, left by a mechanic who did not return.
Foolscap, quills, sealing-wax, and a great many tins that once held something else.
Pitman, Gurney, Taylor: three fierce loyalties in one dusty row.
Spoiled pages, each wrong in a different and instructive way.
Low and wobbly. A girl does not sit in it for pleasure.
Back to chalk and girls.
Retired from shorthand after forty years, she still taps her fingers on every table as if it were one.
Forty shorthand exercises, a pot of ink, a cold cup of tea. A pen lies where I put it down to think of Jonathan.
'Dear Sir, I beg to acknowledge...' in the fastest hand I have. Somewhere in the pile is a letter to Jonathan I have not dared send.
Bradshaw's Guide in four monthly numbers, the Bible, Tennyson, and a Baedeker for places I shall not see.
My favourite reading. I could take the 7.15 to Plymouth with my eyes shut and tell you where it stops.
The cathedral towers over the chimney-pots. The rooks quarrel about it every evening.
Horsehair, and ruthless to the spine. Lucy says it was designed by someone who hated guests.
The gas-ring and its kettle. I have boiled a thousand eggs on it and loved none of them.
Down the stairs and across the Close.
Ten minutes' walk to the station, eight if I do not look at the shop windows.
My landlady, who keeps the draper's below and a ledger of every letter that comes to the house.
Lucy, in a travelling dress, with a flush of excitement and a hat-box she has forgotten to unpack.
A slanting stand under glass, with a rail for the great books.
A standing train: a carriage with a lamp for the dark and hard seats for the honest.
A brass grille in a mahogany box. Behind it a young man listens to the whole country ticking.
Someone has carved 'Tiverton 14' in the seat, for reasons known to the carver.
A lamp that is lit at four every afternoon, even in June.
Stamped with the name of a Devon farm and a number I find reassuring.
'To the city and the Close.'
A man in a frock-coat who has not been late in nineteen years and does not intend to begin.
A young clerk with ink on his cuffs and a faraway look, as if the wires hummed in his teeth.
A big man leaning on a barrow, eating a pasty with the concentration of a scholar.
Tide-tables, picture post-cards, and a clear space exactly the size of my notebook.
Cold, with a ship in a bottle on the mantel that Mrs. Westenra thinks is an ornament and the landlord thinks is sacred.
Murray's Guide, Mrs. Radcliffe, and a single volume of sermons that has never been opened.
Lucy's place. She lies on it and reads the end of novels.
Mine, by right of possession.
Boats come in by the dozen at four. From here I can count them and make myself no happier.

interact.go_fail: It is still day, and I have one thing to do before I go up: I have something in mind to hang by a cord.
interact.look: Fourteen steps, of which the ninth complains.
Out to the cliff, the churchyard and the sea.
Lucy, rosy from the sea air, with a pencil behind one ear and the post-card of a lighthouse in her hand.
Lucy's mother, in grey silk and a lace cap, enjoying her tea with the air of a woman who has been told not to excite herself.
A bench of black wood, carved with the initials of four generations and one rude word.
It leans toward the sea, as if it wanted to be a sailor too.
Broken against the red sky. The sexton says a White Lady is seen in the great window at sunset.
A zig-zag path down the cliff toward the pier.
A lamp that the harbour-master lights when it pleases him.
The road back to our lodgings.
An ancient fisherman with a face like a walnut, smoking a pipe nobody has ever seen him light.
Two bats out hunting early, turning over my head in tighter and tighter circles. I do not like how they look at me.

do.say: The sun is going down behind the Abbey. A tiny bat flickers over the nearest tomb, and then another.

interact.look: Charts weighted with a mug, a knife and a sleeping cat.
A long brass glass lashed to its stand. It points at nothing at all right now, which is the best sort of target.
A stove that is always lit. The tea on it is a legend.
Neat coils of spare line, tarred and ready.
Lead-lines and a dented flask. Locked, and it looks as if it likes being locked.
Out to the cliff path.
A broad man who talks to the sea in a low voice, as one might to a large and doubtful dog.
Lucy sleeps with one hand under her cheek, like a child in a picture.
I have not slept in it yet. I am writing at the foot of it, which is almost the same.

mina_records_candle.say: I set the candle in its dish and strike a match. One flame, standing quite still.

interact.use_fail: That does not belong on the table.
interact.look: A candle-dish, a prayer-book and a pencil.

water.say: I pour the water into the basin, slowly. It laps once against the china, and laps again.

interact.use_fail: The basin wants water.
interact.look: A china basin on a washstand, white as milk.

interact.take_text: I take the jug's water, a cupful poured into my little flask.
interact.look: A big jug of cold water, sweating on the boards.

mina_records_plumb.say: I knot the cord to the bracket and let the plumb hang. It turns, very slowly, with a small bright eye in the candle-light.

interact.use_fail: Nothing hangs from there.
interact.look: A dead gas bracket that nobody has lit since the gas was cut off.
A rocking-chair that came with the room and has opinions about it.
A ship in a bottle and a small brass clock that has stopped at ten past three.
Sheets, lavender, and the ghost of Mrs. Westenra's moth-balls.
Hair-brushes, a hand-glass, and a small mirror that has never once flattered me.
Back down to the sitting-room.
Lucy, fast asleep, murmuring something about a ring. She looks entirely happy. I would not wake her for the world.

do.say: The ninth stair complains behind me. I turn. Nobody is there, but the curtain is moving, and the window is shut.

interact.look: Locked, rope-bound, wet to the touch. Wherever it was bound, it was not meant to be opened by me.
It swings. It is the only thing in the room that moves with the water, and it is all I can look at.
A neat coil of rope. One end leads up, into the dark, toward a square of grey that might be the sky.
A ladder, and a cord beside it, a thread so fine I can feel it more than see it.
A square of the room I fell asleep in.

do.say: Water laps. Timber creaks. My own breath sounds like someone else's. I tell myself it is a dream and that I may wake whenever I choose; I am not sure that is true.

do.card: Brazos country, Texas. Spring, 1884.

interact.look: The big double door of the stable, propped open on a bar.

interact.set_text: Sawn, and sawn quietly. Wash's dogs were fed first: there are bits of meat in the dust. This was planned.
interact.look: The top rail has been sawn through, not broken. Whoever did it came with a file and patience, and the dogs never barked.

interact.take_text: A fifty-foot lariat, Wash's best. I coil it over my shoulder.
interact.look: Bridles, girths and a coil of good manila rope.
A half-barrel of rainwater. The horses were watered here last night. Now there are no horses.
Where Santa Fe's saddle usually rests. It is bare. I feel it in my chest.
A pan of corn bread under a cloth, and a note: 'Eat something before you go, Mr. Quincey. Maria.'
The ranch foreman, sixty if a day, with a bloody rag tied to his scalp.
She wrings her apron and crosses herself every time she looks at the empty corral.

interact.go_fail: Wash is right. I will not ride out against Dunning's gang with an empty rifle. Powder and lead, and the loading bench in the stable.
interact.look: The east gate, and beyond it nothing but grass and a long day's riding.
Burnt down to the wick. It was dark when the thieves came.
Daylight and a cold draught.

quincey_hunt_lead.say: I melt the lead over the lamp and pour it into the mould. Ten neat slugs lie cooling on the bench.

quincey_hunt_powder.say: I measure the black powder into the brass cases, grain by grain, as my father taught me.

quincey_hunt_slugs.say: I seat the slugs in the cases and crimp them with the vise. Ten cartridges for the Winchester.

interact.use_fail: That does not belong on the loading bench.
interact.look: A vise, a powder-measure and a bullet-mould. Lead is cast here into slugs, and slugs are charged with powder to make cartridges.

interact.take_text: I dig the spent slugs out with the bowie and tap them into a lump. Enough lead for a few good cartridges.
interact.look: Wash's old shooting post. Years of misses lie buried in the wood.
Saddle-soap, hoof-oil, harness buckles.
Oats. The lid has been put back askew.
Collars and breeching, smelling of leather and old sweat.

interact.take_text: Her saddle-blanket, worn soft, still smelling of her. I fold it under my arm.
interact.look: Her name, painted on a board by a boy of fifteen. The straw is still pressed in the shape of her.

interact.take_text: Arthur's hand. I pocket it. It can be read later.
interact.look: A tin cup, a pipe, and a letter with a Buenos Aires stamp.
A hurricane lamp swinging from a nail.
A day's ride home, or a quarter of one when you are in a hurry.

interact.set_text: East, then. They did not hurry, which means they feel safe: low ground, soft going, no sky-line.
interact.look: A string of horses crossed here, walking close, loose-herd pace. Santa Fe's own print is among them: unshod behind. Where the tracks leave the water-hole they bend east, toward low ground.

interact.set_text: Cottonwood ash. They burn what they find in the creek bottoms, and they were there a night ago.
interact.look: A ring of stones and cold white ash. Cottonwood: light, fast-burning, no coal. There is no cottonwood within fifteen miles of here except one place.

interact.set_text: Red flannel with canebrake burrs: a man who has ridden through the bottoms and lately.
interact.look: A scrap of red flannel snagged on a thorn, burrs of canebrake clinging to it. Canebrake grows only in wet ground.
Where the water-hole's paths diverge: north to the Cap Rock, east to the cottonwood bottoms, south across the mesquite flat.
Muddy water, tracked all round by cattle and, lately, by horses.

interact.go_fail: I do not know which way they went. Three trails, and I have only one chance to be right. Read the signs first.
interact.look: The trail runs downhill into a green line on the horizon: cottonwood.
A trapper in a buckskin coat, whittling at nothing.
A Tejano drover sitting his horse, watching the horizon with the patience of his people.

rope.say: I send the loop over the stub on the second throw, make fast, and swing across hand over hand, the way we did as boys. The far bank is firm and my boots are dry.

interact.use_fail: The channel is too deep and cold to swim with a rifle. Something to throw over that snag, perhaps?
interact.look: A dead cottonwood leaning far out over the deep channel, with a stub like a hook on its limb. The ford is a swimming-hole; the far bank is firm.
Two gaunt grey wolves, hunger-mad after a dry season. They have noticed me.

interact.take_text: A big silver Mexican spur, engraved with a P. Someone from Dunning's gang, called Pike, lost it at the ford.
interact.look: Half sunk in the mud, with the buckles still done up. Whoever lost it was in a hurry.
Frogs are loud under it.
A calf with Wash's brand, killed for meat and left to the buzzards. They are not even trying to hide it any more.

interact.go_fail: The wolves are between me and the water, and the channel is too deep to swim. First deal with the wolves, then find a way across.
interact.look: Fresh horse-dung and the smell of woodsmoke. Dunning's camp is close.
The way I came.
Cottonwood embers. A coffee-pot and a bottle of mescal beside it.
The leader. A black coat, a hat set square, and hands that never leave his belt.
He leans on a saddle, snoring through a three-day beard.
My mare, dancing on her picket, ears flat, sweat on her flanks. She has seen me.

quincey_hunt_sugar.say: She takes the lump with her soft lips, and the shaking stops. 'Hey, little girl. Easy. I'm here.'

knife.say: One stroke of the bowie and the line falls slack. She tosses her head once, and stays where she stands, which is how I know she trusts me.

interact.use_fail: The knot is wet rawhide, hard as iron. A blade would be better than my fingers.
interact.look: A rawhide line staked between two posts. Santa Fe has pulled it taut and left the skin raw.

interact.take_text: A running-iron: the thieves' tool for turning one brand into another. Evidence enough for any sheriff.
interact.look: Saddles with other men's brands, a ship's chronometer, a dozen watches.
A chuck-wagon full of other people's cattle ropes.
A dung fire in a ring of stones, a kettle, and a place for a man to talk.
Young, fair, cleaning his rifle with a tenderness he should keep for people.
Notebook on his knee, spectacles in his hand, and no sleep in his eyes.
Our guide, bow-legged, smoking a corn-husk cigarette. He has not looked at the fire once; he looks at the sky.
She came all the way from Texas on a steamer. She has never once complained.

interact.take_text: A bundle of thick, dry thistle-stalks. They burn long and smoke thickly.
interact.look: Dry thistle-stalk and cattle-dung: the only fuel for a hundred miles.

interact.take_text: A tin of lamp oil, a little more than a pint.
interact.look: Biscuit, jerked beef, a flask of lamp oil.
Canvas hood, iron tyres, and a seat worn smooth.
Three men to a tent, in theory.
My saddle, my blankets and, for tonight, a rifle at hand.

interact.go_fail: Not yet. I want to hear what the gaucho has to say first, and to sit by the fire a while with the others.
interact.look: Where the horses are picketed for the night, out in the tall grass.

wood.say: I pile the thistle-stalks in the pit and light it. A thick white smoke rolls across the lines. Bats do not like smoke, Anselmo says; it stings their noses.

interact.use_fail: It needs fuel that burns slow and smokes thick.
