interact.look: A shallow pit between the picket-posts. Dry grass would burn out in minutes, but something thick and smoky would burn till dawn.

quincey_hunt_lantern.say: I hook the lantern on the nail at the top of the post, where its light will fall on every horse.

oil.say: I fill the font, trim the wick and strike a match. A white steady flame fills the glass.

interact.use_fail: A lantern hung high would keep a wide ring of light, with oil in the font. The post is waiting.
interact.look: A stout post. A lantern hung high on it would light the whole of the lines.
She stands head-down, nostrils wide, shifting from hoof to hoof as if the ground itself were uneasy.

quincey_hunt_blanket.say: I throw her own saddle-blanket over her neck and withers, knot it under her throat, and tuck in the corners. 'There, girl. Nothing gets in under that.'

interact.use_fail: She needs something over her neck: a blanket she knows.

interact.look: Where I will not be sleeping tonight. My Winchester lies across it.
The glow of the camp, two hundred yards off through the grass.
She stands, but only just, trembling, grey about the lips. There is a small neat wound at her neck, and her blanket is stained.
Kneeling in the grass with his bag open.
Pale, silent, holding the mare's halter-rope out of habit.

interact.set_text: No beast sleeps in a circle. A bat would hang, not trample. Something stood here, and then rose.
interact.look: A circle of grass pressed flat, about the size of a cartwheel, with every blade lying one way as though some great creature had wheeled and risen from it. The grass in the middle is dead, grey and brittle.

interact.set_text: Alien earth: someone carried it here. Something that cannot rest without it?
interact.look: A handful of black, dry soil, dropped on the green. There is no black soil within a hundred miles of the Pampas; the ground here is red clay.

interact.set_text: It walked in, and it did not walk out. The prints stop and the bat begins.
interact.look: Long bare footprints, human in shape, that cross the grass and stop between the picket-posts. They do not return. They begin again at the ring.

interact.take_text: I cut off the wing, as a proof for Seward, who will say it needs a better word than 'bat'.
interact.look: A bat the size of a hen. One wing is broken. It is the only part of last night I understand.
A mound of red clay under a cross of picket-posts. A last blanket of grass will cover it by spring.
A narrow cot with a grey blanket folded square. A man who knows where he stands folds his blanket.
A deal table, scrubbed. The only thing in the room I am allowed to arrange.
Bread, a tin cup and a smear of margarine. The attendants count the spoons; one is always missing, and they always blame me.
Enamel, chipped. It smells of the thing it is for.
A three-legged stool, bolted to nothing but to my patience.

renfield_mercy_spoon.say: The spoon-handle bites under the board. Beneath it, wrapped in a handkerchief with a crest I have not shown anyone in thirty years, lies my notebook of lives.

interact.use_fail: That will not lift a board. Something thin, with a lever's patience.
interact.look: One board by the cot-leg sounds hollow under the heel. It wants something thin and strong to lever it.

interact.take_text: I take the jar. An empty jar is an invitation.
interact.look: A clean jam jar on the shelf by the window. Hodge lets me keep it for my 'pets'.

renfield_mercy_sugar.say: I set the sugar on the sill, a white crumb on grey stone. Within a minute the flies are there, small and humming and entirely mine.

interact.use_fail: That is not what a fly wants.
interact.look: A bare stone sill. A few flies bump against the glass, but nothing holds them. They will not stay for nothing.

renfield_mercy_jar.say: I drop the jar over the sugar, slide my palm beneath, and lift. A small furious life in glass. Eleven, by my count. The ledger will hold it.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: Eleven flies, eleven lives. 'Each one a tithe,' I write, and the pen goes through the paper. Dr. Seward would say it is a dozen flies on a lump of sugar. Perhaps it is both.

interact.use_fail: Nothing to do with that.
interact.look: A dozen flies feed on the sugar, which is all that is happening, whatever the ledger says.
Tallies scratched low on the padding, in groups of five. Mine. I do not remember whether they count days or lives.
Issued, counted and collected. I light it at dusk and give back the stub at dawn.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Mr. Hodge has not yet decided what sort of man I am today.
interact.look: Heavy, with a grating. On the other side it has a lock; on this side it has me.
A big, tired, kind man in a white coat, with the keys on his belt. He has been bitten twice and bears no grudge.

do.say: Morning at Purfleet. Tray, cup, a grey light on the padding. I am Renfield, R. M., once of a good house and a better profession; and I am in a cell with a ledger I cannot reach. First Hodge. I shall have to be a gentleman.

interact.look: Narrow, made square. Whoever sleeps here has stopped expecting to be moved.
A bed under the window. The pillow is damp from some weeping nobody mentioned.
A scarred table where the patients play dominoes and nobody keeps the score.
Turned low. One of nine lamps; I have counted them.
A board of the ward's inventory in Dr. Seward's neat hand, kept under glass against the patients' fingers.
A tall press with a brass dial of three wheels. Dr. Seward keeps the patients' sugar ration in it, so they cannot hoard it.
Ten past three, always, for the one day it was right. The nurses wind it on Sundays and it forgets by Monday.
Where the patients sit to watch weather they are not allowed in.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: The coat is a tall man, patient and pale-eyed, who has come to ask after his debtors. I look again. It is Hodge's greatcoat, and it smells of pipe-smoke and wet dog. Both of these are true, and I do not know which is the lie.

interact.use_fail: It will not take that.
interact.look: An attendant's greatcoat on a peg. In the half-dark it has the shape of a tall man waiting.
My room, with its door open and its tray untouched.
The doctor's door. Brass plate, black letters. It is open when I have been good.
To the scullery and the kitchen. The warm smell leaks under the door.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Hodge has the key somewhere about him, and he is awake and watching the door.
interact.look: Iron-bound, and kept locked at dusk. Beyond it, the wall, the water-butt, and Carfax.
Hodge, leaning against the wall, with his keys and his thoughts. He has the look of a man who is owed a pipe.
A small, grey, precise gentleman, counting under his breath. He was a clerk in the Customs and has not stopped.
A tall old gentleman with a rug over his knees, sitting very straight. He wears a collar nobody has ever seen him fasten.
Hodge on the night watch, a lamp at his elbow and his eyelids at half-mast.
Hodge, snoring in the big chair with his chin on his chest. The brandy has done what it was asked.
A desk of case-notes, ink and cigar ash. Somewhere in there is a page headed 'R. M. R., aet. 59'.
Maudsley, Esquirol, Pinel, and a volume of Carpenter that has been read to pieces.
Banked low. The mantel holds a stopped clock, a pipe, and a photograph of a young woman I am too polite to name.
The chair in which a great many troubled people have explained themselves. It is worn at the front.
Two fingers gone. Brandy is not a cure; it is a postponement.
Some Greek, with a pencil-moustache added by an earlier patient. Seward leaves it.
Under its cloth, a wax cylinder half full of someone's confessions. Doctors are the priests of this century.
Three candles, burnt to the same stub. He sits up under them most nights.
Back to the ward.
A grave young man in his thirties with the eyes of a man who has stopped sleeping and kept working. He is the only person in the house who writes down what I say.
A great black kitchen range, polished with a patience that deserves a better employer.
Flour, a rolling-pin and a half-plucked fowl. It is a scene of moderate and orderly slaughter.
Dusty to the rim. Mice have been at it, and Cook has been at the mice.
Rain-water for washing the greens.
Oatmeal, coarse and damp at the bottom.
Blue plates, copper pans and, behind them all, a bottle Cook says is for the gravy.

renfield_mercy_flies_jar.say: I tip the flies into the web. The old spider drops down, takes them one by one, and in the stir the thing in the web comes loose: an iron key, lost long ago behind the plate-rack, on a loop of tape marked 'GARDEN'. Hodge dropped it, Dr. Seward would say. The spider kept it, I would say. I am not troubled by the difference, only by the key.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: A spider is a clerk who keeps accounts in silk. Every fly a line. This one has a very handsome set of books.

interact.use_fail: The spider is not interested in that.
interact.look: A wide old web in the corner behind the plate-rack, thick with dust and with something small and metal caught in it. The spider is large, fat in the way of a spider who has been fed by nobody.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: I look at the cat and the ledger looks at me. 'The cat has eaten forty sparrows,' I write, 'and the sparrows ten thousand flies.' It does not close. Nothing in this ledger closes.

interact.use_fail: The cat declines.
interact.look: A fat tabby asleep in the warm. In my ledger he is the last account in the chain: sugar, flies, spiders, sparrows and the cat.
A tin lamp, always lit. Cook says the dark in a kitchen breeds beetles.
Back to the ward.
A broad, floury woman who has raised six children and fed forty patients and has never in her life been afraid of a man.
The way back in, to Hodge, the cot and the tray.
Ten feet of old brick, topped with broken glass. Beyond it, Carfax.

interact.go_fail: I cannot go through while the night-man is on his round, and not without the garden key.
interact.look: A little door in the old wall, rusted shut on the Carfax side. It has a keyhole on this one.
A fat water-butt against the wall, deep in shadow. A man who knew his hour could kneel behind it.
The bench where Dr. Seward sits with the quiet patients in the afternoon.

interact.take_text: I cup it in both hands. It is warm and it weighs nothing. It looks at me with a bead of eye, and I cannot read what it says.
interact.look: A sparrow on the path with one wing hanging wrong. The cat will find it before morning.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: It is not a man. It is a heap of whitewashed stones the gardener left. It is also a patient Master waiting for the debt to be paid. The ledger does not choose between them; I will have to.

interact.use_fail: It does not respond.
interact.look: Something pale in the lee of the wall, as tall as a man. It has not moved since I came out.
The night-man hangs it here when he goes to the far wall. A lantern is a clock if you watch it.
A jumble of stones. A good place for beetles.
A pear tree that stopped bearing the year the last Lord died. The sparrows love it.
A thick-necked man with a lantern and a stick. Blunt has the night round, ten and two, and the temper of a man who thinks the patients are animals.
A stone altar stripped of its cloth. Someone has laid a ring of earth where the cross should stand. A voice lives here.

renfield_mercy_ledger.say: I open the ledger on the lid and total the whole of it: every fly, every spider, every sparrow, the cat. Eleven, forty, three hundred, a thousand. It is a column that grows and never rises to the sum he promised. 'Lives', he says, and gives me none of them. He has not paid a penny in all the weeks I have kept his books.

interact.use_fail: The box does not answer that.
interact.look: A long box of black oak, new earth spilling over the lid. Whatever is within, it is a foreigner and it is patient.
A silver crucifix thrown into the corner, its arms bent. I do not touch it. Not yet.
A pew with the end split off. Boots have been up on it.
A pew with a small brass plate: 'The Gift of J. H.'
Cold as a gravestone.
The glass is gone from the lancet. Through it, a sliver of moon and the free air.
Whose hand lit it? There is a pool of wax and a smell like a burnt feather.
A heap of plaster and dust where the north roof has begun to think about the floor.
The little door through the wall.

do.say: Carfax. A chapel I watched from the window for three months and never entered. The air is thick and sweet as a root cellar. Something is here that is not entirely here, and my hands, for the first time in weeks, are quite steady.

interact.look: Case-notes in rows, a blotter, an ink-well and a good deal of cigar ash. The desk of a man who works because he cannot sleep.
Maudsley, Esquirol, Pinel, Carpenter on dreams, and a gap where a volume was borrowed by nobody.
Banked low. On the mantel the clock has been wrong for a week, and I have not had the heart to correct it.
Two fingers gone since Sunday. Brandy is not a cure; it is a postponement.
Three candles, burnt to the same stub. I have sat up under them every night this week.
The records room, where every patient is a handful of ruled pages.

interact.go_fail: Locked. I always keep the ward key somewhere sensible, which means I never remember where.
interact.look: The ward door. It is kept locked, and I keep the key where I will not forget it.

do.say: Three nights without sleep. Lucy Westenra has refused me, kindly, and I have gone on doctoring as if nothing had happened. Perhaps the day's work will tire me. I begin with the ward, which means finding the key.

interact.look: A narrow bed with the blanket folded square. Whoever sleeps here folds it every morning, whatever the night did.
A bed under the window. The pillow is damp from some weeping nobody mentioned.

seward_asylum_clock_key.say: The mainspring bites. The clock strikes ten past three, ticks, and goes on. A small door in the case swings open, and behind it hangs the dispensary key on a nail, where Hennessey has hidden it.

interact.use_fail: It will not respond to that.
interact.look: A tall case-clock, hands stopped at ten past three. It has been stopped as long as I have kept the house.

interact.take_text: I take a grey wool blanket from the stack.
interact.look: Sheets, towels, a stack of grey blankets. Everything smells of soap and boiled cotton.
A scarred table where patients play dominoes and nobody keeps score.
Where the patients sit in the afternoon to watch weather they are not allowed in.
Turned low. The attendants say a patient will not sleep in true dark, nor in true light.
My study.
The garden door. Hennessey locks it at dusk.
A heavy door with a grille. The brass plate says 12.

interact.go_fail: Locked. Hennessey says the key is 'kept safe', which is no answer.
interact.look: The dispensary. It is locked, and the key is not on my ring.
A large, kind man in a white coat who has been bitten twice and bears no grudge.
A small grey man in a cardigan, who keeps glancing at the stopped clock as if it owes him an apology.
A governess of fifty, upright on the window bench, a sheaf of unsent letters on her knee.
A thin lad of seventeen with violet-stained fingertips, sweeping a floor that is already clean.
The night nurse, grey-faced and steady, a lamp in her hand.

do.say: Two in the morning. Smoke is coming under the dispensary door, Room 12 is standing open, and somewhere down the corridor a lad is crying.
The ward in the grey of the afternoon. They look up as I come in, as they always do: the same faces, the same private weather.

interact.look: Made with the tightness of a soldier's. The mattress has been unpicked and sewn again, twice.
Sugar in a saucer, in lines, drawing the flies from the window.
A sugar-smeared jar, perhaps two dozen flies, buzzing without hope. They are counted every morning.
Webs hang in the corner like a hammock, and a fat house-spider sits in the centre of it. It has not been disturbed in weeks.
A cat's basket. The cat is not mentioned in the ward, and nobody looks at the basket for long.
A wicker cage the size of a loaf. The door stands open. The sparrows are written down in the ledger, and nowhere else.
Bolted to the floor. Dr. Seward's stool, when he comes to listen.
The heavy door, always locked from the outside.
A thin, pale man near sixty, calm, with an eye on the window and a little line of sugar before him.

interact.take_text: I take a bottle of chloral crystals from the cupboard, signing the register out of habit.
interact.look: Laudanum, chloral, morphia, strychnine, each in its own labelled bottle. The key hangs on a string; I will not have it locked up where a man cannot reach it in the night.
Mortars, a graduated glass and a pair of brass scales, all scrubbed bright.

interact.take_text: I fill a clean glass from the jug.
interact.look: Distilled, for mixing. Take what you need; it is the only thing here that cannot kill.

seward_asylum_wet_blanket.say: I throw the sodden blanket over the burning shelf and lean on it with my whole weight. The flames die in a hiss of steam and a stench of scorched spirit. Black smoke curls up, and then nothing.

water.say: I fling the water on the flames. They leap and spread across the shelf: ether floats on water and burns on it. Fool. It must be smothered, not drowned.

interact.use_fail: That will not stop it.
interact.look: The shelf of ether and spirits is ablaze, and the flames are climbing the wall. Water will only spread an ether fire; it must be smothered.
Black and steaming, but standing. The chloral, thank God, was on the other side.
Smelling salts, in bulk.
A shaded lamp with a glass chimney, safely away from the spirit shelves.
The ward door.
Patients who have gone home, patients who have died, and a few who are neither.
The house is full of paper. Madness, it turns out, is chiefly clerical.
A copying-press, three ink-bottles and a rack of pens. The ink is violet, the clerk's ink, which stains the fingers for a week.
A chest of old forms, ribbons and a wooden box marked 'Edison'.
A screw press for copying letters. It leaves a violet ghost on the tissue.
A green-shaded lamp.
My study.

do.say: The records room, where the dead and the discharged still sit in neat rows. Somewhere in here is a wax cylinder for the phonograph, and a bundle of letters from Amsterdam.

interact.look: The garden door, back to the ward.

seward_asylum_blanket.say: I duck the grey blanket in the cold water and wring it just enough that it will not drip all over me. It is now a heavy, sodden shroud.

interact.use_fail: That does not need to be wetted.
interact.look: A great oak butt of rain-water, cold enough to make your teeth ache.
Greer's bench. He sits here in all weathers, and the weather is polite about it.
The boundary wall of Carfax, ivy and broken glass. The empty house is on the other side.
Ivy, and the stub of a ladder that someone left by a wall where no ladder is needed.
Higher than a man, and tall enough to be an ill-wisher's idea of a fence.
The old chapel, sunk behind the wall. No one has said a service in it for a long time.
Struck by lightning years ago. The sparrows still roost in it.
Lit at dusk by Hennessey. It makes the dark beyond it darker.
An old sailor in a pea-coat, with a face like a tarred rope, sitting very straight and facing the sea that is forty miles away.
Renfield, in the garden after midnight, shirt torn, a smear of earth on his hands. He has found the wall and cannot be reasoned with; he is staring at the moon and snarling at it.

seward_asylum_draught.say: I hold out the glass, speaking low: 'The sugar, Mr. Renfield. You will want your sugar.' He drinks as a child drinks medicine. In ten minutes he is quiet, and I walk him back to Room 12.

chloral.say: I press a dose of chloral into his hand in a glass of water, and he swallows it, still glaring. Slowly the glare fades. It is the dose I should have measured; luck has measured it for me.

interact.use_fail: That will not calm him.

interact.look: Renfield, hunched under the wall, breathing hard. But I have read his ledger, and I think I know what he is feeling.
Renfield, sitting on the gravel with his hands between his knees. He looks like a clerk, which he once was.
Quills, pounce, a blotter ruled by years of thinking, and a Latin note pinned flat under a paperweight.
A slip in a small crabbed hand, from Arminius's last parcel. 'Read it before you read anything else', he has added in German.

interact.take_text: I take my casebook. A man who lectures on evidence should carry some.
interact.look: Cases, dates, observations. I write what I saw and what I was told in separate columns, as a physician should.
Boerhaave, Sydenham, Hunter. My dead masters, standing shoulder to shoulder.
Paracelsus, Agrippa, Glanvill on witches, Calmet on vampires. 'Read the madmen too', my teacher said. 'Madmen are sometimes right by accident, and then you must know it.'
The great Boerhaave in plaster, who taught that the bedside is the only true library.
It loses four minutes a week, and I forgive it, because it was my father's.

vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.say: The lock gives. A bundle of letters in a small clear hand, tied with black tape.

interact.use_fail: The cabinet is locked. I laid its key somewhere sensible, which means somewhere I cannot remember.
interact.look: Where I keep what my friend Arminius sends from Buda-Pesth. I lock it because I do not wish my students to see how many of my theories began in somebody else's letter.

host.say: I lay the consecrated Wafer on a clean linen square. The heart of the thing.

vanhelsing_lore_child_cross.say: The small silver cross, set beside the Wafer. It was made for a smaller hand than mine, and it is no less strong for that.

garlic.say: Garlic, braided with red thread, for the doors and the windows and the throat.

interact.use_fail: That does not belong in the ward. It wants a Wafer, a cross, and garlic.
interact.look: A bare oak table scrubbed white. Here I mix, mend and put things together.

interact.take_text: I fold the linen over and bind it with the red thread. It weighs nothing, and it weighs a great deal.
interact.look: Linen, silver, red thread and white bread: all that I know of protection, folded small.

interact.set_text: I check the case: two stakes of ash, a hammer of good steel, my small crucifix. I take the whole.
interact.look: My travelling case, packed for the field. Ash stakes, a mallet, a crucifix, and Hunter's lancet for the sort of cases that need one.

interact.take_text: The ash stake goes inside my coat.
interact.look: Ash, seasoned, sharpened by my own hand.

interact.take_text: I take the hammer.
interact.look: A mallet of good steel.

interact.take_text: I put the crucifix in my breast pocket.
interact.look: The little crucifix I have carried since my ordination to nothing in particular.
A globe, worn pale across the Carpathians where my thumb goes.
Upstairs to the stove, and my wife.
To the Herengracht and the world.
Black-edged, it has come while I was in Styria. I know the hand before I turn it over.
My wing-chair, with a lamp at its elbow. A man should read bad news sitting down.
The bed is turned toward the window so that she can see the canal and the skaters and the boys who do not fall.
Blue Delft tiles, a fire of peat and a kettle that has never been allowed to go off the boil.
Not a cradle any more; she has put her sewing in it. She will not let the maid move it. I have not asked her to.
Half a child's coat, in grey wool, never finished. The needle is still in it.
Scrubbed pine. A dish of onions, a loaf, a jug of Hollands gin that the doctor does not need to know about.
Mine, by the bed, wherever the bed is.
Where the maid sits when I am at the University.
The housekeeper hangs these for the cook-pot and for the winter ague. Mostly for the winter ague.
Down the narrow stair to my books.
She is thin and very straight against the pillows, and she greets me with the small dry joke she uses instead of complaint.
Floured to the elbow. Stout, sixty, and a better judge of the sick than half the Faculty.
Number 44, with the brass knocker polished by Mevrouw Bakker.
The Faculty's grey arch. 'Veritas', says the keystone, and a hundred and fifty years of pigeons have commented.
Under the Latin motto, a smaller notice: 'Silence'.
A low door beneath a lantern, and the smell of wax.

interact.go_fail: Not yet. I must go prepared: the ward made up, stake and hammer in my bag, the Latin note understood and my friend's letters read.
interact.look: The coach for the Rhine, the railway and then south, to the Styrian mountains. Arminius's friend, the pastor, has written. I should go, with whatever I can carry.
Lit at four in winter, and always a minute late.
A bench for watching skaters and not noticing the cold.
Pickled herring, the fuel of the Dutch intellect.
Wrapped in three coats, in the way of men who wait out of doors for a living.

npcs.name: A student with a stack of books

interact.look: One of mine. Bright, anxious, and carrying the wrong volume under the right one.

interact.set_text: I read the board twice. The Dean will use my own words against me, so I had better know them.
interact.look: In a square hand: 'BELIEVE NOTHING YE CANNOT TEST. DISBELIEVE NOTHING YE HAVE NOT TESTED.' Below, two columns. TESTED: the bite of the rabid dog; the trance under mesmerism in Charcot's wards; blood passed from a sound man to a dying one. UNPROVED: the evil eye; a hanged man's rope as a cure for fever; the ringing of bells to turn the hail.
Scarred oak with a brass lamp. A drip of tallow marks the page where I lost my place in 1858 and found a new theory.
A plaster skull on a wooden stand, with the sutures painted in. A student has hung a cap on it.
Initials carved through two generations, and one drawing I will not describe.
The back row. All the best students sit here, and all the worst.
The front row, for those who wish to be seen to understand.
Jars, calipers and a stomach in spirits. I do not say whose.
A tall iron stove that warms the first row and no one else.
Back to the canal.

A tall man in a perfect black coat, who has been exactly right in public for thirty years. He holds the key to the rare-book press and the Faculty's good opinion, and I want the first more than the second.
A visiting student from London. Earnest, quiet, and clever in the way that frightens his tutors. He has a half-healed scar on the back of his hand.

vanhelsing_lore_library_key.say: The brass lock turns. I take down the one volume I came for, an old Ordo, in a binding gone black with handling.

interact.use_fail: Locked. The key is with the Dean, and the Dean does not lend it to men he disagrees with.
interact.look: An oak press with a brass lock, kept by the Dean. Inside, behind iron grilles, the books no one wants to be seen reading.
Aquinas, Suarez, and a thousand folios of the Fathers. Nobody has taken out Suarez since the Treaty of Utrecht.
Boyle, Newton, Leeuwenhoek. A man could be happy here and never need the truth.

interact.set_text: Among the travellers I find an old German account of a Styrian village that 'sealed its north grave with ash and iron in the year of the great snow'. I copy the page number and say nothing.
interact.look: Voyages to Muscovy, Carpathian tales, Calmet. They are shelved with Natural History, which is about right.
A green lamp, an inkstand and a ticket for borrowed books, forty-two of them in the name of one Van Helsing.
The constellations in gilded wire, many of them wrongly placed.
Three students, asleep, and a fourth pretending to be.
Erasmus, who laughed at the Church and loved it all the same.
A single steady flame, the only kind a library trusts.
Back out into the cold.
Pale as his parchment and twice as dry. He speaks in a whisper, even when the library is empty.
Plain stone under a white cloth. A small altar, for a small chapel, kept as though a bishop might arrive.
Silver, worn at the arms by generations of lips.
Beeswax, honey-sweet, and burning straight.

interact.take_text: Father Pieter nods from the altar. I take the tin of unblessed wafers; they are only flour and water, as yet.
interact.look: Albs, stoles, corporals and a tin of unleavened bread for the next Mass. Father Pieter has marked the tin: 'Not yet blessed.'
A shallow basin with a skin of ice at the edges. Even the holy water is cold in St. Nicholas.
Wood worn smooth by the sailors' wives.
The sailors' widows' pew. It is always full.
Mine, when I come, which is less often than Father Pieter hopes.
St. Nicholas and three drowned boys, in lead and blue glass.
The canal, and the bells of the Oude Kerk.
Fifty, round, mild. A confessor first, a scholar second, and a very good Latinist whenever there is no one to see.
Deaf in the left ear, and fiercely proud of the candle-ends he has saved for forty years.
A small church with an onion-spire, whitewashed against the weather and clearly built to be looked at nervously.
'Zum Schwarzen Hahn', says the sign: the Black Cock. A lantern burns by the door in daylight.

interact.go_fail: The sexton stands before the gate with his arms folded. 'Not without the Pfarrer's word, Herr, and not unless you know which grave you are going to.'
interact.look: A roofed gate of black timber, hung with dried herbs and a very recent iron nail.
Iced over. The women fetch water in pairs and in daylight.
A sledge piled with hay and a pitchfork stuck, tines up, in the top of it.
Frozen sauerkraut.
'Graz, 31 Kilometer.' Somebody has scratched a cross under the 31.
Lit well before dusk.
The village priest, tall, grey and badly shaved. He has not slept properly in a month, and is ashamed to have written for help.
Stooped and strong from forty years of digging. He leans on his spade as though the village might ask him to dig another.
Black shawl, black skirt, a white face like a shaved apple. She was eight when the great snow came, and she has not forgotten it.
Green tiles, a bench round it, and all the village's feet stretched toward it.
Scarred, wine-stained, with a bowl of dumplings going cold because nobody has the heart for them.
The wall side. Nobody sits there.
Marzen, and a little plum brandy.
Pewter plates, a Bible, and a very old tarot pack that the landlord claims is for patience.
Strings of it over every window. There is more garlic than the soup could ever need.
Carved lime-wood, painted, with a fresh sprig of fir behind it.
The snow, and the church.
A big man with a small voice. He has stopped telling anyone it is late.
Sits with his back to the wall and his eyes on the door.
Back to the village and the lamps.

vanhelsing_lore_ward.say: Nothing stirs. The snow is smooth, and the old woman sleeps as she was told to.

interact.use_fail: This is not the place.
interact.look: 'ANNA PFEIFER, WIDOW. DIED 1791, AGED EIGHTY. SHE SLEPT WELL.' The lichen has overgrown the 'well'.

vanhelsing_lore_ward.say: I kneel in the snow and lay the linen square upon the stone. I scatter the garlic in a ring, the Wafer at the head, the little silver cross at the foot, and I draw the circle closed with my finger in the frost. Then I wait, and the cold comes down.

interact.use_fail: Nothing I carry will serve here but the ward.
interact.look: 'KATHARINA LINDNER, WIFE AND MOTHER, DIED 1812, AGED NINETEEN, IN THE SPRING AFTER HER WEDDING.' Three iron nails have been driven in a row across the top of the stone. The soil about it is not frozen.

vanhelsing_lore_ward.say: Nothing stirs. A thief is only a thief, and he is dead.

interact.use_fail: This is not the place.
interact.look: 'JOSEF HAUER, 1799. HANGED AT GRAZ FOR SHEEP-STEALING.' Poor wretch. The village has put a cross on him to make him comfortable, and perhaps to keep him down.
Worn smooth. Whoever it was is no longer anyone's business.
One arm is gone.
A small stone with a lamb on it. I look away, then back. Then I look away again.
A squat tomb of the Pfeifer family, shut, and clean of snow.
A yew older than the church, black and hollow.
The sexton's. It will not stay lit beyond the third stone.
She wears a wedding-dress gone grey. She has no footprints in the snow, and she has turned her face toward me with great interest.

do.say: The moon stands over the north wall. I can smell cold earth, and under it, faint and sweet, something that is not earth. Three stones, three stories. I must be sure of the right one, because the right one is the only one I can afford to kneel at.

n0.speaker: Jonathan Harker
n0.text: A narrow stair goes down beneath the chapel. A heavy door bars the foot of it; the Count's keys hang in my hand. Below, I can hear the Szgany loading boxes of earth.

n1.speaker: Jonathan Harker
n1.text: The key turns. This is my last throw. Whatever lies below - better to die like a man than to wait for those women.

do.card:
30 June. Castle Dracula.

"I shall try to scale the castle wall once more, and get away. It is the last chance I have. Good-bye, all! Mina!"

But that night, far away on the English coast, another story had already begun...

n0.speaker: Hostess
n0.text: Must you go, Herr Harker? It is the eve of St. George's Day. Do you not know that at midnight all the evil things in the world will have full sway?

choices.text: I must. A client waits at the castle.

n1.speaker: Hostess
n1.text: Then take this for your mother's sake. Wear it round your neck.

do.say: She hung the crucifix round my neck. I did not like it - a stern Englishman's creed - but I took it.

n2.speaker: Hostess
n2.text: Ah, the Count's land is not as ours. At night the dead ride fast. Please, take this.

n0.speaker: Landlord
n0.text: Herr Engländer... the Count's castle is no place... *he stumbles, shakes his head*. Eat. Rest. The coach comes at midnight.

n0.speaker: Driver
n0.text: *In a deep, hollow voice* We are early tonight, sir. The wolves have been bold. Get in.

n1.speaker: Driver
n1.text: *His eyes glint red.* Everyone in this land knows the Count, sir. Few have seen him.

n0.speaker: Count Dracula
n0.text: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will! The night is cold, and you need to eat and rest.

choices.text: I am pleased to be here. I have the papers for Carfax.

n1.speaker: Count Dracula
n1.text: I am anxious to speak as the English do. Here I am noble; I am a Count. But in London no one would know me. I should be as the others - a stranger.

n2.speaker: Count Dracula
n2.text: Good. Whenever you want anything, ring. Only - you will remember? - do not sleep anywhere in my house save in your own room.

n0.speaker: Fair woman
n0.text: 'Go on! You are first, and we shall follow. Yours is the right to begin.' *They giggle, silvery and cold.*

n1.speaker: Fair woman
n1.text: *She hisses, falls back.* 'Take that away! He will not let us feed on you tonight. Not yet.'

do.say: A great flurry of wind - the Count was there, furious. 'How dare you touch him? This man belongs to me!'

n0.speaker: Lucy
n0.text: Mina, darling! I was just thinking of you. Do sit with me.

choices.text: Tell me about the three proposals, Lucy.
Poor Dr. Seward, among his madmen. Let me hear how he fares.

p1.speaker: Lucy
p1.text: Oh Mina, such a day! Three proposals, and I have not breathed since. Dr. Seward first, grave and kind, very much in earnest, so I said no and felt like a wicked girl.

p2.speaker: Lucy
p2.text: Then Mr. Quincey P. Morris, from Texas, who came in so drolly. I was in the middle of laughing when he told me it was serious, and then I was quite undone. He took it like the gentleman he is.

p3.speaker: Lucy
p3.text: And then dear Arthur, Lord Godalming's son. He had only to look at me, and I had only to say yes. Oh Mina, why can't a girl marry three men, or as many as want her, and save all this trouble?

choices.text: You must marry the man you love, and no regrets.
Tell them gently, and tell them soon. Delay is cruel.

p4.speaker: Lucy
p4.text: You are the sweetest. I shall write to them tonight, and if I weep on the paper you must not tell. Now, what shall I do with all this happiness?

sew.speaker: Lucy
sew.text: Dr. Seward? He sent me a long letter, quite exhausted. He is a man of science, he says, and likes best to be among those whose minds are broken, because he can learn from them. Poor man. Poor madmen.

choices.text: [Let your thoughts go to the asylum]

sew2.speaker: Mina
sew2.text: I close my eyes, and for a moment I am somewhere else, in a study full of books and the smell of carbolic. A phonograph is waiting...

do.card: Dr. Seward's Diary, 25 April. Kept in phonograph.

sleepw.speaker: Lucy
sleepw.text: Like a top, Mina! Only I woke two nights ago with my feet wet and my slippers on the wrong feet, and you scolding me. Oh, and I dreamed of the sea.

choices.text: You walk in your sleep, Lucy. We must be careful tonight.

sleepw2.speaker: Lucy
sleepw2.text: Do you really think so? Mother will be so alarmed. Promise not to tell her. Lock the door, if you must, and keep the key, and I will not mind a bit.

decl.speaker: Lucy
decl.text: Tired. Terribly tired, Mina, and I sleep all night and wake worn out. The marks on my throat sting a little. I must have scratched myself on the pin, you know. You were so very good to pin my shawl.

choices.text: Let me see. [Look at her throat]
You must rest. I will not leave you.

decl2.speaker: Mina
decl2.text: Two tiny punctures, white-edged and red-rimmed, such as I would not give to a pin. They are very small. I do not like the look of them, or of how pale she is.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n0.text: Mina, dear, there is a draught, I'm certain. Lucy takes such risks with her health, you know, and her father's death, and my heart... We must keep her quiet.

choices.text: Does Lucy have a habit of walking in her sleep?
Where do you keep the spare key to Lucy's door?
Mr. Holmwood has proposed, I hear.

walk.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
walk.text: As a child, indeed. It left her after her father died. But please don't speak of it to her; she is so sensitive. And Mina, you are such a comfort.

key.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
key.text: The spare? Lock it up in the drawer, or the basket, or the old bookcase. I always put things where I shall remember them and then I don't. Look about the sitting-room, dear.

arthur.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
arthur.text: Arthur Holmwood! His poor father is so very ill. She does not know how ill, and I will not tell her until it is quite necessary. Her happiness comes first.

n0.speaker: Housemaid
n0.text: Beg pardon, miss. Cook says the sea-fret will be in by tea, and she's boiled up garlic broth, as her mother taught her for fever.

choices.text: May I have a head of that garlic?
Is there news of the town?

g.speaker: Housemaid
g.text: Cook says take two, miss, if you'll swear not to tell the mistress how much she puts in.

gossip.speaker: Housemaid
gossip.text: The new searchlight on the East Cliff, miss, they're to try it out. Folks say a storm's brewing, the fishermen's wives won't have the washing out. And there's an old lady at the Abbey sees the White Lady every dusk.

n0.speaker: Postman
n0.text: Letter for Miss Murray, miss. From foreign parts, the stamp says Buda-Pesth. A convent's seal on the back, if you don't mind me noticing.

t.speaker: Mina
t.text: My hand trembles as I break the seal. At last, at last, news of Jonathan.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: My trunk. The Sister's letter says Jonathan is in the hospital of St. Joseph and St. Mary, Buda-Pesth, broken down with brain fever, and has asked for me. I must go to him. But Lucy...

choices.text: Pack and go. Jonathan needs me, and Lucy has her mother and Arthur.
I need to read the Sister's letter and see how Lucy is first.

go.speaker: Mina
go.text: I will write to Dr. Seward as I leave and ask him to look at her. He is the one man I can think of. And I will pray, if there is any praying that will serve.

do.card: Mina goes to Buda-Pesth, to Jonathan. Lucy grows paler every day. Arthur, from his father's deathbed, writes to Dr. Seward: 'Come, for God's sake.'

nope.speaker: Mina
nope.text: I cannot go until I know both: the Sister's news for Jonathan, and how Lucy truly is.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: The glass has fallen two-tenths since morning. Mr. Swales told me he can smell the storm in his bad knee, and the sunsets have been blood-red.

choices.text: Take Lucy's arm and go to the East Cliff to watch the sky.

go.speaker: Mina
go.text: The whole town is up on the cliff to see the new searchlight tried, and a hush has fallen over the sea.

do.card: 6 August, near midnight. The sea-fret rolls in and the wind rises.

n0.speaker: Hennessey
n0.text: Evening, doctor. Number 12 is in good spirits tonight, which is to say, in his usual spirits.

choices.text: What exactly does Renfield do all day?
Has anyone else been able to manage him?

r.speaker: Hennessey
r.text: Collects flies, doctor. Sugar on the window-sill and the flies come. Then he eats them. Last month it was spiders; he fed the flies to the spiders. Then he found a sparrow...

m.speaker: Hennessey
m.text: Only me, sir, and only when he wants. He's polite to a man who doesn't argue. He asked me yesterday whether I knew the difference between a flea and a cat.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: Doctor, you must excuse me; the flies are very busy this evening and I should not like to neglect them. I have a purpose, you see.

choices.text: Why do you eat flies, Mr. Renfield?
I would like to see your notes on the spiders.
Do you wish for anything, Mr. Renfield?

flies.speaker: Renfield
flies.text: The blood is the life, doctor, as the Scripture tells us. Flies are small lives; spiders eat flies; sparrows eat spiders; a cat would eat sparrows, and a man... a man would eat many lives and grow strong. It is the life that matters.

spiders.speaker: Renfield
spiders.text: They are all numbered in a book, doctor. Each fed from the one before, and each given a place in the account. Would you not call that mathematics? You, who work with numbers of the soul?

wish.speaker: Renfield
wish.text: A kitten, doctor. A little one. I would be very good to it. And a great deal of sugar. No, I did not say that. Please forget it. You are a good man, doctor, and I should be sorry to see you hurt.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: The cylinder is ready, the needle trimmed. Lucy's refusal is still raw, but work heals more than sympathy.

choices.text: Record today's entry on R. M. Renfield.
Close the lid and think of Whitby.

rec.speaker: Seward
rec.text: Patient, R. M. Renfield, aetat 59. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbidly excitable. Periods of gloom ending in some fixed idea which I cannot make out. I fancy he is himself a dangerous man, and I think...

back.speaker: Seward
back.text: And there, for tonight, is that. I will go on with my rounds, and think kindly of Miss Westenra, who has made a good choice, and of her chosen friend who writes such letters.

do.card: Whitby. Mina Murray's Journal, 24 July.

n0.speaker: Mr. Swales
n0.text: Ah, 'tis the young leddy. Sit ye down, miss, and I'll tell ye the truth, which is more than the parson will. I've sat here since afore your mother was born.

choices.text: May I sit and hear you talk?
What do you mean, the stones lie?
Tell me about the Abbey and the legends.
Will the weather hold, Mr. Swales?
You are known to every officer on the quay. Would you vouch for me if I need to see something there?

sit.speaker: Mr. Swales
sit.text: Ye're a nice lass. Now these stones, they're all lies, every one. There's folk lying under 'em as ne'er were 'drowned', as ne'er were 'beloved', as ne'er did a dozen things the stone says. 'Tis the Judgement Day I fear for the carver more than the dead.

lies.speaker: Mr. Swales
lies.text: Aye. Look at 'em! 'Sacred to the memory.' Tchah. But there's one big lie in this yard that's a rare comfort, miss: the mother's stone, the widow's, for the lad that fell at Kettleness. 'Only son.' Aye, so it said. I'd not be surprised if a clever man who knew that lie hid something where nobody'd think to lift it.

legend.speaker: Mr. Swales
legend.text: Old Hilda's Abbey. There's the White Lady in the window at sunset, and the Barguest dog that walks before a death. And them that took their own lives lie yonder, where your seat is, though the parson says nowt. I sat on that stone as a lad.

weather.speaker: Mr. Swales
weather.text: Mares'-tails and a sun like blood. There's a storm in 'em, miss. Afore the week's out ye'll see the sea come up and swallow the piers. And God help any ship at sea.

vouch.speaker: Mr. Swales
vouch.text: Aye, miss, I'll say a word. The constable's my nephew's lad, and he'll mind his granddad. Ye need only say: Swales sent me.

n0.speaker: Lady from Leeds
n0.text: My dear, did you know that this very churchyard inspired the author of that famous ballad? The guide-book says so. Or the guide-book says something. And that Abbey, would you credit it, is the only ruin in England with its own ghost.

choices.text: Excuse me, I'm looking for old Mr. Swales.

g.speaker: Lady from Leeds
g.text: No, but the cab-driver has, twice, and the second time he was sober. The guide-book has a footnote on it.

s.speaker: Lady from Leeds
s.text: The old man by the bench? Oh, my dear, he says the most shocking things about the stones. Quite refreshing, in a churchyard.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Pinder
n0.text: Morning, miss. Rope, twine, tar and tallow, and the best garlic for sailors' wives. What'll it be?

choices.text: A length of good rope, if you please.
A second head of garlic, for a friend.
What are the sailors saying about the weather?

rope.speaker: Mrs. Pinder
rope.text: There y'are, six fathoms of the tarred hemp. No charge for a young lady who looks like she'll make good use of it.

garlic.speaker: Mrs. Pinder
garlic.text: Two heads, then, tied with a bit of twine. Sailors swear it keeps off the ague. The old women say it keeps off worse.

weather.speaker: Mrs. Pinder
weather.text: That's not for me to say. But look at the gulls, miss; they've all come in off the sea, and not a one flying out. They're no fools.

n0.speaker: Old fisherman
n0.text: Mind the nets, miss. Aye, the sky wants watching. I've seen mares'-tails like that but twice, and both times someone died.

choices.text: What's your opinion of old Swales?

cg.speaker: Old fisherman
cg.text: Dunn? He keeps the hut locked, miss; he's careful. But he's a forgetful man; he leaves his spare in the churchyard, under one of them lying stones, for safety. I'd not tell you where, but I know the stone is for a widow's son. Off you go.

sw.speaker: Old fisherman
sw.text: Swales? He's older than the pier. He says the dead are all liars, and the living are worse. Not a bad man to sit beside.

n0.speaker: Constable
n0.text: Back, miss, if you please. The ship's under guard till the Board of Trade man comes. The dead captain's still aboard.

choices.text: Mr. Billington said I might look.
Please, constable. It is an extraordinary thing, and I'd like to see it.

swales.speaker: Constable
swales.text: Old Swales? My grandfather's friend? Why, he'd have my hide. Go on, miss, but mind your skirts, and don't touch anything you don't have to.

bill.speaker: Constable
bill.text: From Mr. Billington, the solicitor? He said that? Go on, miss, but touch nothing that's evidence.

plead.speaker: Constable
plead.text: I'm sorry, miss, but I can't let anyone aboard on a feeling. Come with the owner's solicitor, or someone I know.

n0.speaker: Mr. Billington
n0.text: Madam, I am Samuel F. Billington, of 7 The Crescent. The wretched ship is consigned to me, and I assure you I know nothing of what is in it.

choices.text: May I look at the vessel? I should like to describe it for friends.
Where were the boxes to go, Mr. Billington?
I have seen the consignment note. Who is Count Dracula?

leave.speaker: Mr. Billington
leave.text: Eh? I suppose so; it is not as if the Board of Trade will let anyone else near it. Tell the constable I said so. My clerk is distraught as it is.

carfax.speaker: Mr. Billington
carfax.text: Ah! That note. Fifty boxes of clay to be taken to Carfax, an estate at Purfleet, bought through Mr. Hawkins of Exeter. Carter, Paterson and Co. are to cart them. It is quite regular, and quite incomprehensible.

dracula.speaker: Mr. Billington
dracula.text: A foreign nobleman, a client of Mr. Hawkins. Beyond that, madam, I know only that he bought a house in England and sent his earth ahead of him. The ways of the gentry are strange.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: A notice-board, thick with pins. Among the tide-tables and warnings, a hand-written note: 'In case of lock-out, spare key kept with the stone of the widow's only son. Do not tell the boys. - Dunn.'

n0.speaker: Officer Dunn
n0.text: Miss Murray, is it not? Come in, and mind the oil. I've been sixteen years on this coast and never seen a glass drop like that.

choices.text: What do you think is coming?
Might I borrow a little brandy for Lucy's nerves?
I have read the log of the Demeter. What do you make of it?

storm.speaker: Officer Dunn
storm.text: A big blow out of the north-east, if I'm any judge. And I'm judge of nothing else. If a ship's caught outside the piers tonight, God help her.

brandy.speaker: Officer Dunn
brandy.text: Ay, here, take a nip's worth in this flask. Mind, I'd not give it to every lady.

log.speaker: Officer Dunn
log.text: I read it, miss, in the coroner's office. A man who kept a log in a gale, and a mate who went for a knife at a ghost. I've no explanation, and neither has the coroner. He said 'open verdict.' I say a devil rode that ship.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: A bare desk, ink-stained. If I had the leaves of the ship's log, I could lay them in order here, and read what happened. I should need all four.

choices.text: Lay out the four leaves of the log.

done.speaker: Mina
done.text: I have read it three times, and it has not changed.

o1.speaker: Mina
o1.text: Four leaves, all of different sizes, all dated. Which comes first?

choices.text: The leaf dated 4 August, in a shaky hand.
The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August, with the mate's name.
The leaf dated 17 to 28 July, about the stranger.
The leaf headed Varna, 6 July to 16 July.

w1.speaker: Mina
w1.text: No. That speaks of men already missing. Something must come before it.

o2.speaker: Mina
o2.text: Varna: the cargo of silver sand and boxes of earth, the Bosphorus, the Dardanelles, a man gone off the watch off Cape Matapan. And next?

choices.text: The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August.
The leaf dated 17 to 28 July, about the stranger.

w2.speaker: Mina
w2.text: That cannot be next; it assumes the stranger, and no one has yet seen him.

o3.speaker: Mina
o3.text: Olgaren saw the tall thin man. The crew searched the ship, found nothing. Then Biscay and the fog, and the second mate gone. And now?

choices.text: The leaf dated 29 July to 3 August, with the mate.

w3.speaker: Mina
w3.text: He is alone in that one. The mate must still be alive in the one before.

o4.speaker: Mina
o4.text: The mate stabs the pale figure, and the knife passes through. He opens a box with a tool-chest, screams, and leaps into the sea. That leaves the last leaf.

r1.speaker: Captain's log
r1.text: 4 August. Alone, with the thing aboard. I am lashing my hands and a crucifix to the wheel. If we go down, bury me with this where my body is found, so that He may not have my soul. Whatever comes, I have done my duty as captain and as a Christian. The knots I tie with my teeth.

r2.speaker: Mina
r2.text: A tall, pale thing came out of a box in the hold and killed the crew one by one, until the captain alone remained to bring the ship to harbour. That man, and the dog that leaped ashore, were no creatures I know. Fifty boxes. Mr. Hawkins. Jonathan's firm. I feel quite cold.

n0.speaker: Sexton
n0.text: Afternoon, miss. Mind the old slabs; one of 'em tilts. They say an abbot lies under it.

choices.text: The White Lady, sexton, have you seen her?
Is there anything of value in the Abbey?
Lucy loves the seat on the cliff. Do you know it?

lady.speaker: Sexton
lady.text: At sunset, in the east window, the figure of a woman in white. 'Tis only the light, and the stones, and the Westerley wind on the glass. But I'd not be the one to stand there after dark.

silver.speaker: Sexton
silver.text: Digging a drain last spring, I turned up a little coin: silver, worn smooth, a sailor's penny maybe. You may have it, miss, if you promise not to throw it in the sea.

seat.speaker: Sexton
seat.text: That's on a suicide's grave. The parson says it matters not. I say a seat is a seat, but I'd not sleep there. There's folk have seen things at it, in the dark.

n0.speaker: Mr. Swales
n0.text: I told 'ee so, miss! There's a hollow sound in the sea, like a giant beating on the Judgement. And a ship is out there tonight, mark my words, with her sails afire.

choices.text: You are a prophet, Mr. Swales.

p.speaker: Mr. Swales
p.text: I'm an old fool, miss, who's watched the sea sixty year. The wind was the Lord's, but the warning was mine.

f.speaker: Mr. Swales
f.text: Aye, and so ye should be. But fear's honest, miss. 'Tis the folk that aren't afraid I worry for.

n0.speaker: Officer
n0.text: Stand back! Miss, you must keep clear of the searchlight. She's untried, and the sea is a madman tonight. A schooner is making for the piers.

can.speaker: Officer
can.text: Not by seamanship. By fool's luck, or the Devil's. The searchlight shows her sails, then loses her. She has no crew on deck that I can see.

flag.speaker: Officer
flag.text: Russian, by her cut. From Varna, I'd stake my pension. She's trying for the entrance, but the wind is dead on shore.

n0.speaker: Onlooker
n0.text: Ye gods, did you see that wave? Over the piers, it was, as high as the church! And the fog like hands, miss, like the wet hands of the drowned, touching everyone.

choices.text: Is anyone out in a boat?

boat.speaker: Onlooker
boat.text: Not on the Lord's life. The lifeboat crew's gathered, waiting. There's a ship, though. Look! She's making straight for the harbour mouth, and no one at her helm.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: The wind tears at my hair. The sea below is white and black, and the fog rolls in like a wall. The searchlight swings out over the water, and stops.

choices.text: Look where the light has stopped.

w1.speaker: Mina
w1.text: A schooner! Every sail set, plunging between the piers, with a gale behind her and no hand on the sheets. 'She will be dashed to pieces,' someone cries. The searchlight lights her helm: a man stands there, bowed, quite still.

w2.speaker: Mina
w2.text: She runs full tilt on the sand of Tate Hill Pier. And from below her decks an enormous dog, the size of a mastiff, leaps out upon the shore and bounds straight up the cliff, toward the churchyard, into the dark.

w3.speaker: Mina
w3.text: The crowd cries out. Men run for the pier. The fog is thick as milk. I cling to the railing and see nothing more.

choices.text: Go home to Lucy, shaken and soaked.

end.speaker: Mina
end.text: Lucy is sound asleep when I return. She has been out of bed twice, Mother says, and had to be coaxed back. We shall talk in the morning.

do.card: Next morning. The wreck lies at Tate Hill Pier.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: Lucy sleeps. It is past eleven. I remember how she walked in her sleep as a girl, and what Mother said. I should make sure of the door, the window, a warm shawl and a pin laid by me, in case the worst comes.

choices.text: Lie down and sleep, everything being in order.

nope.speaker: Mina
nope.text: I lie down but cannot rest. The door is not locked with the key in my keeping, or the window is not fastened, or the shawl and pin are not laid ready. And is the ship's log read? Something is wrong.

sleep.speaker: Mina
sleep.text: I lock the door, put the key under my pillow, and sleep. Some hours later, I wake to a sound like a sigh. The moon is in the room.

do.card: Night of 10-11 August. 1 a.m.

wake.speaker: Mina
wake.text: Lucy's bed is empty. The door is still locked, with the key under my pillow. The window, which I bolted, is open on the night. She cannot have gone by the door. I take the shawl, the pin and the key, and go.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: She is lovely, asleep. I should not like to wake her. But her hands are cold, and I tuck the quilt about her as I would for a child.

n0.speaker: Watchman
n0.text: Out late, miss, and in a nightdress under that coat? Looking for someone? A girl in white went by an hour since, walking like in a dream, up to the churchyard.

choices.text: Which way? Did she say anything?

way.speaker: Watchman
way.text: Up the steps, miss, quick and quiet. Barefoot. I called, but she never turned her head. And, begging your pardon, I saw something black behind her in the fog.

n0.speaker: Street boy
n0.text: Yer lookin' for a white lady, miss? She went down to the quay, she did, I seen her. Ghost, mebbe.

choices.text: Are you sure it was the quay?

sure.speaker: Street boy
sure.text: Pretty sure, miss. It was dark. Or she might 'ave gone t'other way. But the watchman 'ud know, 'e saw 'er, 'e did.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: I run up the last steps, calling her name. Something long and black stoops over the white shape on the seat, bent low, as if to whisper.

choices.text: Call her name as loudly as I can.

f1.speaker: Mina
f1.text: The thing raises its head. In the moonlight I see a white face, and red eyes, such as Lucy described in her dream. Then a flapping of dark wings; a great bat wheels up out of the churchyard and is gone. All is quiet.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: Lucy sits upright on the seat, her eyes half shut and her head thrown back. She breathes in long, heavy sighs. Her lips are parted. At her throat... I can scarcely see for the shadows.

choices.text: Wrap her in the shawl and fasten it with the safety-pin.

pin.speaker: Mina
pin.text: I wrap the shawl about her and fasten it at the throat with the pin, but my hands are shaking, and I fear I must have pricked her, for she gives a little cry and puts her hand to her neck.

throat.speaker: Mina
throat.text: Beneath the shawl, on her white throat, two small red spots. I think the pin has marked her. But the marks are far apart, and I know in my heart that the pin does not make such marks.

wake.speaker: Lucy
wake.text: Mina? Where am I? Oh, I was dreaming. There was a sea, and a voice calling, and I walked on air. Why is my throat sore? And why are my feet wet? Did I walk in my sleep again?

home.speaker: Mina
home.text: She leans heavily on my arm. We go down the steps together in the grey light, I praying under my breath, she silent and dreamy.

do.card: 12 August. Mina's journal: 'Lucy is not herself. She is very pale. I do not like it.'

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward (phonograph)
n0.text: I turn the crank and the cylinder begins to speak in my own tired voice. 'Patient: R. M. Renfield, aged fifty-nine. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbidly excitable, periods of gloom ending in some fixed idea. Fixed idea: that he must absorb life. I note that he has begun to make a ladder of it.'

n1.speaker: Dr. Seward (phonograph)
n1.text: 'Also noted: two letters from Arthur Holmwood, three from Lucy, none from Quincey. Lucy writes of Whitby, of sleepwalking, of a pale and anxious friend, Mina. I do not like what I read between the lines. Practical matters: the dispensary key is mislaid again; Renfield's dose will need to be weighed correctly, for he is not what he was; and Hennessey will be wanting me.'

n0.speaker: Case ledger
n0.text: The asylum ledger lies open. Each patient has his column: weight, temper, treatment, notes.

n_dose.speaker: Case ledger
n_dose.text: In my own hand, in pencil in the margin: 'Chloral hydrate, ten grains for a man of nine stone; fifteen for twelve stone; thirty for a bull. Never above his weight, and never when he is already dosed.' I underline 'nine stone' and the word 'never'.

n_file.speaker: Case ledger
n_file.text: 'R. M. Renfield. Wt 9 st 4 lb, wasting. Eats little at table. Hoards sugar. Keeps a jar of flies, a box of spiders, and a sparrow. Asked this week whether he might have a kitten. Refused.' Beneath, in a different ink: 'Count the sugar.'

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: I spread what I have found across the table. Sugar in his pillow, a jar of flies, a box of spiders, his notebook of figures. I need all four before I trust my own deduction. 'What', I ask the room, 'does this man do?'

choices.text: He is a harmless naturalist who loves small things.
He hoards sugar because he has a sweet tooth, and keeps the rest as pets.
Sugar draws flies; flies feed spiders; spiders feed sparrows. He is building a ladder of lives to feed on, and he wants a cat for the next rung.
I have not gathered enough yet.

n_wrong1.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_wrong1.text: A naturalist keeps what he studies. He does not count them every night, and does not look at the sparrow like that. No.

n_wrong2.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_wrong2.text: A sweet tooth does not hide sugar under a pillow and keep a ledger of insects. No.

n_ok.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_ok.text: It is not a hobby; it is a method. He is feeding life into life, link by link, and believes the strength gathers in him. I wrote 'zoophagous mania' on his sheet this morning without understanding what I was writing. He is a maniac, and the maniac has a plan.

n0.speaker: Dr. Hennessey
n0.text: Morning, Doctor. Renfield was at it all night, counting out loud, sometimes in a whisper and sometimes not. I wouldn't go in without a sedative. He's been like a man listening for something.

choices.text: Has he tried to get out?
I will take a pull from that flask of yours, if you can spare it.

n_eats.speaker: Dr. Hennessey
n_eats.text: Nothing at table, hardly. But Dobbs found sugar hidden in his pillow, and he lives on bluebottles, I swear it. He swallowed a spider in front of me. He said it was 'a very fine one'.

n_escape.speaker: Dr. Hennessey
n_escape.text: Twice since June, once at night, and Pocock found him in the Carfax garden at dawn. How he gets from his cell to the wall I don't know; but the wall, now, is another matter. Ask Pocock about the fence.

n_key.speaker: Dr. Hennessey
n_key.text: You always put it somewhere clever, Doctor. Last time it was behind Lombroso. The time before, the mantel clock. If I were you, I'd look in your own study before you look anywhere else.

n_flask.speaker: Dr. Hennessey
n_flask.text: Take what you need. You've earned it. Between us, if the old fellow's quiet at last, I'd drink to that myself.

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: Scales, a graduated glass, a brass measure. Chloral crystals dissolved in water: but how many grains? The ledger has the rule; the weighing table has the weight. A mistake here is a mistake in a man's body, not a ledger.

choices.text: Five grains: a mild draught, in case he is already tired.
Ten grains: right for nine stone.
Thirty grains. Make a certainty of it.

n_weak.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_weak.text: Five would make him drowsy and furious. A furious Renfield does not stay drowsy. No.

n_ok.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_ok.text: Ten grains in a measure of clean water: not a grain more than his nine stone can carry. I stopper it and put it in my pocket.

n_mid.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_mid.text: Fifteen is for a man of twelve stone, and Renfield is nine and wasting. He would sleep all night and wake raving with a bad heart. No.

n_strong.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_strong.text: Thirty is a bull's dose. It would stop his heart. I put the measure down with a shaking hand.

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: Rainwater, clean enough, and a tin dipper hanging on its chain.

do.say: I fill the glass to the mark.

n0.speaker: Dobbs
n0.text: Evening, Doctor. I'd not go in alone, if I were you, not unless he's had his draught. He bit Mr Hennessey's glove in half last week, and wasn't sorry.

n_a.speaker: Dobbs
n_a.text: Like a clock wound too tight, sir. He's been talking to the window. Not praying, sir, just talking, as if someone were out there answering.

n_b.speaker: Dobbs
n_b.text: The sparrow, sir. He's tamed one, and it sits on his shoulder. And last night he asked me, very civil, whether the 'Master' had come. I said I didn't know any master in the building, only you. He laughed at that. Laughed for a quarter of an hour.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: Ah, Doctor Seward. How very good of you to call. I have had the strangest sort of calm. I was wondering whether we might speak as gentlemen.

choices.text: Why do you keep flies, Renfield?
Is it true you asked for a kitten?
What do you see from the window?
Do you know a lady called Lucy Westenra?

n_flies.speaker: Renfield
n_flies.text: They are lives, Doctor. Each is a little, glittering life, and it takes so many to make one great one. A spider eats a hundred flies. A sparrow eats a hundred spiders. And a cat... a cat has the lives of the whole garden in her.

n_kitten.speaker: Renfield
n_kitten.text: A kitten. A nice little sleek playful kitten, that I can teach and feed and feed, and feed. I should not hurt it. Not until it was grown.

choices.text: No, Renfield. You may not have one.

n_k_no.speaker: Renfield
n_k_no.text: (He is not angry; he is quiet. He says, softly:) Then you will regret it, Doctor. Not me. I shall not.

n_k_yes.speaker: Renfield
n_k_yes.text: (He brightens horribly.) You will? Oh, Doctor, then you are a friend! (I wish I had not said it. I shall not repeat it.)

n_master.speaker: Renfield
n_master.text: He is coming, Doctor. Not yet, not tonight, but he is near. He promises me lives, and more lives, a world of flies... I only want to be ready. I was a poor mad creature, and he has said that I shall be honoured. (He looks at the window and weeps.)

n_window.speaker: Renfield
n_window.text: Carfax. There are lights in it now, at night. Boxes. Great boxes, carried by men who sweat and swear in a foreign tongue. Mr Hawkins's clients, perhaps. Whoever it is, he has more patience than I.

n_lucy.speaker: Renfield
n_lucy.text: Lucy? A sweet name for a sweet creature. I believe I have seen a letter. Sweet things go to waste, Doctor, in a house with an open window. Do you know, you should be very careful, very careful indeed. (He is not mocking me. He is frightened.)

n0.speaker: Pocock
n0.text: Doctor. Fine day for the fruit trees. You're not here for the fruit trees.

choices.text: Mr Hennessey says someone has been through the wall.
Carfax. What do you know of it?

n_wall.speaker: Pocock
n_wall.text: Aye. Slat by the elms, hangin' by one nail. There's a track through the long grass to Carfax's garden, worn like a sheep-path, and the grass bent the wrong way, sir; towards the house. I told Mr Hennessey. Told 'im last month.

n_hammer.speaker: Pocock
n_hammer.text: Toolbox in the shed, sir. Don't leave any nails about. They find them.

n_carfax.speaker: Pocock
n_carfax.text: Sold in the spring. Men have been carrying boxes in at night, like coffins. I don't ask, sir. The fruit doesn't ask me.

n0.speaker: Telegraph boy
n0.text: Telegram for Dr. Seward, sir! Came at four, sir, by Hampstead. The sender looked proper upset.

n_t.speaker: Telegraph boy
n_t.text: No reply paid, sir. Thank you, sir!

n0.speaker: Mr. Bilder
n0.text: Berserker? Lord love you, sir, the gentlest great beast in the Gardens. Dog-gentle. Would let the Missus scratch him through the bars. Yet that night, sir. That night.

choices.text: What happened the night he went?
May I have the newspaper cutting?

n_night.speaker: Mr. Bilder
n_night.text: Storm, sir, thunder and lightning. He began to howl before it started. I was in the cottage when I heard iron bend. Went out with a lantern, and the bars were wrenched. He was gone by morning, and not a track in the mud, not a sign of him over the wall.

n_stranger.speaker: Mr. Bilder
n_stranger.text: Aye. A tall, thin man, hooked nose, black moustache and a pointed beard with a few white hairs. A tight-lipped gent, with red in his eyes under the lamp. He'd been standing at Berserker's cage the evening before, and Berserker, who never so much as shifted for visitors, put his head on the bars and looked at him. Nothing more. They knew each other, I'd swear.

n_cut.speaker: Mr. Bilder
n_cut.text: It's on the table, sir. A reporter wrote it down as I said it, and he got one thing right and nine things wrong. Take it. The Missus reads it aloud and I can't abide it.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Bilder
n0.text: Mr. Bilder says it was a storm, sir. I say a wolf in a storm would stay in his cage and howl. This one went where he was wanted. Mark me.

n1.speaker: Mrs. Bilder
n1.text: He was a pet, sir, a great soft dog of a thing, till somebody whistled. Don't ask me who. I only say there are things that go when they are called.

n0.speaker: Berserker
n0.text: The wolf stops pacing and looks at you. For a moment you are sure he is about to speak, and then he drops his head, and begins again, back and forth, back and forth, with his eyes on the north.

n0.speaker: Sister Agatha
n0.text: You are Miss Murray. I wrote to you. He has been calling for you in his sleep, and sometimes in his waking. The doctors say it was a brain fever, brought on by some great shock. What shock, he will not say.

choices.text: Where is his journal? I have heard of it.
Sister, may we be married here, today?

n_how.speaker: Sister Agatha
n_how.text: Weak, and very quiet. He wakes sometimes in the night and asks whether the windows are barred. I tell him they are not, and he is comforted. I have watched men who fought on battlefields. He has seen something worse.

n_diary.speaker: Sister Agatha
n_diary.text: Under his pillow, Miss. He asked me to keep it from him, then asked for it back. He says he cannot bear to read it, but that you may, if some solemn duty ever demands it. Ask him gently. It is his to give.

n_wed.speaker: Sister Agatha
n_wed.text: I would be proud to witness it, child. I will arrange a priest, and the chapel. Bring a ring, bring your husband's consent, and let that journal be sealed first, so neither of you is tempted. Black ribbon is in the basket, wax on the desk. Some promises are better kept by a seal than by a vow.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: Mina? Is it really you? I had been afraid... I thought it was another dream, with a kind face on it.

choices.text: Rest, Jonathan. I am here, and I shall not leave you.
Sister Agatha says there is a journal, Jonathan.
Jonathan, will you marry me, here, today?

n_rest.speaker: Jonathan
n_rest.text: (He takes my hand with both his. His fingers feel like twigs.) The Count... no, I shall not say it. Not now. Only that when I walked out of the Castle, I walked out of every door I had ever believed in.

n_diary.speaker: Jonathan
n_diary.text: Here, take it. I wrote it all, every night. Read it if you must, never if you needn't, and do not ask me to confirm one line. I want to be married before I remember what is in it. (He pushes the little black book across the blanket.)

n_marry.speaker: Jonathan
n_marry.text: Yes. Oh, yes. There is a ring in my coat, I think, in the waistcoat pocket. I bought it in London the week before I left, and could not bring myself to throw it away. Mina, if you will have a broken man...

n0.speaker: Sister Maria
n0.text: He is a very good patient, Miss. He eats everything. But he sleeps with the light on, and the Sisters say he talks of wolves. We do not mention wolves.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: A table by the window, and good light. If I could close Jonathan's journal so that it can only be opened by our decision... black ribbon, wax, and the book itself.

choices.text: Tie the journal with the ribbon and seal it with wax.

n_ok.speaker: Mina
n_ok.text: I tie the ribbon in a bow and let the red wax fall, a drop, a seal. It is nothing, a book and a ribbon, and I feel as though I have closed a door in my own house. Whatever is in it is safe from us until we need it.

n0.speaker: Father Hermann
n0.text: My child, Sister Agatha says you wish to be married. It is not the usual hour, and not the usual reason. Tell me.

choices.text: We are ready, Father: the ring, his consent, and the journal sealed.

n_need.speaker: Father Hermann
n_need.text: A ring, my child, and the bridegroom's consent, which he must give freely and in his right mind. Sister Agatha mentions something about a journal that must be sealed first; I confess I do not ask. And a witness, which she is.

v1.speaker: Father Hermann
v1.text: Wilhelmina Murray, wilt thou have this man to be thy wedded husband, to live together after God's ordinance? Wilt thou love him, comfort him, honour and keep him in sickness and in health?

v2.speaker: Mina
v2.text: 'I will.' (My voice is not mine. It is smaller, and certain.) 'I will, in sickness and in health, and I think the sickness is the part that matters.'

v3.speaker: Jonathan
v3.text: 'I will. I, Jonathan, take thee, Wilhelmina, to my wedded wife. To have and to hold, from this day forward... and I will not let go.' (His fingers are shaking. He puts the ring on, and it does not slip.)

v4.speaker: Father Hermann
v4.text: Those whom God hath joined together let no man put asunder. Go in peace, Mrs Harker.

do.card: Hillingham, 7 September.  The wire from Dr. Seward was answered, in the end. Van Helsing is on the step.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: I can stand if you hold my arm. If I could ask one more thing, Mina: that we never talk of the Castle unless we must. I want to remember being happy before I remember anything else.

n0.speaker: Sister Agatha
n0.text: I have put my hand to many a bedside, child. This is the first altar I have been asked to stand at in sixteen years. Go on. The priest is waiting, and the candles do not last.

n0.speaker: Bradshaw's Guide
n0.text: The Continental pages are open, and someone has underlined a line in pencil. Amsterdam: the Hook of Holland boat leaves at night for Harwich, the boat-train for Liverpool Street. The day services by Calais and Dover take half as long again, with two changes.

n1.speaker: Dr. Seward
n1.text: Night boat from the Hook; boat-train reaches Liverpool Street at five minutes past six. And the telegraph at Hampstead closes at eight, with a boy who must be paid before then. If I want Van Helsing here by breakfast, my wire must name the night boat.

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: A box of garlic flowers from Haarlem, with the Professor's own scrawl on the lid. 'Not for the kitchen.'

choices.text: Take a handful of the flowers.

do.say: I take three heads of the pale, rank flowers. The whole hall smells of them.

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: The fire is low. The house is silent. The wire is gone; there is nothing to do but wait for morning, and the train.

choices.text: Sit by the fire until morning.
Not yet. There is more to do first.

n1.speaker: Dr. Seward
n1.text: I sit in the armchair, and the fire gutters, and Lucy's breathing comes down the stairs like a clock. Somewhere, Jonathan Harker is lying in a foreign bed, and Mina has gone to find him. I have not even had time to think of them.

do.card: Meanwhile, in Buda-Pesth, a fortnight earlier.  24 August.  Mina Murray crosses Europe to find a man she is not yet married to.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n0.text: Dr. Seward! How good of you. Lucy is so very much better, I think. She only wants her window open and a little air. Girls will make such a fuss about the stuffiness of a sickroom.

choices.text: And you, Mrs Westenra? Your own heart?
I should like her room kept quiet and undisturbed tonight.
About the garlic in Lucy's room, madam...

n_a.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_a.text: She sleeps so much. She was never so languid at Whitby, and those sea airs were supposed to have done her such good. She cries out in her sleep sometimes, poor child. I have thought of sending for Dr. Hargreaves, but Arthur says to wait for you. You may go up. She is sleeping, I think.

n_heart.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_heart.text: Oh, a little fluttering. It is nothing. I have it every evening. Dr. Hargreaves says I must not be startled. I tell him I am never startled; nothing ever happens in Hampstead.

n_quiet.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_quiet.text: Of course, Doctor. I shall not so much as put my head round the door. Although I do think the poor child is too much alone at night; the house is so large, and the maids are so far.

n_g.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_g.text: Those dreadful flowers! I confess I threw them out, and opened the window. A girl cannot get well in a room that smells like a kitchen drain. Dr. Seward, it is my house and my child.

choices.text: They are a fashionable Dutch remedy, madam, nothing more.
Professor Van Helsing has many degrees. He prescribes it.
Madam, they are as real a medicine as digitalis. If they are moved again, I fear Lucy may not wake. I beg you to trust a physician who has seen this before.

n_g_bad1.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_g_bad1.text: A fashionable remedy! Then it will be out of fashion by Sunday. No, Doctor, I think not.

n_g_bad2.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_g_bad2.text: Degrees! Dr. Hargreaves has several, and he does not tell me to hang a vegetable round my daughter's neck.

n_g_ok.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_g_ok.text: (Her hand has gone to her heart.) Oh, my dear Doctor. Put like that... I would never forgive myself. I promise, on my honour. Touch nothing in that room. I shall not even pass the door.

n0.speaker: Maid
n0.text: Oh, sir, begging your pardon. I've worked here nine years, and I never saw Miss Lucy like this. She isn't herself in the mornings, sir, and she never was a one to walk about.

choices.text: Does she walk in her sleep?
Where is the key to Miss Lucy's room kept?

n_a.speaker: Maid
n_a.text: At Whitby, Mrs W. says, sir. But here, I found her slippers wet one morning, standing by the window. I thought: she's been walking on the dew. Then I thought: no, I'm being silly.

n_key.speaker: Maid
n_key.text: On the rack in the hall, sir, with all the other keys. Miss L.'s room, in the housekeeper's hand. We keep them all there. Mrs Westenra says it makes the house feel safe, sir.

n0.speaker: Maid
n0.text: (She mumbles, 'The port, the port... the gentleman said it was for the mistress.' Her head rolls. She is as insensible as a log.)

n1.speaker: Dr. Seward
n1.text: I shake her, slap her wrists, call her name. Her eyes roll open, and shut. Whatever she took has her fast. Smelling salts might do what shaking cannot; Mrs Westenra has a bottle in her dressing-case upstairs.

n0.speaker: Arthur
n0.text: Jack! Thank God. Is she... how bad is it? They would not let me stay at the Hall, with my father as he is, and I have been going out of my mind.

choices.text: Arthur, Van Helsing says she needs a man's blood tonight. Will you give it?
Arthur, there is something I must tell you about the transfusions.
She is sleeping, Arthur. Be patient a little.

n_help.speaker: Arthur
n_help.text: Take what you want, Jack. Take all of it. I'd give my last drop and think it cheap. (He is already rolling his sleeve.)

n_pat.speaker: Arthur
n_pat.text: Patient. Yes. I have been told to be patient since June.

n_secret.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_secret.text: (The Professor has told me, bluntly, that Arthur must never know another man's blood has gone into her. A lover has jealousies even for gifts.) Arthur... I mean to tell you the truth about this.

choices.text: I gave her blood too, Arthur.
Nothing. Only that you saved her life.

n_s_truth.speaker: Arthur
n_s_truth.text: You gave... then in a manner of speaking, she is... (He is white.) No. No, Jack, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. You saved her too. I am the lowest kind of fool to be jealous of a doctor's arm.

n_s_keep.speaker: Arthur
n_s_keep.text: Then I am the happiest man in London tonight, and I would not have it otherwise.

n0.speaker: Quincey Morris
