n_ring.text: The Ring is the house, the land, and four hundred people who think it will outlast them. It is a burden, Arthur. I hope you will carry it better than I.

n0.speaker: Dr. Lenox
n0.text: The Lord rallies when he has company, Mr. Holmwood. Anything that interests him is medicine. But no excitement.

n_ill.speaker: Dr. Lenox
n_ill.text: The heart, and the strain of carrying too much. Worry is the real disease. He has been worrying for years. About what, I have never been told.

n_hope.speaker: Dr. Lenox
n_hope.text: Weeks, perhaps. He wants to see you settled. I would see to it, if I were you. The green bottle in my cabinet will steady him for conversation.

n0.speaker: Bates
n0.text: Master Arthur. The household is at your disposal, sir, as it always was at his.

choices.text: Have you seen my father's desk-key?
Who is Crowle of Crowle & Aske?

n_key.speaker: Bates
n_key.text: His lordship hid it himself, sir, in the hall, and told no one where. He said once it was safest in company with something that had never been opened: books, old Sir Hugh, or the chest.

n_crowle.speaker: Bates
n_crowle.text: The Lord's banker, sir. He came often in the winter. The Lord asked me never to announce him. I thought it discreet.

n0.speaker: Tom
n0.text: The brougham will go as soon as you say, sir. Only the Lord gave me orders. No one goes to Hillingham without a word of his blessing, and a letter from him to carry.

choices.text: I will have both before I go.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n0.text: Mr. Holmwood. Lucy has told me nothing, which means she has told me everything. Have you anything for me, from your father?

choices.text: Thank you for your kindness, madam.

n_none.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_none.text: Respects are very nice, but a mother likes a signature.

n_thanks.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_thanks.text: Go on. Lucy is waiting. I have never seen her so fond of a lawn.

n_letter.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_letter.text: I see. He writes beautifully. But a mother must ask what a letter cannot say. Is the Ring in good heart? I do not ask about money. Only whether it will keep my daughter warm.

choices.text: It is sound, madam. Entirely sound.
It is burdened, madam. My father's illness has cost us dear. But my honour is not for sale.

n_lie.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_lie.text: Splendid. I am so glad. (She says it too quickly, as if she had made up her mind first and asked afterward.)

n_truth.speaker: Mrs. Westenra
n_truth.text: Thank you. That is the first plain answer a gentleman has given me in thirty years. I shall not hold your father's debts against you; I shall hold your honesty for you. Go and find my daughter.

n0.speaker: Quincey Morris
n0.text: Say, Art. I had a speech ready. Three fine paragraphs. I reckon I'll keep it for the next wedding. Go on. She's by the roses.

choices.text: You are a better man than I, Quincey.

n1.speaker: Quincey Morris
n1.text: Hell, no. I'm a worse shot at the heart. You hit it dead centre without even aiming. I'd call that luck, but I'd rather call it honest.

n0.speaker: Lucy
n0.text: Arthur! You have come after all. Mamma has been unbearable about it. She says you shall decide to like us on a full stomach.

choices.text: [Offer the wild rose and the ring]
I have something to ask you, but I am not ready.
I am so glad to see you.

n_notready.speaker: Lucy
n_notready.text: Then I shall wait. A girl who has had three proposals in a day knows the smell of a fourth. (She smiles.) Mamma must approve of the thing first, and the rose arbour is so lovely this month.

n_glad.speaker: Lucy
n_glad.text: And I of you. Go and sit in the summer-house, we are expected for tea.

n_ask.speaker: Arthur
n_ask.text: Lucy, my father is dying. The house I shall inherit is old and tired and heavy with duty. I have nothing to offer you but the whole of myself and my mother's ring. Will you take it?

n_yes.speaker: Lucy
n_yes.text: Oh, Arthur. Yes. I have been saying yes for six weeks; you were simply not listening. (She laughs, and takes the rose, and puts the ring on, and wipes her eyes with her wrist.)

do.say: She gives me a blue ribbon from her hair, 'for luck, and for remembering'.

n0.speaker: Lucy
n0.text: Sit by me, Arthur. No one has the right to look so solemn in a summer-house.

choices.text: Tell me what you would do with the Ring.
I want to remember every hour of this.

n_ring.speaker: Lucy
n_ring.text: Open all the windows. And invite the whole village to tea. I am quite certain nobody has ever done it.

n_rem.speaker: Lucy
n_rem.text: Then look about you. The mallets, the music-box, the poems. They are all here, and they will keep.

n0.speaker: Footman
n0.text: A telegram, Mr. Holmwood. From the Ring. I am sorry to bring it.

n1.speaker: Arthur
n1.text: 'LORD GODALMING SINKING. COME AT ONCE. BATES.' Lucy turns her face into my shoulder, and does not speak, and does not need to.

do.card: Hillingham stood on its lawn in the last of the light. By the time the train reached the Ring, the Lord had died.

n0.speaker: Mr. Pennefather
n0.text: My lord. I mean, the title is yours, as of this morning. I am obliged to tell you the estate is encumbered. I am not at liberty to tell you how. Mr. Wilkes can; the muniment room can; I should rather not.

choices.text: Who holds the key to the muniment room?

n_key.speaker: Mr. Pennefather
n_key.text: The steward holds the key, and, I fancy, an oath to the late Lord not to give it up. You will have to persuade him, my lord. With the ledger, I should think.

n_seal.speaker: Mr. Pennefather
n_seal.text: Your father's signet. It lies with him, in the vault, as is the custom. A custom, my lord, is only a rule you have not been asked to break.

n0.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n0.text: My lord. My deepest sympathy. Business can wait a day, but only a day. May I speak plainly?

choices.text: I have read the deed, Mr. Crowle.

n_terms.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_terms.text: Your father borrowed against the Ring. It is no scandal; half the peerage does. But the debt is large, and the interest is hungry. Sell the Home Wood and the Green to a syndicate I know, say nothing to the village, and the whole matter dissolves by Michaelmas. No one need ever know.

n_terms_again.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_terms_again.text: As I said, my lord. A comfortable arrangement. Bring me the deed when you have read it, and I shall draw it up.

n_decide.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_decide.text: Then you know. Now, my lord: your father's way was a lie, and mine is a quiet sale. What will you do?

choices.text: [Refuse, and tell the truth to the tenants]
[Refuse, but I am not ready yet]

n_wait.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_wait.text: My lord, you do not have the tenants with you. A truth with nobody behind it is only a confession.

n_end_lie.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_end_lie.text: A wise young man. The Wood will be down by spring. Nobody will say your name unkindly; nobody will say it at all.

do.card: Arthur signed. The Home Wood was sold by Michaelmas. The Ring was saved, and the village never knew what it had been spared or what it had lost. He wore the signet for the rest of his life and never quite got used to its weight.

n_end_truth.speaker: Mr. Crowle
n_end_truth.text: I see. Then you are your father's son after all, in the way that matters. I shall extend the term. I would rather lend to a man who tells me how it stands.

do.card: Arthur read his father's letter aloud on the village green, with the deed in his hand and Gideon Marsh at his side. The Ring was mortgaged for twenty years more; the tenants gave what they could; the Home Wood stood. In the autumn he stood at Lucy's side in Hillingham church, and was, for an hour, only a man.

n0.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n0.text: My lord. Condolences. The funeral was well attended. The estate is... in its customary order.

choices.text: Show him the ledger of arrears.
Tell me the truth about the estate.
Thank you for your thirty years, Mr. Wilkes.

n_truth.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n_truth.text: The estate is... as it has been. I am sworn to say no more, my lord. You must look in the ledger on my desk yourself, if you want proof.

n_thanks.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n_thanks.text: It was a privilege, my lord. I hope I have not cost you more than I saved.

n_ledger.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n_ledger.text: ...Where did you find it? Never mind. It is on the page. There is no sense hiding what you can read. The Lord made me swear. I have served him thirty years and I will say it plainly: he borrowed to keep every cottage warm. And I let him.

choices.text: You did right, Mr. Wilkes. Give me the key to the muniment room.
You lied to me for four years.

n_blame.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n_blame.text: I did, my lord. Dismiss me if you like. But the Lord asked, and I owed him more than I owed you. I do not know whether that was loyalty or cowardice. Perhaps they are the same.

choices.text: Forgive me. Give me the key, and stay.

n_key.speaker: Mr. Wilkes
n_key.text: Here, my lord. It opens the muniment room, but the lock has a recess for the seal, and the seal is your father's signet. It lies with him in the vault.

n0.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n0.text: Lord Godalming. We're sorry for your loss. We're sorrier, I'll not lie, for our own. A new Lord is a new landlord.

choices.text: Hobbs says there are men in the Home Wood.
The Home Wood is clear, Mr. Marsh.

n_fear.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_fear.text: That the rent goes up, that the Wood goes down, that the Green goes to a railway. Your father kept it all as it was. We never asked how.

n_help.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_help.text: Words. Fine words. Show us. There's men in the Home Wood, snaring the Lord's hinds and worse, and no one's gone in. If the new Lord will walk in his own wood by night, we'll listen to what he says by day.

n_wood.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_wood.text: Aye. Go and see to them yourself. Not Hobbs. You.

n_proof.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_proof.text: Hobbs has told us. You went in yourself. That's something none of your family's done since the old Sir Hugh. Now tell us the rest, my lord. The whole of it.

choices.text: The estate is mortgaged to its roof, but not a cottage will be sold.
The estate is entirely sound, Mr. Marsh.

n_liar.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_liar.text: ...Sound. Is that so. The miller's rent was paid by a bank, my lord, and every one of us knows it. Come back when you can look at us and tell it straight.

n_honest.speaker: Gideon Marsh
n_honest.text: ...Well. That's a new thing to hear from a Lord. (He takes his hat off, and the miller does the same.) We've a petition. Thirty names. We'll stand surety for the interest, if you'll stand surety for the cottages.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Marsh
n0.text: Gideon speaks for all of us. I only speak for the one who'd rather you didn't pretend. Your father pretended beautifully, and never fooled any of us.

choices.text: What would you have me do?

n1.speaker: Mrs. Marsh
n1.text: Tell us the truth. Even a bad truth. People can build a house on it.

n0.speaker: The miller
n0.text: The mill-race was your father's loan, my lord, and I'll be paying it till I'm dead. I never knew who he borrowed from. I thought it came from the Lord's own pocket.

choices.text: It came from a bank. I am sorry.

n1.speaker: The miller
n1.text: A bank! Well. I'd rather have known. A man likes to know whose bread he's eating.

n0.speaker: Hobbs
n0.text: My lord! Don't come further. There are three of them by the old beech, and I swear one is a wolf, or something wolfish. There hasn't been a wolf in England since the Stuarts.

choices.text: I will deal with them myself.
Where did the hind come from?

n1.speaker: Hobbs
n1.text: God bless you, my lord. Aim for the dog first. The men will run when the dog does.

n2.speaker: Hobbs
n2.text: Dead by the log, my lord. Throat torn, not cut. I thought the poachers killed it. Now I think the poachers are as frightened of it as we are.

n0.speaker: Pike
n0.text: My lord. The Wood gate was open last night, though I locked it myself. Hobbs says there's trouble in there.

n0.speaker: The kneeling woman
n0.text: Hush, Master Arthur. It's only old Nan, who nursed you and your mother. I come when the bell tells me there's a Holmwood in grief. I thought you would find the vault.

choices.text: How does one open the vault, Nan?

n_bell.speaker: Nan
n_bell.text: It rings for the family. It rang for your mother, and for your father this morning. The sexton says it's the wind. Wind or not, I answer.

n_vault.speaker: Nan
n_vault.text: It's a lock of years, dear. The first Lord's 'resting', the old brass says. Read the brasses. Not when he fell, my dear. When he came home.

n0.speaker: The vault lock
n0.text: A dial of years. 'HERE HE RESTS.' Which year is that?

n_wrong.speaker: The vault lock
n_wrong.text: The dial turns. Nothing. Not that year.

n_right.speaker: The vault lock
n_right.text: The dial clicks. The black door sags inward onto a stair that has not been used since Mother's funeral.

n0.speaker: Arthur
n0.text: My father is in there. The signet lies on his folded hands, as the custom is.

n1.speaker: Arthur
n1.text: His fingers are cold. The ring slips off the way it does when a man has grown thin. I whisper that I shall wear it better than I have worn the weeks.

n2.speaker: Arthur
n2.text: Our father, who art in heaven. I cannot get past 'forgive us our debts', and I stand there for a long time.

n0.speaker: Clerk
n0.text: Captain! The bill of lading, signed and sealed as Herr Hildesheim promised. Fifty boxes, silver sand and earth, consigned to Mr. S. F. Billington of Whitby. A very odd cargo for July, but the freight is paid in full.

choices.text: Who orders earth by the shipload?

n1.speaker: Clerk
n1.text: Take care of it, Captain. The customs officer will want to see it, and the officer is not a man who forgets. Nor does he stamp for nothing.

n_who.speaker: Clerk
n_who.text: A foreign nobleman, Captain. He did not come himself. Everything was by letter and by agents, and the earth came down from the mountains on Szgany carts. He paid in gold. I did not ask questions.

n_why.speaker: Clerk
n_why.text: A quiet harbour, little watched, with deep water by the pier. That is what the gentleman's letter said. I thought it a strange thing for a gentleman to know.

n0.speaker: Customs officer
n0.text: Papers.

n1.speaker: Customs officer
n1.text: Fifty boxes of earth. Irregular. Extremely irregular. For a small consideration, however, a ship may be regular in everything.

n2.speaker: Customs officer
n2.text: Everything is in order, Captain. A good voyage. I shall never see that ship again, I think, and I do not mind it.

n_hint.speaker: Customs officer
n_hint.text: A stamp costs silver, Captain. The paper first; the coin second. That is how the law is read in Varna.

n0.speaker: Candle-seller
n0.text: A beeswax candle for the icon, Captain? One silver. It has been blessed in St. Constantine's and will burn all night, whatever the wind does.

choices.text: What do the sailors say about this ship?

n1.speaker: Candle-seller
n1.text: Light it before the icon on the quay. Father Nikolai will say the words. A ship that has not been blessed is a ship with no mother.

n_say.speaker: Candle-seller
n_say.text: That the Slovaks who loaded her would not look at the boxes. That they crossed themselves each time they put one down. That the last one was warm.

n0.speaker: Father Nikolai
n0.text: A ship may sail without a blessing, my son. Sailors may not.

choices.text: What is in the boxes, Father?

n1.speaker: Father Nikolai
n1.text: Lord, who rebuked the winds and the sea, keep this ship and every soul aboard her. Here is water from the font, Captain; use it where you must. And keep a cross about you. A cross is better than a pilot.

n_q.speaker: Father Nikolai
n_q.text: I do not know. I know that the Szgany kissed the ground before they would touch them, and I know that the earth has a smell I have smelled once before, in a vault where a man was buried who should not have been.

n0.speaker: Slovak foreman
n0.text: Fifty. Not one more, not one fewer. We counted them twice.

choices.text: Who carried them to the quay?

n1.speaker: Slovak foreman
n1.text: Szgany. They came down in the night, with their carts and their dogs, and they would not take payment from us. They took it from the clerk and rode away.

n2.speaker: Slovak foreman
n2.text: The last box was warm, Captain. In July that is nothing. But it was warm through the night, and not from the sun.

n0.speaker: Amramoff
n0.text: Captain. The ship is stowed. The tide is turning. If you want to sail, we can sail.

n_go.speaker: Amramoff
n_go.text: At noon, then. East wind, fresh. She will go like a bird.

do.card: 6 July. Varna. At noon the Demeter set sail, east wind, fresh. Crew: five hands, two mates, the cook, and myself, the captain. Cargo: silver sand and fifty boxes of earth, for Whitby.

n_hint.speaker: Amramoff
n_hint.text: The papers must be stamped by the customs officer, and the men will not cast off without a priest's blessing. They are Russians, Captain. You know what that is.

n_key.speaker: Amramoff
n_key.text: I locked the hold when the boxes were stowed. The key I hung where a captain keeps keys: near where he sleeps, or where the cook keeps his spoons, or in the locker where we keep our tools. If it is not there, the carpenter's crowbar will do the same work.

n0.speaker: Amramoff
n0.text: Captain. What are your orders?

choices.text: I want the whole ship searched.
The men want a double watch. I mean to grant it.
Do you believe there is a man aboard?
[It is here, I know it now...]

n_men.speaker: Amramoff
n_men.text: Frightened women, Captain. A handspike will cure it. A man who is afraid of a deck-house is a man who needs more work.

n_search.speaker: Amramoff
n_search.text: A fool's errand. Sixty feet of boxes, and no man can hide in a box. I shall take the helm, and let the men search. But it is folly, and it will demoralise them.

n_watch.speaker: Amramoff
n_watch.text: Then give me the dark watch, Captain. The men will not stand with me, and I will not stand with them. I will stand with you, with a handspike and a lantern, and between us we shall keep the middle watch.

n_man.speaker: Amramoff
n_man.text: There is no man aboard. There is what comes of men who sleep too little and think too much. I will find the cause. I shall find it if I have to open every box.

n_mad.speaker: Amramoff
n_mad.text: It is here. I know it now. On the watch last night I saw It, like a man, tall and thin and ghastly pale. It was in the bows, looking out. I crept behind It and gave It my knife, but the knife went through It, empty as the air.

choices.text: Mr. Amramoff, go to your bunk.

n_mad2.speaker: Amramoff
n_mad2.text: It is in the hold, perhaps in one of those boxes. I shall unscrew them one by one and see. You work the helm.

do.say: He takes the tool-chest and a lantern and goes down the forward hatchway. I cannot leave the wheel. I hear him knocking in the hold, patient as a carpenter.

n_mad3.speaker: Narrator
n_mad3.text: Then a sudden startled scream, and he comes up the hatchway as though shot from a gun, with his eyes rolling and his face convulsed with fear. 'Save me! Save me!' He looks round on the fog, and his horror turns to despair.

n_mad4.speaker: Amramoff
n_mad4.text: You had better come too, Captain, before it is too late. He is there. I know the secret now. The sea will save me from Him, and it is all that is left!

do.card: 3 August. He sprang on the bulwark and threw himself into the sea. I suppose I know the secret too, now. Lord, help me. How am I to account for all these horrors when I get to port? When I get to port! Will that ever be?

n0.speaker: Petrofsky
n0.text: Captain. Good watch.

n1.speaker: Petrofsky
n1.text: I sleep with my boots on, Captain. The floor has begun to feel cold. Cold the way a cellar is cold, not a sea.

n2.speaker: Petrofsky
n2.text: No. Nothing. Only that I take the larboard watch tonight, and Abramoff relieves me at eight bells, and I would rather he came early.

n0.speaker: Dmitri
n0.text: Captain. It is cold on deck.

n1.speaker: Dmitri
n1.text: That Petrofsky did not drown. A man who drowns makes a noise. They say he walked forward and the fog took him. Do not laugh, Captain. I will go and stand by the lantern.

n0.speaker: Ivan
n0.text: At the wheel, Captain. Steady as a rock.

choices.text: Would you stand a watch alone?

n1.speaker: Ivan
n1.text: No. Not alone, Captain. If I stand it, Bolotin stands it with me. He is my kinsman, my mother's cousin's boy. He does not leave my side, and I do not leave his.

n0.speaker: Olgaren
n0.text: Captain.

choices.text: Something is on your mind, Olgaren.

n_fear.speaker: Olgaren
n_fear.text: No, Captain. A little uneasy. I will tell you more tomorrow.

n_tale.speaker: Olgaren
n_tale.text: In my watch, Captain, I was sheltering behind the deck-house from the rain, when I saw a tall, thin man come up the companion-way, who was not like any of the crew. He walked forward along the deck and disappeared. I followed softly, but when I got to the bows, there was no one, and the hatchways were all closed.

n0.speaker: Stepan
n0.text: Captain. Soup in a quarter-hour. It will be hot, whatever else is not.

choices.text: What do you make of all this?

n_garlic.speaker: Stepan
n_garlic.text: Garlic? There is a string over the stove. My grandmother hung it over the cradle, against what, she never said. Take it. A man should have something in his pockets besides his hands.

n_gulls.speaker: Stepan
n_gulls.text: The gulls have all gone inland, Captain, and the porpoises are running to the west. A cook knows when to put the fire out. Weather, and soon, from the south-west. I have not seen it so since Odessa.

do.say: I note it. Gulls inland, the cook's weather-sense, and I have the sky and the glass besides.

n_mood.speaker: Stepan
n_mood.text: They say there is a stranger aboard, Captain. I say there are fifty strangers aboard and I have been feeding them for a week. Fifty boxes. A man who eats little and sleeps all day. That is no stranger. That is a passenger.

n0.speaker: Abramoff
n0.text: Captain. Mending.

n_watch.speaker: Abramoff
n_watch.text: Olgaren and I sail together, Captain, or we do not sail at all. He is my friend. If he goes on deck alone, I go; if I go alone, he goes. That is understood in the forecastle.

n_pet.speaker: Abramoff
n_pet.text: At eight bells, as arranged. I came up and found the deck empty and the lantern burning. I looked in the bows. I did not look in the hold.

n0.speaker: Bolotin
n0.text: Captain. The wheel is steady.

choices.text: Will you take a watch with Ivan?

n_ivan.speaker: Bolotin
n_ivan.text: With Ivan? Gladly. He is my kinsman; I would stand with him on a burning ship. I will steer and watch, sir, if you let me. Let the others sleep.

n0.speaker: Slate
n0.text: In three different hands the men have chalked: 'We ask for double watch. We do not go on deck alone. Not one of us.' Under it, in a fourth, a note: 'Not with the mate.'

n1.speaker: Captain
n1.text: A round robin, in the sailors' way: names in a ring, so that no one signs first. I will keep it, and I will grant what it asks. Double watches. It is the least I can do.

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: The sail-plan. What do I know about the weather, and what will I do about it?

choices.text: Carry all sail: the sky is clear and the wind is fair.
Take in sail: weather from the south-west by morning.

n_know.speaker: Captain
n_know.text: Let me count the signs. The glass:

n_know2.speaker: Captain
n_know2.text: falling long and slow, if I have read it (the barometer by the wheel). The sky: mares'-tails from the north-west, if I have looked at it (from the deck). The birds and fish: the cook's own word (galley). Three signs; they must agree.

n_wrong1.speaker: Captain
n_wrong1.text: No. I do not trust a clear sky with a falling glass. Let me think again.

n_wrong2.speaker: Captain
n_wrong2.text: A harbour in this wind is a reef with a name. We hold our course; we only shorten sail.

n_right.speaker: Captain
n_right.text: Glass falling, mares'-tails to the north-west, gulls inland, porpoises running west. That is a south-westerly gale before the next forenoon. We reef down, secure the boats, and get everything lashed. I give the orders.

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: The watch bill. Three watches, three pairs, and no man alone. I must match them by what the men have told me.

n_know.speaker: Captain
n_know.text: Abramoff says Olgaren stands only with him. Ivan and Bolotin are kin and will not be parted. The mate says the men won't stand with him and he will stand the dark watch with me. And the round robin: nobody alone. I need to hear all of it first.

n_done.speaker: Captain
n_done.text: The bill is chalked up: First watch, Ivan and Bolotin. Middle watch, the mate and myself, armed. Morning watch, Olgaren and Abramoff.

r1.speaker: Captain
r1.text: The first watch, eight bells to midnight. Who?

choices.text: Ivan and Bolotin (kin, they won't be parted).
Stepan the cook, alone, by the stove.

w1.speaker: Captain
w1.text: No. The men have said they will not stand with the mate. It would be better to have no watch at all.

w2.speaker: Captain
w2.text: Alone? The round robin says not one man alone. No.

r2.speaker: Captain
r2.text: The middle watch, midnight to four, the darkest. Who?

w3.speaker: Captain
w3.text: No. Ivan is already on the first watch with Bolotin and Olgaren will only stand with Abramoff.

w4.speaker: Captain
w4.text: No. They belong on the morning watch, a pair for the grey hours, and the middle watch needs the strongest.

r3.speaker: Captain
r3.text: The morning watch, four to eight. And the last pair?

w5.speaker: Captain
w5.text: No. Bolotin is on the first watch with Ivan, and the mate is with me.

r4.speaker: Captain
r4.text: There. A ship has never been better watched, and there is not a single man alone. If anything can be done by arithmetic, I have done it.

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: The ship's log lies open. A log is not a diary; it must say only what is true, in the right order, in a steady hand.

n_read.speaker: Captain
n_read.text: I read the log back. It is short and honest, and every line of it frightens me more than the one before.

l1.speaker: Captain
l1.text: What do I write of the cargo?

choices.text: Fifty boxes of Carpathian clay for Hamburg.
Silver sand and fifty boxes of earth, consigned to Mr. Billington, Whitby; customs stamped, Varna.

w_l1a.speaker: Captain
w_l1a.text: That is not what the bill of lading says. A log that lies is not a log. I strike it out.

w_l1c.speaker: Captain
w_l1c.text: The cargo is the whole point of the voyage. I strike it out.

l1b.speaker: Captain
l1b.text: And the weather I have read?

choices.text: Glass falling, mares'-tails NW, weather from SW by morning; reefed down.

w_l1d.speaker: Captain
w_l1d.text: No. I did not read it so, and I will not write it.

l1e.speaker: Captain
l1e.text: Written, and signed, and sanded. The cargo and the weather.

choices.text: Searched stem to stern, found nothing at all; crew's fears are folly.
Searched stem to stern with lanterns: no man; but earth spilled from box thirteen to the bows, and Petrofsky's cap.
Found a stowaway and put him in irons.

w_l2a.speaker: Captain
w_l2a.text: That is what the mate would write. It is not what I found.

w_l2c.speaker: Captain
w_l2c.text: There is no stowaway in irons. I would have remembered.

l2b.speaker: Captain
l2b.text: A strange entry, but a true one.

l3.speaker: Captain
l3.text: How many men have I lost since Varna?

choices.text: Three: Petrofsky, Dmitri and the second mate.

w_l3a.speaker: Captain
w_l3a.text: Bolotin is alive; I saw him at the wheel. Let me count again.

w_l3c.speaker: Captain
w_l3c.text: A man does not desert a ship in the middle of the Atlantic. No.

l3b.speaker: Captain
l3b.text: Two men. Both off watch, neither seen again. I write it exactly so.

l4.speaker: Captain
l4.text: The final entry. What do I tell the people who find this bottle?

choices.text: The mate murdered the crew and then himself.
The mate saw It: tall, thin, pale. The knife went through It. He leapt overboard. I know the secret now, and I will lash my hands to the wheel with the cross.

w_l4a.speaker: Captain
w_l4a.text: No. That is what the inquest will say, and it would be convenient. It is not what I saw.

w_l4c.speaker: Captain
w_l4c.text: I will not make up a pirate for the Board of Trade.

l4b.speaker: Captain
l4b.text: I write it as steadily as I can, and I seal it in the bottle with wax from the lamp, so that those who find it may understand. If not, all men shall know that I was true to my trust.

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: A few hours of sleep, if the ship allows it. But every night that I lie down, the ship is a man short in the morning.

choices.text: [Turn in: the Archipelago, Matapan, the 16th of July]

do.card: 16 July. The mate reported in the morning that one of the crew, Petrofsky, was missing. He took the larboard watch at eight bells, was relieved by Abramoff, and never reached his bunk. The men are more downcast than ever.

choices.text: [Turn in: Gibraltar and the Bay of Biscay, 24 July]

do.card: 24 July. There seems some doom over this ship. Already a hand short, and entering the Bay of Biscay with wild weather ahead, and last night another man lost. Like the first, he came off his watch and was not seen again.

29 July. Another tragedy. The morning watch found no one but the steersman; the second mate is gone. 30 July. Last night, both the man of the watch and the steersman missing. Only myself, the mate, and two hands left to work the ship.

2 August, midnight. Woke up from a few minutes' sleep by hearing a cry, seemingly outside my port. Nothing in the fog. I ran on deck and into the mate; he heard the cry too. The hold hatch is open, and from the hold comes the sound of the boxes moving.

choices.text: [What is left to do before I can rest?]

n_hint.speaker: Captain
n_hint.text: Let me count what is wanted.

n_h2.speaker: Captain
n_h2.text: In general: read the weather, count the hold, write the log (July 6th to 16th); search every corner and find the trail (17th); set the watch and gather garlic (22nd to 29th); open the box and deal with it (2 August).

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: Black earth, damp, the shape of a man pressed into it. There is a smell I knew in a vault, once. This is where It lies by day. What shall I do?

choices.text: [Pour the holy water into the earth]
[Pour out the oil and set a torch to it]

n_hw.speaker: Captain
n_hw.text: The water hisses where it touches the earth, like water on a hot stove. The black soil blisters and goes grey; the smell changes from the grave to something that is only a smell. Whatever lay here has lost its bed.

n_burn.speaker: Captain
n_burn.text: The oil takes, and the torch with it. The flame is low, blue at the heart and does not like the earth. Smoke rolls along the hold. The box burns badly and the others do not burn at all; and across the boxes, in the dark, something is awake.

n0.speaker: Captain
n0.text: The wheel. The fog. The night coming on. The hands are the ship's, now; they must be tied to it.

n_need.speaker: Captain
n_need.text: A rope for my hands. The crucifix and my mother's beads, which He dare not touch. The log, sealed in the bottle, in my pocket, with the cabin key. The mate gone, and the last entry written. When all is ready, I shall tie myself to the wheel.

n_end.speaker: Captain
n_end.text: I lash my hands to the spokes with the manila, wind the rosary through my fingers, and set the crucifix between them. Come good wind or foul, I shall save my soul and my honour as a captain. I am growing weaker, and the night is coming on. God, the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.

do.card: 6 August. In the great storm the Demeter ran before the wind into Whitby harbour, all sails set, and struck the sands under the East Cliff. As she struck, a great dog sprang from the deck to the shore and ran up the cliff path into the dusk; no trace of it was ever found. The captain was found lashed to the wheel, dead, his hands bound over a crucifix and a string of beads, a corked bottle and a cabin key in his pocket. The folk of Whitby buried him as a hero, on the cliff, near the seat where a girl and her friend sat watching the sea.

n0.speaker: Stanciu
n0.text: My lord. Severin has been under siege six weeks. Boyar Vlaicu says we cannot afford the grain to relieve it. I say we cannot afford not to. The council waits for your word, and your father's seat.

choices.text: What is the state of the border?
Tell me of the Order of the Dragon.
What must be done before I march?

n_border.speaker: Stanciu
n_border.text: The Turk comes at us across the Danube every spring, my lord, as the tide comes up the beach. We are the beach. Your father held it for twenty years with a fist; you will have to hold it with a head.

n_order.speaker: Stanciu
n_order.text: Your father's collar: the Dragon. The lock on the chest in your chamber bears the Order's year, not your father's. Do not mix them. The founding was in the king's reign, at the very beginning of this century, in 1408, when the Turk was still a rumour. Your father was merely accepted into it much later.

n_todo.speaker: Stanciu
n_todo.text: The order sent to the camp must be written, sealed with the Voivode's ring, and carried. The signal on the tower should be fired to call the ridge garrison. And your brother Radu has been seen in the corridors at odd hours; I do not like corridors at odd hours. Bring your father's hammer, my lord: the men follow what they remember.

n_council.speaker: Stanciu
n_council.text: Then to the matter. Two hundred starving villagers are camped in the courtyard. They want the granary opened. Boyar Vlaicu says the granary is the army's, and will be needed for the siege. A prince must choose, my lord, between a kindness that may cost a battle and a hardness that may cost a conscience.

choices.text: Open the granary to the villagers. The army will march lighter.
Close the gates. The army eats first, and the weak must bear it.

n_open.speaker: Stanciu
n_open.text: (He bows, very slowly.) It is the harder choice, my lord, and perhaps the wrong one. But I will see it done, and I think you will remember it. They will.

n_closed.speaker: Stanciu
n_closed.text: (A long silence.) As you command. The gates will be shut. Some of the villagers will walk away at dawn. Some will not walk. I shall see to it that none of this is said in the Voivode's name.

n0.speaker: Vlaicu
n0.text: My lord. Three hundred spears at your service, naturally. At my own expense, naturally. One only asks that the boyars be consulted in the matter of the spoils. Of the matter of the spoils, I have a great many thoughts.

choices.text: The spoils are for the soldiers who bleed, Vlaicu.
You shall have your share when Severin is relieved.

n_honour.speaker: Vlaicu
n_honour.text: A noble sentiment, my lord. Admirably young. I trust you will find your army grows lighter in the night when it hears it.

n_share.speaker: Vlaicu
n_share.text: Then we understand each other. And may I say how like your father you are, in the matter of understanding.

n0.speaker: Radu
n0.text: Brother. Prince. Voivode. I never know which to use first. It is a strange thing to come home and find that everyone defers to the boy who used to cheat at dice.

choices.text: You returned from the Sultan's court. How was it?

n_court.speaker: Radu
n_court.text: Very warm, very civilised, and quite unlike what the priests say of it. They gave me a horse. I did not have to cut off anyone's head to be given a horse. I commend the arrangement.

n_confront.speaker: Radu
n_confront.text: (He reads. He does not blush. He sets it down, very exactly.) Yes. I wrote it. 'The ford at the new moon, the boyars divided, the Voivode young.' I wrote it, brother, because the Sultan's hand is longer than ours, and I wanted to be on the right end of it. I did not think it would be you who read it.

choices.text: You will leave this castle tonight. I do not want to see a Turkish banner in your wake. Go with your life.
Take him to the cells. He will answer for treason.

n_exile.speaker: Radu
n_exile.text: (Quiet.) You are very like father at his best, Vlad. It is not a compliment. I shall be at the Sultan's court. I shall not forget your mercy, and I think it will not be quite enough.

n_chain.speaker: Radu
n_chain.text: (He smiles, with a sort of tenderness.) That, too, is like father. Do as you will. When I scream, remember who taught you to put a man in a hole.

n0.speaker: The Order chest
n0.text: The dial is a ring of years, the iron cold under the thumb. 'The year the Dragon was founded.' Which year?

n_wrong.speaker: The Order chest
n_wrong.text: The dial turns. Nothing. A year, but not that year.

n_right.speaker: The Order chest
n_right.text: The dial clicks over. The lid breathes up an inch on a smell of cedar and old wax.

n_in.speaker: The Order chest
n_in.text: Under a folded cloak lie my father's collar, an Order medal, and his signet, a dragon coiled round a cross. I put the ring on, and the room seems a little smaller.

n0.speaker: The seal-press
n0.text: Wax, a candle and the brass press, waiting for a ring.

choices.text: [Seal the draft order with my father's ring]

n_seal.speaker: The seal-press
n_seal.text: The wax is green. The dragon stands up out of it, tail in its teeth. For the first time in its history, the order is real.

n_need.speaker: The seal-press
n_need.text: A written order, and the Voivode's signet. The first is on the clerk's table. The second is, I think, somewhere my father hid it.

n0.speaker: Petru
n0.text: My lord, I can carry anything to the camp in a day and a night. But the captains won't take my word and I won't bring them a word they cannot read.

n_send.speaker: Petru
n_send.text: The levy will be at the camp below the Reed ford by the third night, my lord. God keep you.

n0.speaker: Ileana
n0.text: You have your father's chair and your father's frown. Both look better on him. Are you going to speak to me, or only to your counsellors?

choices.text: What do you think of Radu?

n_afraid.speaker: Ileana
n_afraid.text: Of course you are. If you were not, I would marry Radu instead. (She smiles, and it hurts.) Fear is not the enemy. Not knowing what to do with it is.

n_radu.speaker: Ileana
n_radu.text: He comes into this room when you are away. He looks at your desk, not at me. A man who looks at a desk is a man deciding what to do with the room.

n_back.speaker: Ileana
n_back.text: Say it again when you are in the doorway, Vlad, with the army behind you. I will believe it then. (She presses a ribbon of grey silk into his palm.) For a ring, until you have time to buy another.

n0.speaker: Dan
n0.text: The ridge answers if we fire the beacon, my lord. There's a platoon on the far crag, forty spears. But the beacon's dry as a priest's sermon. It wants lamp-oil, and a torch to set it going. The oil is down in the hall: the garrison barrel. The torch is in the bracket by the stair-door; the others are burned out.

n0.speaker: The grandmother
n0.text: You are the new Voivode. You have your father's eyes, and your father's chin. Your father left the villages out of his reckoning. I hope you will count us in.

choices.text: Take what you need from my pack.

n_from.speaker: The grandmother
n_from.text: From beyond Severin, where the Turk has been burning the barns. We walked ten days. The wolves have followed us for three. They are patient, my lord. Wolves usually are.

n_gift.speaker: The grandmother
n_gift.text: Then God bless you, young lord. It is the first kind word I have had from a man in armour.

n0.speaker: Mircea
n0.text: My lord. The scouts say the Turk will raid across the river before dawn, in the dark of the moon. They cannot cross at the Stone Ford, nor the Wolf's Ford. We should know which. You will find the map on the table.

choices.text: What do you remember of Kossova, Captain?
What do the men say of me?

n_kossova.speaker: Mircea
n_kossova.text: Don't ask. I was a boy. Three days in the heat, and on the third the Hungarian king ran, and the Crescent stood in the field where we had been. Your father said afterwards that the shame was not that we had lost but that we had not been trusted to lead.

n_men.speaker: Mircea
n_men.text: They say you are your father's son. Some say it to praise you. Some say it as a warning.

n0.speaker: Cristea
n0.text: My lord. I lay in the reeds two nights. They are coming down the old creek bed in the dark, from the north-east. They walk their horses, they wrap the hooves in felt: no clatter on stone, no splash. It must be a place with reeds to hide in and soft mud to cross; not a rocky ford.

n_wolf.speaker: Cristea
n_wolf.text: Four hours upstream, past the old mill, west of the hills. They would have to march round the whole army to reach it. No, my lord.

n_stone.speaker: Cristea
n_stone.text: A causeway of slabs, a quarter-mile of echoes. A felt-wrapped horse is still a horse. They would not choose it. It is too proud a crossing for a night raid.

n0.speaker: The Akinji
n0.text: (He speaks a little Wallachian, with the care of a man spelling a word he hates.) I will not talk. I am of the Sultan's household. You may do what you please.

choices.text: [Offer him water and a blanket, and ask him plainly]
[Threaten him with the boot and the iron]

n_parley.speaker: The Akinji
n_parley.text: ...I did not expect it. (He drinks.) We cross at the Reed Ford, where the river is slow, before dawn. Do not harm the reeds. My cousins are in them. If you must kill, kill quickly. That is all I ask.

n_break.speaker: The Akinji
n_break.text: (He talks, white-faced, for a quarter of an hour. When he is finished he does not look at me, and I do not look at him.) The Reed Ford. The reed-ford. Before dawn. I have told you everything. Cut my cords.

n0.speaker: The map
n0.text: Three fords marked in red wax. The scout says the Turks are coming down the old creek from the north-east, with felt on their hooves, to a place with reeds and soft mud. Where do I put the army?

n_stone.speaker: The map
n_stone.text: A causeway of slabs. A quarter-mile of echoes. They would not choose a ford where every hoof rings.

n_wolf.speaker: The map
n_wolf.text: Four hours upstream, far from the north-east creek. The Turks would have to round the whole army to reach it.

n_reed.speaker: The map
n_reed.text: The wax shows a broad slow river, reed-banks on both shores. A creek runs in from the north-east. It is the one place where felt-wrapped horses would make no sound. I move the stones.

n_go.speaker: The map
n_go.text: [You take the track to the river]

n0.speaker: The scholar
n0.text: A quick sword, Voivode. A quicker mind. A pity both are in service of a throne which has just been sold. Do you know that? The ford was told to the enemy by one of your own. You were meant to lose tonight.

choices.text: What do you want of me?

n_who.speaker: The scholar
n_who.text: A man who collects those who do not wish to end. I keep a school, under a mountain, by a lake in Hermannstadt. A small school, ten places at a time. The tenth is the Devil's. Everyone is told that. Nobody believes it until the end of term.

n_sold.speaker: The scholar
n_sold.text: I could tell you. But a prince should learn to read faces himself. You will read your brother's face long before you read my school-books.

n_want.speaker: The scholar
n_want.text: To teach you to be a king who is not beaten, Voivode. Not by Turks. Not by brothers. Not by time. The price is a winter of your life and a risk you will be told about in plain language. Come, if you dare.

n_go.speaker: The scholar
n_go.text: Then take this token. It will open the ferry to those who carry it. Nine days' ride, and we shall begin.

do.card: The Voivode held the ford that night, and the Turks went home across the water with fewer men than they came with. But the betrayal at Severin was done, and the border fortress fell on the third day. It was the first victory he could not enjoy. He went with the pale scholar the next dawn, without a word to any of his captains, to the school under the mountain that takes every tenth of its sons.

n0.speaker: The ferryman
n0.text: (No sound. A long, pale finger points at the open palm. Then, in a voice like water in a cistern:) The toll. One silver, from a scholar's own hand.

n_pay.speaker: The ferryman
n_pay.text: (The coin vanishes. The gull on his shoulder does not stir.) Board, scholar. Do not look at the water.

n_nocoin.speaker: The ferryman
n_nocoin.text: Nine fall short; the tenth pays more. A coin lies in the cairn, with the drowned scholar's cross. He kept it. He kept it badly.

n0.speaker: The Master
n0.text: Voivode. You came. I remember very few who come. The winter is long and the lessons are plain. First, the lesson of names: every thing has a name that is not its name. Learn to speak to a thing in the voice it hears itself in.

choices.text: What is the rite I must learn?
I want to read your library.

n_rite.speaker: The Master
n_rite.text: Three vessels, three acts, and an order that matters more than any of them. It is written in the Clavis Minor, in the library. A scholar who cannot read it will not be able to perform it, and a scholar who cannot perform it will not earn the stair.

n_lib.speaker: The Master
n_lib.text: The key is Vasile's. I give nothing away; the school teaches by taking. You must get it from him as best you can. Princes are used to getting things from men.

n_tithe.speaker: The Master
n_tithe.text: When the winter ends, ten scholars sit in a ring. One is the Devil's. He pays the tuition of all of us. Don't look so grave, Voivode. It is only a custom. The roll in the library says whose turn it is.

n0.speaker: Vasile
n0.text: The new boy. A prince in a scholar's gown. I have the key to the library, you know. The Master gave it to me because I do not want what is in it. You do. That makes you very interesting.

choices.text: [Offer him your friendship, and a share of what you learn]
[Lay a hand on the dagger and ask for the key]
What are you running from, Vasile?

n_friend.speaker: Vasile
n_friend.text: (He laughs, a surprised, boyish laugh.) You are very strange, Vlad. All right. A share. But the first thing you learn, you'll teach me. (He lifts the cord over his head.) Do not lose it. And do not lose me.

n_cow.speaker: Vasile
n_cow.text: (He goes quite white, and does not move.) You would not. (A long breath.) Take it. Take it. I'll remember this when I'm Master.

n_from.speaker: Vasile
n_from.text: From a town that taught me my place and then did not give me one. My father drank, my mother prayed and nobody did either well. I came here to be taken seriously.

n0.speaker: Teodor
n0.text: They say one of us goes down the stair at the end of the winter, my lord. They say it is chosen by the roll. They say the roll can be read by anyone with the key, and altered by anyone with ink. I have not said any of this.

n_ink.speaker: Teodor
n_ink.text: Everywhere, and nowhere. The Master leaves a pot out for the beginners and moves it every night. Look where a clerk would put it, and where a child would hide it.

n0.speaker: Maria
n0.text: I have learned to call the weather. It takes about three hundred hours and the loss of one's eyebrows. Do not look at me like that, prince. Do not look at any of us like that. We are all here for the same reason: nobody at home was going to teach us anything.

n_third.speaker: Maria
n_third.text: The Wolf-Tongue. In the spring the Master takes us out on the heath and teaches us to call the beasts of the wood. A wolf-tooth is the pledge. If you have ever fought wolves, they may remember you.

n0.speaker: The rite-altar
n0.text: Three hollows: a bowl, a disc, a lamp. Water, silver, flame. In what order do I begin?

n_bad.speaker: The rite-altar
n_bad.text: The hollow cracks with cold and the stone spits. The order is wrong. I must start again.

n_w.speaker: The rite-altar
n_w.text: Water in the bowl. The hollow drinks. What next?

n_ws.speaker: The rite-altar
n_ws.text: The disc settles. The stone hums. And last?

n_wsf.speaker: The rite-altar
n_wsf.text: The lamp lights without a match. The three hollows glow, and a cold calm falls on the room. I feel, for a moment, that I have been heard.

n0.speaker: The Roll
n0.text: A scroll as tall as a man. Ten names for this winter, in this order: Nicolae. Gheorghe. Vasile Cernat. Maria. Teodor. Anca. Bogdan. Lupu. Cosmin. And, last, in ink still wet: Vlad, Voivode of the Wallachians. The tenth to enter is the Devil's.

choices.text: [Dip the quill and write Vasile Cernat in the last place]
[I have no ink to change it]

n_forge.speaker: The Roll
n_forge.text: The quill scratches. I have made a name that was Vlad's into one that is not. I have made a tenth out of a man who did nothing but tell me the truth. The ink dries at once, and does not look wet or recent. The roll accepts it, as paper accepts anything.

n_noink.speaker: The Roll
n_noink.text: The last line is wet and sullen. A change would need ink, and I have none.

n0.speaker: The Master
n0.text: The winter is over. Ten stand in the ring. The roll is read. (He turns the scroll in the green light.)

n_self.speaker: The Master
n_self.text: The tenth to enter is the tenth to pay. It is you, Voivode: Vlad, son of Vlad, of the House of the Dragon. It is an honour of a kind. It is not an easy one.

choices.text: I will pay. It was my choice to come.
Take Vasile Cernat. He is the better scholar, and the weaker man.

n_pay.speaker: The Master
n_pay.text: (A long, slow smile.) Good. Hold my hand. Below the grate a sound like a great beast breathing grows loud, and then it gathers itself, and rises. When it reaches you, I think you will not scream. You will never scream again.

n_betray.speaker: The Master
n_betray.text: (Interested.) A prince's choice, quick and cold. Very well. The name, spoken in the ring, becomes the debt. Vasile, come. Do not weep: you have been a good scholar.

n_vasile.speaker: The Master
n_vasile.text: (He reads, and stops. His eyes, for a moment, flick to mine.) The tenth to enter is Vasile Cernat. (A pause.) Strange. I had remembered it otherwise. But the roll says what the roll says, and the debt follows the ink. A prince's art, Voivode. I should have guessed.

n_end.speaker: The Master
n_end.text: The term is ended. Whatever comes up that stair belongs to the Devil and the one he leaves behind. Take this book, Voivode. It teaches the speech of wolves and the weather. It is a poor payment for what you have just seen, and it is the one I give. Go home. Rule. You will not need to wait for death to find a kind of eternity.

do.card: He left the school with a book of black leather, a ring of pale grey rime that never melted from his hand, and a voice that wolves came to when he spoke. Some years later, the Turk crossed the river again and the Voivode rode out to meet him, and did not ride home. The boyars carried him back by night in a closed bier, and Father Dragomir said the office over him in a hurry, and sealed the vault with lead. They were wrong to think that this was the end of it.

n0.speaker: Ileana's tomb
n0.text: 'Ileana Corvin, who waited.' The ring on the stone is the silver ring I never gave her, which she must have had made herself.

n_ring.speaker: Ileana's tomb
n_ring.text: It is very small. I can close my fist around it. I do not know why that is the thing that finally does it.

n_stay.speaker: Ileana's tomb
n_stay.text: 'Say it again when you are in the doorway, Vlad,' she said. I am in the doorway. She is not here. I say it anyway.

n0.speaker: Father Dragomir
n0.text: (He tries to rise, and fails.) My lord. You are... You are cold. I sealed you myself. I said the office. And yet you stand there, and the candle does not move when you breathe. (He is quite still.) Forgive me. Are you my Voivode, or something he has become?

choices.text: I am your Voivode, Father. Tell me what has happened.

n_tell.speaker: Father Dragomir
n_tell.text: The Turks took the gate the night you were laid in the vault. The boyars have gone; Vlaicu to the Sultan, they say. I stayed. Someone had to. I took a spear in the side defending the door I ought to have barred, and I think, my lord, that I will not see the morning.

n_turks.speaker: Father Dragomir
n_turks.text: They have the courtyard and the gate, and the boyars have gone, Vlaicu to the Sultan, they say.

n_radu_s.speaker: Father Dragomir
n_radu_s.text: He rides with them, under the Sultan's green banner. You gave him his life, my lord, and he has used it to take yours.

n_radu_c.speaker: Father Dragomir
n_radu_c.text: He died in the cells, in the first cold. The village has not forgiven you, and does not mean to.

n_ileana.speaker: Father Dragomir
n_ileana.text: She waited, my lord. She came every morning to the tower. When the news came, she walked into the lake and the people found her ring on the shore. I buried her under the stone. You will see it. She said you would come back. She said it quite crossly.

n0.speaker: The altar
n0.text: I am standing at the altar of my own chapel, a hundred paces from where I was laid. A priest who may die by dawn lies against a pew. A wolf is howling in the hills; I understand it. I understand every word. And I am more thirsty than I have ever been. Nobody is here to tell me what to do. That, I think, is the whole point.

choices.text: [Take what I need from the dying priest]
[Go out to the hills and call the wolves]
[Kneel by Ileana's tomb and wait for the sun, whatever it may do]

n_priest.speaker: The Voivode
n_priest.text: He does not scream, which is the worst of it. He puts out one hand, as if to bless me, and then it falls. I think he understood. I think he forgave me. I cannot be sure which is the greater sin.

n_wolves.speaker: The Voivode
n_wolves.text: I open the doors and call, in a tongue taught under a mountain. They come out of the dark with their breath steaming, and I choose the weakest, an old one, whose time was nearly done. It is not what I wanted. It will keep a priest alive. It will keep the chapel's door unbarred.

n_vigil.speaker: The Voivode
n_vigil.text: I kneel by her stone with her ring in my fist and ask whatever I have become to wait for the sun. The sun rises. It does not kill me: it only turns the whole world to glass, and the priest, who is still alive, sees that I am weeping, and says my name, and dies.

ep_r_spared.speaker: The Voivode
ep_r_spared.text: A brother sent away alive, with a green banner at his back.

do.card: His brother Radu, whom he had spared, returned with the Sultan's army and was given the throne of Wallachia as a prize. He ruled it quietly, and was loved by nobody and feared by nobody. He died in bed. It was, in its way, the cruellest outcome.

ep_r_chained.speaker: The Voivode
ep_r_chained.text: A brother left to rot in a cell, and the village that watched me do it.

do.card: His brother Radu, whom he had chained, died in the cells within the winter, and his name was struck from the family roll. The castle's servants learned the new Voivode's justice and did not forget it. When the Turks came, nobody manned the walls with any enthusiasm.

ep_t_self.speaker: The Voivode
ep_t_self.text: I paid what I owed, in the coin I chose.

do.card: At the school, the Voivode had stood in the ring and taken the tithe upon himself. The Master was fascinated by this. Vasile Cernat, who lived and was a scholar to the end of his days, taught for a time at the Scholomance and left behind a book of lessons that Van Helsing would later read with a chill.

ep_t_vasile.speaker: The Voivode
ep_t_vasile.text: I paid what I owed with another man's life.

do.card: At the school, a name in wet ink had moved the tithe from one scholar to another. Vasile Cernat went down the stair and was not seen again. The Master never reproached the Voivode for it. It was a very princely art, and he set it among his best lessons.

ep_end.speaker: The Voivode
ep_end.text: The thirst, the choice, the debt. Seven hundred years, and not one day of them without the memory.

do.card: The Voivode rose at dusk, and fed on the only warm thing in the chapel. It was the first death for which he was, in the strictest sense, responsible. It would not be the last. By the time the Turks left the castle, he had gone into the hills, and the village learned to leave a door unbarred for the lord who no longer slept. Seven hundred years passed. The hunger did not.

The Voivode rose at dusk, and learned that the beasts of the hills would keep his secret. He fed on the old and the dying, and left the living to their hearths. The shepherds called him the Wolf-Lord, and their children's children told it to strangers, and in time Harker heard it. In the strictest sense, he never took a man's life. It was a very thin sense, and he knew it. Seven hundred years passed.

The Voivode rose with the sun and was not destroyed. He was something worse: the same man, with the same thirst, in a different world. At dusk he took Ileana's ring and went out. He did not feed that night, nor the next, nor for a long time, and he grew very strange and very sorrowful. Eventually he did, and the bell in the village was never rung for it. Seven hundred years passed.

n0.speaker: Cabman
n0.text: Morning, Mr. Harker. Where to? Your Mr. Hawkins has the cab-rank in his pocket, so I take it you are going somewhere dear.

choices.text: To the station - for the London train and the Museum.
To the station - and then, God willing, the East.
Not yet. I have a few things to finish.

n_london.speaker: Cabman
n_london.text: Paddington by the 9.15, then. The Museum is a step from the Underground. Mind the pickpockets in the Reading Room: they read, too.

do.card: By the morning train to London.

n_east.speaker: Cabman
n_east.text: The Great Western to town, sir, and the boat-train after that. You are the first man from this street who ever went so far. I'll tell your landlady you looked cheerful.

do.card:
THE SOLICITOR'S ROAD

By rail and river, through Munich and Vienna, to Bistritz and the Borgo Pass...

A month later: the castle.

n_wait.speaker: Cabman
n_wait.text: I am here until four, then the horse insists on his oats.

n0.speaker: Flower-seller
n0.text: Violets, sir? Penny a bunch. For Miss Murray, is it? She was by this morning for geraniums and told me you were off to a great foreign place.

n1.speaker: Flower-seller
n1.text: You walk like a man counting his steps to a station, sir. I've seen soldiers go to war with less spring.

n2.speaker: Flower-seller
n2.text: Modesty. And faithfulness. A gentleman about to go abroad could do worse than both.

n0.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
n0.text: Ah, Jonathan. Come in, come in. You look as though you had not slept. Are the Count's letters still on my desk? I should like you to master them before you go.

choices.text: Tell me again about the Count's commission.
I have the surveys, sir. Let me tell you which house will suit the Count.
The Count wants nothing but Carfax, I think. May I have my instructions?
Do you think I shall like Transylvania, sir?
Is there anything else I should know before I go?

task.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
task.text: A foreign nobleman, Count Dracula, has bought a house in England through us. He wants it large, old and solitary, with a chapel, a high wall, and no neighbours who can overlook him. The surveys are in the deed-box in the muniment room, but Pell has the key, and he will give it up only for good reasons.

choices.text: The Count's letters, sir - may I take them?

letters.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
letters.text: They are on the desk. Take them. Show them to Pell; he will not move without papers.

pick.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
pick.text: I am all attention. Which of the three would you recommend? He is a man of wealth and old habits, and he does not care to be watched.

choices.text: The Hampstead villa: handsome, but near a good deal of neighbours.
The house at Whitby: quiet, and by the sea.
Carfax at Purfleet: old, walled, with a chapel, a pond and only a madhouse for neighbour.
I need a little more time to study them.

wrong_hampstead.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
wrong_hampstead.text: Hampstead? The Count asks for seclusion; the villa has fourteen neighbours, a vicar and a bandstand. Look again at the surveys.

wrong_whitby.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
wrong_whitby.text: Whitby is a fine place, but it has no chapel, and a villa on the cliff is overlooked by half the town. Look again at the surveys.

right.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
right.text: Carfax. Yes. Ancient, enclosed by high stone, with the old chapel and a pond like a well. And the nearest house is Dr. Seward's asylum. A quiet neighbour, as the Count remarks. I think we have our man the house.

choices.text: Then I must go and see him in person, sir.

instr.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
instr.text: Quite right. The Count is no common client, and I am too old to travel. You are to go to Castle Dracula, find his house of business, and have the deed signed. Take these - a letter of credit and the particulars - and visit the British Museum before you leave: learn what you can of the country. And, Jonathan - say goodbye to Miss Murray.

think.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
think.text: A country of beauty and ignorance, I am told. Be careful what you eat, and keep your own counsel. The Count writes in a very good English, but the English of a man who has read much and spoken little.

farewell.speaker: Mr. Hawkins
farewell.text: Only this, my boy: when you are ready to marry that girl, do it quickly. I am old; I like to see good things done in good time. I shall give you a partnership when you return.

n0.speaker: Mr. Pell
n0.text: Mr. Harker. The muniment room is not a public thoroughfare. May I ask what business takes you there?

choices.text: Mr. Hawkins wants the Transylvanian surveys. Here are the Count's letters.
Why do you keep the key so close, Mr. Pell?
What do you think of the Count's letters?

give.speaker: Mr. Pell
give.text: Letters. Hmm. A good hand, a foreign seal, and a request in four pages. Yes, I see you are expected. Here. Lock up after you, and put the box key back where you found it; I hide it in the room itself.

why.speaker: Mr. Pell
why.text: In thirty-one years, Mr. Harker, nothing has been lost from that room. That is not luck; that is a chain.

opinion.speaker: Mr. Pell
opinion.text: A well-bred hand, and a seal with a wolf on it. I dislike a seal with a wolf on it. I have no reason. The ink is very black, and the paper very cold.

n0.speaker: Copy-book
n0.text: Nine letters of the firm's side of the correspondence, in Mr. Hawkins's own pressed copy. Which would you like?

l1.speaker: Letter 1
l1.text: 'My dear Sir: I am a foreigner who desires a house in England, near London, of ancient build, with ample grounds and a chapel. My friend Mr. Hawkins is recommended to me as a gentleman of probity. I am, Sir, yours truly, Dracula.'

l2.speaker: Letter 7
l2.text: 'The house must be large, secluded, well walled, old, and not overlooked. I care little for the comforts of modern life, but a pond or well, and a chapel are required. I am not young, and I have habits.'

l3.speaker: Letter 9
l3.text: 'I expect Mr. Harker at the Borgo Pass on the 5th of May. A carriage will await him. I trust he will not mind the journey, which is long; the people are simple, and their superstitions many. Be assured, I shall be a good host.'

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: Jonathan! You came, and in school hours. The headmistress has gone to the dentist, so we may talk, if we are quick and a little bit improper.

choices.text: I am going to Transylvania, Mina. A month, perhaps more.
Mina, I have something of my mother's to give you.
Mina, will you wait for me?
I should go. I just wished to see you.

go.speaker: Mina
go.text: I knew it, Jonathan. Mr. Hawkins told the whole parish. You will write to me. You will write to me every day, even if you cannot post it. Promise.

ring.speaker: Mina
ring.text: A ring? It was your mother's? Oh, Jonathan. Put it on, then - quickly, before I lose my nerve. No: keep it safe, Jonathan, for the day itself. I shall wear it on my finger then, and no sooner.

wait.speaker: Mina
wait.text: Wait? I should wait for a Pasha's decision, Jonathan, but for you I'll do it gladly. Take this. It is the ribbon from my hair; tie your diary with it, and write to me in shorthand, and I shall learn to read it faster than a clerk.

short.speaker: Mina
short.text: Look at the board. I wrote you a line in Pitman's: 'Come back safe.' It is quite the shortest sentence in the world, and the hardest to keep.

n0.speaker: Small pupil
n0.text: Are you Miss Murray's gentleman? She cries when she looks at the map. She says it is the chalk dust.

n1.speaker: Small pupil
n1.text: And she draws your name in the margin and rubs it out. I can read it, though. It begins with a J. Is it Jonah?

n0.speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
n0.text: Mr. Harker! The trunk has stood there since the day you came, and I shall be glad to see something done with it. A man should not live with a locked box in his bedroom. It is not healthy.

choices.text: Do you know where the combination might be?
What shall I do about the dreams, Mrs. Dunmore?

combo.speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
combo.text: Combination? Your father had it from the Admiralty, I was told, and he used it for the year he stopped sailing. A man puts the saddest year of his life in a lock like that. Ask the verger at St. Petroc's; he buried him.

pack.speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
pack.text: Then pack with what's in the trunk and what's on the table: your diary, the Count's papers and the notes from the Museum. I'll have the cab ready for the morning.

dream.speaker: Mrs. Dunmore
dream.text: Dreams? I never remember mine. I find it saves a deal of explaining at breakfast.

n0.speaker: Father's trunk
n0.text: A brass-bound trunk with a four-wheel lock. The wheels read 18-- . You must set the last two digits. What year did your father die?

choices.text: I do not remember. I shall find out.
(The trunk is open.) Look inside again.

bad.speaker: Father's trunk
bad.text: The wheels click, but the lock does not yield. It is not the right year. Somewhere there is a stone with the date on it.

good.speaker: Father's trunk
good.text: The wheels fall into place, and the hasp springs free. Inside: my mother's ring in a twist of tissue, my father's last letter to me, and a small crucifix. The smell of camphor and thirty years.

again.speaker: Father's trunk
again.text: The trunk is empty but for tissue and lavender. My mother's ring and my father's letter are in my pocket now.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: I lie down for an hour. In the half-sleep I see a long road winding up into mountains, and a lit window high on a rock. Somebody is standing in it, waiting. I do not know why that should make me afraid.

n0.speaker: Verger
n0.text: Harker, is it? I knew your father. A decent, tired man, and the fever took him in a week.

choices.text: What year did he die, Mr. Pascoe?

year.speaker: Verger
year.text: Read it from the stone, young sir; I'm not a clerk. It's the Harker stone by the yew. But I'll tell you this: it was the winter of the great frost, and the Exe froze to the bridge.

who.speaker: Verger
who.text: I do. And the one who leaves the snowdrops, I won't say, though I know. She has nice handwriting.

n0.speaker: Reading-table
n0.text: A heap of folios and one reader's lamp. What do you look up?

bradshaw.speaker: Bradshaw
bradshaw.text: Bradshaw's Continental Guide: Munich to Vienna, thence to Klausenburg and Bistritz. There is a ten-hour delay at Klausenburg. 'Passengers are advised to take their own provisions.' I mark the page.

n0.speaker: Superintendent
n0.text: Slip, pen, and a press-mark? We do not retrieve books by hope, sir.

choices.text: Press-mark K.7: Geography and Ethnology of the Carpathians.

bad.speaker: Superintendent
bad.text: That press-mark belongs to a treatise on cattle-breeding, sir. I recommend you consult the catalogue: the entry on Transylvania has a red ticket.

noslip.speaker: Superintendent
noslip.text: The tray of slips is by the catalogue. We are a library, sir, not a mind-reader.

good.speaker: Superintendent
good.text: K.7. Yes. A rare work, and a good one. I shall have it brought. You will find a table prepared.

end.speaker: Jonathan
end.text: I read for three hours. The country lies in the horseshoe of the Carpathians; it is a whirlpool of races, Saxon, Wallach, Magyar and Szekely; and the Szgany, who are its gypsies. The people believe in the Evil Eye. I copy what I can. I note a mention of the Borgo Pass, and a name, Dracula, which means 'son of the dragon' and 'devil'.

n0.speaker: Elderly reader
n0.text: You are reading the Carpathians, sir. Go no farther than the facts. The superstitions of that country are so numerous that every bridge has a ghost and every ghost a recipe.

choices.text: Do you know the Dracula family?
I'll leave you to your Hungarian wills.

n1.speaker: Elderly reader
n1.text: The Evil Eye, for one. At midnight on St. George's Eve every evil thing in the land is abroad. The peasants hang garlic over their doors, and leave wild roses at the cross.

n2.speaker: Elderly reader
n2.text: A voivode's line. One of them held the Danube against the Turk, and was either a hero or a devil according to which shore you lived on. The name means 'dragon'. I should not ask about it in the village.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: I lean from the sill and look down. A drop of three hundred feet, and a ledge. The Count went down this wall like a lizard, head first, with his cloak spread out. If I am to follow, I must know the way. What can I use?

choices.text: Try the handholds, starting with the ivy.
Try the handholds, starting with the iron ring.
Try the handholds, starting with the loose stone.
Wait. I must study the wall.

s1_ivy.speaker: Jonathan
s1_ivy.text: I catch the ivy and lower my weight. It holds, and I let myself down a foot at a time to the first anchor. Now: the iron ring, or the stone?

s1_ring.speaker: Jonathan
s1_ring.text: I try the ring first. My hand slips; the rust is smooth and I cannot reach the ivy. My fingers fail, and I scramble back to the sill, shaking.

s1_stone.speaker: Jonathan
s1_stone.text: I put my foot on the stone. It shifts, and a block falls into the dark, a long time before it strikes. I scramble back with my heart in my mouth.

s2_ring_after_ivy.speaker: Jonathan
s2_ring_after_ivy.text: The ring takes my weight. It is bright where a hand has used it. Now I can reach the stone with my toe.

s3_good.speaker: Jonathan
s3_good.text: The stone, which is loose only on the outside, takes my foot as it must. From there, the eastern corner is within reach. I cross the face on my belly, a foot at a time, and drop through the open window into the Count's room.

fall.speaker: Jonathan
fall.text: I put a hand wrong and lose my grip. For a moment I hang by one arm over the abyss before I scramble back to the sill. I will try again, in a better order: ivy first, then iron, then stone.

done.speaker: Jonathan
done.text: The window is waiting. I drop through into the room.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: The Count lies in the box, looking younger than I have ever seen him. His eyes are open and stony; there is a bloated look about him; his lips are red as if with blood. A key should be on him, but I do not find one.

choices.text: Search his pockets for the key.

search.speaker: Jonathan
search.text: I search him as one searches a dead man. No key. No watch, no purse; a few gold coins loose in a pocket, and nothing else. He does not move. I cannot bring myself to look at his face again.

strike.speaker: Jonathan
strike.text: I raise the spade, and his eyes turn toward me. The face is a mask of hate. I cannot do it. The spade slips from my hand and strikes the box, and I run.

n0.speaker: Footbridge
n0.text: The middle plank is gone, and the gully below is a black throat of water. A single plank, if you had one, might bridge it.

choices.text: Lay the plank across and cross.
Go back and look for something.

cross.speaker: Jonathan
cross.text: I lay the plank across and take it step by step with the roar of the water below. On the far side a track runs down toward a valley that is, God willing, the road to civilisation. My legs give way beneath me; I rest against a boulder and the dark comes down.

do.card:
Who can say how long, or by what road?

The next that Jonathan Harker knows is the smell of linen and the sound of a woman's voice, praying in German.

n0.speaker: Szgany woman
n0.text: Ah, the English gentleman, who walks on the mountain at night and is white as milk. Sit. Eat. The Count's people do not eat with us, but you are not one of his.

choices.text: May I ask about the Count?

food.speaker: Szgany woman
food.text: Gold of the old kings! That has not been seen in these hills for three hundred years. Take the bread and the goat-cheese, and a flask. I'll not ask where you found it, for I do not wish to know.

count.speaker: Szgany woman
count.text: We carry his boxes. We take his coin. We do not ask what is in them, nor why they are filled with earth. Our grandfathers bowed to his grandfathers, and we have kept the habit.

help.speaker: Szgany woman
help.text: I cannot take you down the mountain; the men will say I betrayed the master. But the herdsman by the woodpile may take you to the footbridge. He is not afraid of the old man.

n0.speaker: Slovak herdsman
n0.text: Dobry vecer, pan. You have the look of a man who has seen something in the castle. Hush! I do not need to hear what.

choices.text: Is there a way over the gully?

way.speaker: Slovak herdsman
way.text: Down the path, left at the cross, and over the gully by the old bridge. The plank is gone, but there is wood by the pile. You'll find a plank long enough.

bridge.speaker: Slovak herdsman
bridge.text: Plank, rope, courage. Courage you have, or you wouldn't be here. Plank is at the woodpile.

n0.speaker: Sister Agatha
n0.text: Sh, sh. Do not try to rise. You have been very ill, mein Herr, a brain fever, and you spoke much in your sleep, in English, of wolves and women and a wall. I was afraid.

choices.text: What day is it? What month?
My name is Jonathan Harker. I am an English solicitor.
Sister, I must write to a lady in England.
Sister, may I have my pocket-book and diary?
Sister, I want to seal my diary. I do not want to know what is in it.

where.speaker: Sister Agatha
where.text: In the Hospital of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary, in Buda-Pesth. A herd-boy found you on the road to Bistritz, weeks ago, and the doctors say you came by wagon and cart and charity. You are among friends.

when.speaker: Sister Agatha
when.text: It is the second week of September, mein Herr. You were brought in at the end of August. We counted every day.

name.speaker: Sister Agatha
name.text: Harker. Yes, the name was in your pocket-book, but you spoke it in your sleep, so I knew it was true. Rest. The doctor will see you at noon.

letter.speaker: Sister Agatha
letter.text: I will tell you what to write: the date, the place, that you are alive, and nothing more. Your friend must hear you are safe before she hears anything else. Use the writing-desk, mein Herr.

diary.speaker: Sister Agatha
diary.text: Your coat is torn. Your diary is in the lining. I have not read it; it is in shorthand, and I'm only a Sister. Take it from the patient's chest.

seal.speaker: Sister Agatha
seal.text: You give it to me to seal? No - to your friend. That is better. I shall pour the wax, if you will say the words. Give me the ribbon and the book.

choices.text: Do it for me. I cannot bear to touch it.

sealed_ok.speaker: Sister Agatha
sealed_ok.text: There. The ribbon is Miss Murray's, I think? Red-white. The wax is the chapel's. Now say it, mein Herr: why do you not want to read it?

choices.text: Because I do not know whether it was a dream, or whether I went mad. I will not know unless some solemn duty come upon me.

vow.speaker: Sister Agatha
vow.text: That is the vow, then. Not to read it, and not to doubt it, unless duty. Hold the book. I shall say a prayer.

n0.speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
n0.text: Ah, you are awake and sane. Good. I will tell you plainly: it was brain fever of the severest. You will not remember the first three weeks, and I advise you not to try.

said.speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
said.text: You spoke of a castle in the mountains, of wolves, of women with red lips, and of a man who walks down a wall. I took it for delirium. Sister Agatha did not.

write.speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
write.text: By all means. Here, you may keep my pen. A letter soothes the mind better than any bromide.

leave.speaker: Dr. Hartenstein
leave.text: When the lady arrives, and we have married you, and not before. I shall not release an unmarried man in your condition.

n0.speaker: Magyar patient
n0.text: You are the Englishman. You shouted in the night. In German, in English, and once in what I think was Latin. Do you remember?

choices.text: Go back to sleep, old man.

n1.speaker: Magyar patient
n1.text: There are many castles. Only one of them you should not name. Do not name it. It has ears.

n2.speaker: Magyar patient
n2.text: Then you are fortunate. I broke my leg falling from a cart, and I remember every pain.

n0.speaker: Jonathan
n0.text: I lie down on the clean linen and close my eyes. The ward is quiet. At the edge of sleep I hear a soft laughter, like silver bells, and three women are in the moonlight: two dark, with hooked noses like the Count, one fair as the sun with great wavy hair. I feel a wicked, burning desire that they would kiss me with those red lips.

n1.speaker: Jonathan
n1.text: I wake with the sheet in my fists, drenched in sweat. A hand cools my forehead: Sister Agatha. 'You said the word again,' she says. 'It was a woman's name. Not a good one.' I hold her hand until the fear passes.

n2.speaker: Jonathan
n2.text: This time the women stand back. One of them turns her head, and for a moment she has Mina's eyes, then no eyes at all. I wake knowing that I shall never again be quite at ease in sleep. A cab-wheel sounds in the courtyard. It is morning, and a woman is on the stairs.

do.card: Three days later.

n0.speaker: Writing-desk
n0.text: A sheet of hospital paper and the doctor's pen. What shall I write to Mina?

choices.text: 'I am safe, in Buda-Pesth, in the care of the Sisters. I am ill, but mending. I love you.'
'I have terrible things to tell you.'

ok.speaker: Jonathan
ok.text: I fold the letter, and Sister Agatha writes under mine: 'He is well, but weak, and he asks that you come.' She seals it herself. 'Mr. Hawkins will be told,' she says. 'And your friend will not read a word that frightens her.'

bad.speaker: Jonathan
bad.text: I stare at the page, and the pen shakes. I cannot say it; she must not read it. I cross it out, and begin again.

n0.speaker: Mina
n0.text: Jonathan. Oh, Jonathan. Sister Agatha has told me everything; she has also told me nothing that matters. I am here. I am not going away.

choices.text: Mina, I have something to ask.
Mina, I have my diary. I cannot read it. Will you keep it?
Mina, a Sister says the chaplain can marry us tomorrow.

ask.speaker: Mina
ask.text: Ask, then. I have come across the sea, and I have six hours of train in my bones.

choices.text: Will you marry me, here, as soon as you are rested?

yes.speaker: Mina
