yes.text: I will marry you tomorrow. Today if the chaplain could be found. But one condition: that you let me take care of you. And that you tell me, one day, what it was that frightened you.

journal.speaker: Mina
journal.text: A sealed book? You wish me to keep it, unread, and to give it back only if some solemn duty comes upon us? I will, Jonathan. I do not need to know what is in it. I know what is in you.

wed.speaker: Mina
wed.text: Then let us be married. I will find Sister Agatha and the white roses.

n0.speaker: Old gardener
n0.text: The Herr Englishman. I have seen you in your chair on the third bench every afternoon this week. You look better. The cherry-trees are better than the roses; roses are tricky.

choices.text: May I cut a rose for my fiancee?
What flowers do the Sisters prefer?

rose.speaker: Old gardener
rose.text: A white one. White for a wedding, and white for a funeral, but never red; red is for the bold.

flowers.speaker: Old gardener
flowers.text: Lilies for Our Lady. Roses for St. Joseph, who never asked for any. Sage for the kitchen, rue for the fever.

n0.speaker: Young convalescent
n0.text: You are the English one. They say you came with your hair white and your coat in ribbons.

n1.speaker: Young convalescent
n1.text: A white streak, Sister Agatha says. She calls it a mark of grace. I think you look like a pirate.

n0.speaker: Altar
n0.text: The altar is bare but for a vase of white roses and two brass candlesticks. A prayer-book lies open.

choices.text: Write a letter to my parents.

write.speaker: Jonathan
write.text: I write at the altar-rail: 'Father, Mother: I have been far from home, and nearly did not come back. I found your letter again - you never said that you were proud of me, but I knew. I am to be married. I wish you could see her. I wish you could see me now, and not the boy who ran along the Exe with a kite.' I fold it, and my hand is steadier than it has been in weeks.

kneel.speaker: Jonathan
kneel.text: I kneel. I do not pray in words; I only think of the long road that brought me here, and of the chain of kindly hands: a herdsman, a carter, a Sister. I am not yet quite sane, but I am nearer.

n0.speaker: English chaplain
n0.text: You are the young man from Exeter. I have been sent a letter by your Mr. Hawkins, who writes, I may say, a very fine hand.

choices.text: Is it permitted, in a hospital chapel?

perm.speaker: English chaplain
perm.text: With the Sisters' leave, and the doctor's, and the Bishop's lack of objection, which I have in writing. It is not usual, but it is not forbidden. Come back when the lady is ready.

yes.speaker: English chaplain
yes.text: Gladly. Is there a ring? A bride must have a ring.

choices.text: I have my mother's ring, sir.

n0.speaker: English chaplain
n0.text: Dearly beloved. We are gathered together in the sight of God, in a little white chapel in a foreign city, to join together this man and this woman. If any man can show just cause...

vows.speaker: English chaplain
vows.text: Jonathan, wilt thou have this woman to thy wedded wife, to live together after God's ordinance?

mina_vows.speaker: Mina
mina_vows.text: I will. For better, for worse, and for the unspoken things in the sealed book.

ring.speaker: Jonathan
ring.text: I slip my mother's ring on her hand. It fits. Sister Agatha weeps openly into her veil. The chaplain says the final words; the white roses breathe in the candlelight; and the world, which has been a nightmare for so long, is only a room full of people who love us.

final.speaker: Mina
final.text: Now we are husband and wife, Jonathan. Whatever comes. Whatever you saw, we shall face it together, and perhaps the sealed book can stay sealed for ever. 'Unless some solemn duty come upon us.'

do.card:
Jonathan Harker and Mina Murray were married in the hospital chapel in Buda-Pesth on the twelfth of September.

Their journey home was long. Ahead, there was a house at Purfleet; a girl called Lucy; and a sealed book that would be opened at last.

But that is another story.

n0.speaker: Hannah
n0.text: Miss Lucy! Mrs. Westenra says there are to be gentlemen to tea and the parlour vase is to be a credit to the house. And the flowers want doing properly, if I may say so.

choices.text: How do you arrange a vase properly, Hannah?
What do you think of my gentlemen, Hannah?

n_rule.speaker: Hannah
n_rule.text: Mrs. Westenra's rule, miss, and her mother's before her: height at the back, then the middle, then the shortest in front, so the eye can walk in. Lilies behind, rose between, little blue things before.

n_men.speaker: Hannah
n_men.text: I think the doctor will bring a book, and the American will bring a horse, and Mr. Holmwood will bring his whole heart in his two hands and not know where to put it. I'd say that last is the one for you, miss, but it's not for the likes of me to say.

n0.speaker: Mamma
n0.text: Lucy, there is a tea at four and a vase that looks as though it has been in a fight. I want a bouquet in this room before the doctor comes, and I shall not be put off with half the garden in a jam-jar.

choices.text: What do you want in the vase, Mamma?
Mamma, may we speak of Whitby?
I am very tired today, Mamma.

n_flowers.speaker: Mamma
n_flowers.text: Flowers, child. White lilies, a wild rose from the arbour, and the forget-me-nots Mina sent seed for. Arrange them yourself; you have the best eye in Hillingham and the worst patience.

n_tired.speaker: Mamma
n_tired.text: You have been tired all spring, my darling, and rosy with it. It is the gentlemen. When they are settled you will sleep like a log. (She pats my cheek, and her hand is trembling a little.)

n_bq.speaker: Mamma
n_bq.text: Oh, Lucy. It is exactly right. The lilies stand up, the rose looks out, and the little blue things hold hands in front. I could weep. Take Mina's key; I have been keeping it from you since Tuesday for no reason except that I like to be asked.

n_whitby.speaker: Mamma
n_whitby.text: Whitby! Mina has been scribbling about it for weeks, and the sea air will do you good, and so shall poor Mrs. Murray's gossip. Pack your trunk, Lucy. The Crescent is taken, and I shall travel with you.

do.card: In the summer Lucy went to Whitby, with her mother and her best friend, and a trunk full of white frocks. She took a bright laugh with her, and the sea took notice.

n0.speaker: Lucy
n0.text: A green jar, empty. I have the stalks to fill it, if I have the flowers.

n_miss.speaker: Lucy
n_miss.text: I need three things: white lilies, a wild rose and forget-me-nots. All in the garden, if I know the garden.

n_back.speaker: Lucy
n_back.text: Which flowers go at the back of the jar, to stand highest?

n_wrong_back.speaker: Lucy
n_wrong_back.text: I put it there, and it sinks. The jar looks lopsided and apologetic. The tallest should be at the back, I think, so the others can lean on it.

n_mid.speaker: Lucy
n_mid.text: And in the middle, standing between the lilies and the front?

n_wrong_mid.speaker: Lucy
n_wrong_mid.text: The forget-me-nots flop forward like little blue sleepers and the rose is left behind them. I take them out. The middle is the rose's.

choices.text: The forget-me-nots, in a fringe at the front.
Nothing; leave it with its lilies and its rose.

n_wrong_front.speaker: Lucy
n_wrong_front.text: It looks bare. There is a rule against bare vases, and I am married to rules at the moment. The blue ones go in front.

n_done.speaker: Lucy
n_done.text: I stand back and look. The tall lilies stand and the wild rose looks out between them, and the small blue things hold hands in the front. It is the first thing I have done well all spring.

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: Miss Westenra... Lucy. I came to speak to you. I have a note somewhere, but I think I had better say it myself. I have thought of nothing else. I should like very much to ask for your hand.

n_ask.speaker: Lucy
n_ask.text: He is the dearest man, and I cannot marry him. But what shall I say?

choices.text: Not yet, John. Ask me again in a year, and I'll see how I feel.
Dr. Seward, I like you better than almost anyone, and I cannot marry you. I will not keep you hoping.
You are far too grave for me, John! You would bury me in your casebooks.

n_hope.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_hope.text: A year. Yes. Of course. I shall wait. I am a patient man, you know; it is the whole of my profession. (He smiles, and my heart sinks, because I have given him a hook to hang a year on.)

n_cruel.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_cruel.text: ...I see. I beg your pardon. (He turns his hat in his hands, and says nothing, and I am ashamed of myself for the rest of the day.)

n_right.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_right.text: Thank you. That was kind, and it was plain, and I would rather have it so than the other way. I knew, I think, before I asked. May I still be your friend?

choices.text: Always. You will be Jack to me as long as you like.

n_end.speaker: Dr. Seward
n_end.text: Then I shall go and be of use to someone. Good day, Lucy. Be happy; it is a medical prescription.

n0.speaker: Quincey Morris
n0.text: Miss Lucy. I'll be as brief as a Texan can. I've ridden a long way and shot a few things and I'd like to ask if you'd take me on as a husband. That's the whole speech. The rest is for you.

n_ask.speaker: Lucy
n_ask.text: I must not make him sit through a speech. But I must not be too short either.

choices.text: Mr. Morris, one cannot speak so quickly of such things, and one must consider the whole situation, and the position, and one's dear Mamma, and the prospects, and...
No, Mr. Morris. I am sorry. I am proud you asked, and I should like us to be friends.
Perhaps, if you were to stay in England a few more months, I might think of it.

n_long.speaker: Quincey Morris
n_long.text: That's a heap of words, ma'am, for what I reckon is a no. I'd have gone easier with the plain article. (He takes off his hat, and puts it on again.)

n_hope.speaker: Quincey Morris
n_hope.text: More months? Hell, Miss Lucy, I'd stay years. I'd stay till the Thames froze over. (He is smiling. I have just made a very kind, very stupid mistake.)

n_right.speaker: Quincey Morris
n_right.text: No hard feelings, ma'am. A man gets to say it, and a woman gets to say the other, and neither of us gets to be sorry for the saying. But if you ever want a man to ride out in the rain for you, you whistle.

choices.text: I shall whistle badly, Quincey, but I shall whistle.

n_end.speaker: Quincey Morris
n_end.text: That's the girl. Now, I reckon there's a gentleman waiting for you behind that rose-bush who's been standing there for half an hour. Good luck, Miss Lucy.

n0.speaker: Arthur Holmwood
n0.text: Lucy... I had a long speech and I've dropped it somewhere in the lilies. I only want to ask whether you could be happy with me. If you could, I should be the most fortunate man in England. If you couldn't, I should try to deserve it.

n_ask.speaker: Lucy
n_ask.text: I do not need a speech either. I only need to be myself for once, and plain.

choices.text: I must ask Mamma, Arthur, and then I shall tell you, at some convenient time next week.
Yes, Arthur. Plainly, and you shall not have to ask a second time.
Ask me tomorrow. I shall think it over.

n_mamma.speaker: Arthur Holmwood
n_mamma.text: Of course. Mrs. Westenra. Next week. (His face is a perfect picture of a man who has been ordered to stand in the rain.)

n_think.speaker: Arthur Holmwood
n_think.text: Tomorrow. Yes. I shall be at the Station Hotel and I shall not sleep. (And I know, watching him go white, that I have done wrong, and I want to run after him.)

n_right.speaker: Arthur Holmwood
n_right.text: Lucy! ...Lucy. (He takes my hand, and discovers the rose in his buttonhole, and puts it in my hair, and I laugh until I cry.) My mother's ring is in my pocket. May I?

n_end.speaker: Lucy
n_end.text: It is a small old ring with a pale stone, and it fits. I wish, oh I wish one girl could marry all three of them. Jack, who sees what is wrong; Quincey, who is the one you want in a storm; Arthur, who is the one you want at home. But there is only one of me, and I have said yes to the one I love.

n0.speaker: Lucy
n0.text: A desk, a window and the best light in the house. Mina's letters are always so careful. Mine always have the postscript first.

choices.text: I have nothing to tell her yet.
I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.
I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.
I need ink, paper and Mina's last letter first.

n_notyet.speaker: Lucy
n_notyet.text: I have nothing settled to tell her. Not about the gentlemen, anyway. I shall come back when my heart has stopped changing its mind.

n_missing.speaker: Lucy
n_missing.text: The ink from my room, the paper from Mamma's escritoire, and Mina's own letter to answer. It is in the left-hand drawer.

n_read.speaker: Mina
n_read.text: 'Dearest Lucy, you must tell me everything, but not in the order it comes to you, for your letters are all middle. do.card: She did not know it, but it was the first time she had walked into that country on purpose. Years later, in a London drawing-room, the Professor would say: 'Where are you now, Madam Mina? What do you hear?' And she would answer him with the very words she found tonight.

a.speaker: Mina

a.speaker: Mina
a.text: The great timber groans as the hull settles. It has a voice, long and patient, like an old man shifting in his sleep. I listen until I can tell it from my own heartbeat. Wood, the second of the three.

I shall tell no one. Not yet.

do.card: The Typewriter and the Trance. She kept the ribbon from the Remington and the notebook from Whitby in the same drawer, and neither was ever empty of use. When Dr. Seward's asylum, the Count's Carfax and a ship called the Demeter drew the threads together, she knew the sound of the dark, because she had been listening to it for years.

do.card: One year later. The Pampas of Argentina, winter 1885. Arthur Holmwood and Jack Seward, my friends, had asked me to hunt with them in the south. Santa Fe came too.

do.card: Years later, in London, a Dutch doctor with a pointed beard spoke of bats at a window and a girl who grew pale. I did not need him to say the word. I said it myself. I had already seen it on the Pampas, and I had not forgotten.

do.say: Hodge's arms are like a barrel's hoops. He holds me till the strength runs out of me, and then he opens the door as gently as though I had been a child. I hate him for it. I hate myself rather more.

choices.text: A drop of something, Mr. Hodge, for your nerves. I could not drink it myself. You have been so kind.

sleep.speaker: Hodge
sleep.text: None of us can, sir. Go on, now. Back to your room, and I'll bring you a cup of cocoa.

brandy.speaker: Hodge
brandy.text: Well. Well, that's very handsome of you, sir. Just the one, mind. For the damp. I never saw you do a mean thing in all the time I've known you, not once, whatever they write in the book...

do.say: He drinks, sighs, sets his chin on his chest. In five minutes he is breathing like a bellows, and the keys on his belt do not stir. I tell myself I have done him no harm. A man should be allowed to sleep.

n0.speaker: Mr. Quill
n0.text: Seven, seven, seven. One, two, three. Do you know, Mr. Renfield, that in this room there are nine lamps? I counted them as a boy of ten at my mother's. They all go out at the same hour, and still I count.

choices.text: How many beds are in this room?

beds.speaker: Mr. Quill
beds.text: Seven beds. Seven. You'd say eight, because of the one by the stair, but it isn't a bed. It's a bier.

windows.speaker: Mr. Quill
windows.text: Three, with bars, and a fourth that is only a painting of one. The doctor calls them 'inventory'. He puts them in his book in the order: beds, windows, lamps. A tidy man, the doctor.

why.speaker: Mr. Quill
why.text: Because if I stop, sir, I begin to think about the things that can't be counted. And those are what put me in here.

n0.speaker: Mr. Ashby
n0.text: Renfield. You were once Mr. Renfield of the firm, I think. A good house. There is a crest on your handkerchief, and in my day we did not carry the crest of a bad house in our pockets.

choices.text: I was a man of business once, Mr. Ashby. My father kept a good library.
Do you hear the voice, Mr. Ashby?

family.speaker: Mr. Ashby
family.text: I knew it. One can tell a man of breeding by what he does with the cutlery. Whatever they say of you, you have never once been vulgar. Hold to that, Renfield. It is the only furniture we are permitted to bring in with us.

voice.speaker: Mr. Ashby
voice.text: The voice? My dear fellow. Everyone in this house hears a voice. Mine tells me the price of consols. Yours, I think, promises you something. Be careful what you accept from a voice that has never once been in need.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: The ward inventory, under glass, in Dr. Seward's hand: 'Beds, 7. Windows (barred), 3. Lamps, 9. Clock, 1 (defective).' And below it, in a fainter pencil, 'Sugar ration: Press, key by dial. Do not tell R.'

copy.speaker: Renfield
copy.text: Seven. Three. Nine. In that order, beds, windows, lamps. I never forget a figure. It is the last sane thing about me.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: The linen-press, with its three brass wheels. The sugar ration is in there, and with it the whole of my little world of flies.

bad.speaker: Renfield
bad.text: The wheels turn and stop. The press does not budge. An error of arithmetic; I will not make another.

good.speaker: Renfield
good.text: Seven. Three. Nine. The wheels click, the latch drops and there it is, on a blue paper, fine as snow: a lump of sugar. Just one. Dr. Seward counts them. I count him.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: A case-book open on the blotter: 'R. M. Renfield, aet. 59. Zoophagous (life-eating) maniac. Sanguine temperament, great physical strength, morbid selfishness. Collects: flies (sugar), spiders, sparrows, a cat. Keeps accounts. Perfectly lucid on matters of family and law.'

more.speaker: Renfield
more.text: 'His dread of the unseen is genuine. He does not lie. He says a Master will come for the lives, and that he has been promised a great number. I do not know what to make of a delusion so well-regulated. He is the only patient who thanks me for my notes.'

n0.speaker: Dr. Seward
n0.text: Renfield. Good morning. Sit, if you wish. I confess I did not expect to see you out and about so early. You look, if I may say, like a man who has not slept.

choices.text: [Ask to be moved from this house]
[Ask what the doctor thinks of the notes]

notes.speaker: Dr. Seward
notes.text: My notes? I note what I see. You collect, you count, and you cannot be argued out of the account. I find it rather admirable and I do not know what to do with it.

ask.speaker: Dr. Seward
ask.text: Moved? Where? This is a good house, as houses go, and I have no other bed.

choices.text: He is coming, doctor. I feel him through the wall. I beg you, send me away before he comes! [Raving]

bad.speaker: Dr. Seward
bad.text: I see. 'He is coming.' It is a symptom, Renfield, I wish it were not; I wish you could say it to me without rolling your eyes. I will note it. Come back when you can tell me what you mean in plain figures.

good.speaker: Dr. Seward
good.text: Your ledger. Good God, man. Every fly, every sparrow, in a clerk's hand. It is a perfectly rational document, and I have never read a sadder one. Very well. I shall move you to the quiet wing on Monday, and I want no more of this 'Master'. Take this note to the day-room; Hodge will see it honoured.

wary.speaker: Dr. Seward
wary.text: You are the man who raised his voice at Hodge this morning, Renfield. But this ledger is the first honest thing you have shown me. Very well, Monday, the quiet wing. Hodge will keep an eye on you; you will not mind.

thanks.speaker: Dr. Seward
thanks.text: Do not thank me yet. Monday is Monday. Try to be quiet tonight, Renfield. It is a thing I can say to you without writing it down.

n0.speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
n0.text: Mr. Renfield! Get along with you, out from under my feet. Though if you've the wit for it, I've a riddle. Sing a song of sixpence, a pocket full of rye; four and twenty blackbirds, baked in a...?

choices.text: Why do you keep the cat so fat, Mrs. Pargeter?

wrong.speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
wrong.text: Ha. No, no, no. Not that. The nursery rhyme, dear. I had a brother who told it the wrong way too, God rest him, and they put him in a place like this one.

cat.speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
cat.text: He earns it, the beast. He's the bravest in the house, sir. Eats whatever the garden sends, and sleeps in the warm. I keep him fat so he doesn't need to hunt.

pie.speaker: Mrs. Pargeter
pie.text: ...Baked in a pie! There, you've a head on your shoulders. Now: Doctor says you're not to have anything stronger than cocoa, and I say a man who can finish a rhyme can have a drop in a cup for his nerves. Take it, hide it, and do not tell the Doctor that Cook says so.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: The cot, and the grey blanket. It is early afternoon and the whole house is waiting for something.

choices.text: [Think what a prudent man needs before the dark]

notyet.speaker: Renfield
notyet.text: A prudent man gets his house in order before the dark: a key to the garden, a drop of brandy for the keeper. And a ward to wait for, only when I hold them all.

wait.speaker: Renfield
wait.text: I lie down and let the afternoon pass over me. When I wake the lamps are lit and the house is quiet. Somewhere a bell strikes ten.

do.card: That night, at Purfleet.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: I crouch behind the water-butt, in the wet. The night-man's lantern comes along the gravel, swinging. He is walking out to the far wall.

choices.text: [Run for the wicket now, while he is walking away]
[Wait until he has stopped under the far lamp and bent over his pipe]

run.speaker: Renfield
run.text: I get three strides before the lantern swings round. 'Who's that?' I am back behind the butt with my heart in my mouth. He turns again. The lantern goes on.

late.speaker: Renfield
late.text: I wait, and wait. He does not go in; he is on the bench with his pipe. It is a long, cold, wet quarter of an hour. Nothing has changed.

wait.speaker: Renfield
wait.text: He reaches the far wall, stops under the lamp, bends to his pipe, a match flaring in his cupped hands. His back is to me. I cross twelve yards of gravel in my stockinged feet, and not a stone speaks.

n0.speaker: The Voice
n0.text: Renfield. You have come. You have kept my books faithfully, and I have kept my promise. I told you: lives. Not flies, not spiders, not a bird in the grass: lives. Great ones. Do you hold something for me?

choices.text: [Offer the sparrow: 'Yes, Master. A life, as you taught me.']
[Say: 'I have totalled the ledger. It does not close, Master. You owe me, not I you.']
[Write something for Dr. Seward on the altar cloth]
[Say you have nothing yet, and withdraw]

note.speaker: Renfield
note.text: I tear a clean page from the back of the ledger and write, in the clerk's hand I have never lost: 'Doctor, he is real. The box is in the chapel. Do not come alone. Garlic, a cross, and the sunlight. I am sorry for the trouble. R. M. R.' I tuck it beneath the candle where the morning will find it.

loyal.speaker: The Voice
loyal.text: Ahh. Yes. Good servant. Give it me, and the bird shall be the first of many. Seven, then seventy, then seven thousand. You have only to be faithful.

loyal_end.speaker: Renfield
loyal_end.text: I do what I have done a hundred times. It is a small, warm, brief thing and it is over before the voice has finished its blessing. And then there is no blessing: only the pale smell of earth, and a feather on my thumb, and the silence of a house that has taken what it asked for and will give nothing back.

do.card: In the morning they found Mr. Renfield asleep on the chapel floor with a feather in his hand. He said very little. He did not eat for two days, and then he asked, very civilly, for a clean ledger. He never again counted a fly. Dr. Seward wrote it down. He did not write down what it cost him to see it.

refuse.speaker: The Voice
refuse.text: You dare. You, who ate a thousand little lives in my name! You are mine, Renfield. You are a vessel, a thing I fill. What is one sparrow to a man who has eaten ten thousand?

choices.text: [Stand quite still. 'I am Renfield. I was a man of business, and I have totalled the account. Nothing is owed.']
[Scream at it, strike the altar, and beat the box till my knuckles split]

calm_end.speaker: Renfield
calm_end.text: The word 'Renfield' goes through the chapel like a coin on stone. The voice thins. I cross to the broken window, open my hands, and the sparrow shakes itself once, and flies out of my fingers and over the wall into the grey. It does not look back. It is the best bookkeeping I have ever done.

do.card: In the morning they found Mr. Renfield in the chapel, wide awake and quite calm, with a torn page beside him and nothing in his hands. He asked for Dr. Seward, and he was gentle with Hodge. In his last hour he gave the doctor what a sick man has to give: a little courage, a little brandy and the truth. Seward never forgot it.

frenzy_end.speaker: Renfield
frenzy_end.text: I roar. I beat the lid until the voice is a sound like paper tearing, and when I come to myself I am on my knees with split hands, and the sparrow is still alive, trembling in the crook of my arm. I lift it to the window. It goes, in a flurry. I laugh, I think, or weep.

do.card: In the morning they found Mr. Renfield in the chapel, bruised, bleeding and quite awake. He asked for Dr. Seward and said, 'I have been a long time wrong, doctor, but I think I have been right once.' In his last hour he repaid it as best he could. Seward never forgot him.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: The phonograph waits, the wax cylinder in its place, the horn turned toward me like an ear.

what.speaker: Seward
what.text: It records a voice, so that I do not need to write by candlelight. I have kept a diary since I first saw a ward, but I cannot yet say a thing aloud and let it stand. The machine keeps its counsel better than I do.

rec1.speaker: Seward
rec1.text: 'Twenty-fifth May. Lucy Westenra has refused me. She was gentle, and clear, and entirely right. I do not blame her, nor Arthur, nor myself, which is a nuisance, since a man wants someone to blame. I shall not sleep. I shall dose myself with chloral, in the proper measure, and be a better doctor for it.'

rec2.speaker: Seward
rec2.text: I let the cylinder run out. The voice that comes back is thinner than my own, and braver.

fin1.speaker: Seward
fin1.text: Dawn comes grey over Purfleet. The dispensary is a black ruin of one shelf, Pettit is bargaining with his conscience in the ward, and Renfield sleeps in Room 12 with his sugar untouched. I wind the cylinder and begin.

fin2.speaker: Seward
fin2.text: 'Case notes, the twenty-sixth. A night in which three things went wrong and none was the worst. I used judgment where I might have used force, medicine where I might have used a stick, and nerve, I hope, where I might have run. I write this partly for the Board, but chiefly for myself, who must not forget it.'

fin3.speaker: Seward
fin3.text: 'I shall write to Van Helsing in Amsterdam tomorrow. He taught me that a doctor's chief duty is to doubt himself carefully. I shall tell him that I doubted, and went on.'

choices.text: [Seal the cylinder and end the night]

do.card: Within a fortnight Lucy would be pale, and Arthur would send a telegram, and Dr. Seward would write, with a hand he did not quite trust, to Amsterdam. But that was later. This night he had kept his house, his patients and his head, and that was enough to be going on with.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: Lucy's note, on thick cream paper in her round, schoolgirl hand. It has been folded and unfolded until the creases are soft.

n1.speaker: Lucy (letter)
n1.text: 'Dear Dr. Seward, I cannot say what you wish. You have been kind and gentle and clever, and I would not lose your friendship for the world. But I am promised, in my heart, to another, and it would be cruel to let you hope. Please do not think the less of me. Lucy.'

n2.speaker: Seward
n2.text: I stood in the Hillingham drawing-room with my hat in my hand and she said it more kindly than I deserved. I said I understood. I said I wished her happy. I said it twice, to be sure that I had.

choices.text: Keep it. A doctor should keep his case-notes.

burn.speaker: Seward
burn.text: I hold it to the candle. And I cannot. I fold it back along the creases and put it in the drawer, which is a different kind of weakness, but a more honest one.

keep.speaker: Seward
keep.text: I shall keep it. It is no use to anyone, which is the best reason I know for keeping a thing.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: The armchair, with a dent in it the shape of my sleeplessness.

choices.text: [Not yet. There is more work in the house]

go.speaker: Seward
go.text: I have the draught measured, the letters read, and Renfield's secret half understood. If I am to sit up with any of it, it may as well be tonight.

do.card: Purfleet. Two in the morning.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: A bundle of letters from Amsterdam in a crabbed, forceful hand. Van Helsing, my old master.

l1.speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
l1.text: 'My dear John. On the chloral, remember the three lines I taught you. Fifteen grains for a woman or a frail man; twenty for a strong man in his full strength; never more than thirty for anyone; and sixty is not a sedative but a funeral. Weigh twice. A sleepy patient is a patient; a sleeping doctor is a catastrophe.'

l2.speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
l2.text: 'John, you doubt too much, and then you believe too much, and the middle you never visit. Believe nothing because I say it; doubt nothing because you have not seen it. Write it all down, and then look at what is written. Madness is often a theory the world has not yet been told.'

l3.speaker: Van Helsing (letter)
l3.text: 'You thanked me again in your last. I do not recall that winter's dying, John. I recall only that you sat for three nights with a man who was nothing to you, and that I could not leave a fever to do what you had not allowed it. You owe me nothing. But if you wish to pay, then be to some other sleepless fool what I was to you.'

n0.speaker: Hennessey
n0.text: Good afternoon, sir. All quiet, bar Mr. Pym, who is taking an interest in the weather again.

choices.text: Why is the ward clock stopped?
Can you write the ward log tonight, if I am busy?

ward.speaker: Hennessey
ward.text: Mr. Pym, the watchmaker; Miss Vane, who writes letters to a man who died in India; old Mr. Greer, who sits in the garden talking to the sea. And Number Twelve, sir, who you know. All good as gold, so long as the weather holds.

clock.speaker: Hennessey
clock.text: Ah. That was Mrs. Pym's clock. Stopped at ten past three, the hour she went, and he's never allowed it touched. Not once. If you tell him you know what the hour was, I think he might be persuaded. But only just.

key.speaker: Hennessey
key.text: Safe, sir. I've put it where Mr. Pym would never let anyone look. That's the safest place in the house.

mark.speaker: Hennessey
mark.text: I'd be glad to, sir, but I can't, being no scholar. I sign with my mark, and a bad one. Mother couldn't spare me to the school. The log's best left to Nurse Dowling.

n0.speaker: Mr. Pym
n0.text: Don't touch it. Don't touch the clock. It is quite right. It has been right ever since.

choices.text: Why is it stopped, Mr. Pym?
It stopped at ten past three, the hour your wife died.

why.speaker: Mr. Pym
why.text: Because it is my clock, doctor, and it has told the time quite long enough.

key.speaker: Mr. Pym
key.text: ...Who told you? Hennessey. He is a kind man and a poor liar. Ten past three, in the morning. I had the watch in my hand, and I counted her breaths, and they stopped. I was a watchmaker forty years and I could not mend that.

choices.text: It need not stay stopped. A clock that runs again is not a clock that forgets.

give.speaker: Mr. Pym
give.text: Hm. Hm. Perhaps. Here, doctor: the winding key. Wind it, and set it, and then give me back the key. I am not ready to hold it. But I would like to hear it tick.

n0.speaker: Miss Vane
n0.text: Dr. Seward. I am writing to Edmund, as you see. He is a poor correspondent, but a very faithful one.

choices.text: How is the ward at night, Miss Vane?

edmund.speaker: Miss Vane
edmund.text: He was to be my husband. He is in India. Mrs. Pritchard tells me he is dead, but I am sure that is a mistake of the post.

night.speaker: Miss Vane
night.text: Oh, quiet enough. The boy comes in at night, you know, the one with the violet fingers. He sits in the dispensary with the lamp and practises writing a name on the back of old labels, over and over. I thought it a love-letter. It is rather a long way to travel for a love-letter, to practise one signature.

n0.speaker: Mr. Greer
n0.text: Sit, doctor. I was mate on the old Lizzie out of Sunderland, forty years back. D'you know what happens when spirit catches in a hold?

choices.text: What do you see out there?

fire.speaker: Mr. Greer
fire.text: You never throw water on it. The spirit floats and spreads it, burning, to every plank. We wet the blankets and smothered it. That's all there is to it, doctor: soak the blanket, drop it on, and lean. Mind you, I've forgotten my own wife's name, but I never forgot that.

sea.speaker: Mr. Greer
sea.text: A ship, doctor. She will come in out of the east with a dead crew and a dead master lashed to her wheel. Mind you, we all know that story. Do you? Well, then.

n0.speaker: Pettit
n0.text: Doctor. Shall I do the dispensary jars again, sir?

choices.text: Where do you learn your Latin, Pettit?
Pettit, I have a slip for sixty grains of morphia. Written in my name.

latin.speaker: Pettit
latin.text: From the labels, sir, and from the dispenser. He lets me copy the prescriptions so as I learn the hands. My mother's very ill, sir, in Barking. She cannot be left alone.

choices.text: The ink is violet, and Miss Vane saw you practising. Hennessey cannot write, and Mrs. Dowling was on the ward. Only one person could have done it.
Someone has been practising my hand, Pettit. Who might it be?

deny.speaker: Pettit
deny.text: I don't know, sir. I swear I don't. Perhaps Mr. Hennessey. Perhaps...

conf.speaker: Pettit
conf.text: ...It was for my mother, sir. The doctor in Barking has given her up and the pain is... she begged me. I thought sixty grains would carry her through a month. I tried it three times before I could do your S. Then I couldn't, and I started the fire to burn the slip, and it caught the ether...

choices.text: [Send him to the Board for it]
[Tell him his mother is a patient of mine from tomorrow]

report.speaker: Seward
report.text: I do the thing the law requires, which is to say, I write to the Board and let a boy of seventeen pay for what a doctor ought to have prevented. I do not feel clean. I do not think I am meant to.

help.speaker: Seward
help.text: I make a bargain: a proper prescription, signed in my own hand, to be dispensed by the dispenser and no one else; a bed for his mother in the cottage hospital at Purfleet; a boy who works off the damage in the dispensary under Hennessey's eye. It is not in any book of regulations. It is, I think, in one of Van Helsing's.

n0.speaker: Nurse Dowling
n0.text: Doctor, thank God. Number Twelve is empty; the grating was forced from within. Hennessey's gone out after him. And there's smoke in the dispensary.

choices.text: Who was last in the dispensary?

ren.speaker: Nurse Dowling
ren.text: The garden, sir. He always goes to the garden wall, to look at Carfax. If I may say so, doctor, leave the stick at home. Three men would be needed.

who.speaker: Nurse Dowling
who.text: Pettit, to sweep. And me. And I don't write, sir, except the log, and my hand's not a bit like yours.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: A prescription slip, half-burnt at the corner. 'Morph. mur. gr. lx. Pro J. Pettit.' The body of the slip is clerkly. The signature, 'J. Seward', is a very careful forgery.

choices.text: [Pick it up and examine the ink]

e.speaker: Seward
e.text: The ink is violet, the clerk's copying ink, which stains the fingers for a week. Sixty grains of morphia: enough to kill three men. The signature is perfect, and somewhere a hand has practised my S fifty times to get it.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: The brass scales and the tray of weights. I have measured chloral on them a hundred times. I will not do it by guesswork tonight.

what.speaker: Seward
what.text: For Renfield. If he breaks out, and the garden wall keeps its mortar poorly, a draught that is neither too weak nor too strong may be the difference between a man put to bed and a man put in the ground. I need both chloral and a clean glass of water, and I need to know the right number.

ten.speaker: Seward
ten.text: Ten grains. For Renfield, who is strong and wakeful, it would simply make him cross. I pour it away.

thirty.speaker: Seward
thirty.text: Thirty grains: the limit, not the dose. It might put him down; it might stop his heart. I pour it away.

sixty.speaker: Seward
sixty.text: Sixty grains is not a sedative but a funeral. I set it down before I have thought about it, and wash my hands.

twenty.speaker: Seward
twenty.text: Twenty grains for a strong man in his full strength, as Van Helsing wrote. I weigh it twice and dissolve it in the water. Clear, bitter-sweet, innocent. A bottle I hope never to use.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: The poison register, a ledger of every grain that has left this room, in my hand and the dispenser's.

r.speaker: Seward
r.text: 'R. M. Renfield, aet. 59. Sanguine; great physical strength; fourteen stone; sleeps ill. Chloral, if needed, to the full strong-man dose, to be witnessed by the attendant.' I wrote that three months ago, and have been careful with it since.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: Hennessey's diet ledger for Room 12, his big round hand, week after week. I have read it a dozen times, but not as a series.

f.speaker: Seward
f.text: 'Flies, caught on sugar, 3-4 a day. Mr. R. keeps them in a jar, to hold the lives, in his own words. Eats none for first fortnight. Third week: eats them. Says they are quite delicious, and so full of life.'

s.speaker: Seward
s.text: 'Spiders. He feeds the flies to spiders, and swallows the spiders. Says: one spider is worth a hundred flies, for the life in it.'

b.speaker: Seward
b.text: 'Sparrows. He tamed one. Wanted a cat to eat the sparrows. Now keeps them, begs for more, and one morning there is a heap of feathers. He says he should like a cat, for the spider's life is little, and the sparrow's is more. Not a word to the doctor.'

k.speaker: Seward
k.text: 'A kitten, brought by the housemaid. Wanted by him, begged for. The kitten went into his room on Tuesday and came out on Wednesday as a cap-ribbon of fur and a smear. Mr. R. ill, afterwards, as if he had been sick with grief.' I have written nothing under it. I do not need to.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: Doctor Seward. I am quite at your service, and as sane as any man in England. Might I trouble you for another saucer of sugar?

choices.text: How are you sleeping, Mr. Renfield?
I have read the ledger. I think I understand what the flies were for.

sleep.speaker: Renfield
sleep.text: Poorly, Doctor. A man in my position has so much to keep track of. I find I count, and the counting does not stop.

flies.speaker: Renfield
flies.text: Flies are lives, Doctor. Small lives, but each a life. I keep them, as you keep your patients. Is it so different?

theory.speaker: Seward
theory.text: You do not eat the flies because you are hungry, Mr. Renfield. You eat them because each one is a bit of life, and you wish to gather more life into yourself. The spider for the flies, the sparrow for the spiders, and the cat for the sparrows. Each is a step up a ladder. And what did you wish to be at the top?

theory2.speaker: Renfield
theory2.text: ...Doctor. You have a cleverer head than I took you for. Life, Doctor. 'The blood is the life.' I am a collector of it, in a small way. You see how the system works. I am not at all mad; I am merely early.

theory3.speaker: Seward
theory3.text: I write that down, in the ledger, in my own hand: 'Zoophagous mania, systematised; the patient believes life may be taken in by eating living things; progression from small to large.' It is a good case. It is a very bad case. I wonder what he is waiting for, that he must be early.

n0.speaker: Seward
n0.text: Renfield, hunched under the wall, eyes on the moon. I take a step and he turns his head, and for a moment I see the whole ladder of lives written on his face.

choices.text: Mr. Renfield. You are not hungry. You are afraid of being too late.
[Try to bring him down by force]

reason.speaker: Renfield
reason.text: ...Afraid? Yes. Of being late. Doctor, you are the first who has ever said so. I thought there was time. I kept the flies, and the spiders, and now the wall is so high. Something is coming. Something is coming and I should like to be tidy, if it comes.

reason2.speaker: Seward
reason2.text: 'Come in out of the dew, Mr. Renfield. Number Twelve is warm, and the sugar is still there. We shall be tidy together.' He lets me take his arm, and I walk him in across the gravel while the moon sets behind Carfax.

n0.speaker: Renfield
n0.text: Doctor. Forgive me. I was not myself, which is perhaps a mercy. I should like the sugar, in the morning.

ok.speaker: Renfield
ok.text: And Doctor: I was truthful, about being early. Be a little early yourself.

n0.speaker: Latin note
n0.text: 'Mortuus non est qui nocte surgit. Per diem in terra sua iacet. Ligno cor transfige, caput abscinde, os allio imple.' Beneath: 'And beware of the sacrament, A. - it is a thing, not a sentiment.'

choices.text: 'He who rises at night is not dead. By day he sleeps in his own earth. Pierce the heart with iron, burn the body, fill the mouth with earth.'
'He who rises at night is not dead. By day he lies in his own earth. Pierce the heart with wood, cut off the head, fill the mouth with garlic.'
'The dead do not rise at night. By night he lies in his own earth. Bind the heart with wood, hide the head, fill the mouth with salt.'

n_bad.speaker: Van Helsing
n_bad.text: No. 'Ligno' is wood and 'transfige' is pierce; 'os allio imple' will not turn into salt however much I wish it. And 'per diem' is by day. A careless translation could get a man killed.

n_good.speaker: Van Helsing
n_good.text: Wood, not iron; day, not night; garlic, not earth. It is exact, and it is horrible, and my friend Arminius has not troubled himself to say how he came to know.

n0.speaker: Arminius's letters
n0.text: Three letters, tied with black tape. The paper is Hungarian, the hand beautiful, the content not.

n1.speaker: Arminius
n1.text: 'My dear Abraham, you ask who he was. A Voivode of the Wallachian line, a general, a statesman, a man of cunning and of iron. Beaten at Kossovo and, they say, betrayed. In the Szekelys' tales his blood is the river of a nation. I do not believe a word, my friend, but I have never found his grave.'

n2.speaker: Arminius
n2.text: 'The tales speak of a school: the Scholomance, in the mountains over the Hermannstadt lake, where the Devil himself was said to take ten scholars in seven, and keep the tenth as his due. They learned the language of beasts, the weather, the use of thunder. One of those scholars, the Szekelys say, was of this Voivode's blood.'

n3.speaker: Arminius
n3.text: 'Now a practical matter. Pfarrer Albrecht of Kirchdorf, in Styria, has written me about a grave in his churchyard. The village will not let him open it. I cannot go, being old and immovable. You are neither. Go prepared, Abraham, and do not go to disprove it. Go to find out.'

n0.speaker: My wife
n0.text: You are late, Abraham, which means you have found a theory. Tell me, quickly, before Mevrouw Bakker scolds us both.

choices.text: Tell me about the little coat.

n_how.speaker: My wife
n_how.text: The doctor says my lungs are 'no worse'. I told him that was not a diagnosis, it was a courtesy. I watched the skaters today. One boy fell and got up again. I counted it a sign.

n_coat.speaker: My wife
n_coat.text: I began it in March, for a boy who would have been four. I stop when I think I will finish it. Do not look at me like a case. It is only wool.

n_coat2.speaker: My wife
n_coat2.text: You are the cleverest man in Amsterdam, my dear, and you cannot save a child who has already gone. But you will save somebody's. I think that is why you read the heresies.

n_need.speaker: My wife
n_need.text: Yes. There is a silver cross in the cradle, under the wool. It was his christening gift from Arminius. It is made for a small hand. I would rather it went into the world doing a work than lay in a cradle. Take it, Abraham. Take it for the next one.

n_sit.speaker: Van Helsing
n_sit.text: I sit by her until the lamp needs trimming. We do not talk of the child. We talk of Boerhaave and her father's boat and whether the ice will hold until Sunday. It is the best afternoon of the winter.

n0.speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
n0.text: She ate two spoons of the barley broth, Herr Professor. Two! If you could see your face, you would think it was the end of the world.

choices.text: Mevrouw, I need garlic for a ward.
What do you make of all this, Mevrouw?

n_garlic.speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
n_garlic.text: A ward? Is that what they call it at the University? My grandmother hung garlic in Zeeland to keep the plague away. Take the best braid, Professor, and put it where it does the most good.

n_think.speaker: Mevrouw Bakker
n_think.text: I think you work too hard, I think she is braver than any of us, and I think a house with a sick-room needs one woman who says nothing clever. That is me. Eat something.

n0.speaker: Jan
n0.text: Cold, Herr Professor. Colder than the Zuider Zee in March. Cab? The coach for Cologne goes from the corner when you are ready, and not before.

choices.text: What do you hear of the south?
Where might a man lose a key in my house?

n_south.speaker: Jan
n_south.text: The post-boys say the Styrian road is cut at Kirchdorf with snow, and that no one in the village will say why they close their doors at four. A rumour, Professor. I always say: a rumour is a draught that has found a keyhole.

n_key.speaker: Jan
n_key.text: Where would a clever man hide a thing from himself, Professor? Under his own nose. I once found my watch in my boot. Check what you look at every day without seeing it.

n0.speaker: The student
n0.text: Professor! Is it true the Dean means to have you disgraced on Friday? They say he has the whole Faculty behind him.

choices.text: Never mind the Dean. What does he say about me?
What are you reading under that Boerhaave?

n_dean.speaker: The student
n_dean.text: That you put stories of ghouls in your lectures and call them medicine. That a physician who believes in peasants' tales has no business teaching the sons of the Burghers.

n_book.speaker: The student
n_book.text: Calmet. On vampires. I thought it was a joke, but Herr Seward from London says you gave it him to read. Are you cross?

n_book2.speaker: Van Helsing
n_book2.text: I am delighted. A student who reads the foolish book is a student who learns to ask what is true in it. Keep it. But read the column that is written in the margin, not the one that is printed.

n0.speaker: John Seward
n0.text: Professor! I thought it best to be early, in case the Dean tried to take the best seat.

choices.text: How is your hand, Mr. Seward?
Does the Dean ask the same questions every time?

n_hand.speaker: John Seward
n_hand.text: Healed, Sir. Thanks entirely to you. I cut myself at the dissection of the septic case, and the surgeon wished to take the hand. You would not allow it. You opened the wound with your own knife and drew out the poison with your mouth. I remember thinking you were mad.

n_hand2.speaker: Van Helsing
n_hand2.text: I was mad with fear, Mr. Seward. I had lost enough that winter. A physician may refuse to lose another. It is a very stupid thing and an excellent reason.

n_dean.speaker: John Seward
n_dean.text: Always the same three, Sir: the peasant's remedy, the mesmerist, and the thing he calls your 'Carpathian superstition'. If I were you I would look at your own blackboard. Everything he needs is there, and everything you need.

n0.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n0.text: Van Helsing. Still pinning ghost-stories to your lectures, I hear. The Faculty is gravely concerned that a physician of your gifts has gone to the dogs.

choices.text: I have come for the key to the rare-book press, Dean.
I think we should settle this today, in the open.
(That blackboard has the answers. I should read it first.)

n0b.speaker: Van Helsing
n0b.text: I will study the board before I give him my reasons. A man ought to know his own argument.

n_key.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_key.text: The key stays where it is. Prove to me that you are a man of science and not a man of rumours, and you shall have it. I shall ask you three questions. Fail one, and we begin again.

n_start.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_start.text: Splendid. Three questions, then. The first: the peasants of this country swear that a hanged man's rope, bound round the brow, cures a fever. Fact, or superstition?

choices.text: Fact. The peasants have observed it for centuries.
Superstition. It has never been tested.
It is none of a physician's business what peasants believe.

n_fail1.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_fail1.text: Centuries of observation by whom? By people who also stopped hail with bells? It seems your own blackboard disagrees with you, Van Helsing. Again.

n_fail3.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_fail3.text: A physician who will not look at what the peasants believe will never learn what the peasants know. That is no answer. Again.

q2.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
q2.text: Good. The second: the mesmerism in the Salpetriere, where a sleeper obeys a command given hours before. Another peasants' marvel?

choices.text: No. It is observed under witness and repeated; it is fact, though we do not understand it.
Yes. If we cannot explain it, it cannot be real.
It is a hoax of the French.

n_fail2.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_fail2.text: 'If we cannot explain it, it cannot be real.' You wrote the opposite on the board. Begin again.

q3.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
q3.text: And the third. In the Carpathians, they say, the dead rise by night and drink the blood of the living. I take it you will call that superstition by your own rule.

choices.text: By my rule I may not call it so until I have tested it. I will not deny what I have not examined.
It is nonsense, of course, as I have always said.
It is certainly true. I have seen it.

n_fail4.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_fail4.text: Neither of those is your own doctrine. You are either lying to me or to yourself. Begin again.

n_won.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_won.text: ...Hm. 'Disbelieve nothing you have not tested.' You have beaten me with my own favourite sentence. Very well. Take the key. But understand I will watch the day you bring the Faculty a case.

n_won2.speaker: Professor Verhoeven
n_won2.text: And, Van Helsing. For what it is worth, my own grandmother hung garlic at her door. I should be very sorry to find she was right.

n0.speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
n0.text: (whispering) Professor. The Ordo you want is in the press. The Dean has the key. The Dean also has the opinion that you should not have it.

choices.text: What have you in the way of Styrian travellers?
Does the Dean ever read the rare books himself?

n_ordo.speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
n_ordo.text: A rituale of the old Dutch rite. It is dull in ordinary hands. The chapter on the blessing of bread and the making of a circle is the only part anyone has ever read, and that only once, in 1731.

n_styria.speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
n_styria.text: The Folklore and Travels. Third shelf from the west, among the Natural History where they cannot do any harm.

n_dean.speaker: Mijnheer de Vries
n_dean.text: Every Sunday, in the dark, with the lamp turned down. He thinks I do not know. I should hate to be the one to tell him I have always known.

n0.speaker: Father Pieter
n0.text: Professor. You come into my chapel perhaps twice in the year. Either you are very troubled, or you are working.

choices.text: I have the Ordo and a tin of wafers. I need to consecrate them, Father.
What do you think of a man who tests his religion?
What makes the Host the Host, Father?

n_test.speaker: Father Pieter
n_test.text: I think he is a better Christian than the man who never tests it. Faith that cannot bear a question is not faith but fear.

n_host.speaker: Father Pieter
n_host.text: Nothing you could measure on a scale. The bread is bread, until the words and the intent are laid on it in the right order, and then it is what it is. The order matters, Professor. Do not let any man tell you it is only ceremony.

r0.speaker: Father Pieter
r0.text: Hm. You have the Ordo. Then let us do this properly. I will not guess at the order; you shall read it to me, and I will do as you direct. What comes first?

choices.text: The Collect is said over the bread.

f1.speaker: Father Pieter
f1.text: (frowning) No, that is not what the Ordo says. 'Before the bread is blessed the hands must be washed; before the hands are washed the priest must be shriven.' Let us begin again.

r1.speaker: Father Pieter
r1.text: (He kneels, speaks low, rises lighter.) I am shriven. What now?

choices.text: The Collect is said over the bread.

r2.speaker: Father Pieter
r2.text: (He washes his hands in the font, breaking the ice with his knuckles.) Clean. And now?

choices.text: The Collect is said over the bread.

r3.speaker: Father Pieter
r3.text: (Over the wafers, in a voice I have not heard him use before, the Latin runs like water.) And last?

r4.speaker: Father Pieter
r4.text: (He closes the little silver box and presses the cross on its lid.) It is done. These are no longer bread. Take them with the blessing of this house, and may you never need them. And if you do, Professor, remember that the Host is not a charm but a reproach: it works only on those who know what it is.

n0.speaker: Old Gerrit
n0.text: WHAT? Ah, the Professor! I was saying, the Father is a good man but he washes his hands with a great deal of ice about it.

choices.text: Is there anything in the order of the Mass that people forget?

n_order.speaker: Old Gerrit
n_order.text: Forget? Forty years I have set the table for it. Confess first, wash after, bless the bread, close the box. The Father mutters if I put the water out before he has been to the box. Sacristans know these things, Professor. We just never get asked.

n0.speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
n0.text: Professor Van Helsing? Thank God. I have written to nine men and been answered by one. I had begun to think my letter was a kind of madness.

choices.text: I wish to see the churchyard, Pfarrer.

n_tale.speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
n_tale.text: Four children of the village have wasted this winter. Pale, listless, two small marks at the throat. I buried one of them. Then I found, at dawn, that the snow on the north side of the churchyard had gone as if a fire had been lit under it. One grave only. I will not say which, for I have not the courage. Ask the old ones.

n_leave.speaker: Pfarrer Albrecht
n_leave.text: (He closes his eyes.) You will do it by night? I have no right to refuse; I have only the fear of a priest who has seen what a Christian burial cannot hold. Go. Matthias has the gate. Say a Pater for me at whichever grave it is.

n0.speaker: Matthias
n0.text: I do not talk of it, Herr. I dig. I do not ask who it is I dig for.

choices.text: The grave that has no snow upon it. Do you know which?
A girl, nineteen. A wedding-dress. Is it Katharina Lindner?
Is there anything I should know about the gate?

n_snow.speaker: Matthias
n_snow.text: Three stones are by the north wall. Anna Pfeifer, who was a saint. Josef Hauer, who was a thief. And a third. Ask the old Frau Lindner; she is the only one who still says the name.

n_yes.speaker: Matthias
n_yes.text: (He crosses himself.) I have driven three iron nails into that stone with my own hand. Twice the nails were out by morning. Yes, Herr. She is the one. God help me for saying it aloud.

n_gate.speaker: Matthias
n_gate.text: The lantern will not stay lit beyond the third stone. Go by the moon. And, Herr, do not step on the snow where it has thawed.

n0.speaker: Frau Lindner
n0.text: A stranger. A doctor, they say. Then you are the one who will open the grave, and I will tell you what I should have said to the Pfarrer's face seventy years ago.

choices.text: [Sit and listen to the whole story]

n_who.speaker: Frau Lindner
n_who.text: My aunt. She was nineteen, a bride of the spring, and the prettiest girl in three parishes. Ask me no more until you have listened.

n_story.speaker: Frau Lindner
n_story.text: It was the year of the great snow, when the wolves came into the street. My aunt Katharina wed the miller's son in March and was dead by Easter. She lay in the church for three days with a bloom on her cheek like a living girl. The priest, who was old and wise, drove an ash-nail through the coffin-lid, and the sexton nailed three more to the stone. Still the children sickened.

n_story2.speaker: Frau Lindner
n_story2.text: My mother used to say she walked on the night of the great thaw, and that she asked for her husband by name at his window. Katharina Lindner. A bride of the spring. Say it once to the sexton, Herr, and he will give you the gate.

n0.speaker: Landlord Huber
n0.text: A hot wine for the Herr Doctor. Or a hot soup. We have both, and I fear that is all we have.

choices.text: Why so much garlic on the windows?

n_garlic.speaker: Landlord Huber
n_garlic.text: My wife's idea. Do not ask me if it works; ask me if I sleep. I do. That is all the evidence I need.

n_begin.speaker: Landlord Huber
n_begin.text: At the first thaw. A child at the Meyer farm, then a girl at the mill. By the Feast of the Three Kings the village shut its doors at four. They say the Pfarrer wrote for help to a man in Holland. We did not think he would come.

n0.speaker: The herdsman
n0.text: You are the learned gentleman. Tell me, Herr, is it true that you can tell by looking at a man whether he is sick of body or sick of mind?

n_why.speaker: The herdsman
n_why.text: My daughter Resi has been weak since the thaw. She says a pretty lady stands at her window and sings. I told her it was a dream. The Pfarrer says it is not, and I dare not hear him say why.

n0.speaker: Van Helsing
n0.text: Arminius has written again. The black edge is not for himself; it is for the friend who died in Buda-Pesth last month. At the foot, in his shaking hand, a postscript: 'Abraham, what I told you of the Voivode - a letter came to me from a Transylvanian monk. The name that he used for the family in the end was not Voivode, but Dracula.'

n_end.speaker: Van Helsing
n_end.text: I sit with it for a long time, the lamp low, the snow falling across the canal. Upstairs she coughs and sleeps. I had thought I was putting a ghost to rest. It is very clear to me tonight that I have only learned what the ghost looks like. The fight is not over, and I am not, I think, the man who will finish it. But I shall teach the man who will.

do.card: Years later, a London doctor wrote to an old teacher in Amsterdam: 'Come at once, if convenient; if not, come anyhow.'

lantern.text: I took the lantern. It will serve in the dark places.
lantern.hint: Someone left a working lantern against the wall.

lantern.text: Behind the barrel, a lantern, still warm. Someone was here just now.
lantern.hint: The barrel stands a little away from the wall, as if moved.

lantern.text: A lantern sits in the shadow at the foot of the column. I take it.
lantern.hint: A faint glint at the column's foot.

key.text: Hidden in the hollowed pages of a book: an iron key. Why would the Count hide it here?
key.hint: One thick volume stands out on this shelf. It feels hollow.

key.text: Behind the row of law books, an iron key on a nail.
key.hint: The dust is wiped away behind one row of books.

key.text: Under the London directory lay an iron key.
key.hint: The directory is lying a little crooked, as if lifted.

key.text: Under the candelabra's base, a flat iron key.
key.hint: The candelabra stands on something that is not quite flat.

key.text: In the cushion of the Count's chair - an iron key sewn into the lining.
key.hint: One seam of the cushion is freshly stitched.

key.text: Under the pillow of my own bed lay an iron key. Left for me, or for someone else?

brass_key.text: A brass key lies in the folds of the cushion.
brass_key.hint: Something small glints in the cushion.

brass_key.text: In the rain barrel, under the water: a brass key.
brass_key.hint: Something yellow glimmers beneath the water.

brass_key.text: Under the table cloth, taped to the underside: a brass key.
brass_key.hint: One corner of the table-cloth hangs oddly.

brass_key.text: Wedged in a crack of the column: a brass key.
brass_key.hint: There is a crack in the column's base.

a2_lucy_door_key.text: Under the blotter, a small brass key labelled 'Lucy's door' in Mrs. Westenra's careful hand.
a2_lucy_door_key.hint: The blotter lies crooked on the writing table.

a2_lucy_door_key.text: Behind the Bible, a brass key on a ribbon: 'Lucy's door'.
a2_lucy_door_key.hint: The Bible stands a little out from the row.

a2_lucy_door_key.text: Under the embroidered cushion, a brass key tagged 'Lucy's door'.
a2_lucy_door_key.hint: The cushion of my writing chair sits lumpily.

a3_dispensary_key.text: In the false back of my own desk drawer: the dispensary key, where I hid it from myself.
a3_dispensary_key.hint: The drawer is a half-inch shallower than it should be.

a3_dispensary_key.text: Behind Lombroso, where I put it last Thursday: the little brass dispensary key.
a3_dispensary_key.hint: One volume has been pushed forward from the rest.

a3_dispensary_key.text: Under the mantel clock, on a scrap of blotting-paper: the dispensary key.
a3_dispensary_key.hint: The mantel clock sits crooked, on something small.

a3_transfusion_kit.text: My transfusion kit, in its black bag, at the bottom of the instrument chest where it has lain since Edinburgh.
a3_transfusion_kit.hint: The chest is lighter than a locked chest should be.

a3_transfusion_kit.text: Under a pile of clean linen in the ward trunk: my black bag with the silver tubing.
a3_transfusion_kit.hint: The trunk lid does not shut; something black is under the linen.

a3_transfusion_kit.text: At the back of the gardener's shed, wrapped in sacking: my black bag. Hennessey must have stowed it.
a3_transfusion_kit.hint: There is a black corner of leather under a sack.

a3_window_pin.text: Hanging on a nail in the potting-shed: a stout iron pin with a ring head.
a3_window_pin.hint: Among the rakes, an iron rod shines like a new coin.

a3_window_pin.text: Thrust in among the umbrellas: an iron pin from some old shutter.
a3_window_pin.hint: One 'umbrella' is straighter and colder than the others.

a3_window_pin.text: Under the potting-bench, an iron pin with a ring head.
a3_window_pin.hint: Something metallic glints between the bench and the wall.

a4_pawn_ticket.text: Under the corner of the rug, where the maid dropped it in haste: a pawn ticket for one small gold crucifix.
a4_pawn_ticket.hint: One corner of the rug has been lifted and put back crooked.

a4_pawn_ticket.text: Tucked in the Prayer Book, folded small: a pawnbroker's ticket for a small gold crucifix.
a4_pawn_ticket.hint: The Prayer Book on the shelf sticks out a little.

a4_pawn_ticket.text: Under the coffin's brass handle, folded flat: a pawnbroker's ticket for a small gold crucifix.
a4_pawn_ticket.hint: A scrap of paper pokes from beneath the coffin's handle.

a4_key_blank.text: In the drawer, among odd wards, a blank of good brass, uncut. It will do.
a4_key_blank.hint: The drawer rattles with odd wards and blanks.

a4_key_blank.text: Beneath the other keys in the biscuit tin lies an uncut blank. Odd that I forgot it.
a4_key_blank.hint: The tin is heavier than a few old keys should make it.

a4_key_blank.text: Under the blotter, where I put it for safety months ago: a brass blank.
a4_key_blank.hint: The blotter lies a little proud of the leather.

a5_cabinet_key.text: Under the inkstand's felt base, a small brass key.
a5_cabinet_key.hint: The inkstand sits a little crookedly on its blotter.

a5_cabinet_key.text: The bust's head lifts; in the hollow neck, a small brass key. I knew Hippocrates had a use.
Tucked in the candelabra's base, a small key on a bit of ribbon.
a5_cabinet_key.hint: A scrap of ribbon peeps from the candelabra's foot.

a5_chapel_key.text: In a crack of the gatepost: a rusty iron key. Someone left it there, years ago.
a5_chapel_key.hint: Moss has been scraped off the gatepost recently.

a5_chapel_key.text: Inside the dry well-head, wrapped in oiled cloth, the chapel key.
a5_chapel_key.hint: The well-cover is not as heavy as it looks.

a5_chapel_key.text: At the foot of the weathered cross lies an iron key under a flat stone.
a5_chapel_key.hint: One flat stone at the cross's foot has been turned.

a6_whetstone.text: I pocketed the whetstone. I shall leave a coin on the barrel for the chandler.
a6_whetstone.hint: A chandler's whetstone lies on its rim.

a6_whetstone.text: Under the rope in the chest lay a flat grey whetstone. I took it.
a6_whetstone.hint: Something flat and heavy is wedged under the coil.

a6_whetstone.text: Behind the broken slats was a flat grey whetstone, hidden by a careless carter.
a6_whetstone.hint: A hard grey shape shows between the slats.

arthur_burden_desk_key.text: Taped to the underside of the plaster bust's base, a small brass key: the desk-key.
arthur_burden_desk_key.hint: Sir Hugh's plaster base sits slightly crooked.

arthur_burden_desk_key.text: Behind the red Bradshaw, a small brass key hung on a nail: the desk-key.
arthur_burden_desk_key.hint: The red Bradshaw sits one inch proud of the rest.

arthur_burden_desk_key.text: At the bottom of the hall chest, in the toe of an old riding-boot, a small brass key: the desk-key.
arthur_burden_desk_key.hint: The hall chest lid has been put down in a hurry.

demeter_voyage_hold_key.text: Under the straw of the bunk, a big brass key on a lanyard: the hold key.
demeter_voyage_hold_key.hint: The straw in the bunk lies lumpily.

demeter_voyage_hold_key.text: On the cook's key-hook, among the spoons, a big brass key: the hold key.
demeter_voyage_hold_key.hint: One of the spoons on the cook's hook is a key.

demeter_voyage_hold_key.text: At the bottom of the deck locker, in a coil of marline, a big brass key: the hold key.
demeter_voyage_hold_key.hint: The deck locker has been rummaged and put back in a hurry.

demeter_voyage_cabin_key.text: Behind Lloyd's Register, hanging on a nail, the small iron key of the cabin door.
demeter_voyage_cabin_key.hint: Lloyd's Register stands a finger out from the shelf.

demeter_voyage_cabin_key.text: Under a corner of the chart, the small iron cabin key, where I put it myself and forgot.
demeter_voyage_cabin_key.hint: The chart is lying crooked on the table.

demeter_voyage_cabin_key.text: Hooked behind the swinging lamp, the small iron cabin key.
demeter_voyage_cabin_key.hint: The lamp swings from its gimbals with a faint jingle.

dracula_voivode_radu_letter.text: Folded under the pillow, a letter in a neat hand, sealed with a stranger's wax: Radu's letter.
dracula_voivode_radu_letter.hint: The pillow has been plumped again, too carefully.

dracula_voivode_radu_letter.text: Between two volumes of the annals, a single sheet in Radu's writing: the letter to the Turkish agent.
dracula_voivode_radu_letter.hint: One volume of the annals sits proud of the rest.

dracula_voivode_radu_letter.text: Slipped behind the marble bust's plinth, a letter in Radu's neat hand: the letter.
dracula_voivode_radu_letter.hint: My father's marble bust has been turned a quarter of the way round.

dracula_voivode_ink.text: Under the lectern's candlestick, a small pot of black ink that dries at once.
dracula_voivode_ink.hint: The lectern's candles have a ring of black underneath.

dracula_voivode_ink.text: Wedged under the scholar's bench, where a beginner has been hiding it: a pot of black ink.
dracula_voivode_ink.hint: Something rattles beneath the bench when you lean on it.

harker_road_box_key.text: Under the stool's flat cushion, a small japanned key tied with a pink thread.
harker_road_box_key.hint: The cushion of the stool lies lumpily.

harker_road_box_key.text: In the barrel of old seals, a small japanned key hidden under a lump of green wax.
harker_road_box_key.hint: One of the lumps of wax in the barrel looks fresh.

harker_road_box_key.text: On the hook behind the lantern, a japanned key on a pink thread.
harker_road_box_key.hint: The lantern hangs a little crooked from its hook.

harker_road_vault_key.text: Among the keys on the ring, one heavy iron key with a worn bow, stamped with a tiny cross, the stair-door's own.
harker_road_vault_key.hint: One key on the ring hangs apart from the rest, as if used recently.

harker_road_vault_key.text: Under the plate on the inlaid table, a heavy iron key with a worn bow.
harker_road_vault_key.hint: One of the gold plates on the table sits crookedly.

harker_road_vault_key.text: Behind the Latin ledger, a heavy iron key with a worn bow, on a nail.
harker_road_vault_key.hint: The ledgers on the shelf stand a hand's breadth out from the wall.

lucy_summer_pressed_letter.text: Under the last layer of tissue in the trunk, flat and a little crumpled, Papa's letter, where I put it so that nobody would sit on it.
lucy_summer_pressed_letter.hint: The trunk lid does not quite close.

lucy_summer_pressed_letter.text: Down the back of the cretonne window-seat, where I must have dropped it while watching the harbour: Papa's letter, safe.
lucy_summer_pressed_letter.hint: The cushion of the window-seat is rumpled, as though someone had searched it in a hurry.

lucy_summer_pressed_letter.text: Tucked behind the board at the back of the cliff seat, damp at one corner but intact: Papa's letter, with its forget-me-nots.
lucy_summer_pressed_letter.hint: The cliff seat has a loose board at the back.

mina_records_ribbon.text: At the back of the stationery cupboard, in a tin that says 'Biscuits', a fresh black ribbon in its paper.
mina_records_ribbon.hint: One tin in the cupboard is far too clean to hold biscuits.

mina_records_ribbon.text: Behind Taylor's primer, a new typewriter ribbon in its wrapper.
mina_records_ribbon.hint: One primer stands proud of the row, as if something is behind it.

mina_records_ribbon.text: Under a drift of spoiled pages, a spare ribbon, quite good, and cast away by a girl who knew no better.
mina_records_ribbon.hint: The basket rustles in a way that suggests it is hiding something.

mina_records_candle.text: Behind the ship in the bottle on the mantel, a tall white candle.
mina_records_candle.hint: The ship in the bottle sits oddly on the mantel.

mina_records_candle.text: Wrapped in a sheet at the top of the linen chest, a tall white candle.
mina_records_candle.hint: The linen chest smells of wax as well as lavender.

mina_records_candle.text: In the dresser's top drawer, among the hair-pins, a tall white candle.
mina_records_candle.hint: One drawer of the dresser sticks as if something rolls inside.

quincey_hunt_powder.text: Behind a row of saddle-soap tins, wrapped in oilcloth: Wash's horn of black powder, dry as a bone.
quincey_hunt_powder.hint: One tin on the shelf sits proud of the others.

quincey_hunt_powder.text: Buried in the oats, in a waxed pouch: a powder horn. Wash hides everything in the feed.
quincey_hunt_powder.hint: The lid of the feed barrel has been put back crooked, and dust has not settled on one side.

quincey_hunt_powder.text: Under the breeching, wrapped in an old shirt: a full powder horn.
quincey_hunt_powder.hint: The harness chest is heavier than a chest of leather ought to be.

quincey_hunt_lantern.text: Under the wagon-seat, on its side, wrapped in a sack: a stout hurricane lantern.
quincey_hunt_lantern.hint: Something glass-and-iron glints under the wagon seat.

quincey_hunt_lantern.text: On the tent floor, between Arthur's valise and Seward's notebooks: a hurricane lantern, unlit.
quincey_hunt_lantern.hint: Something round and metal pokes out of the tent flap.

quincey_hunt_lantern.text: Wrapped in my own spare shirt inside the saddle-roll: the hurricane lantern I had forgotten I carried.
quincey_hunt_lantern.hint: My saddle-roll is lumpier than I left it.

renfield_mercy_spoon.text: Under the bread, flat against the tin: the missing spoon.
renfield_mercy_spoon.hint: The bread on the tray sits oddly.

renfield_mercy_spoon.text: Hooked over the inside rim of the bucket, a bent tin spoon.
renfield_mercy_spoon.hint: The bucket has a faint ring of tin-polish round its rim.

renfield_mercy_spoon.text: Wedged into the crack under the stool-seat, a tin spoon.
renfield_mercy_spoon.hint: The stool wobbles on one side, as if something were pushed into it.

renfield_mercy_pencil.text: Behind Pinel, a pencil stub, the sort a doctor loses for a month.
renfield_mercy_pencil.hint: One volume on the shelf sits out of line.

renfield_mercy_pencil.text: On the mantel behind the stopped clock, a short pencil stub.
renfield_mercy_pencil.hint: The mantel is dusted everywhere but one corner.

renfield_mercy_pencil.text: Down the back of the cushion, a pencil stub, no doubt dropped by a thoughtful patient.
renfield_mercy_pencil.hint: The cushion has been sat on and then disturbed.

seward_asylum_ward_key.text: Under the blotter, a small iron key on a loop of tape, labelled 'WARD' in my own hand.
seward_asylum_ward_key.hint: The blotter lies crooked on the desk.

seward_asylum_ward_key.text: Behind Maudsley, a small iron key on a loop of tape: 'WARD'.
seward_asylum_ward_key.hint: One volume of Maudsley sits out of line.

seward_asylum_ward_key.text: On the mantel, behind the stopped clock, the small iron ward key.
seward_asylum_ward_key.hint: The mantel is dusted everywhere except one corner.

seward_asylum_spare_key.text: Under the folded blanket, a brass spare key tagged 'DISP.' in Hennessey's laboured capitals.
seward_asylum_spare_key.hint: The blanket on this bed is folded too neatly.

seward_asylum_spare_key.text: Pushed down the back of the window bench, a brass key tagged 'DISP.'
seward_asylum_spare_key.hint: The cushion of the bench has been disturbed.

seward_asylum_spare_key.text: Tucked under the pillow, a brass key tagged 'DISP.'
seward_asylum_spare_key.hint: The pillow on this bed is lumpy.

seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.text: In the old chest, wrapped in tissue, a blank wax cylinder in its cardboard tube.
seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.hint: The old chest has been opened recently; the lid does not quite sit.

seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.text: In the desk drawer, among the pens, a blank wax cylinder in its tube.
seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.hint: The drawer of the copying desk is not quite closed.

seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.text: Behind the case-books, a cardboard tube: a blank cylinder, still smelling of new wax.
seward_asylum_blank_cylinder.hint: Something rattles faintly behind the case-books.

vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.text: Under the plaster bust of Boerhaave, a small brass key: the cabinet key.
vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.hint: Boerhaave stands a finger's width off his usual ring on the shelf.

vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.text: Taped inside the case of the tall clock, a small brass key: the cabinet key.
vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.hint: The tall clock has been opened; the pendulum is lopsided.

vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.text: Behind a volume of Sydenham, on a nail, a small brass key: the cabinet key.
vanhelsing_lore_cabinet_key.hint: One volume of Sydenham sits proud of the rest.

door_old.fail: Too dark. I need a light before I go beyond that door.
It is locked. The keyhole is small and brass-bright.

a2_d_cabin_door.fail: Locked. The captain must have kept the key by him.
The padlock is rusted shut. A lever might shift the hasp.

a3_door_cell.fail: I should speak to Hennessey before I go in alone to a man like that.
Hennessey has the other key, and the sense not to let me in without a word.

demeter_voyage_d_hatch.fail: Barred and padlocked. The hold key is kept somewhere in the ship, not far from where the captain sleeps.
Barred and padlocked. The carpenter's crowbar would take the hasp off.

harker_road_r_door.fail: Locked. The lock is as old as the door; a heavy key must hang somewhere in this room.
Locked. The bolt is old and rusted; a lever might break the hasp.

harker_road_o_door_archive.fail: Locked. Mr. Pell keeps the key to the muniment room, and Mr. Pell keeps it like a relic.

mina_records_w_stairs.fail: It is still day, and I have one thing to do before I go up: I have something in mind to hang by a cord.

quincey_hunt_gate_range.fail: Wash is right. I will not ride out against Dunning's gang with an empty rifle. Powder and lead, then the loading bench.
A full cylinder, and I will want a lariat from the tack chest before I leave the yard.

seward_asylum_w_door_disp.fail: Locked. Hennessey says the key is 'kept safe', which is no answer.
Locked. There must be a spare somewhere on the ward; Hennessey is not the only one who hides things.

a1_j1.title: 3 May. Bistritz
a1_j1.text: Left Munich at 8:35 P.M. The impression I had was that we were leaving the West and entering the East. At the Golden Krone the landlord's wife begged me not to go: it is the eve of St. George's Day. She gave me a crucifix.

a1_j2.title: The driver
a1_j2.text: Four black horses stood where there had been none. A tall driver with a long brown beard and eyes that seemed red in the lamplight. Wolves howled all about us.

a1_j3.title: The Count
a1_j3.text: A tall old man, clean shaven save for a long white moustache, clad in black from head to foot. His hand was as cold as ice. 'Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!' I am not to sleep in any other part of the castle.

a1_j4.title: The shaving glass
a1_j4.text: I was shaving when I felt a hand on my shoulder. I had seen no one come in, and in the glass there was no reflection of him at all. I cut myself. The Count seized my throat - then drew back at the crucifix.

a1_j5.title: The three women
a1_j5.text: In the forbidden part of the castle, in the moonlight, three young women whispered by my couch: 'He is young and strong; there are kisses for us all.' The Count's fury dispersed them. I am a prisoner.

a1_j6.title: Fifty boxes of earth
a1_j6.text: In the old chapel I found fifty great boxes of earth. In one of them lay the Count - eyes open, stony, without colour. Not dead and not alive. I took the keys from his belt.

a1_j_cat.title: Beneath the chapel
a1_j_cat.text: With the Count's keys I tried the low iron door beside his box. A stair, worn hollow by feet long turned to dust, led down into the earth. The air was cold and stale, and somewhere far below water dripped. If this castle has a heart, it lies under here.

a1_j_cliff.title: The iron door
