a1_j_cliff.text: The iron door gave at last under the hammer. Beyond lay a ledge of rock, the wind, and a drop into the black gorge. Across the gap rose the castle's south wall, and in it one window. I knew that window. It was mine. There is no road out this way - only the road I already know.

a1_j_gold.title: The heaped gold
a1_j_gold.text: In a vaulted chamber lay a great heap of gold - Roman, British, Austrian, Hungarian, Greek and Turkish coin - under a film of dust. None of it, I noticed, was less than three hundred years old. A man with such a hoard has no need to keep a guest, unless he wants something more.

a1_j7.title: 30 June. The last chance
a1_j7.text: The Szgany are loading the boxes onto wagons. The Count means to go to England. If I can escape, I may warn them. Good-bye, all! Mina!

a2_j_undercroft.title: Under the abbey
a2_j_undercroft.text: A stair behind the founder's slab goes down beneath the abbey: an undercroft of old monks' graves, cold as a cellar and reeking of something sharp and animal. Someone has been here, and not a monk. The dust is scuffed, and a rag of white lawn hangs from a nail. I think of Lucy's sleeping feet, and how far they have wandered.

a2_j_arrive.title: 24 July. Whitby
a2_j_arrive.text: Lucy met me at the station and drove me to the Crescent, which looks out over the harbour and the East Cliff and the sea. I have had no letter from Jonathan since the 29th of June. Lucy's mother is sweet, and Lucy is lovelier than ever.

a2_j_proposals.title: Three proposals
a2_j_proposals.text: Dr. Seward, Mr. Quincey P. Morris and Arthur Holmwood all asked for my hand on the same day. I refused two and accepted one. Why can't a girl marry three men? I am so happy and so wretched at once.

a2_j_seward_intro.title: Dr. Seward's study
a2_j_seward_intro.text: Lucy has refused me, as I feared. I must turn to work. My most interesting case is R. M. Renfield: sanguine, strong, excitable, with a fixed idea that he must eat living things to gain their life.

a2_j_seward_diary.title: Renfield
a2_j_seward_diary.text: Patient Renfield collects flies, spiders and now a sparrow. 'The blood is the life,' he says. A homicidal maniac of a peculiar kind, perhaps. I will watch him closely, and write down what he wants.

a2_j_east_cliff.title: The East Cliff
a2_j_east_cliff.text: The churchyard is the nicest spot in Whitby, with seats to sit on and the sea laid out below. Lucy loves the seat on the suicide's tomb. Old men sit on the benches and talk all day, and the oldest is Mr. Swales.

a2_j_swales.title: Old Mr. Swales
a2_j_swales.text: 'It be all lies,' said Mr. Swales of the stones. I think he is the most honest man in Whitby. He tells me the Barguest, the Abbey ghost and the dead are no worse than the living. He is ninety-five.

a2_j_stones.title: The lying stones
a2_j_stones.text: Mr. Swales says one stone, the widow's, for the only son George Canon who fell at Kettleness, is a bigger lie than most, and a clever man would hide something there. Is that the coastguard's spare key?

a2_j_harbour.title: Tate Hill Pier
a2_j_harbour.text: The harbour is full of boats, the quay is full of gossip, and the sky is full of gulls. The coastguard keeps a hut under the cliff with a heavy padlock. The fishermen talk of mares'-tails and bad weather.

a2_j_hut.title: The coastguard's hut
a2_j_hut.text: Officer Dunn keeps his hut in good order: a stove, charts, a tool-chest, a storm lantern and a notice-board. He tells me he has never seen the glass drop like this. There is a desk where I may set out papers.

a2_j_hut_clue.title: Dunn's notice
a2_j_hut_clue.text: 'Spare key kept with the stone of the widow's only son.' That is George Canon's stone in the East Cliff churchyard, whose epitaph Mr. Swales so detests. The coastguard hides his key in a lie.

a2_j_abbey.title: The Abbey
a2_j_abbey.text: The Abbey is the loveliest ruin in the land. The sexton says the White Lady shows in the great window at sunset. I picked wild roses and found a clean ash bough and a font brimming with rain.

a2_j_storm_rises.title: 6 August. The storm
a2_j_storm_rises.text: Sunset blood-red, mares'-tails across the sky, and a hush on the sea. Then the wind rose, and the waves came over the piers. All the town stands on the cliff in the fog, and the searchlight sweeps the water.

a2_j_storm.title: The Demeter runs ashore
a2_j_storm.text: A schooner ran between the piers with every sail set and a dead man lashed to the wheel. When the keel struck sand an immense dog sprang from below, bounded up the cliff and was lost in the fog. It made for the churchyard.

a2_j_wreck_morning.title: 7 August. The wreck
a2_j_wreck_morning.text: The Demeter of Varna lies on Tate Hill Pier, her sails in rags. A constable keeps the crowd back. Mr. Billington, to whom she is consigned, is greatly distressed. All the town speaks of the dog and the dead steersman.

a2_j_pass.title: Leave to go aboard
a2_j_pass.text: The constable let me through. A word from Mr. Swales, or from the consignee, is as good as a warrant in Whitby. I shall see the dead captain and the ship.

a2_j_wreck.title: Aboard the Demeter
a2_j_wreck.text: The deck is wet and bare. The wheel is lashed with cords and the dead man's hands are bound over a crucifix. His eyes are shut; his face is quite calm. Whatever he saw, he met it as a man.

a2_j_captain.title: The captain
a2_j_captain.text: He fastened the knots with his teeth. In his pocket, a corked bottle and a cabin key; in his hands, a crucifix and a rosary. He wished it known that he was captain, and a Christian, and he did his duty.

a2_j_boxes.title: Fifty boxes of earth
a2_j_boxes.text: The hold is full of great boxes of mould, marked for Mr. Billington. One is open, and the earth in it has been lain in. Another has its nails bent out from within. They came from Varna with the ballast.

a2_j_log.title: The Log of the Demeter
a2_j_log.text: Crew uneasy off Cape Matapan; a tall thin stranger seen; men vanish one by one in fog and storm; the mate stabs the figure and the knife passes through; he opens a box, screams, leaps into the sea. The captain, alone, lashes himself to the wheel.

a2_j_carfax.title: Carfax
a2_j_carfax.text: The fifty boxes were consigned to a house called Carfax at Purfleet, bought through Mr. Hawkins. Jonathan's firm! I cannot rid myself of the feeling that Jonathan's long silence and this ship are connected.

a2_j_swales_dead.title: 10 August. Mr. Swales is dead
a2_j_swales_dead.text: The captain was buried today, with a hundred boats at the funeral. When we came to Lucy's seat, Mr. Swales was lying there, his neck broken, his face frozen in horror. 'He had been dreading it,' someone said. And the dog...

a2_j_gone.title: 11 August. Lucy is gone
a2_j_gone.text: I woke at one in the morning and found Lucy's bed empty. The door was still locked, the key under my pillow, but the window stood open. I took the shawl, a pin and the key, and went out.

a2_j_trail.title: Tracking Lucy
a2_j_trail.text: The fog lamps burn like dull coals. Bare footprints in the wet, a strip of her nightgown on a railing, a watchman who saw her go up the steps toward the churchyard. I must be quick.

a2_j_arrive_seat.title: The churchyard at night
a2_j_arrive_seat.text: The moon is full. The clock of St. Mary's has stopped. On the seat I can see something white, and something dark that bends over it.

a2_j_seat.title: Red eyes on the seat
a2_j_seat.text: A long, black form leaned over Lucy, and when I called it raised a white face with red, gleaming eyes. Then it was gone, and a great bat wheeled over the churchyard. Lucy sat quite still, breathing hard.

a2_j_pin.title: The safety-pin
a2_j_pin.text: I wrapped her in the shawl and fastened it at her throat with a pin, so she should not catch cold. I must have pricked her, for she cried out. Two tiny red spots lay on her skin beneath it.

a2_j_decline.title: 12 August. A pale Lucy
a2_j_decline.text: Lucy sleeps all night and wakes weary. Her cheeks are white and her lips colourless. Mrs. Westenra says it is the sea air; I fear it is something else. Those marks on her throat do not heal.

a2_j_decline2.title: The marks on her throat
a2_j_decline2.text: Two small punctures with white edges and red rims, a quarter-inch apart. Lucy blames my pin. A pin never made such a mark, and I never pinned her twice. She is growing paler by the day.

a2_j_agatha.title: Sister Agatha's letter
a2_j_agatha.text: 'Mr. Harker is with us and has had a sharp attack of brain fever. He has been raving of wolves, poison and ghosts, and of things I dare not name. Come to him, if you can; he asks for you.' - Sister Agatha.

a2_j_dog_driven.title: The dog
a2_j_dog_driven.text: I faced the great dog under the pier, and it fled up the cliff toward the churchyard. A mastiff was found dead there the next morning, torn open, they say, by some savage thing.

a3_j_cellar.title: The old cellar
a3_j_cellar.text: Under my own asylum lies the old cellar where my predecessors kept the violent cases: padded stalls, iron staples, a dripping tap. Renfield has no business knowing of it, and yet he spoke of 'the cold dark under the house' only last week. I find I do not like the coincidence.

a3_j_cellar_cell.title: The cell of a hundred hands
a3_j_cellar_cell.text: With the orderly's key I opened the grated door in the cellar. The plaster is scratched from floor to ceiling with one sentence in a hundred hands: HE IS COMING. On the straw lay a crucifix and a braid of garlic, left by some earlier patient who believed it. I took them. I have never believed in such things, and I did not like how glad I was of them.

a3_j_cellar_grating.title: How Renfield gets out
a3_j_cellar_grating.text: At the far end of the cellar the old coal grating hangs from one hinge, the bars bent outward and the mud beneath it fresh. No orderly bent those bars. It opens on the grounds, and from there it is an easy walk to Carfax. Hennessey asked how Renfield leaves his cell. I think I have found where he goes after.

a3_j_casebook.title: An old case-book
a3_j_casebook.text: Margin notes in my predecessor's hand: 'Zoophagy - the madman eats lives to gain life. Seen once before, and he spoke of a Master then also.' I read it twice, and wish I had not. Whatever Renfield serves, it has served itself of other minds before his.

a3_j_seward_diary.title: Phonograph diary
a3_j_seward_diary.text: My patient Renfield is the interest of my days: a life-eater, a zoophagous maniac who collects flies, then spiders, then sparrows. I keep this diary on the phonograph; it records my voice and my doubts alike. Lucy's name keeps surfacing, and Arthur's letters worry me.

a3_j_dose.title: The chloral rule
a3_j_dose.text: My own pencilled rule: chloral hydrate, ten grains for a man of nine stone, fifteen for twelve, thirty for a bull. Renfield is nine stone and wasted. Ten grains, then, in water, and no more.

a3_j_sedated.title: Renfield sleeps
a3_j_sedated.text: Ten grains in clean water, a quiet word, and Renfield went down like a lamb. I do not like how easily he took it. A man who eats lives should resist the needle more.

a3_j_zoophagy.title: The ladder of lives
a3_j_zoophagy.text: Sugar for flies, flies for spiders, spiders for sparrows, and in time, he asked me, a kitten. Renfield believes that to swallow many lives is to gain life. He calls it 'the blood is the life'. He says 'the Master' is coming.

a3_j_fence.title: The loose slat
a3_j_fence.text: A slat in the wall by the elms was hanging by one nail, and a path through the long grass leads straight to Carfax. I have nailed it fast. Pocock swears it is not the first time.

a3_j_arthur_wire.title: Arthur's telegram
a3_j_arthur_wire.text: The boy came at four. Arthur's father is dying and Arthur dare not leave him; Lucy is ill, and he trusts me to see her. I go to Hillingham tonight. Renfield is quiet; for that I am grateful and, I admit, a little uneasy.

a3_j_hillingham.title: Hillingham
a3_j_hillingham.text: Lucy is bloodless, breathing heavily, and sleeps with her window open. Mrs Westenra says she is much better. I find no disease I can name, and that frightens me more than any I can.

a3_j_lucy_exam.title: Lucy's throat
a3_j_lucy_exam.text: Two small punctures on her throat, white-edged and torn, and no fever. Her gums are pale as paper. Whatever drains her is drawing it from outside the body. I cannot do this alone: I will write to the one man who might know, my old teacher Van Helsing.

a3_j_bradshaw.title: The timetable
a3_j_bradshaw.text: Bradshaw: the night boat leaves the Hook of Holland for Harwich and the boat-train reaches Liverpool Street at five minutes past six in the morning. The telegraph closes at eight tonight. A wire sent before then, and Van Helsing can be at Hillingham by breakfast.

a3_j_wired.title: The wire to Amsterdam
a3_j_wired.text: Sent, before the office shut: 'Come by the night boat from the Hook; boat-train reaches Liverpool Street 6.05; urgent, a matter of life.' The boy ran off through the dusk. I cannot do more tonight.

a3_j_mina_hospital.title: Buda-Pesth
a3_j_mina_hospital.text: Sister Agatha's letter said he was alive, and weak, and calling for me. I found him in the corner bed, white-haired and looking through me as if I were a window. When at last he knew me, he wept. I will not leave him again.

a3_j_mina_diary_sealed.title: The sealed journal
a3_j_mina_diary_sealed.text: He has given me his journal of the Castle, and begged me never to read it unless some solemn duty demands it. I sealed it with black ribbon and red wax before witnesses, so that neither of us shall be tempted. It is the first thing we have decided together.

a3_j_wedding.title: Mina Harker
a3_j_wedding.text: We were married in the chapel of St Joseph, with Sister Agatha for a witness and an English priest for a voice. I am Mina Harker now. Jonathan does not remember his terror at the altar, but I do: he held my hand as if I were a rope over a pit.

a3_j_vh_arrival.title: Van Helsing
a3_j_vh_arrival.text: He came as the clock struck seven, small, deliberate, with a leather case and a hundredweight of questions. One look at Lucy and he sent for blood. 'Let us not waste time on words, friend John. She needs blood, or she will die this night.'

a3_j_vh_exam.title: The Professor's examination
a3_j_vh_exam.text: He examined her throat with a lens, her eyes with a candle, and her wrist with his watch. He asked what no physician asks: did she sleep with her window open, did she walk at night, did anything fly at the pane? Then he said: 'Arthur is her lover. His blood first.'

a3_j_garlic_rules.title: The garlic
a3_j_garlic_rules.text: He gave me flowers of garlic from Haarlem with the gravity of a priest giving the Host. 'The window. The door. The chimney. And a wreath for her neck, friend John. Do not laugh. It is medicine.' I did not laugh. I was, rather, afraid.

a3_j_tx1.title: The first transfusion
a3_j_tx1.text: Arthur's blood passed into Lucy and the colour came back to her face as dawn comes to a window. Van Helsing's hands never trembled. He told us afterward: 'Arthur must never know that any hand but his own gave her life. A husband has jealousies even for gifts.'

a3_j_night1.title: The garlic has been moved
a3_j_night1.text: At dawn the wreath lay on the floor, the garlic had been swept from the window-sill, the window itself was ajar. Lucy was white again and could say nothing. She had not rung. She had not stirred, and she does not remember.

a3_j_sleepwalk.title: Lucy walks in her sleep
a3_j_sleepwalk.text: Garlic petals on the carpet from the bed to the window-seat; her slippers by the sill, wet with dew. Lucy herself undid the wards, asleep, and does not know it. Van Helsing is quite sure it is not her will but another's. We lock the door, pin the window, and watch.

a3_j_tx2.title: The second transfusion
a3_j_tx2.text: I gave my own blood this time. 'You are strong, friend John, and the secret is the more safe in a doctor's arm than a lover's.' The bed swam a little; brandy set it right. Arthur does not know. Lucy sleeps, and for an hour, so did I.

a3_j_mother_removed.title: The open window
a3_j_mother_removed.text: Mrs Westenra, whose kindness has done more harm than any wolf, found the flowers 'stuffy' and flung them out, and opened the windows to the dawn. We came back to a room cold as a cellar and a girl whom the night had emptied again. Van Helsing wept, and I saw him do it.

a3_j_tx3.title: The third transfusion
a3_j_tx3.text: Van Helsing gave his own blood, saying only: 'Devils or no devils, we fight him all the same.' He will not say who 'him' is. Lucy's cheek has a little rose in it; Mrs Westenra has promised on her honour to touch nothing in the room.

a3_j_peace.title: Four days of peace
a3_j_peace.text: A box of garlic arrives each morning from Haarlem. Lucy eats a little, laughs a little, reads Arthur's letters aloud. Van Helsing sleeps in a chair with a hand on the door. Something flaps at the window each night. He says it is a bat. He does not say it with a smile.

a3_j_wolf.title: The wolf in the window
a3_j_wolf.text: At midnight the glass burst inwards, and a great grey wolf was on the bed. We drove it back, and it fled, howling, into the garden. Mrs Westenra rose to see, and her heart stopped at the sight. She fell across her daughter and lay still. Lucy lay under her in a swoon.

a3_j_mother_dead.title: Mrs Westenra
a3_j_mother_dead.text: She is dead. She had not slept since the shutters failed. A woman who had borne so much so lightly was killed by an animal's face at the window. The garlic that might have kept it out she herself had cleared away.

a3_j_servants.title: The drugged maids
a3_j_servants.text: The maids lay insensible round the kitchen table, smelling of laudanum, and the decanter on the sideboard was left half-full. Van Helsing sniffed it and said nothing. This was not a drunkard's sleep. Someone wished to be undisturbed in that house.

a3_j_tx4.title: The fourth transfusion
a3_j_tx4.text: Quincey Morris came in, rumpled and weather-worn, and held out his arm before we could ask. 'A brave man's blood is the best thing on this earth when a woman is in trouble.' Four men have now given Lucy their blood. She sleeps; I do not.

a3_j_lucy_death.title: Lucy's last night
a3_j_lucy_death.text: Her breath is slow and snoring; her teeth look longer, the gums have drawn back. Arthur kissed her forehead at Van Helsing's word, and that was all. Between one breath and the next she was dead, and for a moment, lovelier than ever she had been.

a3_j_teeth.title: Her teeth
a3_j_teeth.text: Van Helsing drew her lip back with a finger. The canine teeth are longer and sharper than any I have seen in a living mouth. 'You have eyes, friend John. Remember this; remember it well.' He would say no more.

a3_j_memo.title: The paper at her breast
a3_j_memo.text: Lucy's last memorandum was found against her heart: a scrap of a night's fear, 'Arthur, forgive me', in a hand that fails by the end of the page. Van Helsing read it twice and pocketed it. I asked him what it meant, and he answered: 'Another day.'

a3_j_zoo.title: Berserker
a3_j_zoo.text: Mr. Bilder, keeper of the wolves, says Berserker is the gentlest great beast in the gardens, and that on the night of the storm he went mad, tore at the bars, and was gone by morning. A tall thin man had been watching him that evening, he says, with a hooked nose.

a3_j_burial.title: Rain on the yews
a3_j_burial.text: The coffin went down an hour ago. The clergyman has gone; the mourners have gone to the carriages; and the Professor has not moved from the vault door. I have never seen a man look so little like a mourner and so much like a sentry.

a3_j_funeral.title: Kingstead
a3_j_funeral.text: We laid her in the Westenra vault. Arthur wept like a boy; Quincey wept like a man; I did neither, and shall, I think, hereafter. Van Helsing stood at the door and said, 'It is not finished.' I did not ask him what he meant.

a4_j_catacombs.title: The old vaults
a4_j_catacombs.text: Beneath Kingstead lie older vaults than the Westenra tomb: lead coffins in niches, a gallery of the long dead. Lucy is not the first this churchyard has held. I look in each niche for the signs: a lid forced, earth fresh, a face too red. Most are only dead. That is not the same as being at peace.

a4_j_lower.title: The lower gallery
a4_j_lower.text: In the lower gallery one coffin lid has been prised from within; the splinters point outward. Others hunted here before us, and lost. Their stake lies in the dust, its point stained to the grain. We are not the first to learn what that kind of sleep means, and we need not be the last to pay.

a4_j_heath.title: 26 September. Hampstead
a4_j_heath.text: The Gazette tells of children lured on the Heath by a 'bloofer lady', found with small throat wounds. Van Helsing went white when he read it, and has said only that I must see for myself. I do not like the look in his face.

a4_j_gazette.title: The Westminster Gazette
a4_j_gazette.text: A HAMPSTEAD MYSTERY. Children have been missing on the Heath and found, after an interval, with small wounds on the throat. They say a 'bloofer lady' enticed them. It is a pretty name for a horrid thing.

a4_j_bloofer.title: The Bloofer Lady
a4_j_bloofer.text: A nursemaid and a ragged child both speak of a kind lady in white who kisses children on the neck. Children do not invent such tales. I begin to wonder what walks the Heath at night.

a4_j_heath_trail.title: The trail
a4_j_heath_trail.text: A red shoe, a thread of fine lawn, a woman's bare footprints, all pointing north to Kingstead. The Professor says the trail is as clear as the Gazette. I see it, and I do not wish to.

a4_j_child_wound.title: The wound
a4_j_child_wound.text: I saw the child's throat at the North Hospital. Two punctures, a finger apart, white-edged and ragged. I have seen the same on Lucy's neck. There is a doctor in me who says it cannot be, and an observer who says it is.

a4_j_doubt.title: Doubt
a4_j_doubt.text: I told Van Helsing it was madness; he did not rebuke me. He asked for belief in things unseen, and said there is a woman in Paddington whose typewriter will do what his words cannot. I am too weary to quarrel.

a4_j_mina.title: Mrs Harker
a4_j_mina.text: She has the courage of a soldier and the hands of a clerk. She reads her husband's journal and does not weep. If the world is saved, it will be by such women. I ask her only for what she can give.

a4_j_typed.title: The typed pages
a4_j_typed.text: The ribbon was fresh, the keys clean, the shorthand surrendered. By evening the whole of Jonathan's foreign journal lay typed, clear as print. I pray it will convince the doctors, since it has convinced me.

a4_j_jonathan.title: Jonathan's recovery
a4_j_jonathan.text: Jonathan wept when the Professor told him the journal was true. He has been a different man since: pale but whole. He saw the Count in Piccadilly, and fainted; but now he says he will help to the end.

a4_j_belief.title: Belief
a4_j_belief.text: I have read Mina Harker's pages and seen the child's wound. I cannot call it madness any longer. Van Helsing says we shall look into the Westenra tomb. If it is empty, I shall have no more reasons to disbelieve him.

a4_j_papers.title: Lucy's papers
a4_j_papers.text: Lucy's papers are in order, Mr. Marquand's work. Among them the undertaker's bill, which gives the make of the vault lock, and a note in her own hand about walking in her sleep. The Professor smiled sadly: 'it is all here.'

a4_j_crucifix.title: The crucifix
a4_j_crucifix.text: The little gold cross was stolen by the maid, who is poor and frightened. I redeemed it, and forgave her. A wretch in need is not to be punished; a wretch in power is.

a4_j_lock.title: Keys
a4_j_lock.text: I cut a key for a four-lever falling lock by the undertaker's description. An hour of filing at the bench; it fits as if made by Chubb. I feel like a criminal and a physician at once.

a4_j_dinner.title: Dinner at the Castle
a4_j_dinner.text: We dined at Jack Straw's, I with little appetite. The Professor explained his plan and chose the dark path by Hampstead Lane to avoid the patrol. Then, with turnscrew, saw, candle and cross, we set out for Kingstead.

a4_j_night1.title: The empty coffin
a4_j_night1.text: We opened the vault by night. The Professor unscrewed the lid, cut through the lead with a tiny saw, and held the candle over the satin. The coffin was empty. I felt as though the ground gave way.

a4_j_child_found.title: The child
a4_j_child_found.text: We watched from under the yew. A white figure came with a child in her arms. The Professor opened the lantern, and I saw Lucy's face, her mouth wet with blood. She dropped the child and fled into the tomb.

a4_j_handoff.title: The constable
a4_j_handoff.text: We laid the child on a bench under the lamp and hid behind the hedge. The constable found it within minutes, and we slipped home across the Heath. The Professor said nothing, and neither did I.

a4_j_day2.title: The afternoon
a4_j_day2.text: By day we opened the coffin again. Lucy lay sleeping, redder and more beautiful than in death, with fresh blood on her lips and her teeth sharper. The Professor said: 'Now do you believe?' I did.

a4_j_lucy_sleeping.title: Lucy sleeping
a4_j_lucy_sleeping.text: She lay as in sleep, but not at rest. The Professor says she is Un-Dead and that we must fetch Arthur: it is his right, and his burden, to see her released.

a4_j_arthur.title: Arthur's consent
a4_j_arthur.text: Arthur agreed to come. He was white as paper, but he said that if there was any chance of releasing her, he would take it. Quincey Morris stood beside him, silent and unshakeable.

a4_j_vigil.title: The vigil
a4_j_vigil.text: We watched under the alders. The Bloofer Lady came with a child on her arm and called Arthur by name. The Professor held up the golden crucifix, and she fell back, hissing, as if burned.

a4_j_lucy_down.title: At dusk
a4_j_lucy_down.text: At sunset she rose, with a smile that was not hers. We drove her back with the cross and our hands until she lay helpless. The Professor said, 'Now, friend Arthur, strike.'

a4_j_stake.title: The stake
a4_j_stake.text: Arthur set the point above her heart and drove the stake home with three blows. The body arched, screamed, and was still. The Professor read the prayers while the tomb breathed out.

a4_j_peace.title: Peace
a4_j_peace.text: We did what remained: the head, the garlic, the lead case soldered shut. The face wore the sweetness of the girl I had loved. Arthur said, 'She smiled at me.' I think she did.

a4_j_vow.title: The vow
a4_j_vow.text: We swore on the vault door to hunt down the creature that did this. The Professor asked me for the use of my asylum, and for all the help I could give. It is a hard road, but I shall walk it.

a5_j_cellar.title: Beneath the chapel
a5_j_cellar.text: Under Carfax chapel lies a cellar of damp dressed stone, older than the house. The boxes above were carried up from here; the drag-marks on the flags are plain. Fifty boxes came to Carfax and only twenty-nine stand in the nave. The rest went out by cart, and carters keep ledgers.

a5_j_labels.title: Torn shipping labels
a5_j_labels.text: Among the straw, half-torn labels in a clerk's hand: 'Carter, Paterson and Co.' - 'Jamaica L...' - 'Piccad...' - 'to be called for'. The twenty-one missing boxes did not vanish. They were ordered, and what is ordered is written down.

a5_j_vault.title: The lower vault
a5_j_vault.text: Below the cellar, a second vault of brick where the damp stands in puddles and the air tastes of copper. If the Count made a bed in England, he made it where no church bell could reach. The cold that rises here is not the cold of stone.

a5_j_arrival.title: 29 September, Purfleet
a5_j_arrival.text: Jonathan Harker and his wife arrive at the asylum. He is grey at the temples, and she is brave beyond words. Van Helsing greets them as old friends. At last, one house holds all of those who know.

a5_j_harker_meet.title: Jonathan Harker's journal
a5_j_harker_meet.text: Jonathan has handed Dr. Seward every page of his Transylvanian journal. I am to copy it and everything else. I know of no better use for a typewriter.

a5_j_cylinders.title: The locked cabinet
a5_j_cylinders.text: I unlocked the cabinet with the little key and gave Mrs. Harker the cylinders of my phonograph diary. She wept at Lucy's death, but said she must hear it all.

a5_j_typed_cyl.title: Typed: the phonograph diary
a5_j_typed_cyl.text: Seward's cylinders typed. Renfield's fits, Lucy's wasting, the night at Hillingham. And a note: Renfield's wildest days fall when the Count is near the house.

a5_j_typed_harker.title: Typed: Jonathan's journal
a5_j_typed_harker.text: Jonathan's journal typed. The castle, the Count's boxes of earth, fifty of them in the chapel. And the shipping to Whitby, to London, to Carfax.

a5_j_typed_whitby.title: Typed: the Whitby papers
a5_j_typed_whitby.text: My Whitby diary typed with the cuttings. A great dog leapt ashore from the Demeter, and Lucy's sleep-walking began the same week.

a5_j_typed_vh.title: Typed: the memorandum
a5_j_typed_vh.text: The Professor's memorandum typed: the Un-Dead cannot rest save in earth sanctified to them. They lie in their boxes by day and walk by night.

a5_j_typed_renfield.title: Typed: Renfield's tallies
a5_j_typed_renfield.text: Renfield's notebook typed. His columns of flies and sparrows lie in a pattern. They climb and fall with the nights the Count visits.

a5_j_link_carfax.title: The Count's lair
a5_j_link_carfax.text: Jonathan's fifty boxes and Mr. Hawkins' deeds for Carfax. The Count sleeps among them in the old chapel next door to the asylum.

a5_j_link_renfield.title: Renfield is the door
a5_j_link_renfield.text: Renfield's moods and the Count's visits keep step. He is the Count's pawn, and perhaps the only one who can tell us when the Count is near.

a5_j_link_whitby.title: The road from Whitby
a5_j_link_whitby.text: The Demeter's cargo of fifty boxes consigned to Billington of Whitby, then by rail to London, then by carrier to Carfax. A road can be followed.

a5_j_records_done.title: The records are complete
a5_j_records_done.text: The papers are in order. Fifty boxes; the Count must rest in each of them. Destroy their holy sanctuary, and he has nowhere to hide. I told the Professor what I had found.

a5_j_council.title: Council of war
a5_j_council.text: We sat round the long table. Van Helsing told us all that science does not teach, and we, who laughed at it, listened. I never felt so small, nor so resolved.

a5_j_rules.title: What the Un-Dead are
a5_j_rules.text: He is strong as twenty. He casts no shadow, no reflection. He cannot enter unless invited. He is powerless at noon, and cannot cross running water save at slack or flood tide. Crucifix, garlic, the Host: these he shuns.

a5_j_mina_joins.title: Madam Mina is one of us
a5_j_mina_joins.text: They have admitted me to counsel. The Professor says: no more secrets. I felt a great weight lift, and a greater one settle upon my heart.

a5_j_carfax_enter.title: Carfax by lantern light
a5_j_carfax_enter.text: We went through the wall at dusk with the keys in Harker's hand. The house breathed damp. The chapel door took two of us to open. The smell of the earth was ripe.

a5_j_rats.title: The rats of Carfax
a5_j_rats.text: Thousands of rats, eyes like coals, poured from the crypt. Arthur's terriers went in like furies. When the lamps were held high, the swarm broke.

a5_j_boxes29.title: Twenty-nine of fifty
a5_j_boxes29.text: We counted twenty-nine boxes, sterilised each with a crumb of the Host. Fifty came from the castle. Twenty-one are elsewhere in London, and the Count knows we are hunting.

a5_j_ledger.title: The carriers' ledger
a5_j_ledger.text: Mr. Smollet's ledger: six boxes to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town; six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey; the rest nine boxes to a man called Bloxam. A sovereign opens a ledger.

a5_j_bloxam.title: Sam Bloxam of Walworth
a5_j_bloxam.text: Bloxam carried the nine boxes to a stone-fronted house in Piccadilly, bow window, high steps, a white church nearby. An old man with a white moustache lifted a box himself.

a5_j_agent.title: Mitchell, Sons & Candy
a5_j_agent.text: The house agents confirm: 347 Piccadilly sold for cash to Count de Ville. A word of Lord Godalming's, a letter and a clerk's nerves, and I have the keys.

a5_j_renfield_plea.title: Renfield asks to go
a5_j_renfield_plea.text: Renfield begged to be released: 'Do not let Him find me.' Not mad then, or not entirely. He feels the Count's attention. I have told Van Helsing.

a5_j_renfield_dead.title: Renfield dying
a5_j_renfield_dead.text: We found Renfield with a broken back and a smashed skull. 'I tried to stop Him. He promised me life, and I was weak.' We are all weak. We are sworn nevertheless.

a5_j_attack.title: The Count in the bedroom
a5_j_attack.text: The door burst. Moonlight, mist, and Mina on her knees at the Count's chest, drinking. Jonathan in a stupor. Van Helsing held out the Host. The Count cowered back, and went.

a5_j_unclean.title: Unclean
a5_j_unclean.text: 'Unclean! Unclean!' The Host burned my forehead like a hot iron. The Professor says the scar will fade when the Count is dead, and not before. I shall wear it as a sign.

a5_j_piccadilly.title: 347 Piccadilly
a5_j_piccadilly.text: Eight boxes in the Piccadilly hall, sterilised. Then the front door, and the Count on the threshold. He leapt through us like a cat through rats. His keys and his money fell in the hall.

a5_j_keys_money.title: The Count's pocketbook
a5_j_keys_money.text: Notes and gold, and the bunch of keys with labels in a neat hand: Mile End, Bermondsey. He is not omnipotent. He bleeds money like any man, and he is afraid of us.

a5_j_mile_end.title: Mile End
a5_j_mile_end.text: Six boxes in a boarded cellar. Arthur's keys turned in the Count's locks. A crumb of the Host on the earth, and the hideous smell was gone.

a5_j_bermondsey.title: Bermondsey
a5_j_bermondsey.text: Six more at Jamaica Lane. Forty-nine boxes destroyed. One remains in the Count's hands, and he knows it.

a5_j_bond.title: The bond
a5_j_bond.text: I feel him, like a cold wind with a taste. When the sun is rising or setting I seem able to follow him a little way. The Professor says this may be our only road to him.

a5_j_trance1.title: At sunrise
a5_j_trance1.text: Under the Professor's hand I heard lapping water, creaking wood, a rope taut, the hollow tramp of feet above. Darkness, and cold. I am afraid for what I said.

a5_j_trance2.title: At sunset
a5_j_trance2.text: At sunset again: dull ringing of a bell, hawsers, a cry from the deck. 'We are going, we are going.' I could not say where. The Count was close, and aware.

a5_j_ship.title: The Czarina Catherine
a5_j_ship.text: Lloyd's reports: the Czarina Catherine cleared the Thames for Varna. A ship, water and wood, an eastbound hawser. He is returning to his own land. We must race him.

a5_j_plan.title: Van Helsing's plan
a5_j_plan.text: By rail to Paris and the Orient Express, then Varna. The Count's ship is slow, ours fast. We shall be there first and wait for the box. All of us, save one.

a5_j_left_out.title: Left behind
a5_j_left_out.text: They have decided to go and I am not in the plan. 'It is for your safety.' I watched the cab out of sight with Jonathan's face still in my eyes. I do not mean to stay behind.

a6_j_ward.title: The outer ward
a6_j_ward.text: By day the Count's stronghold is only a ruin: fallen merlons, a gate that no longer closes, and a keep rotted open to the snow. But a fire was lit here not two days past, and the cold ashes lead toward the gate. He has not left his house empty. He has left it waiting.

a6_j_oath.title: 11 October. The promise
a6_j_oath.text: Before we left London Mina asked each of us to swear that, if she turned, we would do for her what we did for Lucy. Quincey swore first. Jonathan was to read the Burial Service. We are in God's hands, and we must be steady.

a6_j_varna.title: 15 October. Varna
a6_j_varna.text: Three days by the Orient Express. Mina slept almost the whole way. Now we are at Varna, and the Czarina Catherine has not arrived. Lord Godalming wires Lloyd's daily. We have nothing to do but wait.

a6_j_trance1.title: Mina at sunset
a6_j_trance1.text: The Professor put me in trance. I heard lapping water, rushing by. I heard creaking, as of masts and cordage, and the tramp of feet overhead. I felt a motion under me. The ship is moving, and the ship is not here.

a6_j_lloyds.title: Lloyd's report
a6_j_lloyds.text: The Czarina Catherine was reported passing the Dardanelles on 4 October. Nothing since. A fast steamer would be here already; she is not. Either the sea has her, or she is making for some other port.

a6_j_deduce.title: The ship is elsewhere
a6_j_deduce.text: Van Helsing says the Count knows we are at Varna: he learned it through Mina's mind, and has cut her off. The ship will not come where we wait. We must watch the wires and be ready to run.

a6_j_telegram.title: 28 October. Galatz!
a6_j_telegram.text: A telegram from Lloyd's: the Czarina Catherine has entered Galatz at one o'clock. We have been tricked, and by a margin of a day. Mina, the 'train fiend,' says the only train leaves at 6.30 in the morning.

a6_j_timetable.title: The 6.30
a6_j_timetable.text: The Continental Bradshaw gives one train a day from Varna to Galatz: leaving at half-past six, arriving in the afternoon. Jonathan laughs at me for my 'train fiend' ways, but he is glad of them now.

a6_j_galatz.title: 30 October. The Czarina Catherine
a6_j_galatz.text: The ship lies in the river harbour, and the box is gone. Captain Donelson says the box was taken ashore at dawn by men acting for a Hildesheim. Our one hope now is to follow the trail before it is cold.

a6_j_donelson.title: Captain Donelson's tale
a6_j_donelson.text: A fog went with the ship from the Bay of Biscay to Galatz, and the crew would not touch the long box. The Captain swung a handspike at the mutiny. 'If the Deil did have any luggage aboord the ship, it was nane ither than that.'

a6_j_hildesheim.title: Hildesheim
a6_j_hildesheim.text: Immanuel Hildesheim was bought at a fair price and delivered a receipt. The box was handed to a Slovak named Petrof Skinsky. The price was paid by an English note cashed at the bank. Hildesheim hopes we shall not trouble him again.

a6_j_skinsky.title: Petrof Skinsky
a6_j_skinsky.text: Skinsky was found in St. Peter's churchyard, his throat torn. The priest says wolves; the neighbours say a very tall man. But in his coat was a slip for a boat and a crew of Slovaks, to go up the river by night.

a6_j_memorandum.title: Mina's memorandum
a6_j_memorandum.text: By exclusion: not by road, since horses fear him; not by rail, since he must be seen at stations; therefore by water, on the Sereth, then the Bistritza, which is the water that runs by the Borgo Pass. It must be so.

a6_j_council.title: The council of war
a6_j_council.text: Lord Godalming and Jonathan go by steam launch. Quincey and I ride the bank. Van Helsing takes Mina by train and carriage to the Borgo Pass and the castle. Jonathan protested; Mina quieted him. Money brought us a launch, horses and maps in three hours.

a6_j_launch.title: Night on the river
a6_j_launch.text: We steam day and night, overhauling every boat. The Slovaks fall on their knees when our electric lamp strikes them. They say a boat with a great box passed before us, bound up the Bistritza with Szgany at the oars.

a6_j_rapids.title: The rapids
a6_j_rapids.text: The launch struck a rock below the rapids and lost her keel plank. We mended her with a spar, a coil of rope and canvas, and lost half a day. Lord Godalming bought horses at a farm above the falls.

a6_j_trail.title: The bank road
a6_j_trail.text: Quincey and I have ridden three days along the right bank. At Fundu we heard that the launch went up the Bistritza. Snow threatens; if the road closes we shall take a sledge and go on, Russian fashion. Wolves howl behind us.

a6_j_veresti.title: 31 October. Veresti
a6_j_veresti.text: The Professor bought a carriage, horses and furs. The landlady packed a great basket and wept. We are truly in the hands of God. I write this to Jonathan, who may never see it.

a6_j_road.title: The Borgo road
a6_j_road.text: I knew the road at the Pass. Have not my Jonathan travelled it, and written of his travel? I am strangely sleepy all day and wakeful at dusk. The peasants cross themselves at my scar. The Professor watches me and says nothing.

a6_j_circle.title: 4 November. The holy circle
a6_j_circle.text: The Professor crumbled the Host into a ring around me and the fire. I cannot step out of it, though I long to. The horses scream and cower in the snow. Mist forms in the dark, and three white women are calling me sister.

a6_j_sisters.title: The three sisters
a6_j_sisters.text: They begged, and laughed, and wept, and held out their arms. 'Come, sister. Come to us.' The Professor held the Host toward them and they could not cross. At dawn they thinned into the snow, and we found the horses dead.

a6_j_castle.title: 5 November. The castle
a6_j_castle.text: By day the castle is only stone. I broke the rusted chapel door with a blacksmith's hammer, and my heart was a stone also. I must not look at the faces in the tombs too long.

a6_j_brides.title: The three tombs
a6_j_brides.text: In the first tomb lay a woman so lovely that I felt the madness of her call. I heard Mina's wail, and the spell broke. Stake, then knife; the dust fell and she was at peace. So with the others. Three souls made free.

a6_j_tomb.title: The Count's tomb
a6_j_tomb.text: I laid a piece of Host in the Count's own tomb, which was empty, and made it unclean for him forever. The doors I sealed with the Wafer also. He cannot come home to rest, whatever else he may do.

a6_j_hollow.title: 6 November. The hollow
a6_j_hollow.text: We rested in a hollow between two great stones. The Professor drew a circle around the rock and looked out through the glasses. 'They are racing for the sunset. We may be too late. God's will be done!'

a6_j_final.title: The sunset
a6_j_final.text: We rode to death of some one. The Szgany closed around the wagon. I cut through to the box; Quincey beside me. I swung the kukri at the Count's throat while Quincey's knife went to his heart. Before our eyes he crumbled into dust.

a6_j_quincey.title: Quincey Morris
a6_j_quincey.text: Quincey was stabbed in the side and bleeding fast. The setting sun fell on my forehead, and he cried, 'See! The snow is not more stainless than her forehead! The curse has passed away!' He died with a smile. A gallant gentleman.

arthur_burden_j_sickroom.title: The long illness
arthur_burden_j_sickroom.text: My father has been dying since Candlemas. We have a nurse, a physician and a rug over his knees. He would prefer his spectacles, his cordial, and news from Hillingham, in that order. I have not slept a whole night in a fortnight.

arthur_burden_j_blessing.title: My father's blessing
arthur_burden_j_blessing.text: He read Mrs. Westenra's telegram with trembling hands and told me to go to Lucy. There is a ring in his desk, a letter, and a key hidden somewhere in the hall. He looked ashamed when he spoke of the key. I did not ask why.

arthur_burden_j_hillingham.title: Hillingham
arthur_burden_j_hillingham.text: Lucy in the garden, Mrs. Westenra under her parasol, and Quincey Morris making an elegant exit with the air of a man who has lost a bet and enjoyed it. I had come to propose and my hands were damp.

arthur_burden_j_mrs.title: Mrs. Westenra's question
arthur_burden_j_mrs.text: She asked whether the Ring was in good heart. I answered as I did. Whatever I said, she watched my face while I said it, and I knew I would remember her look when I was older.

arthur_burden_j_proposal.title: The ring and the rose
arthur_burden_j_proposal.text: She said yes. I said many foolish things first. She gave me a blue ribbon from her hair, and I have worn it against my watch since, and I think I am the happiest man in England.

arthur_burden_j_summer.title: The summer-house
arthur_burden_j_summer.text: Three weeks of tea, croquet and Tennyson. I had not known that life could be so light. Lucy cheats at croquet. Mrs. Westenra pretends not to see. Quincey, to his credit, loses at it with great ceremony.

arthur_burden_j_telegram_back.title: The telegram
arthur_burden_j_telegram_back.text: 'LORD GODALMING SINKING.' I left Hillingham in the dusk with Lucy's hand in mine until the carriage moved. I did not reach the Ring in time. He had died at four, with Bates beside him, and a window open that he had asked for.

arthur_burden_j_death.title: My father is dead
arthur_burden_j_death.text: I am Lord Godalming. The title sits on my shoulders like a coat cut for a larger man. Bates has wept, Dr. Lenox has not, and Mr. Pennefather has the face of a man bringing me a bill. He is, I think, bringing me a bill.

arthur_burden_j_office.title: The steward's office
arthur_burden_j_office.text: Wilkes keeps the ledgers as another man keeps a conscience: carefully and out of sight. There was a book on his desk with a strap round it. The red ink in it looked less like arithmetic than like a wound.

arthur_burden_j_steward.title: Wilkes confesses
arthur_burden_j_steward.text: Thirty years' service, and he held the secret for my father for four of them. I could not be angry for more than a minute. He gave me the key to the muniment room, and the knowledge that I would need my father's signet to use it.

arthur_burden_j_village.title: The village green
arthur_burden_j_village.text: The tenants did not take off their hats. I did not blame them. Marsh spoke for them, with Mrs. Marsh listening and the miller scowling. They want to see whether the new Lord will do more than inherit.

arthur_burden_j_wood_in.title: The Home Wood
arthur_burden_j_wood_in.text: A hind with her throat torn. Three shapes in the dark, and something growling that was not entirely a dog. I will not be afraid in my own wood. I will merely be careful.

arthur_burden_j_chapel.title: The family chapel
arthur_burden_j_chapel.text: The bell rang once, though the rope was still, and there was a woman kneeling at the far pew. She was Nan, my nurse. I have decided that the bell was the wind, and that I am not afraid of it.

arthur_burden_j_vault_open.title: The year of resting
arthur_burden_j_vault_open.text: 'Here he rests.' Not the year Sir Hugh fell, but the year his son carried him home. A house which marks its burials as homecomings is a house I do not wish to disgrace.

arthur_burden_j_vault.title: My father's coffin
arthur_burden_j_vault.text: The vault is dry and ordered. My mother is here. He is by her. I stood a long time. The signet was on his hands, as custom says. I took it and I will wear it.

arthur_burden_j_tenants.title: The tenants' petition
arthur_burden_j_tenants.text: I told Marsh the truth: the estate is mortgaged to its roof, and not a cottage will be sold if I can help it. He took off his hat. They have given me thirty names and their promise to stand by me.

arthur_burden_j_muniment.title: The muniment room
arthur_burden_j_muniment.text: I broke the seal of silence. My father left a deed and a letter, side by side on the blotter, as though he were waiting for me. He is, in a manner of speaking. I read them standing.

arthur_burden_j_terms.title: Mr. Crowle's kindness
arthur_burden_j_terms.text: A very reasonable man. Sell the Wood, say nothing, be rid of it all by Michaelmas. It is the most comfortable thing anyone has offered me in a month, and I know that is exactly what is wrong with it.

arthur_burden_j_end_lie.title: The comfortable lie
arthur_burden_j_end_lie.text: I signed. The Wood is gone, the debt is small, and no one spoke of it again. I am a very good Lord Godalming by every measure but one, and that one I do not take out to look at often.

arthur_burden_j_end_truth.title: The hard truth
arthur_burden_j_end_truth.text: I stood on the green and said it all. The village did not cheer; it did something better and went home to count what it could give. I know now that a name can bear a debt but not a lie. I wear the signet in good conscience.

arthur_burden_j_wood_out.title: The Wood is clear
arthur_burden_j_wood_out.text: Two poachers and a starved wolf, driven out of my grandfather's oaks by a man with a club and a worse temper than he knew he had. Hobbs wept. The tenants will want to hear it from me.

demeter_voyage_j_varna.title: Varna
demeter_voyage_j_varna.text: 6 July. The quay is loud and the cargo is quiet. Fifty boxes of earth and sand, for a gentleman in Whitby whom no one has met. The freight is paid in full and I am asked no question. I have been twenty years at sea and I do not like a cargo that nobody wants to talk about.

demeter_voyage_j_cargo.title: The bill of lading
demeter_voyage_j_cargo.text: Fifty boxes of earth, silver sand, consigned to Mr. S. F. Billington of Whitby. The papers are clean. The man who ordered it did not come himself, and the Slovaks who loaded it would not look at it. I put the bill in my coat and I say nothing.

demeter_voyage_j_cleared.title: Customs
demeter_voyage_j_cleared.text: The customs officer found the boxes 'irregular' until I found a silver coin. Then they were perfectly regular. I have been in business long enough to know that this is how the world works, and long enough to hope that it will not always be so.

demeter_voyage_j_blessed.title: The blessing
demeter_voyage_j_blessed.text: Father Nikolai blessed the ship and gave me a small flask of holy water. 'A cross is better than a pilot,' he said. I do not argue with priests, and on this voyage I am not sure I argue with anyone.

demeter_voyage_j_sail.title: Departure
demeter_voyage_j_sail.text: At noon we cast off. East wind, fresh. The men sing at the capstan, a little too loudly. Five hands, two mates, the cook, and myself; a good crew who have sailed with me before. I expected nothing, and I am already uneasy.

demeter_voyage_j_cabin.title: My cabin
demeter_voyage_j_cabin.text: My own cabin, my own lamp, my own cross in the sea-chest. I have kept the log here for twenty years. I shall keep it as long as I can hold a pen.

demeter_voyage_j_hold.title: The hold
demeter_voyage_j_hold.text: Fifty boxes in five rows. The ship sits lower than clay would make her. I count them twice. It is the same number, and it should be a comfort.

demeter_voyage_j_galley.title: The galley
demeter_voyage_j_galley.text: The cook is the most superstitious man aboard, and the only one I would trust with the ship. Garlic over the stove, salt on the step. He laughs at me, then crosses himself.

demeter_voyage_j_fore.title: The forecastle
demeter_voyage_j_fore.text: The men have nailed more holy pictures over their bunks than a church has walls. I say nothing. A man who prays is a man who has not given up.

demeter_voyage_j_weather.title: Reading the weather
demeter_voyage_j_weather.text: Glass falling, mares'-tails in the north-west, gulls inland, porpoises running west. The cook, the sky and the needle agree. We reef down before the blow; the men are quicker than I ever saw them. It is good to give orders that make sense.

demeter_voyage_j_log1.title: 11 July, the Bosphorus
demeter_voyage_j_log1.text: 11 July at dawn entered Bosphorus. Boarded by Turkish Customs officers. Backsheesh. All correct. Under way at 4 p.m. 12 July, through the Dardanelles. More Customs officers. Want us off soon. At dark passed into the Archipelago. I write it exactly, so that it can be checked.

demeter_voyage_j_petrofsky.title: Petrofsky
demeter_voyage_j_petrofsky.text: 16 July. Petrofsky is missing. He took the larboard watch at eight bells and was relieved by Abramoff, but he never went to his bunk. The men say they expected it. They will say no more than that there is something aboard.

demeter_voyage_j_olgaren.title: A tall thin man
demeter_voyage_j_olgaren.text: 17 July. Olgaren tells me that behind the deck-house, in the rain, he saw a tall, thin man, not like any of the crew, come up the companion-way and go along the deck, and disappear. He followed and found no one, and every hatch closed. I fear that panic may spread.

demeter_voyage_j_log2.title: The search
demeter_voyage_j_log2.text: Searched stem to stern with lanterns, all keeping abreast. No man found; only earth spilled from box thirteen to the bows, and Petrofsky's cap. The men are relieved. The mate scowled and said nothing. I did not say what I thought.

demeter_voyage_j_dmitri.title: Dmitri
demeter_voyage_j_dmitri.text: 24 July. Dmitri is gone. A second man off his watch, and not seen again. The crew have sent me a round robin asking for a double watch. They fear to be alone. The mate is angry. I fear that either he or the men will do some violence.

demeter_voyage_j_log3.title: Two men gone
demeter_voyage_j_log3.text: Two men lost since Varna: Petrofsky and Dmitri. Both off watch, neither seen again. I write it exactly. A log does not weep, and neither will I, until I am ashore.

demeter_voyage_j_roster.title: The watch bill
demeter_voyage_j_roster.text: I chalk up the watches: Ivan and Bolotin for the first, the mate and myself for the middle, Olgaren and Abramoff for the morning. No man alone. If anything can be done by arithmetic, I have done it.

demeter_voyage_j_storm.title: Four days in hell
demeter_voyage_j_storm.text: 28 July. Four days in a maelstrom; no sleep for anyone. 29 July: the second mate gone, and only the steersman on deck. 30 July: both watch and helmsman gone. Without second mate, crew in a panic. The mate and I agree to go armed henceforth and wait for any sign of the cause.

demeter_voyage_j_box.title: Box thirteen
demeter_voyage_j_box.text: With the crowbar I opened the box with the bright nails. Black earth, and in it the shape of a man. I have done what I can: it will not be a bed again. But there are forty-nine more, and I am one man.

demeter_voyage_j_cry.title: The cry
demeter_voyage_j_cry.text: 2 August, midnight. A cry outside my port. The mate heard it too, and ran. No sign of the man on watch. One more gone. I take lantern and club to the hold, where the boxes are moving.

demeter_voyage_j_dark.title: The dark in the hold
demeter_voyage_j_dark.text: In the hold, with a lantern and a cross, I held off the dark until dawn. Whether it was bats, or rats, or the thing that walks on deck, I cannot swear. Something with a white face. Olgaren is gone. God, help me.

demeter_voyage_j_log4.title: The final entry
demeter_voyage_j_log4.text: I have written the last entry, sealed it in a bottle, and kept the cabin key in my pocket. If we are wrecked, mayhap this bottle may be found, and those who find it may understand.

demeter_voyage_j_mate.title: The mate
demeter_voyage_j_mate.text: 3 August. The mate came on deck as if shot from a gun, his eyes rolling. 'You had better come too, Captain, before it is too late. The sea will save me from Him.' And he leapt overboard. I suppose I know the secret now.

demeter_voyage_j_bow.title: The bows
demeter_voyage_j_bow.text: The bow is where Olgaren saw It, and where the mate saw It. It is where the fog begins. I stand on the foredeck and I am sure that if I turn my back, it will be behind me.

demeter_voyage_j_wheel.title: The wheel
demeter_voyage_j_wheel.text: The wheel is the only thing aboard that still obeys. I put my hands where a hundred captains have put theirs, and I decide, quietly, that mine are the last that will.

demeter_voyage_j_end.title: Lashed to the wheel
demeter_voyage_j_end.text: 4 August. I shall tie my hands to the wheel, and along with them I shall tie that which He dare not touch; and then, come good wind or foul, I shall save my soul, and my honour as a captain. God and the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.

dracula_voivode_j_hall.title: The hall at Severin's hour
dracula_voivode_j_hall.text: My father is two years dead and I am nineteen. The council meets in his hall, in his chair, with his crest on the wall, and not one man here believes I will keep it. Severin burns on the border. They look at me as at a candle, wondering how long before the draught.

dracula_voivode_j_chamber.title: My father's chamber
dracula_voivode_j_chamber.text: I sleep here now, or fail to. There is a chest with a dial, a stand of armour, a portrait of a man I could not please, and Ileana by the window. I was a boy in this room. It has since decided I am not.

dracula_voivode_j_chest.title: The Order's year
dracula_voivode_j_chest.text: The Order of the Dragon was founded in 1408; my father was invested in 1431. The Order is older than the man. I have been inclined to forget that the men who wear a thing are less than the thing. The chest opened with the older date, the right date. It is a lesson.

dracula_voivode_j_sealed.title: The sealed order
dracula_voivode_j_sealed.text: A dragon in green wax. The levy has been a clerk's wish for a week. In one moment, with my father's ring, it becomes an army. I hope no man ever learns how easily paper becomes blood.

dracula_voivode_j_council_open.title: The granary opened
dracula_voivode_j_council_open.text: Two hundred villagers fed from the army's store. Vlaicu stormed and Stanciu bowed. The men will march on thinner rations, and the village will remember who fed it. I do not know whether I have done wisely. I know it is what I would want done to me.

dracula_voivode_j_council_closed.title: The gates closed
dracula_voivode_j_council_closed.text: I told the villagers they could not have the grain, and the army ate. Some of the villagers walked away at dawn. Not all of them could. Stanciu says it was prudent, and does not meet my eyes. The army is fed. I cannot be sure of the rest of us.

dracula_voivode_j_radu_spared.title: Radu sent away
dracula_voivode_j_radu_spared.text: I read the letter aloud to Radu, and then I let him go. He walked out of the gate with a cloak and a horse, and his face was the face of a boy who has been caught and not whipped. I will see him again, and I will not know what he intends.

dracula_voivode_j_radu_chained.title: Radu in the cells
dracula_voivode_j_radu_chained.text: I read the letter aloud to Radu and gave him to the guard. He did not resist. The key in my hand felt as though it belonged to some more severe person. My brother is below my feet in the dark, and I tell myself it is justice.

dracula_voivode_j_tower.title: The beacon on the tower
dracula_voivode_j_tower.text: Old Dan told me what the tower needs: lamp-oil from the hall and a torch from the stair-door bracket. Without a signal the ridge garrison will not know we have left. I am a prince whose first order is to arrange a bonfire.

dracula_voivode_j_beacon.title: The ridge answers
dracula_voivode_j_beacon.text: Oil, a torch, and a pillar of fire above the pass. Across the valley a small light answered, and then another. Forty spears on the far crag. I stood and watched it burn until Dan said politely that the wind would soon turn the sparks onto the thatch.

dracula_voivode_j_road.title: The hungry road
dracula_voivode_j_road.text: The levy goes one way down the mountain and the refugees come the other, and between them the road is no wider than a wagon. A child asked me if the Turk had a face. I said yes. She asked if I had seen it. I said no. She nodded, as one who knew better.

dracula_voivode_j_refugee.title: The grandmother
dracula_voivode_j_refugee.text: I gave her bread and a blanket from my pack. She did not thank me for the bread, only for the blanket. She said the bread was just, but the blanket was kind, and kindness was the thing nobody had spared for her. It cost me nothing, and I am still thinking of it.

dracula_voivode_j_camp.title: The army's camp
dracula_voivode_j_camp.text: A hundred fires, ten thousand men, and none of them certain whose war this is. Mircea tells stories of Kossova and I try not to look too closely at what he leaves out. I am to put them in a ford by the dark of the moon, and I do not yet know which.

dracula_voivode_j_prisoner_parley.title: The Akinji's name
dracula_voivode_j_prisoner_parley.text: He gave me his name, Ahmed, and the ford, for a blanket and a cup of water. The old way says never trust a captive. The newer way, mine, says never trust a man you have starved. I think I am a poor student of both.

dracula_voivode_j_prisoner_broken.title: The Akinji, broken
dracula_voivode_j_prisoner_broken.text: He told me the ford. It took a quarter of an hour. I do not intend to remember how it was done, and I know I shall remember nothing else. Mircea, who has seen worse, put his hand on my shoulder and said it was necessary. That is how it begins.

dracula_voivode_j_map.title: The Reed Ford
dracula_voivode_j_map.text: Felt on the hooves, reeds on the banks, a creek from the north-east: the Stone Ford would ring, and the Wolf's Ford is too far. Reed Ford it must be. I placed three hundred spears among the reeds myself, and a hundred archers at the bend, and then I waited.

dracula_voivode_j_ford.title: The night raid
dracula_voivode_j_ford.text: They came as Cristea said, low and silent, with their horses in felt. I never knew how loud a river could be until it was full of men trying not to be heard. The first one saw me at ten paces. I had my father's hammer, and I did not hesitate.

dracula_voivode_j_hermit.title: The pale scholar
dracula_voivode_j_hermit.text: He knew what I had not told my captains: that the ford was sold. I did not ask who sold it. I think I knew. He offered me a school, and a lesson, and an eternity, in the voice of a man selling a horse. I took the token. I cannot say why, except that I was tired of being beaten.

dracula_voivode_j_lake.title: Lake Hermannstadt
dracula_voivode_j_lake.text: A black lake, a ferryman with no breath and a mountain with its door open. 'The tenth pays more,' said the scratched post. I did not ask what. I paid the first toll in silver, taken from a drowned scholar's cairn. It felt like stealing from a man who was too proud to mind.

dracula_voivode_j_school.title: The Scholomance
dracula_voivode_j_school.text: A stone school under the mountain. The Master teaches with the amused patience of a thing that has had a thousand pupils and remembers each. The lessons are of names, of weather, of the speech of wolves. Nobody laughs. Nobody leaves. In spring, they say, the tenth is taken.

dracula_voivode_j_vasile_friend.title: Vasile's key
dracula_voivode_j_vasile_friend.text: I offered him a share of what I learned instead of a threat. He looked at me as though I had spoken Greek, and then he laughed, and gave me the key. It is a small thing. I find I am proud of it, and ashamed that I am surprised.

dracula_voivode_j_vasile_cowed.title: Vasile's key
dracula_voivode_j_vasile_cowed.text: I laid a hand on my dagger and Vasile gave me the library key as quickly as a child gives up an apple. He has not spoken to me since. I did not need to draw. That, I suppose, is what a prince's reputation is for.

dracula_voivode_j_library.title: The forbidden library
dracula_voivode_j_library.text: Chained books, black candles and a cold that has nothing to do with the weather. I read the Clavis Minor with my teeth clenched. Water to open the way, silver to bind, flame to seal. The order matters more than the things. It always does.

dracula_voivode_j_rite.title: The rite of three
dracula_voivode_j_rite.text: Water, silver, flame. The altar accepted them in that order and hummed like a struck bell. I felt, for one moment, that something large had noticed me and been pleased. I do not know how to make that feeling stop being pleasant.

dracula_voivode_j_tithe.title: The tithe chamber
dracula_voivode_j_tithe.text: Ten seats in a ring, a green fire that gives no heat and, below the floor, something breathing. The Master read the roll in a flat kind voice. Nobody looked at anyone else. Everyone knew that one of us would not be rising from the ring.

dracula_voivode_j_forged.title: The tenth name
dracula_voivode_j_forged.text: I wrote another man's name in my place. The ink dried at once. I told myself it was a prince's choice, and that Vasile would have done the same, and that it made no difference to the Master. The more I told myself, the less any of it was true.

dracula_voivode_j_tithe_self.title: The tenth pays
dracula_voivode_j_tithe_self.text: I stood in the ring and said that the tenth was mine. The Master was surprised, I think, and then very attentive. Something came up out of the grate. I do not remember what happened, only that I was cold when it ended and have been, since, one way or another.

dracula_voivode_j_tithe_vasile.title: Vasile's debt
dracula_voivode_j_tithe_vasile.text: Vasile went down the stair with his head up. I saw his face as he passed, and I will see it as long as I have eyes. He did not accuse me. That was the cruellest thing he could have done, and I think he knew.

dracula_voivode_j_tomb.title: The family crypt
dracula_voivode_j_tomb.text: I woke in a box. I have no idea how long. My throat was dry, and my father's stone lay on the left, and there was a scratching in my mouth as if my teeth were something else. The lid was lead-sealed, and I was strong enough to want it open.

dracula_voivode_j_chapel.title: The chapel, my first night
dracula_voivode_j_chapel.text: The altar candles are down to stubs and the doors are unbarred. A priest lies against a pew with a spear-wound. Ileana's tomb is new. The hunger in me is not a hunger I know the name of, and I am afraid it knows mine.

dracula_voivode_j_end_priest.title: The first blood
dracula_voivode_j_end_priest.text: I took what I needed from Father Dragomir. He did not resist. That was what was unbearable. He had given me the sacraments at my christening, and I gave him this. Whatever begins here, it begins with a priest's blood and my own choice.

dracula_voivode_j_end_wolves.title: The wolf-lord
dracula_voivode_j_end_wolves.text: I called the wolves and fed on the oldest, and kept the priest alive. It was the lesser sin. It was still a sin. They looked at me with a kind of recognition, and I understood that I was now something wolves could follow.

dracula_voivode_j_end_vigil.title: Ileana's vigil
dracula_voivode_j_end_vigil.text: I knelt by her stone and asked to be spared, and the sun rose and spared me, and spared the priest, and that was the worst of all. There was no one to punish me, so I began to punish myself, and have not stopped.

harker_road_j_morning.title: A May morning in Exeter
harker_road_j_morning.text: Exeter, May. Cathedral bells, a fine sun, and Mr. Hawkins's letter in my pocket. I am to go to Transylvania, a country I know only as a smudge on the school globe. The firm trusts me; I wish I trusted myself as much.

harker_road_j_commission.title: Mr. Hawkins's office
harker_road_j_commission.text: Mr. Hawkins has taken a foreign client, a Count Dracula of Castle Dracula, for the purchase of an English house. His letters are formal and exact. I am to prepare the file and, if all goes well, go to him in person. I am rather proud.

harker_road_j_task.title: The Count's wishes
harker_road_j_task.text: The Count wants a house in England: large, old, solitary, with a chapel and a high wall, and no neighbour near enough to overlook him. The surveys are in the muniment room; Mr. Pell has the key, and Mr. Pell is not a man to be hurried.

harker_road_j_surveys.title: Three surveys
harker_road_j_surveys.text: The deed-box held three surveys: a Hampstead villa, a house at Whitby, and a place at Purfleet called Carfax. Only one was old, walled and furnished with a chapel. I begin to see which the Count would choose.

harker_road_j_carfax.title: Carfax is chosen
harker_road_j_carfax.text: Carfax, then. An old house at Purfleet, walled in stone, with a chapel and a pond, and only a lunatic asylum for a neighbour. Mr. Hawkins agrees. I hope the Count is as pleased with it as we are with ourselves.

harker_road_j_letters.title: The Count's letters
harker_road_j_letters.text: I read the Count's letters again. They are admirable: grave, patient, correct. But I notice what he never asks about: price. A man who does not ask the price has too much to lose, or too much to spend.

harker_road_j_instr.title: Instructions
harker_road_j_instr.text: Mr. Hawkins gives me a letter of credit and sends me to the British Museum. Then I am to go east, find the Count and have the deed signed. And, he says, say goodbye to Mina. He says it with the air of a man who is not asking.

harker_road_j_museum_arrive.title: The Reading Room
harker_road_j_museum_arrive.text: London. The great dome of the Reading Room is like the inside of a giant's skull, and the readers sit under it like thoughts. I stand a long time in the door and feel very small, and very provincial.

harker_road_j_museum.title: Notes on Transylvania
harker_road_j_museum.text: In the Museum I learn that Transylvania lies within the Carpathians, a whirlpool of Saxon, Wallach, Magyar and Szekely, with the Szgany among them. The people believe in the Evil Eye and in a name, Dracula, which means both dragon and devil.

harker_road_j_mina.title: Mina at the school
harker_road_j_mina.text: Mina in her classroom, with chalk on her cuff. She says I am foolish to go so far, and hopes I will write every day. There is a blackboard of shorthand behind her. I shall pretend not to read it.

harker_road_j_trunk.title: Father's trunk
harker_road_j_trunk.text: The trunk is open at last. Inside, camphor, tissue, my mother's ring, a small crucifix and a letter in my father's hand. I did not know I had missed him so much. I must wear the ring, at least, to Mina.

harker_road_j_engaged.title: The ring
harker_road_j_engaged.text: I gave Mina my mother's ring this evening, and she put it on a chain round her neck. She says she will wear it openly when I come home. I have never before had so good a reason to come home.

harker_road_j_ribbon.title: Mina's ribbon
harker_road_j_ribbon.text: Mina gave me the ribbon from her hair for my diary. She says I must write in shorthand and she will learn to read it. I tie it round the book and put it next to my heart.

harker_road_j_packed.title: Packed
harker_road_j_packed.text: Valise strapped, diary in my breast pocket, the Count's papers and the Museum notes in the lining. Mrs. Dunmore wept a little into her apron, and denied it. I am, I think, as ready as a man can be for a country he has only read about.

harker_road_j_lodging.title: Packing
harker_road_j_lodging.text: Mrs. Dunmore has laid out my shirts. My father's trunk sits under the window, locked. I will take nothing from it, because I have never opened it, and I wonder whether I should.

harker_road_j_churchyard.title: Churchyard
harker_road_j_churchyard.text: I walked to St. Petroc's to see my parents' stone. The snowdrops were fresh. Somebody tends it; I know who. Mina has never said a word about it.

harker_road_j_wall.title: The wall
harker_road_j_wall.text: I am a prisoner in the Count's castle. All doors are locked; the only way is a ledge and a wall. The Count went down the wall like a lizard. If he can, I can. The alternative is waiting for the women.

harker_road_j_climb.title: Down the wall
harker_road_j_climb.text: I went down the castle wall by ivy, iron ring and loose stone, and in through the Count's open window. My hands bleed; my coat is torn. I have crossed a threshold I do not understand, and I cannot go back.

harker_road_j_gold.title: The Count's gold
harker_road_j_gold.text: In the Count's room, a heap of gold, Roman, Austrian, Turkish, Hungarian, all coated with dust, none newer than three hundred years. There is no mirror in the castle. There is not even a nail left.

harker_road_j_vault.title: The vault
harker_road_j_vault.text: Down the stair to the old chapel: fifty great boxes of earth. In one lay the Count, as if asleep, his eyes open, but nothing living in them. It is the most terrible thing I have ever seen, and I am not yet mad.

harker_road_j_search.title: No key
harker_road_j_search.text: I searched the Count's body for the key and found none. A few gold coins in a pocket; no watch, no purse. He does not breathe. He does not wake. I wonder which of us is more afraid.

harker_road_j_path.title: The mountain path
harker_road_j_path.text: Out through the postern in the moonlight, down a goat-path under the stars. The wolves are near; I can smell them. A fire burns below, with a Szgany wagon. I do not know whether I am escaping or falling.

harker_road_j_szgany.title: The Szgany fire
harker_road_j_szgany.text: A Szgany woman sold me bread and a flask for a handful of the Count's gold, and refused to say more. Her people carry his boxes and ask no questions. I envy them both.

harker_road_j_cross.title: Over the gully
harker_road_j_cross.text: I crossed the gully on a plank with the roar of the river under me. On the far side the track runs down. Then my legs gave way, and the dark came, and I do not know what I did next.

harker_road_j_hospital.title: Buda-Pesth
harker_road_j_hospital.text: I woke in a hospital in Buda-Pesth. Sister Agatha says I have had a brain fever, and have been here six weeks. I have a white streak in my hair, they tell me, and I believe them.

harker_road_j_woke.title: Sister Agatha
harker_road_j_woke.text: A small, quick Sister of St. Joseph has sat by my bed, and sent word to Mr. Hawkins. She says I spoke of wolves and a wall and three women. I told her nothing. I do not trust words yet.

harker_road_j_dream.title: The dream of the three
harker_road_j_dream.text: Again the dream: three women in the moonlight, laughing like silver bells. One fair, two dark. I wake wet to the skin. Sister Agatha says I called a woman's name, and not a kind one. She does not ask whose.

harker_road_j_letter.title: A letter to Mina
harker_road_j_letter.text: Sister Agatha has written for me; I signed. 'I am safe, in Buda-Pesth, ill but mending.' Nothing more. She said the letter must say nothing that would frighten Mina, and I agreed. I hope that I shall always be able to.

harker_road_j_vow.title: The vow
harker_road_j_vow.text: I have sealed my diary with Mina's ribbon and the chapel's wax. I do not know whether it is true or the delirium of a sick man. I will not know unless some solemn duty come upon me. So be it.

harker_road_j_parents.title: To my father and mother
harker_road_j_parents.text: I left a letter to my parents at the Virgin's feet in the chapel. They never said that they were proud of me. I think I know now why a man writes to the dead: because he can say it, and nobody can say no.

harker_road_j_mina_arrives.title: Mina is come
harker_road_j_mina_arrives.text: Mina arrived in Buda-Pesth this morning, in a cab, with a carpet-bag and a face like a lamp. She did not ask what had happened. She took my hand, and said, 'I am not going away.'

harker_road_j_proposal.title: The proposal
harker_road_j_proposal.text: Mina has said yes. Here, in a hospital ward in Buda-Pesth, to a man half-mad with fever and white at the temples. I do not deserve it, and I have never wanted anything so much.

harker_road_j_gave.title: The sealed book
harker_road_j_gave.text: I gave Mina my sealed diary. 'Keep it,' I said, 'and do not read it unless a solemn duty requires.' She tied the ribbon again, as she had before, and kissed my forehead. She is wiser than I am.

harker_road_j_chapel.title: The chapel
harker_road_j_chapel.text: A small white chapel with roses on the altar, and a vase of candles. The Sisters have decked it for us. The chaplain, they say, has been an Englishman in Buda-Pesth for thirty years.

harker_road_j_garden.title: The garden
harker_road_j_garden.text: I sit in the garden under the limes and listen to the bees. I have not been in sunlight for six weeks. The old gardener says I look better. I do not remember when I last looked at all.

harker_road_j_wedding_day.title: The wedding day
harker_road_j_wedding_day.text: Tomorrow we shall be married, with a white rose, a borrowed ring and a chaplain who says he has been waiting thirty years to see an Englishman and a girl turn up with matching faces. I am very happy.

harker_road_j_epilogue.title: The road home
harker_road_j_epilogue.text: Mina and I leave Buda-Pesth for England, with the sealed book in her trunk and the white streak in my hair. I have the road behind me. I shall not look at it again, unless some solemn duty come upon me.

harker_road_j_wed.title: Husband and wife
harker_road_j_wed.text: We were married in the chapel at Buda-Pesth this morning. Sister Agatha wept. I was happy, truly, for the first time since the Borgo Pass. Whatever the sealed book contains, it is not this.

harker_road_j_wolves.title: The wolves
harker_road_j_wolves.text: Two wolves on the mountain path, hungry and bold. I fought them with a poker and a spade. One tooth I kept. I think I was braver than I have ever been, and certainly sillier.

lucy_summer_j_room.title: Hillingham in spring
lucy_summer_j_room.text: The window is open, there is a lawn outside it and three gentlemen coming to tea. I have never felt so bright in my life. Hannah says I am rosy, Mamma says I am tired, and the mirror says I look like a girl who has been told a secret.

lucy_summer_j_parlour.title: Mamma's parlour
lucy_summer_j_parlour.text: The parlour is chintz and bad piano music. Mamma has a theory about flowers and a larger one about gentlemen. I have decided to ignore both and arrange the vase myself.

lucy_summer_j_garden.title: The garden in May
lucy_summer_j_garden.text: Lilies like bridesmaids, a sundial that counts only sunny hours, a bench in the shade. Dr. Seward left a note on it. I read it and pretended not to.

lucy_summer_j_flowers.title: Mamma is pleased
lucy_summer_j_flowers.text: Tallest at the back, the rose in the middle, forget-me-nots in front. Mamma wept a little, which is how she shows she is pleased, and handed me the key of the escritoire as though she were giving me the Crown jewels.

lucy_summer_j_mina_letter.title: Mina's letters
lucy_summer_j_mina_letter.text: A bundle of them in blue ribbon. She writes with a straight back, if letters can; every page begins with the weather and ends with love. I envy her, but only a little.

lucy_summer_j_seward.title: Dr. Seward
lucy_summer_j_seward.text: He asked, and I refused, plainly, because he asked to be refused plainly. He took it like the good man he is, and asked if we might still be friends. I could have wept. He is the sort of man one wishes were one's brother.

lucy_summer_j_quincey.title: Mr. Morris
lucy_summer_j_quincey.text: He asked in four sentences and I answered in two. We shook hands like a pair of fellow-conspirators. He told me there was a gentleman behind the rose-bush who had been standing there half an hour. I am quite fond of him.

lucy_summer_j_arthur.title: Arthur
lucy_summer_j_arthur.text: Oh, my dear Arthur! He dropped his speech in the lilies and gave me his mother's ring instead. I said yes in the plainest words I knew. Why can't a girl marry three men? Jack to heal me, Quincey to defend me, Arthur to love me.

lucy_summer_j_letter.title: To Mina
lucy_summer_j_letter.text: I wrote in order, as she told me: the window, the house, the secret, and the love. It is the first letter I have ever written without a postscript. She will read it on Friday and write me four pages by return, and I shall love every line.

lucy_summer_j_pack.title: Whitby
