lucy_summer_j_pack.text: Mamma wants sea air for me, Mina has taken the Crescent, and I am to bring my trunk and my appetite. The Hillingham lawn looked so well as I left it that I felt, for a moment, as if I were leaving a person.

lucy_summer_j_whitby.title: The Crescent lodgings
lucy_summer_j_whitby.text: Two beds under a sloping roof, a window full of sea and a landlady who has opinions about draughts. Mina has taken the bed nearest the door. She says it is for the light. I think it is for the key.

lucy_summer_j_lost.title: A letter lost
lucy_summer_j_lost.text: Papa's letter has gone. I had it in my hand at Hillingham; I may have put it down anywhere in Whitby. If I find it I shall never put it down again. Mamma thinks the trunk, the window-seat, or the seat on the cliff.

lucy_summer_j_cliff.title: The East Cliff
lucy_summer_j_cliff.text: A churchyard over the sea, an Abbey over the churchyard, and a seat over everything. Mina writes. I watch the ships and the gulls and the great red sun. Everyone is kind. I am so tired, and I cannot think why.

lucy_summer_j_mina_walk.title: Mina's key
lucy_summer_j_mina_walk.text: Mina tells me I walked in my sleep last night. She found me at the window, in my nightgown, looking at the Abbey. I remember nothing. She has taken the key of our door and put it under her pillow, and she says she shall not sleep until I am well.

lucy_summer_j_swales.title: Mr. Swales and the steps
lucy_summer_j_swales.text: A hundred and ninety-nine, he said. He has carried coffins on his shoulder down every one. It is a curious thing to know exactly how far it is from the cliff to the town. I shall remember it.

lucy_summer_j_night.title: The seat in the night
lucy_summer_j_night.text: I woke on the seat on the cliff. I did not walk there. There was a bell, and a man on the Abbey wall, tall and dark and red-eyed, watching me with the patience of the grave. I was not afraid. That was the terrible part.

lucy_summer_j_anchor_a.title: A name to hold
lucy_summer_j_anchor_a.text: I said 'Arthur,' and he flinched. Arthur's ring was cold in my hand, and his name was warm in my mouth, and for that moment I was Lucy Westenra and not a thing on a seat.

lucy_summer_j_anchor_m.title: Another name
lucy_summer_j_anchor_m.text: I said 'Mina.' Her letter was folded in four in my hand, and the first line was a rule for finding the way. Begin with what you see out of the window. I saw a Moon and a dark man and a path.

lucy_summer_j_anchor_p.title: A third name
lucy_summer_j_anchor_p.text: I said 'Papa.' I held his letter against my heart with its stiff old forget-me-nots, and the man on the seat looked at it and could not look at me.

lucy_summer_j_free.title: Walking away
lucy_summer_j_free.text: I turned my back on him and walked. It was the hardest thing I ever did. There was no footstep behind me. In front, the steps went down into the dark, and I went with three names in my mouth like pebbles.

lucy_summer_j_steps.title: The Abbey steps
lucy_summer_j_steps.text: A hundred and ninety-nine steps in a nightgown, between graves, with the sea below and the bell behind. If I lose count I shall be on the cliff all night, and there will be nothing to hold me but the seat.

lucy_summer_j_counted.title: Counted
lucy_summer_j_counted.text: One hundred and ninety-nine, aloud, as I would count Arthur's name. At the bottom, a lamp swung, and somebody ran toward me with a shawl and a plait of dark hair.

lucy_summer_j_mina_rescue.title: Mina found me
lucy_summer_j_mina_rescue.text: She ran all the way in her dressing-gown. She said she woke and the key was under her pillow and the door was locked and I was gone. She has a gift for being right when I am wrong. I am so glad. I am so tired.

lucy_summer_j_last.title: September, Hillingham
lucy_summer_j_last.text: Home, and no better. The pallor has stayed. Dr. Seward sits with me, and Dr. Van Helsing, and Arthur comes when he can. Everyone is very kind, and everyone looks at me as though I were already a photograph. I do not want to be a photograph.

lucy_summer_j_a_release.title: To Arthur
lucy_summer_j_a_release.text: I wrote: 'Do not be small with grief. Live, and love again, when you can. I shall not mind.' It is the hardest line I have ever written. It is also the truest.

lucy_summer_j_a_remember.title: To Arthur
lucy_summer_j_a_remember.text: I wrote: 'Remember me in the garden, with the rose in my hair, and be the man I knew.' He will do it. He does everything I ask, bless him, even when it hurts him.

lucy_summer_j_m_arthur.title: To Mina
lucy_summer_j_m_arthur.text: I wrote: 'Watch over Arthur for me; he does not know how to be alone.' She will. She keeps promises as she keeps her letters, in order and in blue ribbon.

lucy_summer_j_m_write.title: To Mina
lucy_summer_j_m_write.text: I wrote: 'Keep writing, everything you see, in order, as you taught me. One day someone will need it.' She has always written for the pleasure of it. I would like her to write for the use of it.

lucy_summer_j_end_arthur.title: What I left for Arthur
lucy_summer_j_end_arthur.text: Papa's letter, with the forget-me-nots, tied with the ring-ribbon. Arthur will understand. He always does, in the end.

lucy_summer_j_end_mina.title: What I left for Mina
lucy_summer_j_end_mina.text: Papa's letter, tucked in with her own letters in blue ribbon. She keeps everything, and what she keeps, she keeps right.

lucy_summer_j_end_keep.title: What I kept
lucy_summer_j_end_keep.text: I folded Papa's letter in my hands. If it is to be forgotten, let it be forgotten with me. The forget-me-nots, I think, will be glad of the company.

mina_records_j_tomb1.title: Stone of Hannah Brough
mina_records_j_tomb1.text: 'Hannah Brough, born 1785, died 1830, aged 43.' A faithful wife and a good neighbour. I copy the figures to be added up in a quiet moment.

mina_records_j_tomb2.title: Stone of John Anson
mina_records_j_tomb2.text: 'John Anson, master mariner, born 1765, died 1795, aged 30.' Lost off the Scar and not found. The figures are neat and the sum is good.

mina_records_j_tomb3.title: Stone of Mary Dale
mina_records_j_tomb3.text: 'Mary Dale, spinster, born 1790, died 1810, aged 20.' She died as she lived: quietly. The lettering is clean and the sum exactly right.

mina_records_j_morning.title: Exeter. A missing Tennyson
mina_records_j_morning.text: Miss Hallam's speech-day prize, the Tennyson in green morocco, has vanished from a locked cupboard. I am to look into it, as I seem to be the only member of staff who reads the small print. I am rather pleased.

mina_records_j_task.title: Miss Hallam's bargain
mina_records_j_task.text: Miss Hallam will give me the key to the typewriting room if I find the book. I have wanted that key since Christmas. Cupboard, blotter, girls, she said, in that order. I shall keep the order but not, I think, the temper.

mina_records_j_edith.title: Edith's gossip
mina_records_j_edith.text: Dora Pike dusts the staff-room on Wednesdays for a penny. Her mother is ill in Heavitree, and she sews at night to pay the doctor. I do not like where this points; I like it less that it points so clearly.

mina_records_j_blotter.title: The blotter in the mirror
mina_records_j_blotter.text: Held to the glass, Miss Hallam's blotter gives a backward letter in a girl's round hand, with a looped capital D: 'Dearest Mama, I have it safe...' So the thief is a daughter, not a magpie. That is a different crime and wants a different kindness.

mina_records_j_cupboard.title: The unforced lock
mina_records_j_cupboard.text: No scratch on the lock, no mark on the hasp. Only a tiny shining thumb-print of red ink on the brass. Whoever took the book had the staff-room key and had been writing with the staff's red ink. Not a burglar: a borrower.

mina_records_j_redink.title: Red ink, a quarter lower
mina_records_j_redink.text: The red ink is a quarter lower than last week. Red ink is for the staff alone, so someone has been where she should not, and for longer than a moment.

mina_records_j_cuff.title: Dora's cuff
mina_records_j_cuff.text: Dora Pike's hands are clean, but her sleeve-cuff carries a red thumb-mark the exact colour of the staff ink. She keeps turning it inward. I like her, and I wish I did not know what I now know.

mina_records_j_book_found.title: The Tennyson returned
mina_records_j_book_found.text: Dora confessed: she wanted to read the Lady of Shalott to her mother. The book is back in my hands, undamaged. What we do with a child who steals for love is not in any rule-book, and I am glad of it.

mina_records_j_key.title: The key to the typewriting room
mina_records_j_key.text: Miss Hallam asked no questions and gave me the key. A small iron thing; I wear it on a ribbon at my throat like a cross. Tomorrow I shall learn to make a machine speak.

mina_records_j_dictation.title: The dictation sheet
mina_records_j_dictation.text: From Mr. Hawkins's office: the house at Purfleet, called Carfax, with its chapel and twenty acres, secured for the Count, deeds to follow by the post of the ninth instant. A dull letter; I copy it as I would any other, with all my care.

mina_records_j_typed.title: The Remington speaks
mina_records_j_typed.text: I freed the type-bars, oiled the pivots and wound on a new ribbon. Eleven lines, no errors. If Jonathan's firm ever wants a typist, here is one who has never been told she could not.

mina_records_j_reply.title: Mr. Hawkins replies
mina_records_j_reply.text: A clerk writes for Mr. Hawkins: a registered letter for me, in Jonathan's hand, was posted at Exeter and has been lost on the Bristol line. So Jonathan wrote. Whatever else the silence means, he wrote.

mina_records_j_bradshaw.title: Bradshaw, the Bristol line
mina_records_j_bradshaw.text: The morning trains: 10.20, stopping at Tiverton, Taunton at 11.30; 10.50, express, Taunton at 11.40; 11.15, stopping at Tiverton, Taunton at 12.05. I could set a clock by it. I would rather set a man free.

mina_records_j_bradshaw2.title: Where the bag went
mina_records_j_bradshaw2.text: Mr. Pomfret: the bag went on the first train after the half-past-ten sorting, and the guard saw it on the van floor as the train roared through Tiverton. So not a stopper, and not before half-past ten.

mina_records_j_wire.title: The ten-fifty
mina_records_j_wire.text: After the sorting, clean through Tiverton: the 10.50 express. Mr. Pomfret has had Hobbs wire Taunton. Nobody has ever called me a detective, but I do believe I solved a thing with Bradshaw today.

mina_records_j_letter_found.title: Jonathan's letter, at last
mina_records_j_letter_found.text: Under a van seat at Taunton for twelve days. Soft at the corners, smelling of coal and tobacco, and the dearest paper I own. Bistritz, the Golden Krone, the little cross the landlady pressed on him. He wrote. He did write.

mina_records_j_letter.title: 'Wait for me'
mina_records_j_letter.text: 'I wish you were beside me, with your shorthand and your timetables. Wait for me, and do not be anxious.' I read it twice aloud to Lucy and a third time alone. I shall wait. It is what I am best at, though I wish it were not.

mina_records_j_firstdream.title: The dream I told Lucy
mina_records_j_firstdream.text: I told Lucy of the dream: water lapping, wood creaking, and a call I cannot catch. I thought she would laugh; she did not. It is odd how heavy a thing becomes once it is said aloud.

mina_records_j_confide.title: A night of whispers
mina_records_j_confide.text: We lay awake until the rooks began, and Lucy told me of three suitors and I told her of one absent man. She says I shall come to Whitby, and that the sea air will cure my dreams. I am less sure that I want them cured.

mina_records_j_whitby.title: Whitby
mina_records_j_whitby.text: Whitby, on the West Cliff. The harbour, the Abbey, the church on its hill, and Lucy at the window counting boats. I took one look at the sea and felt at once that it knew my name.

mina_records_j_swales.title: Mr. Swales and the stones
mina_records_j_swales.text: Old Mr. Swales swears that every stone in this churchyard lies and that one of three cannot count. I am to find it. He told me this with the cheerful malice of a man who has been telling it for fifty years.

mina_records_j_almanac.title: The sea keeps a calendar
mina_records_j_almanac.text: Mr. Swales gave me his almanac: tides run later by fifty minutes each day. The stone that could not count was Hannah Brough's: forty-five by the calendar, and forty-three on the stone. I shall remember that when anyone tells me a sum is no matter.

mina_records_j_tide.title: The coastguard's tide-table
mina_records_j_tide.text: The table gives only Monday: high water 4.10 in the morning and 4.35 in the afternoon. Somebody has pencilled 'Wednesday?' in the margin and given up. I would not mind helping.

mina_records_j_plumb.title: A plumb-bob
mina_records_j_plumb.text: The coastguard gave me a brass plumb on a cord: 'A pendulum, miss; hang it in a room and it will tell you what the room is thinking.' I have thought of something else to do with it, and I am a little ashamed.

mina_records_j_bats.title: Bats at the Abbey
mina_records_j_bats.text: Two bats at dusk, rather too close to my hair. I took the umbrella to them like a sensible woman, and they went. I do not think they were bats only. I do not know why I think so.

mina_records_j_scare.title: A small fright
mina_records_j_scare.text: The ninth stair complained behind me, and when I turned the curtain was moving, though the window was shut. Lucy slept through it. I told myself it was the draught. I lit the candle all the same.

mina_records_j_window.title: A damp hand on the sill
mina_records_j_window.text: On the sill, a damp mark the shape of a small hand, drying as I watched. The sea air, the damp, a cat. I have a great many reasonable explanations and not one I would put my name to.

mina_records_j_dreamorder.title: Water, wood, swing
mina_records_j_dreamorder.text: From my dream notes: it begins with the water, lapping near; then the wood, a creak; then the dark, a single point turning, and I forget my name. Water, wood, swing. Always in that order, before I wake.

mina_records_j_trance.title: The first deliberate trance
mina_records_j_trance.text: I sat in the rocking-chair, listened to the water in the basin, rocked until the boards creaked, and watched the plumb turn. It worked. I do not know whether to be proud or afraid, and I suspect the two are the same.

mina_records_j_hold1.title: The lapping
mina_records_j_hold1.text: In the dark hold, a barrel drips. The water is near and slow and the sound comes up through the wood into my wrist. Water first, always.

mina_records_j_hold2.title: The creak
mina_records_j_hold2.text: The great timber groans as the hull settles. Wood is the second sound, patient and old. I can tell it now from my own heartbeat.

mina_records_j_end.title: The thread
mina_records_j_end.text: I woke with a candle-stub and a still plumb and a fine cord between my fingers that was not there. Somewhere, a man is breathing in the dark. I shall tell no one yet. But I know that I can follow the thread when I must.

quincey_hunt_j_stolen.title: The remuda is gone
quincey_hunt_j_stolen.text: Dunning's gang filed through the corral rail while the dogs were fed. Eleven head gone, and Santa Fe among them. Wash has a gash on his skull. I mean to bring every horse home, and Santa Fe first of all.

quincey_hunt_j_load.title: Powder and lead
quincey_hunt_j_load.text: Wash says powder is hidden in the stable, out of the damp, and lead can be dug from the target post. With both in hand the loading bench will make ten cartridges. I mean to ride out loaded, not hopeful.

quincey_hunt_j_hobbs.title: The old trapper's advice
quincey_hunt_j_hobbs.text: Old Hobbs says the creek bottoms are thick with wolves and that the channel is too deep to ford. But there is a cottonwood snag leaning over it with a stub on the limb, and a good lariat will swing a man across.

quincey_hunt_j_signs.title: Reading the signs
quincey_hunt_j_signs.text: Hoofprints bent east to low ground. Cottonwood ash at the dead fire. Red flannel with canebrake burrs on a thorn. Three signs, one answer: Dunning and my mare are in the bottoms.

quincey_hunt_j_creek.title: Across the channel
quincey_hunt_j_creek.text: A throw and a half to catch the stub, then hand over hand across black water. It is a boy's trick and I still know it. The wolves have not forgiven me for being on their side of the river.

quincey_hunt_j_wolves.title: Wolves at the ford
quincey_hunt_j_wolves.text: Two grey wolves, thin as rails and twice as mean. The Winchester settled one and the bowie the other. I take no pride in it. They only wanted the same supper I wanted.

quincey_hunt_j_fight.title: Dunning's camp
quincey_hunt_j_fight.text: One against two, in the open, by firelight, and the odds do not improve as one gets older. The bowie settled Dunning's man and the Winchester settled Dunning. His running-iron I mean to take to the sheriff.

quincey_hunt_j_reunion.title: Santa Fe comes home
quincey_hunt_j_reunion.text: She took sugar from my hand and stood still for the saddle. We rode out of the hollow with eleven horses running behind. A man can lose almost everything and keep his life, but not this mare.

quincey_hunt_j_anselmo.title: What the gaucho knew
quincey_hunt_j_anselmo.text: Anselmo says the vampire bat goes for the bare neck. Against it: smoke across the lines, a high lantern, and a cloth the horse knows laid over the neck. He says it as though it were common sense. It is, if you have lost enough steers.

quincey_hunt_j_tale.title: A story by the fire
quincey_hunt_j_tale.text: I told a tale by the fire, and Art laughed in the right places, and Seward corrected the facts. It was the best hour of the whole trip. Odd how often the best hour comes just before the worst.

quincey_hunt_j_bats.title: The vigil
quincey_hunt_j_bats.text: They came out of the moon, three of them, with a sound like wet leather. The smoke thickened and the lantern swung and the Winchester spoke. One went down. Two flew off. The third did not run: it circled twice, looked at me, and then it was gone.

quincey_hunt_j_grass.title: Gone to grass
quincey_hunt_j_grass.text: She was bled in the small hours, through the blanket, through everything we did right. By sunrise she was gone. I buried her under a cross of picket-posts, and Art helped dig. I do not remember the rest.

quincey_hunt_j_mark.title: The mark in the grass
quincey_hunt_j_mark.text: A flattened ring, black earth foreign to the plain, and bare prints that begin at the ring and end at the posts. No bat made these. Something came on its own feet and left on wings. I wrote it all down, and told no one but Seward.

quincey_hunt_j_end.title: What I carried home
quincey_hunt_j_end.text: I have the bowie, the Winchester, and a sheath that a mare once chewed. And a name for a thing nobody believes in. Some day I may need to use it.

renfield_mercy_j_wake.title: Room 12
renfield_mercy_j_wake.text: Morning at Purfleet. A cell padded in grey, a tin tray, a window with the first flies. I am R. M. Renfield, once of a good house and sound mind. Today I must be a gentleman to Hodge, find my ledger, and make myself reasonable to the doctor.

renfield_mercy_j_calm.title: A gentleman at the door
renfield_mercy_j_calm.text: I said, 'I am quite myself, Mr. Hodge,' and Hodge opened the door. It is astonishing what a civil tongue will do for a man in a grey ticking cell. I wish I had known as much in the Strand.

renfield_mercy_j_frenzy.title: The wet sheet
renfield_mercy_j_frenzy.text: I raved at Hodge. He held me in his arms until the strength had left me, then opened the door as gently as for a child. I should not have shouted. It costs me more than it costs him.

renfield_mercy_j_ledger.title: The notebook of lives
renfield_mercy_j_ledger.text: Under the loose board, wrapped in my father's handkerchief: my notebook. Eleven flies, forty spiders, three hundred sparrows, a cat. A column of figures that grows and never closes. It is the only honest document in this house.

renfield_mercy_j_count.title: Seven, three, nine
renfield_mercy_j_count.text: Quill counts everything. The doctor's inventory board gives beds, windows, lamps: seven, three, nine. That is the order in which the doctor writes it, and so the wheels of the linen-press must be set.

renfield_mercy_j_sugar.title: The sugar ration
renfield_mercy_j_sugar.text: Seven, three, nine, and the press gave up one lump of sugar on a blue paper. Dr. Seward locks it away so we cannot hoard. I have hoarded other things from him, and will go on.

renfield_mercy_j_flies.title: The sugar and the sill
renfield_mercy_j_flies.text: Sugar on the sill, and in a minute the flies came. Eleven. Dr. Seward would call it a dozen flies on a lump of sugar. I call it a tithe. I am not certain which of us is the more honest.

renfield_mercy_j_hodge_key.title: The lost garden key
renfield_mercy_j_hodge_key.text: Hodge dropped the garden key in the scullery three weeks ago and told nobody. Between ourselves, he thinks the mice have it. I think the spider has it. We are both of us probably right.

renfield_mercy_j_key.title: The spider's key
renfield_mercy_j_key.text: Fed the spider eleven flies; she dropped the key from her web, an iron key on a loop of tape marked 'GARDEN'. Hodge's, the doctor would say. The spider's, I say. It does not matter which, only that I have it.

renfield_mercy_j_cook.title: Cook and the rhyme
renfield_mercy_j_cook.text: 'Baked in a pie.' Mrs. Pargeter laughed, gave me brandy in a cup and swore me to secrecy. Her brother died in a place like mine. People are kinder than a case-book allows.

renfield_mercy_j_notes.title: What the doctor wrote
renfield_mercy_j_notes.text: In Seward's notes: 'He does not lie. His dread of the unseen is genuine. I do not know what to make of a delusion so well-regulated.' It is the kindest thing anyone has written of me since my father's will.

renfield_mercy_j_plea.title: The plea
renfield_mercy_j_plea.text: I asked Dr. Seward to send me away before the Master comes. The ledger did it: a clerk's hand speaks better than a madman's mouth. He has written a note: the quiet wing, on Monday. Monday is too far, but it is a start.

renfield_mercy_j_round.title: Blunt's round
renfield_mercy_j_round.text: Hodge says Blunt does the garden at ten and two: out to the far wall, a pause to light his pipe, and back. Same every night for ten years. A man who is predictable is a man who can be avoided.

renfield_mercy_j_night.title: Night at Purfleet
renfield_mercy_j_night.text: The lamps are low and the house is quiet. I have the key, the brandy and the list. Hodge sits his watch in the day-room, and I feel the Master through the wall like a second pulse.

renfield_mercy_j_hodge.title: Hodge sleeps
renfield_mercy_j_hodge.text: A cup of Cook's brandy for his nerves, and Hodge sleeps in his chair. I did not hurt him, or lie to him, except in the matter of why. I leave him a blanket.

renfield_mercy_j_garden.title: The wicket
renfield_mercy_j_garden.text: Behind the water-butt I waited for the pipe, and when the night-man bent to his match I crossed the gravel without a sound. A man who counts can wait. It is the only virtue that madness has left me.

renfield_mercy_j_chapel.title: Carfax
renfield_mercy_j_chapel.text: The chapel at Carfax, the box in its aisle and the voice about it. He has not touched the ledger. He has not paid one penny of what he promised. I am quite steady, for once, and quite sure I can add.

renfield_mercy_j_sum.title: The sum
renfield_mercy_j_sum.text: I totalled the ledger on his box: eleven flies, forty spiders, three hundred sparrows, the cat. It never closes, and neither does his promise. He has taken my lives and given me none. A bookkeeper knows a bad debtor when he meets one.

renfield_mercy_j_warning.title: A note for the doctor
renfield_mercy_j_warning.text: I wrote Seward a page and left it under the candle: the box, the voice, the garlic, the cross, the sun. It is the first letter I have written in years. I signed it with my initials and the crest.

renfield_mercy_j_end_mercy.title: The sparrow
renfield_mercy_j_end_mercy.text: I opened my hand at the window. The sparrow went over the wall. It is the only life I ever gave back, and I will take it with me wherever I am sent. I think the doctor will have my notebook. I would rather he had that than anything else.

renfield_mercy_j_end_loyal.title: What I took
renfield_mercy_j_end_loyal.text: The sparrow was warm for a moment and then it was not. The voice said I had done well. I have never felt smaller. I think I understand now what the doctor meant by 'delusion'. It is a debt that cannot be paid.

seward_asylum_j_sleepless.title: 25 May. Three nights
seward_asylum_j_sleepless.text: Three nights without sleep. Lucy Westenra refused me at Hillingham, with great kindness, and I have gone on doctoring as if the thing had not happened. I shall find the ward key, make my rounds and try to tire myself properly. Chloral, in the right measure, will do the rest.

seward_asylum_j_hillingham.title: Lucy's note
seward_asylum_j_hillingham.text: I keep her note, though a doctor should know better. 'I am promised, in my heart, to another.' She was gentle, and clear, and right. I said I understood, and I did. It is the understanding that keeps me awake.

seward_asylum_j_grief.title: Dictated to the phonograph
seward_asylum_j_grief.text: I spoke my grief aloud to the cylinder, and it sounded smaller than it felt. I shall not blame Lucy, nor Arthur, nor myself. I shall be a better doctor for it, if I am not a worse man.

seward_asylum_j_dose.title: Van Helsing on the chloral
seward_asylum_j_dose.text: Fifteen grains for a woman or a frail man; twenty for a strong man in his full strength; never more than thirty; sixty is a funeral. Weigh twice. Renfield is fourteen stone and in his strength: twenty grains, witnessed.

seward_asylum_j_open_mind.title: Van Helsing on doubt
seward_asylum_j_open_mind.text: 'Believe nothing because I say it; doubt nothing because you have not seen it. Write it all down, and then look at what is written.' He wrote this to me about a case of fever. I find it applies to nearly everything.

seward_asylum_j_debt.title: What I owe him
seward_asylum_j_debt.text: That winter I was ill, and Van Helsing sat three nights with me when he could have been abed. He says I owe him nothing but to be, to some other sleepless fool, what he was to me. I shall try. I do not yet know how.

seward_asylum_j_pym.title: Mr. Pym's clock
seward_asylum_j_pym.text: The ward clock stopped at ten past three the night Mrs. Pym died, and her husband has let no one touch it since. Hennessey says that if I name the hour, the old man may give me the winding key. I think I understand the lock he means.

seward_asylum_j_greer.title: Greer on fire
seward_asylum_j_greer.text: Old Greer, mate of the Lizzie out of Sunderland: never water on a spirit fire, since the spirit floats and spreads. Wet the blanket, drop it on, and lean. A mad sailor's memory is better than my own on the subject.

seward_asylum_j_clock.title: The clock wound
seward_asylum_j_clock.text: Pym's clock ticks again, and the dispensary key hung behind it on a nail where Hennessey, wisely, hid it. Pym watched me with the face of a man receiving a verdict. I think it was a good one.

seward_asylum_j_vane.title: Miss Vane's visitor
seward_asylum_j_vane.text: Miss Vane, who writes to a man dead in India, notes that a boy with violet-stained fingers sits in the dispensary at night practising a signature on the backs of old labels. She thinks it a love-letter. I wonder who is being courted.

seward_asylum_j_hennessey_mark.title: Hennessey cannot write
seward_asylum_j_hennessey_mark.text: Hennessey signs with a mark, being no scholar. It had not occurred to me in three years. A man who cannot write cannot forge, so I may strike one name from any list. I feel foolish for having needed to ask.

seward_asylum_j_cell.title: Room 12
seward_asylum_j_cell.text: Renfield's room, as I always find it: the cot made tight, the sugar in lines on the saucer, the jar of flies on the sill. I have read his ledger a dozen times, but I have never read it as a series, and Van Helsing would say that is the whole of the art.

seward_asylum_j_flies.title: Renfield: the flies
seward_asylum_j_flies.text: Flies caught on sugar, kept in a jar 'to hold the lives'. For a fortnight he eats none. In the third week he begins, and calls them quite delicious, and 'so full of life'.

seward_asylum_j_spiders.title: Renfield: the spiders
seward_asylum_j_spiders.text: He feeds the flies to spiders, and then eats the spiders. 'One spider is worth a hundred flies, for the life in it.' The system has a ladder in it; I should have seen that sooner.

seward_asylum_j_sparrows.title: Renfield: the sparrows
seward_asylum_j_sparrows.text: He tamed a sparrow, wanted a cat to eat the sparrows, and kept a heap of feathers for his pains. 'The spider's life is little, and the sparrow's is more.' The ladder climbs, as I thought.

seward_asylum_j_cat.title: Renfield: the kitten
seward_asylum_j_cat.text: The housemaid's kitten went into Room 12 on Tuesday and came out on Wednesday as a smear of fur. He was ill afterwards, as if from grief. I have written nothing under it. I did not need to.

seward_asylum_j_theory.title: Renfield's theory
seward_asylum_j_theory.text: Zoophagous mania, systematised: the patient believes life may be gathered by eating living things, in ascending order. 'The blood is the life.' He says he is not mad, merely early. I wonder what he is early for.

seward_asylum_j_draught.title: The twenty-grain draught
seward_asylum_j_draught.text: Twenty grains of chloral for a strong man, weighed twice and witnessed by the register. A bottle I hope never to use. The house may break, but it will be broken by the book.

seward_asylum_j_night.title: Two in the morning
seward_asylum_j_night.text: Smoke under the dispensary door, Room 12 standing open, and a lad crying in the ward. Three things at once, and a doctor who has not slept in three days. Good. A man with nothing to lose makes a cool physician.

seward_asylum_j_fire.title: The fire in the dispensary
seward_asylum_j_fire.text: Old Greer told me, with the memory of forty years, never to put water on a spirit fire. I smothered it with a soaked blanket, and the chloral was saved. I must remember to thank a mad sailor in the morning.

seward_asylum_j_slip.title: A forged prescription
seward_asylum_j_slip.text: Sixty grains of morphia, in my name, in my hand, forged beautifully, in violet copying ink. Hennessey cannot write. Miss Vane saw a lad with violet fingers practise my S. I think I know the signatory, and it breaks my heart.

seward_asylum_j_pettit.title: Pettit
seward_asylum_j_pettit.text: He did it for his mother, in Barking, in pain. I could report him, and the law would be on my side. I could help him, and the law would not. I choose, and write the choice in the book, so that I cannot pretend I did not.

seward_asylum_j_renfield_night.title: Renfield at the wall
seward_asylum_j_renfield_night.text: I found him in the garden under the Carfax wall, staring at the moon. I did not need force. Judgment, a measure of medicine and a steady voice did it. He said something is coming, and he would like to be tidy. I wrote it down.

seward_asylum_j_end.title: The twenty-sixth of May
seward_asylum_j_end.text: A night in which three things went wrong and none was the worst. I used judgment where I might have used force, medicine where I might have used a stick, and nerve where I might have run. I shall write to Van Helsing. I think I may sleep.

vanhelsing_lore_j_study.title: The study
vanhelsing_lore_j_study.text: My study, with the lamp lit before dark. Arminius's last parcel lies half-opened: a Latin note, a locked cabinet, and a letter I have not dared to read twice. I must see to my wife, my lecture, my friend, and at last that terrible village in Styria.

vanhelsing_lore_j_latin.title: The Latin note
vanhelsing_lore_j_latin.text: 'Wood not iron; day not night; garlic not earth.' Arminius has the exactness of a man who has had it wrong once and paid. I wrote it out three times, since a physician who mistranslates a prescription kills a man.

vanhelsing_lore_j_home.title: My wife
vanhelsing_lore_j_home.text: She lay turned to the window, with the little grey coat in her lap. Mevrouw Bakker says the broth is a triumph. I stood in the doorway and could not enter for a full minute. We have lost one child. I do not intend to lose the rest of the world.

vanhelsing_lore_j_cross.title: The silver cross
vanhelsing_lore_j_cross.text: She gave me the christening cross from the cradle. 'Take it for the next one', she said. I am a Doctor of Medicine and Law, but I could find no word, and so I held her hand. Some wounds are not the business of surgery.

vanhelsing_lore_j_street.title: The Herengracht
vanhelsing_lore_j_street.text: Skaters, a barrel-organ, the bells of the Oude Kerk. The Dean of the Faculty means to humiliate me on Friday. My students are afraid for me. They are fond of me, which is more than I deserve and a great deal more than I can bear in the open street.

vanhelsing_lore_j_lecture.title: The lecture-room
vanhelsing_lore_j_lecture.text: Verhoeven stood where I stand, with his gloves in one hand and my own board behind him. He has the key to the rare books, and a rule: no man gets it who cannot defend his methods. Young Seward, with that scar on his hand, whispered that I should read what I wrote.

vanhelsing_lore_j_debate.title: The Dean is answered
vanhelsing_lore_j_debate.text: Three questions, three answers from my own blackboard. Verhoeven gave me the key and a word I shall not forget: his grandmother hung garlic at her door. Everyone has one such grandmother. The trick is to listen to her before the Faculty tells you not to.

vanhelsing_lore_j_library.title: The rare-book press
vanhelsing_lore_j_library.text: Calf, vellum and a smell of mice. Mijnheer de Vries whispers, and the Dean's press is oak and brass. Inside it is the only book I wanted: a rituale of the old rite, and the order of the blessing of bread, in a Latin that has lasted since the Reformation.

vanhelsing_lore_j_letters.title: Arminius's letters
vanhelsing_lore_j_letters.text: The Voivode, the Scholomance, the Devil's tenth scholar. Arminius does not believe a word, but he copies every one. And at the end a request: a churchyard in Styria, a priest afraid of his own graves. I shall go, but not to disprove. To find out.

vanhelsing_lore_j_chapel.title: St. Nicholas
vanhelsing_lore_j_chapel.text: Father Pieter at his altar, Gerrit counting the candle-ends. The sacrament is not a charm but a rite, and a rite has its order. That is the one thing a physician and a priest can agree on: if you do it out of sequence, you have done something else.

vanhelsing_lore_j_rite.title: The Host consecrated
vanhelsing_lore_j_rite.text: Confession, ablution, the Collect, the seal. I read the order and Father Pieter followed it, and when the little silver box closed, something in the room changed that I have no instrument to measure. I did not pretend that I understood it. I merely wrote it down.

vanhelsing_lore_j_village.title: Kirchdorf
vanhelsing_lore_j_village.text: Snow, an onion-spire, doors shut at four. A priest with a month of sleeplessness in his face. The village is afraid of its own churchyard. I have not yet asked what it is afraid of. I have only looked at the garlic on the windows, and counted.

vanhelsing_lore_j_pastor.title: Pfarrer Albrecht
vanhelsing_lore_j_pastor.text: Four children weak, one buried, and a grave that melts the snow. He asked me to say a Pater at whichever one it is. I said I would. I did not say that I had never until that night said a Pater with a stake in my other hand.

vanhelsing_lore_j_grave.title: Katharina Lindner
vanhelsing_lore_j_grave.text: A bride of nineteen, dead by Easter in the year of the great snow, nailed in by an old priest and an older sexton. Three nails on the stone, and the earth about it not frozen. It is not a theory any longer. It is a name.

vanhelsing_lore_j_vigil.title: The vigil
vanhelsing_lore_j_vigil.text: She came at midnight, hair pale in the moon, as lovely as the legend said. The circle held. She did not. When she lay helpless in the snow, I did what must be done, and I said the Pater, and I wept afterward, as a physician does when a patient is lost. She was somebody's niece.

vanhelsing_lore_j_end.title: What I have learned
vanhelsing_lore_j_end.text: Verhoeven was right to demand evidence, and the peasants were right to be afraid, and the truth was in neither camp but between them. Arminius has sent a name: Dracula. I do not know what lies behind it. I have a casebook, a ward, and a certain faith that works when the evidence runs out.

on_lose.say: The dog knocks me flat and is gone before I can rise; I am bruised, but unhurt.

on_flee.say: I retreat from the pier. It does not follow.

on_win.say: The wolf is gone. Mrs Westenra lies across her daughter's bed, her hand at her heart. Lucy has not stirred.

on_lose.say: I come to on the carpet with a bruised head. The wolf is gone. Mrs Westenra lies dead across her daughter, and Van Helsing is already bending over them.

on_flee.say: We scatter. The wolf, having smashed what it came to smash, is gone. In the silence we find Mrs Westenra dead on the bed beside her daughter.

on_win.say: He lies quiet at last, panting, and I have the cut on my hand to remember it by.

on_lose.say: Hennessey and two attendants carry me out and the attendants hold Renfield down. By evening he is quiet.

on_flee.say: I get the door shut between us. Hennessey fetches two attendants, and Renfield is quieted in the end by sheer weariness.

on_win.say: She falls back before the crucifix, drops the child in the grass, and cannot reach her tomb: the Host along the door-crack holds her out. The Professor takes the child; Quincey lowers his rifle.

on_lose.say: She bears us down for a moment, but the Professor holds the crucifix over our heads, and she shrinks. We rise, bruised. The child is safe in the grass.

on_win.say: She sinks back in the coffin, helpless and silent, as the Professor holds the cross. Now, while she lies, the stake must be set.

on_lose.say: We are flung aside, and for a moment I think it is over. But the Professor presses the cross to her breast; she freezes, cries out, and lies still. The rite can go on.

on_win.say: The terriers go in like furies. The last rat is a blur and a yelp, and the chapel is still. The boxes of earth lie bare in the lamplight.

on_lose.say: We are driven back, bitten and bruised, past the door. Arthur's dogs hold the swarm at bay. The lamps are re-lit; we may try again.

on_flee.say: We fall back to the door and shut it. The rats mass inside, a rustling tide. We will go in again with lamps held higher.

on_win.say: Renfield lies quiet at last, panting. 'Doctor, I am sorry. He is near. He will come for me, and for her. Keep him from the windows.'

on_lose.say: He flings me against the wall and then, as suddenly, sobs. Simmons restrains him. 'Doctor... He is near. Keep him from the windows.'

on_flee.say: I retreat to the door as he cries after me, 'He is near! Keep him from the windows!' It is the sanest thing he has said.

on_win.say: The Count is gone. In the scuffle Jonathan's knife slit his coat from shoulder to waist, and a rain of gold and notes poured onto the hall floor, with a heavy bunch of keys. He leapt through us like a cat through rats, and through the open door.

on_lose.say: We are flung aside, but Jonathan's knife has found the Count's coat. Gold and a bunch of keys tumble on the floor as the Count leaps over us and out of the door.

on_flee.say: We give ground, and in the confusion the Count slashes through us and is gone. In the hall: a bunch of keys and a purse of gold and notes, torn loose by Jonathan's knife.

on_win.card: Back on 31 October, a day and a half before the launch left Galatz, Van Helsing and Mina Harker had reached Veresti on their way to the Borgo Pass.

on_lose.say: The pack drove us back into the lee of the sledge. By the grace of God and a flung brand the wolves drew off before dawn. We must hold the road and try again.

on_flee.say: We wheeled the horses and ran for the inn fire. The wolves lost heart at the lamplight. We must go again.

on_win.say: The wolves slunk back into the trees. The Professor held his crucifix aloft until the last of them was gone. 'They will not come again before dark,' he said.

on_lose.say: The wolves drew back at the Professor's crucifix before they could harm us. We are shaken, but whole.

on_flee.say: We drew in behind the carriage and the wolves lost interest in the horses. For now.

on_win.card: Dawn, 5 November. A cock crowed somewhere far off, and the three white shapes thinned into the snow. The horses were dead in their traces. The Professor lifted Mina out of the ring and set her down, whispering 'Rest. It is over for tonight.' By day he must go up to the castle alone.

on_lose.say: I woke at dawn in the circle. The Professor had held the Host between us and them through the whole night. The fire was embers and the sisters were gone. We must hold the ring until morning.

on_flee.say: There is no leaving the ring. We stay.

on_win.say: Stake, then knife. At the last each of them sighed and crumbled to dust, and on each face as it went was a look of peace. I swept the dust from the tombs and prayed.

on_lose.say: The charm broke me for a moment. I staggered back through the iron door, gasping, and rested against the pew. I must go in again with a steadier heart.

on_flee.say: I withdrew into the chapel. The sleepers did not stir. I must finish what I came for.

on_win.say: The ring of horsemen broke. A rifle bullet took the leader's hat; the others turned and flung themselves on their horses. The box on the wagon is bare to us.

on_lose.say: The Szgany pressed us back. Arthur's rifle held them at the rim, and we drew breath. We must try again before the sun is down.

on_flee.say: We fell back behind the rocks. The sun was shaving the mountain-top. There was no time to waste.

on_win.card: The lid fell. Jonathan's kukri swept across the throat, and Quincey's bowie plunged into the heart. Before our eyes, and almost in the drawing of a breath, the whole body crumbled into dust and passed from sight. Even in that moment of dissolution there was in the face a look of peace such as I never could have imagined might have rested there. The sun was setting; and Quincey Morris was bleeding to death.

on_lose.say: We fell back. The sun hung on the mountain's edge like a coin on a table. Jonathan was bleeding but on his feet. Whatever it cost, we would have to go in again.

on_flee.say: There is no flight. The sun is going. We must end it now.

on_win.say: The Wood is still. I did it myself, and that is the whole of the point.

on_lose.say: I wake against the beech with a split lip. Hobbs found the men gone and the wolf gone, and swears he saw them run from the Lord's name rather than from his arm.

on_flee.say: I retreat to the gate. The wolf does not follow. By morning the poachers have melted away and the village believes I drove them off. I let it.

on_win.card: 3 August. Rejoiced we are nearing England. At midnight I went to relieve the man at the wheel, and when I got to it found no one there. The wind was steady. I dared not leave it, so I shouted for the mate.

on_lose.card: 3 August. Rejoiced we are nearing England. At midnight I went to relieve the man at the wheel, and when I got to it found no one there. The wind was steady. I dared not leave it, so I shouted for the mate.

on_flee.card: 3 August. Rejoiced we are nearing England. At midnight I went to relieve the man at the wheel, and when I got to it found no one there. The wind was steady. I dared not leave it, so I shouted for the mate.

on_win.card: The river ran red until noon. The Voivode stood on the bank with his father's hammer in his hand and the first grey of the day behind him, and was, for a moment, entirely at peace.

on_lose.say: I wake on the bank with my head split. Mircea's archers cut the rest of them down while I lay in the mud. I will not be told how close it was.

on_flee.say: There is no running. I fought, and somehow it was enough.

on_win.say: The alpha leaves a tooth in the mud. I pick it up: a grey fang with a perfect crown. The refugees tell the story on the road for a month.

on_lose.say: I come to on the road with the grandmother pouring water into my mouth. The wolves have gone, with their faces turned away, as if the whole thing had been a mistake.

on_flee.say: I retreat to the cart. The wolves do not follow. They only watch, as if they are saving me for another day.

on_lose.say: They drive me back from the path, but they do not follow. When I can stand, I find myself bruised, bleeding, and alive.

on_flee.say: I run. The wolves do not follow past the cross.

on_lose.say: The bats flurry about my head, but they do me no harm; they are gone before I have found my umbrella.

on_flee.say: I walk very steadily away from the tombs. I do not run. I want that noted.

on_win.say: The pack lies quiet in the reeds. The channel is still to be crossed.

on_lose.say: I come to on my back with torn sleeves and the wolves nowhere. A flung brand from the last of my matches drove them off. I am whole, and sorer than I'd care to admit.

on_flee.say: I scramble up the bank, wolves snapping at my boots. They'll wait. They have all night.

on_win.say: Dunning's gang is on the ground or in the dark. The camp is mine.

on_lose.say: I wake in the dust with a swollen jaw. Dunning's men have run off into the night, afraid, I reckon, of the hanging that I've threatened. The camp is empty but for the horses.

on_flee.say: I back out of the firelight before they can close in. They'll be waiting.

on_lose.card: I woke at sunrise with my head against a picket-post, and no memory of the end of the night.

on_win.say: The gravel is quiet again. A man does not stay a clerk after a night like this.

on_lose.say: I wake behind the water-butt with a split lip. Blunt has gone indoors to fetch the doctor, cursing, and the wicket stands unwatched.

on_flee.say: I scramble behind the butt. Blunt searches, swears, and goes to rouse Hodge. I have a quarter of an hour.

on_win.say: He lies quiet at last, panting, and I have the cut on my hand to remember it by. I should have used the draught.

on_lose.say: I come to on the gravel with a bruised head. Hennessey and two attendants have Renfield between them, and by the time they have carried him in he is quiet.

on_flee.say: I get a dozen yards away. Hennessey and two attendants arrive, and Renfield is quieted in the end by sheer weariness.

on_win.say: It is over. It is not nothing, to have done it.

on_win.card: The snow stops before dawn. The Pfarrer reads the burial service himself over a grave that is at last, and only now, a grave. Two weeks later, Amsterdam.

on_lose.say: I come to myself in the snow with the circle in tatters. The Pfarrer's lantern bobs by the gate, and somebody, I think the old sexton, has done what I could not. The grave is quiet.

on_lose.card: The snow stops before dawn. The Pfarrer reads the burial service himself over a grave that is at last, and only now, a grave. Two weeks later, Amsterdam.

on_flee.say: I retreat through the lychgate with the creature's laughter behind me. Matthias and the Pfarrer, with ash and iron, finish the work by dawn. I am ashamed, and alive.

on_flee.card: The snow stops before dawn. The Pfarrer reads the burial service himself over a grave that is at last, and only now, a grave. Two weeks later, Amsterdam.

a2_dog_pier.name: The dog under the pier
a2_dog_pier.intro: It crouches, hackles up, in the shadow of the pier. It has been fed on something, and not dog-biscuit.
a2_dog_pier.win: The dog yelps and slinks away up the cliff, tail between its legs.

a3_berserker_night.name: The wolf in Lucy's room
a3_berserker_night.intro: The window bursts inward. A great grey wolf lands on the carpet, between us and the bed.
a3_berserker_night.win: The wolf yelps, and is gone through the glass into the dark.

a3_renfield_struggle.name: Renfield in his cell
a3_renfield_struggle.intro: Renfield flings himself at me with a madman's strength, snarling about lives and masters.
a3_renfield_struggle.win: Hennessey and I pin him until he is quiet.

a4_lucy_vigil.name: The Bloofer Lady at the tomb
a4_lucy_vigil.intro: 'Come to me, Arthur. My arms are hungry for you.' The golden crucifix is raised, but the child is still in her arms.
a4_lucy_vigil.win: She shrinks from the cross, hissing, and will not pass it.
a4_lucy_vigil.dawn_text: The first grey light touches the yews. She breaks away with a snarl and is gone toward the vault.

a5_picc_ambush.name: The Count at the door
a5_picc_ambush.intro: The door bursts. The Count is there, a hired ruffian at each shoulder and a bat at his collar. 'Stand aside!'
a5_picc_ambush.win: The hirelings fall. The Count has leapt through the gap like a cat through rats.

a6_wolf_pack.name: Wolves on the bank road
a6_wolf_pack.intro: The howling swells behind us. Yellow eyes show between the pines as the snow begins to fall.
a6_wolf_pack.win: The great wolf breaks off, and the pack melts into the dark. The horses stop trembling.

arthur_burden_poachers.name: Poachers in the Home Wood
arthur_burden_poachers.intro: A shutter drops and a lantern blazes. Two men and a starved wolf come out of the bracken. 'It's the new Lord,' one of them says, and then, to the beast, 'Get him.'
arthur_burden_poachers.win: The wolf bolts. The men cry for quarter and I give it. The tenants will hear of this by dawn.

demeter_voyage_dark_blessed.name: The dark in the hold
demeter_voyage_dark_blessed.intro: The earth in box thirteen is grey and cold. Something that has lost its bed is looking for another. A lantern swings, and the boxes shift on their lashings.
demeter_voyage_dark_blessed.win: I keep the cross between us and the dark. It does not like it.
demeter_voyage_dark_blessed.dawn_text: A grey line at the hatch. The thing among the boxes is gone, and the bat with it.

demeter_voyage_dark_burned.name: The dark in the hold
demeter_voyage_dark_burned.intro: The smoke is rolling; the earth is smouldering in box thirteen. The dark is full of wings and a tall shape that is not afraid of fire, only of me.
demeter_voyage_dark_burned.win: I hold the cross against them, while the smoke thins.
demeter_voyage_dark_burned.dawn_text: A grey line at the hatch. The wings are gone, the shape is gone, and I am alone with the burned box.

dracula_voivode_raid.name: The night raid at the Reed Ford
dracula_voivode_raid.intro: They come out of the reeds in the dark, wet and silent, with knives in their teeth. I draw my father's hammer. There are three of them and there is one of me, and I find, with some alarm, that this makes me happier than I have been in weeks.
dracula_voivode_raid.win: The last of them goes into the river and does not come up. Across the water a horn sounds the retreat. I am shaking, and the dawn is just beginning.

dracula_voivode_wolves.name: Wolves on the mountain road
dracula_voivode_wolves.intro: The wolves have followed the cart for three days. Tonight the great one steps forward and stands in the road. I am a prince, and I have been told that wolves are my people's emblem. Let us see.
dracula_voivode_wolves.win: The alpha limps off. The others look at me, once, with an expression I can only call respect.

harker_road_wolves.name: Wolves on the path
harker_road_wolves.intro: The grey shapes close from either side of the track. I have a poker, a spade and my courage, in that order.
harker_road_wolves.win: The wolves slink back into the gorse, one of them limping.

mina_records_dusk_bats.name: Bats at the Abbey
mina_records_dusk_bats.intro: Two bats wheel over the tombs and drop toward my hair. I have an umbrella, and rather more nerve than I knew.
mina_records_dusk_bats.win: The bats fall back and are gone into the Abbey ruins.

quincey_hunt_wolves.name: Wolves at the ford
quincey_hunt_wolves.intro: Two grey wolves slide out of the reeds, lips drawn back. They are thin and desperate.
quincey_hunt_wolves.win: The last wolf drops. The reeds go quiet.

quincey_hunt_rustlers.name: Dunning's gang
quincey_hunt_rustlers.intro: Dunning's hand slides from his belt. 'Take him!' Boots scrape behind me; the camp is on its feet.
quincey_hunt_rustlers.win: Dunning goes down on his knees. The camp is quiet. Only the horses snort.

quincey_hunt_bats.name: Bats at the lines
quincey_hunt_bats.intro: Three dark shapes, wings like torn umbrellas, drop out of the moon. I fire from the hip.
quincey_hunt_bats.win: The last of them veers out of the lantern-light and is gone. The silence afterward is worse than the noise.

renfield_mercy_scuffle.name: Scuffle with the night-man
renfield_mercy_scuffle.intro: The lantern swings round. 'You! Back to your bed!' Blunt's stick comes up. I am a thin man of fifty-nine with a madman's strength, and I know exactly how that story ends.
renfield_mercy_scuffle.win: He goes down against the wall, winded, and not hurt past a bruise. I step over him and I am not proud.

seward_asylum_frenzy.name: Renfield at the garden wall
seward_asylum_frenzy.intro: He springs at me from the shadow of the wall, with a madman's strength, snarling about lives and masters.
seward_asylum_frenzy.win: Hennessey and I pin him until he is quiet.

vanhelsing_lore_vigil.name: The vigil at Kirchdorf
vanhelsing_lore_vigil.intro: The snow does not crunch beneath her. She stands at the edge of the circle, smiling the smile of a girl of nineteen, and behind her in the dark a great grey wolf comes to heel like a dog. 'You are very far from home, Herr Doktor,' she says in a village dialect seventy years out of date.
vanhelsing_lore_vigil.win: She falls, and does not rise. The wolf is gone. In the snow, there is only a girl in a grey dress, and no more than nineteen.

a2_dog.name: The huge dog
a2_dog.book: ch.7 the immense dog that leapt from the Demeter

a3_berserker.name: Berserker
a3_berserker.book: the escaped wolf of the Zoological Gardens, ch.11

arthur_burden_lean_wolf.name: Starved wolf
arthur_burden_lean_wolf.book: the escaped wolf of the Home Wood (invented)

dracula_voivode_akinji.name: Akinji raider
dracula_voivode_akinji.book: Turkish light horse on the Danube border (Ch.3, invented)

a4_host_putty.name: Host-putty
a4_host_putty.text: The Host crumbled into soft putty, rolled in a clean napkin: a seal for every crack in the vault door.

arcs_list.title: The Lord's Burden
arcs_list.blurb: Arthur Holmwood nurses a dying father, wins Lucy Westenra's hand, and inherits a title with a secret. Will he keep the comfortable lie, or tell the hard truth?
arcs_list.rewards_text: Godalming's signet ring, five silver coins; +4 Nerve, +3 HP and +1 damage for Arthur Gear: a sword-cane and a riding coat.

arcs_list.title: The Last Voyage
arcs_list.blurb: Varna to Whitby with fifty boxes of earth in the hold: the Captain of the Demeter keeps his log, counts his crew and loses them, one by one, to something that walks the deck at night.
arcs_list.unlock_text: Finish the main story to read the Log of the Demeter in full.
arcs_list.rewards_text: The Captain's crucifix and rosary, 2 garlic, 1 holy water; +3 Nerve and +2 HP for Quincey, +2 Nerve for Arthur Gear: the Captain's oilskin.

arcs_list.title: Seven Hundred Years
arcs_list.blurb: Before the legend there was a prince: a besieged border, a ford by night, a school beneath a mountain that takes every tenth scholar, and a first night in the tomb. Who he was decides what he becomes.
arcs_list.unlock_text: Finish the main story to hear the Count's own history.
arcs_list.rewards_text: The Voivode's dragon signet, the Order of the Dragon medal and a wolf-tooth charm; Van Helsing gains +1 Faith and +2 Nerve from knowing the enemy.

arcs_list.title: The Solicitor's Road
arcs_list.blurb: Jonathan Harker's own road: from Mr. Hawkins's office in Exeter and the Count's letters, over the castle wall, to a sickbed in Buda-Pesth and a wedding.
arcs_list.unlock_text: Finish Act I: Jonathan's last chance in the castle.
arcs_list.rewards_text: Jonathan receives a kukri and his sealed journal; +2 HP, +3 Nerve, +1 Accuracy for Harker Gear: a tweed travelling coat.

arcs_list.title: The Last Summer
arcs_list.blurb: Lucy Westenra, three suitors, a garden and a sea she cannot stop dreaming of. A bright life, told in flowers and letters, and what she chooses to leave behind.
arcs_list.unlock_text: Lay Lucy to rest with Arthur at her side (Act IV).
arcs_list.rewards_text: Lucy's pressed-flower letter and two heads of garlic; her gift of courage: +3 Nerve for Arthur, +2 Nerve for Mina.

arcs_list.title: The Typewriter and the Trance
arcs_list.blurb: Before Dracula, there was Mina Murray: a schoolroom mystery, a stubborn typewriter, a lost letter chased through Bradshaw's timetables, and a dream of water and creaking wood that she is only beginning to understand.
arcs_list.rewards_text: +4 Nerve, +1 Faith, +2 Accuracy for Mina; her typewriter ribbon and shorthand notebook; a flask of brandy and a silver coin Gear: a travelling shawl.

arcs_list.title: The Texan's Hunt
arcs_list.blurb: Horse-thieves on the Brazos, a mare called Santa Fe, and a night on the Pampas when something drank where no bat should. Quincey Morris's own story, of the years before he ever met a vampire.
arcs_list.rewards_text: A second Winchester, ten cartridges, Quincey's tooled bowie sheath; +3 Accuracy, +2 HP, +1 Evasion for Quincey Gear: a buffalo coat.

arcs_list.title: The Fly-Eater's Mercy
arcs_list.blurb: Purfleet, the padded cell and the ledger of lives. A man of sharp mind and old family is promised lives by a voice in the dark. When the night comes, he must choose between the Master and the small mercies he owes the sparrow in his hand.
arcs_list.unlock_text: Show Renfield mercy in his last hour (Act V).
arcs_list.rewards_text: Renfield's notebook of lives, a bottle of brandy and a lump of sugar; +3 Nerve for Dr. Seward, Renfield's last gift.

arcs_list.title: Case Notes
arcs_list.blurb: Purfleet, May. A man who cures other men's sleeplessness cannot cure his own; then the asylum goes wrong in a single night, and Dr. Seward must trust his judgment, his medicine and his nerve.
arcs_list.rewards_text: Unlocks the chloral recipe (medicine); 3 chloral and Seward's phonograph cylinder; +2 HP, +3 Nerve, +1 Faith for Dr. Seward Gear: a doctor's greatcoat.

arcs_list.title: The Amsterdam Lectures
arcs_list.blurb: Before London and the Count there was Amsterdam: a study full of books, a sick wife, a rival who calls it all peasant nonsense, and one winter night in a Styrian churchyard that taught Abraham Van Helsing which of his old fears were facts.
arcs_list.rewards_text: The rites are yours: holy-water, sacred-bullet and consecrated-knife recipes unlock. Three Sacred Wafers, the Professor's black medical bag; +2 Faith, +3 Nerve, +1 HP for Van Helsing Gear: a black frock coat.
